title: Your Tests Blocked System.exit With a SecurityManager and Java 25 Will Not Let You Install One
description:
The command line tool
called System.exit
when its arguments were wrong.

Fine in production.

Fatal in a test.

One call
and the whole test run
just stopped.

Years ago somebody solved it.

A small SecurityManager,
installed in the tests,
that threw an exception
whenever code tried to exit.

The test caught the exception,
checked the exit code,
and carried on.

Plenty of teams did the same.

Libraries were written for it.

Plugin hosts did something similar,
sandboxing code they loaded.

You have probably got one of these
somewhere
and forgotten it.

The Security Manager
was deprecated for removal
in Java 17.

You saw the warning.

So did everyone.

In Java 24,
JEP 486
switched it off for good.

You cannot enable it
at startup.

You cannot install one
while the program runs.

System.setSecurityManager
now throws
UnsupportedOperationException.

Java 25 is the long term release
that most teams on 21
are moving to now.

So for many codebases
this is not a future warning.

It is the next upgrade,
failing in the test suite
on day one.

Usually in a helper class
nobody has opened in years.

The good news
is that the real fix
was always the better design.

Do not call System.exit
deep inside your code.

Return an exit code,
or throw a specific exception,
and let main
be the only place
that ends the process.

Then the tests
call the logic, not main,
and check the code it returned.

No trick needed.

If you load code
you do not trust,
the answer is no longer
inside the same JVM.

Run it in a separate process
or a container,
with the operating system
drawing the limits.

The JDK team's position
is that the Security Manager
was rarely used for that anyway,
and expensive to keep.

Before you upgrade,
search for it.

SecurityManager.

checkPermission.

checkExit.

The java.security.manager flag
in your build files.

Count the hits.

That is the size
of the work
hiding behind a deprecation warning
you stopped reading five years ago.

A warning that says
for removal
is a date,
not an opinion.

– Serguey Asael Shinder

title: How to convert a Framer website to React
description:
To convert a Framer website to React, you either rebuild it in React, export selected components with an editor plugin, or convert the whole published site with a tool that writes React source. Framer has no code export. Deframer produces a React 19 project for Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite (Framer to React compares them); if you need a standalone React app, you can lift components out with their CSS modules, styles and the small @/deframer kit.

This post is the how-to. For the background question, whether Framer is "React under the hood" and what that means, see is Framer built on React?. Deframer is an independent tool and is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by Framer.

Why isn't a published Framer site already a React project?

Because it's the output of a build, not the source. A published Framer page is rendered by Framer's runtime from modules the editor publishes, then hydrated with React in the browser. You can see React running, but there's no project to open: no package.json, no component files with names you chose, no routes folder. Framer's help center says plainly that it "does not offer HTML export for self-hosting" and that published sites "are not fully static" (Framer Help).

So "convert to React" means producing source that a React toolchain can build, and there are three different things people mean by it.

Static snapshot vs generated components

Static snapshot Component export (plugin) Whole-site conversion
What you get Saved HTML, CSS, JS and assets Selected components as React files Routes, pages, components, styles and data as source
Is it React source? No; markup plus Framer's scripts Yes, but generated and usually not meant to be edited Yes, readable and meant to be edited
Pages and routing As saved files You build pages and routing Generated
Keeps Framer as the design tool No Yes; you re-export after publishing No
Examples PullPage, NoCodeExport, HTTrack React Export (Unframer), Proofly React Export Deframer (Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router, Vite)

A snapshot is useful for hosting a copy, but it doesn't give you React components to work with. We cover it in Framer to HTML or Framer to Next.js.

Component exporters are built for a different workflow: you keep designing in Framer and drop its components into a React app you already have. Unframer's docs, for example, say the generated files should never be edited by hand and that you re-run its CLI after changes in Framer, and its components run with the unframer package (Unframer). Its full-website guide has you assemble pages and react-router routing yourself in a Vite app (Unframer guide).

A whole-site conversion is the route when you're leaving Framer and want code you'll maintain. Best Framer to Next.js converters in 2026 compares the tools in each group.

A snapshot copies output, a component export keeps Framer as the source, a conversion gives you the source.

When does a standalone React app (Vite) make sense instead of Next.js?

A marketing site usually belongs in a framework that renders HTML on the server, because search engines and link previews read that HTML. Next.js does this out of the box, and so do the other frameworks Deframer writes: TanStack Start renders on the server, and Astro, React Router and Vite prerender every page to HTML at build time. A client-rendered React app built with Vite still makes sense when:

  • The Framer pages are going into an existing React app, such as a product dashboard, and that app is already a Vite single-page app.
  • SEO doesn't matter for these screens, for example pages behind a login.
  • Your team has standardized on a React framework Deframer doesn't write (Remix, for example) and you're adapting components into it. For React Router's framework mode or TanStack Start, convert to it directly instead.

If none of those apply, keeping the converted project is usually less work than moving out of it. It's a normal React 19 app: you write React components, use hooks, and add any npm package.

Converting with Deframer: what you get

Deframer converts the published site into a TypeScript project: Next.js (App Router) by default, or TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite if you choose one. In short:

  1. Paste the published URL (framer.website, framer.app or a custom domain) and convert. Converting is free.
  2. Review the result in the compare view when live previews are on.
  3. Verify the site and download the project (1 credit with a verification tag, 10 without; see pricing).
  4. Run npm install and npm run dev.

The React code lives in predictable places:

  • src/views/ holds one component per page (home.tsx with home.module.css).
  • src/components/ holds the design components, in the designer's folders, each with a CSS module.
  • src/layouts/ holds templates such as navigation and footer.
  • src/styles/ holds color tokens (tokens.ts), text styles and @font-face rules.
  • src/cms/ holds CMS collections as JSON plus a schema module.
  • src/code/ and src/vendor/ hold your own code components and marketplace code.
  • src/lib/deframer/ is the kit, imported as @/deframer, which replaces Framer's runtime.
  • The routes are each framework's own: src/app/ in Next.js, src/routes/ in TanStack Start, React Router and Vite, src/pages/ in Astro. They hold only routes and their metadata; the pages themselves are the same in all five.

The full tour is in what you get in a converted Next.js project, and the step-by-step export is in how to export a Framer site to Next.js.

How do you move converted components into another React app?

You copy the component with what it depends on, then replace the few places the kit talks to its framework. The steps below use a Next.js export as the example. Expect real work for a whole site and modest work for a few sections. Here's what's involved.

1. Copy the component and its dependencies

  • [ ] The component's .tsx file and its .module.css.
  • [ ] Every component it imports from src/components/, src/icons/, src/code/ or src/vendor/, with their CSS modules.
  • [ ] src/styles/ (tokens, text styles, fonts) and src/app/globals.css.
  • [ ] src/lib/deframer/, the kit. Only the modules your site uses are in it.
  • [ ] What the root layout, src/app/layout.tsx, wraps every page in: the kit's <SiteStyles> (given the design tokens), <SiteRouter> and <SVGTemplates>, inside a <div id="main">. Your app's root needs the same wrappers.
  • [ ] src/site/routes.ts, because the kit's links and routing read the site's route table from @/site/routes.
  • [ ] Any CMS files in src/cms/ the component reads.
  • [ ] The npm dependencies from package.json: at least react, react-dom and motion, plus any packages your code components import.

2. Reproduce the TypeScript and JSX settings

The generated code expects two settings from tsconfig.json: the @/ path aliases, and JSX compiled through the kit's runtime:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "jsxImportSource": "@/deframer",
    "paths": {
      "@/deframer": ["./src/lib/deframer"],
      "@/deframer/*": ["./src/lib/deframer/*"],
      "@/*": ["./src/*"]
    }
  }
}

The kit's JSX runtime matters: it applies defaultProps the way React 18 did and passes DOM elements only props they can render, which code written for Framer relies on. In a Vite app you'd mirror this with resolve.alias entries for @/deframer and @/, and the React plugin's jsxImportSource option set to @/deframer. CSS modules work in Vite without extra setup.

3. Replace the Next.js touchpoints in the kit

The generated components themselves don't import next/link or next/image; links go through the kit's own Link, and the project already serves images unoptimized. The Next.js dependencies are inside the kit, in a handful of files (only some will exist in your project):

Kit file Uses from Next.js What you'd do in a Vite app
route.tsx, route-link.tsx usePathname, useRouter, useSelectedLayoutSegments from next/navigation Back them with your router (for example React Router's location and navigate)
styles.tsx, breakpoints.tsx, cms.tsx, content-svg.tsx, effects/appear.tsx useServerInsertedHTML and ServerInsertedHTMLContext, which stream CSS into server-rendered HTML In a client-only app there's no server HTML to stream into; the kit also inserts rules in the browser, so these need a client-side replacement or no-op. Test each breakpoint after the change
cursors.tsx Next's internal router contexts (next/dist/...) Pass your own router context, or drop custom cursors

Treat this table as a map of where to look, not a finished port: we don't ship or test a Vite build of the kit.

4. Rebuild what lived in Next.js routes

Some features are Next.js files rather than components, so they don't come along:

  • Page metadata. Titles, descriptions, Open Graph and canonical URLs are metadata exports in src/app/**/page.tsx. In React 19 you can render <title> and <meta> tags inside a component; for crawlers you still want server rendering.
  • Forms. Each form posts to a route handler, such as src/app/api/forms/contact/route.ts, which calls src/lib/forms.ts (rate limit, honeypot, validation, webhook delivery). Point the form at an endpoint your app provides.
  • Routing policy. src/proxy.ts (trailing slashes, redirects) and the redirects() list in next.config.ts need equivalents on your host.
  • CMS pages. Detail routes like src/app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx list items with generateStaticParams(). Recreate them with your router, reading the same JSON.

5. Check it

Render the moved component inside your app, then compare it with the original at 1440, 768 and 390 pixels wide, hover and click everything, and run npx tsc --noEmit. Code components written in Framer were never type-checked there, so some type errors may be yours, not the port's; Framer code components and overrides in Next.js explains how to tighten them.

Tip

For a component you'll maintain for years, it's often cleaner to use the converted version as a reference and rewrite it in your app's conventions, keeping the CSS values and motion transitions it already worked out.

FAQ

Can Framer export my site as React code?

No. Framer has no built-in React or code export. You can rebuild in React, export selected components with a third-party plugin, or convert the published site with a tool such as Deframer.

Does Deframer output a plain React (Vite) app?

No. Deframer outputs a Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite project with React 19 and TypeScript. You can move components into another React app, but you'll bring the kit along and replace its framework hooks (the Next.js ones are listed above).

Is a Next.js project still "React"?

Yes. Next.js is a React framework: pages and components are React components, and you can use hooks and React libraries as usual. Next.js adds routing, server rendering and metadata on top.

Do converted Framer components need the framer package?

Not with Deframer. The project has no Framer runtime; a readable kit in src/lib/deframer replaces it. Component exporters may rely on their own runtime package instead, such as unframer.

Will animations work after I move components to Vite?

They run on motion/react, which works in any React app, so the animation code itself moves with the component. Check hover, scroll and appear effects after replacing the kit's Next.js touchpoints.

Originally published on the Deframer blog. Deframer converts a published Framer site into Next.js, Astro, React Router, TanStack Start, Vite, Nuxt or static HTML code.

title: Protection-Oriented Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Fault Detection in Power Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.17872v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based fault detectors are increasingly proposed for power system protection, yet aggregate metrics can obscure the consequences of false and missed trips. We present a protection-oriented assessment of three ML detectors and a sequence-current reference on PROTECT-90, comprising 9,022 simulated fault episodes on a 90 kV double-circuit line. The assessment combines five window conditions, causal window-end labelling, episode-grouped cross-validation, and operating-point selection under a fixed security budget. It reports security, dependability, detection timing, decision margins, and episode-level nuisance assertions. Gradient-boosted trees, a convolutional neural network, and logistic regression achieve AUC-ROC values above 0.999, yet at a security budget of $10^{-3}$ their developed-fault missed-trip rates range from 0.007% to 1.99%. Post-clearing false-trip rates of approximately 0.12-0.16% per window coexist with nuisance assertions in 11.3-19.1% of episodes. Among the analysed physical descriptors, missed trips are most consistently associated with higher fault resistance within the sampled range. An analytical current proxy suggests a fault-current gradient only partly reproduced by waveform-derived current (rank correlation 0.62). No single topology state or faulted phase consistently dominates within the sampled domain. Because PROTECT-90 contains fault episodes only, security is assessed on pre-fault and post-clearing windows rather than independent non-fault disturbances.

title: Aligning AI Teams
description:
arXiv:2611.17820v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework. Our findings can help practitioners design agent teams that successfully preserve the behaviors expected of aligned individual agents.

title: Stop Vulnerable Java Code Before Production: SpotBugs, OWASP Dependency-Check, and Sonatype Guide
description:
Stop Vulnerable Java Code Before Production: SpotBugs, OWASP Dependency-Check, and Sonatype Guide

AI coding assistants have changed the way we write software. They help us generate code faster, understand unfamiliar APIs, and implement features in minutes.

But there is another side to this productivity: AI-generated code can introduce bugs, misunderstand API contracts, use insecure coding patterns, or select vulnerable dependencies.

And let's be honest: developers have been making these mistakes long before AI existed!

The solution is not to stop using AI. It is to introduce automated security and code-quality checks into our development workflow.

In this article, we'll look at three tools and how to integrate them into a Java Maven project:

  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin: Detect potential bugs and unsafe coding patterns in compiled Java code.
  • OWASP Dependency-Check Maven Plugin: Identify known vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies.
  • Sonatype OSS Index through Sonatype Guide: Add another source of component vulnerability intelligence to dependency analysis.

The objective is straightforward: make the Maven build fail when configured security or quality rules are violated, before the application reaches production.

All the configurations below use official project documentation and the following versions:

Component Version
SpotBugs Maven Plugin 4.10.5.0
OWASP Dependency-Check Maven 13.0.0

1. SpotBugs: Find bugs in your Java code

What is SpotBugs?

SpotBugs is a static analysis tool that examines compiled Java bytecode to identify potential bugs.

Instead of executing your application, SpotBugs analyzes the generated .class files and searches for known bug patterns.

These patterns can result from:

  • Misunderstanding Java language features.
  • Incorrect usage of API methods.
  • Violating assumptions when modifying existing code.
  • Common programming mistakes, such as incorrect boolean conditions.

For example, it can detect potential null-pointer dereferences, suspicious code patterns, and other programming mistakes.

This is particularly useful when working with AI-generated code. The implementation might compile and look perfectly reasonable while still containing a potential defect.

SpotBugs helps identify these problems before the application is executed.

Add SpotBugs to your Maven project

Add the following configuration to your pom.xml:

<plugin>
    <groupId>com.github.spotbugs</groupId>
    <artifactId>spotbugs-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>4.10.5.0</version>

    <configuration>
        <effort>Max</effort>
        <threshold>Low</threshold>
        <xmlOutput>true</xmlOutput>
        <includeTests>false</includeTests>
    </configuration>

    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>check</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

Let's understand the important configuration options.

effort

Controls the analysis effort used by SpotBugs.

Available values:

  • Min
  • Default
  • Max

Using Max requests the highest analysis effort. It can increase execution time, but is a reasonable choice for a production verification gate.

threshold

Controls the minimum bug severity reported by SpotBugs.

Available values:

  • High
  • Default
  • Low
  • Ignore
  • Exp

Using Low allows the report to include lower-priority findings instead of limiting it to more severe ones.

xmlOutput

Enables XML report generation. This is useful for CI systems and other reporting integrations.

includeTests

Controls whether test classes are included in the analysis. Its default is false, which is generally appropriate when the primary objective is protecting production application code.

check goal

This is particularly important.

The spotbugs:check goal executes SpotBugs analysis and fails the Maven build when violations meet the configured failure criteria.

It is bound by default to the Maven verify lifecycle phase.

This means we can use mvn verify to enforce the analysis rather than simply generating a report for someone to inspect.

Optional configuration recommendations

As your project grows, consider:

  • Include and exclude filters: Use includeFilterFile and excludeFilterFile to control which findings are reported. This is preferable to broadly disabling analysis when dealing with known false positives.
  • Failing on specific priorities: The check goal supports failThreshold, with High, Medium, and Low values. For a strict gate, use Low.
  • Violation allowance: maxAllowedViolations defaults to 0. Keep it at zero if you want the build to fail when matching violations are found.
  • Multi-module projects: Configure the plugin centrally in the parent POM so modules follow the same analysis policy.

For a new project, I would start with maximum analysis effort, a low reporting threshold, and zero allowed violations. For an existing project with many findings, introduce the policy progressively rather than hiding existing problems with broad exclusions.

Official documentation:

  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin – Usage
  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin – Check Goal
  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin – Violation Checking

2. OWASP Dependency-Check: Find vulnerable dependencies

What is OWASP Dependency-Check?

Finding bugs in our own code is only part of the problem.

Most Java applications depend on third-party libraries through Maven dependencies.

For example:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
    <version>...</version>
</dependency>

Even if our implementation is perfectly written, a vulnerable dependency can introduce a security risk into the application.

This is where OWASP Dependency-Check becomes useful.

Dependency-Check is an open-source software composition analysis (SCA) tool. It examines project dependencies and compares identified components against vulnerability information from sources such as the National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

It helps identify dependencies associated with known vulnerabilities, including transitive dependencies.

A transitive dependency is particularly important because you might never explicitly declare the vulnerable library in your pom.xml. Another dependency may introduce it into your application.

Add Dependency-Check to Maven

Add the following configuration:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
    <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
    <version>13.0.0</version>

    <configuration>
        <failBuildOnCVSS>7.0</failBuildOnCVSS>
        <failOnError>true</failOnError>
        <autoUpdate>true</autoUpdate>
    </configuration>

    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>check</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

Let's examine the important configuration options.

failBuildOnCVSS

This is one of the most important properties.

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) provides a numerical score between 0 and 10 to represent vulnerability severity.

Dependency-Check uses this threshold to decide whether a vulnerability should fail the build.

For example:

<failBuildOnCVSS>7.0</failBuildOnCVSS>

This configuration fails the build when a detected vulnerability has a CVSS score equal to or greater than 7.0.

You can adjust the threshold according to your project's risk tolerance.

For a public-facing application handling sensitive data, a stricter policy may be appropriate.

failOnError

Controls whether an error during Dependency-Check execution should fail the build.

Keep this enabled.

A scanner that cannot execute successfully should not silently allow the build to pass.

autoUpdate

Allows Dependency-Check to update its vulnerability data automatically.

Keep it enabled. The project documentation explicitly advises against disabling automatic updates for normal operation.

Understanding the generated report

By default, Dependency-Check generates an HTML report:

target/dependency-check-report.html

The report provides information about:

  • Dependencies scanned.
  • Identified vulnerabilities.
  • CVE identifiers.
  • Vulnerability severity.
  • Dependency coordinates.
  • Analysis evidence.

This is useful when investigating why a build failed and deciding whether to upgrade, replace, or otherwise address a vulnerable dependency.

Optional configuration recommendations

There are several useful configurations worth considering.

1. Generate multiple report formats

Dependency-Check supports multiple formats, including:

  • HTML
  • XML
  • JSON
  • CSV
  • JUNIT
  • SARIF
  • GITLAB
  • JENKINS

For example, SARIF can be useful when integrating security findings with supported CI reporting systems.

2. Scan Maven build plugins

By default, scanPlugins is disabled.

You can enable it:

<scanPlugins>true</scanPlugins>

This extends scanning to Maven plugins and their dependencies, which can be useful when you also want visibility into your build tooling.

3. Manage false positives with suppression files

Dependency analysis is not perfect. Sometimes a vulnerability can be incorrectly associated with a component.

Dependency-Check supports XML suppression files through suppressionFiles.

The important point is to suppress findings only after investigating them. Document why a suppression is necessary and review it periodically.

You can also enable:

<failBuildOnUnusedSuppressionRule>true</failBuildOnUnusedSuppressionRule>

This makes the build fail when unused suppression rules are detected, helping prevent obsolete exceptions from accumulating.

4. Keep the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities analyzer enabled

Dependency-Check includes the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities analyzer, which uses CISA's KEV catalog.

It is enabled by default. Unless you have a specific reason to change it, keep it enabled.

5. Configure an NVD API key in CI

Dependency-Check uses NVD vulnerability data.

The initial execution can take 20 minutes or more because the vulnerability database needs to be downloaded and processed.

The project recommends keeping the database updated regularly and recommends mirroring NVD data for operational integrations.

When using an NVD API key in CI, Dependency-Check recommends passing it through an environment variable rather than putting it directly into the Maven configuration:

<nvdApiKeyEnvironmentVariable>NVD_API_KEY</nvdApiKeyEnvironmentVariable>

Then provide NVD_API_KEY through your CI secret-management mechanism.

This helps avoid exposing credentials in the project configuration or Maven debug output.

Official documentation:

  • Dependency-Check Maven – Usage
  • Dependency-Check Maven – Configuration
  • Dependency-Check Maven – Check Goal

3. Sonatype OSS Index through Sonatype Guide

What is OSS Index?

Sonatype OSS Index provides vulnerability intelligence for open-source components.

It helps identify known security issues affecting the software components used by an application.

For Java projects, this provides another useful source of vulnerability information alongside the NVD-based analysis performed by Dependency-Check.

However, there is an important integration detail to understand.

The old Sonatype OSS Index Maven plugin (ossindex:audit) is now a legacy tool.

According to Sonatype's current documentation, it is no longer supported and does not receive fixes.

Sonatype recommends migrating to maintained integrations, including OWASP Dependency-Check Maven.

Therefore, rather than introducing another unsupported Maven plugin, we can integrate Sonatype's current Guide service directly into Dependency-Check.

This gives us a single Maven dependency-analysis workflow with vulnerability information from both Dependency-Check's configured sources and Sonatype's component intelligence.

Configure Sonatype Guide

Sonatype has migrated OSS Index API authentication to Guide Personal Access Tokens (PATs).

The process is straightforward.

Step 1: Generate a personal access token

  1. Go to Sonatype Guide.
  2. Sign in.
  3. Open Settings from the user menu.
  4. Navigate to Personal Access Tokens.
  5. Generate a new token.
  6. Copy the token immediately.

The token will not be displayed again after creation.

Step 2: Configure Maven credentials

Instead of putting the token directly into your pom.xml, configure it in your Maven settings.xml.

For example:

<settings>
    <servers>
        <server>
            <id>sonatype-guide</id>
            <password>YOUR_GUIDE_PAT</password>
        </server>
    </servers>
</settings>

The file is normally located at:

~/.m2/settings.xml

For production CI environments, store the token in your CI secret manager and provide it to Maven securely. You can also use Maven's password encryption facilities.

Notice that the Guide PAT is configured as the password. Sonatype documents that the username is not required when authenticating with a Guide PAT.

Step 3: Connect Dependency-Check to Sonatype Guide

Now add these properties to your Dependency-Check configuration:

<ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>true</ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>

<ossIndexAnalyzerUrl>
    https://api.guide.sonatype.com
</ossIndexAnalyzerUrl>

<ossIndexServerId>sonatype-guide</ossIndexServerId>

Here is what each property does:

  • ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled: Enables the Sonatype OSS Index analyzer.
  • ossIndexAnalyzerUrl: Specifies the Sonatype Guide API endpoint.
  • ossIndexServerId: References the Maven server credentials configured in settings.xml.

The Maven server ID must match the ID configured in your settings.xml.

This integration uses the existing Dependency-Check analyzer, so we don't need to introduce an additional Maven plugin just to communicate with Sonatype.

Optional configuration recommendations

The OSS Index analyzer supports caching:

<ossIndexAnalyzerUseCache>true</ossIndexAnalyzerUseCache>
<ossIndexAnalyzerCacheValidForHours>24</ossIndexAnalyzerCacheValidForHours>

Caching helps reduce repeated requests for the same components.

The default cache validity is 24 hours, which is a reasonable starting point.

Keep the default remote-error behavior unless you have deliberately chosen a different failure policy. By default, remote errors from OSS Index can fail the execution rather than being reduced to warnings.

This is important: do not configure the scanner to ignore remote errors without understanding the consequences. A failed vulnerability lookup should not automatically be interpreted as a clean security result.

Official documentation:

  • Sonatype – Integrate Build Tools with Sonatype Guide
  • Sonatype – Using Guide Personal Access Tokens with OSS Index API Integrations

4. Putting everything together in one Maven configuration

Now let's combine the three configurations.

The following is a practical configuration for a Java Maven application:

<build>
    <plugins>

        <!-- Static Java Code Analysis -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>com.github.spotbugs</groupId>
            <artifactId>spotbugs-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>4.10.5.0</version>

            <configuration>
                <effort>Max</effort>
                <threshold>Low</threshold>
                <xmlOutput>true</xmlOutput>
                <includeTests>false</includeTests>
                <failOnError>true</failOnError>
                <failThreshold>Low</failThreshold>
                <maxAllowedViolations>0</maxAllowedViolations>
            </configuration>

            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>check</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>

        <!-- Dependency Vulnerability Analysis -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
            <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
            <version>13.0.0</version>

            <configuration>
                <failBuildOnCVSS>7.0</failBuildOnCVSS>
                <failOnError>true</failOnError>
                <autoUpdate>true</autoUpdate>

                <!-- Sonatype Guide integration -->
                <ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>true</ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>
                <ossIndexAnalyzerUrl>
                    https://api.guide.sonatype.com
                </ossIndexAnalyzerUrl>
                <ossIndexServerId>sonatype-guide</ossIndexServerId>

                <!-- Optional cache configuration -->
                <ossIndexAnalyzerUseCache>true</ossIndexAnalyzerUseCache>
                <ossIndexAnalyzerCacheValidForHours>24</ossIndexAnalyzerCacheValidForHours>
            </configuration>

            <executions>
                <execution>
                    <goals>
                        <goal>check</goal>
                    </goals>
                </execution>
            </executions>
        </plugin>

    </plugins>
</build>

A few important details:

  • spotbugs:check runs SpotBugs analysis and checks its findings.
  • dependency-check:check examines dependencies and generates its vulnerability report.
  • Both checks are associated with Maven's verify phase.
  • The SpotBugs configuration uses a strict failure policy.
  • Dependency-Check fails on vulnerabilities with CVSS scores of at least 7.0.
  • Sonatype Guide credentials are retrieved through Maven settings, not hardcoded in the POM.

For multi-module projects, define plugin versions and configuration centrally in the parent POM. For Dependency-Check, its aggregate goal is also available when you prefer a consolidated report across child modules.

5. Make it part of your CI/CD pipeline

Having these plugins in your POM is useful, but the real value comes from enforcing their results.

Run:

mvn clean verify

The Maven build will compile and test the application before executing the verification checks.

If SpotBugs identifies a finding matching the configured failure policy, the build fails.

If Dependency-Check identifies a vulnerability exceeding the configured CVSS threshold, the build fails.

Your CI/CD pipeline should then prevent the merge or deployment from proceeding until the checks pass.

For example:

Developer / AI-generated code
          |
          v
      Pull Request
          |
          v
      Maven Build
          |
          v
    Compile + Tests
          |
          v
      SpotBugs
          |
          v
  Dependency-Check
          |
          v
      Build Result
       /       \
      /         \
   Failure     Success
      |           |
      v           v
  Block merge   Allow merge
                  |
                  v
               Deploy

Make the CI job a required status check on protected branches, and ensure the deployment pipeline cannot bypass the verification stage.

This distinction matters: Maven plugins alone do not prevent someone from pushing a Git commit. Branch protection and deployment rules enforce the gate.

6. What do we actually gain?

We now have three complementary security and quality layers.

Tool What it examines Main objective
SpotBugs Compiled Java bytecode Detect potential bugs
Dependency-Check Project dependencies Identify known vulnerable components
Sonatype OSS Index Dependency component intelligence Add another vulnerability information source

The main advantage is that these tools address different classes of problems.

For example, an AI coding assistant might generate a method that uses an unsafe API incorrectly. SpotBugs may identify the problem.

Alternatively, it might introduce an outdated dependency with a known vulnerability. Dependency-Check, with Sonatype Guide integration, can help identify that risk.

And the same protection applies when the code is written entirely by a human developer.

7. Final thoughts

You don't need an expensive enterprise security platform just to introduce meaningful security checks into a Java development workflow.

SpotBugs and OWASP Dependency-Check are open-source tools that can provide a useful baseline for application code analysis and dependency vulnerability detection.

Sonatype Guide adds an external vulnerability intelligence service to the dependency analysis workflow. It is important to distinguish the open-source scanners from the hosted Sonatype service and check the applicable account and usage terms.

Of course, no automated scanner can guarantee that an application is secure. Static analysis and vulnerability databases have limitations, including false positives and false negatives. They do not replace code reviews, security testing, threat modelling, or regular maintenance.

But they give us something extremely valuable: a repeatable and automated security gate that runs on every build, regardless of whether the code was written by a developer or generated by AI.

And that is a great starting point for building more secure Java applications.

Official documentation and references

All implementation details in this article are based on the following official documentation:

  • SpotBugs Maven Plugin
  • SpotBugs Plugin Usage and Configuration
  • SpotBugs Check Goal
  • OWASP Dependency-Check
  • Dependency-Check Maven Documentation
  • Dependency-Check Maven Configuration
  • Sonatype Guide Build Tool Integration
  • Sonatype Guide Personal Access Tokens

title: Can Agents Keep Up with Time? An Empirical Analysis of Temporal Adaptation After a Conversational Hiatus
description:
arXiv:2611.17806v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at https://github.com/Adoreu2/session-rekindling-benchmark.

title: Electrocardiographic Imaging via Posterior Sampling under Operator Discrepancy
description:
arXiv:2611.17851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface potentials, an ill-posed inverse problem. Diffusion posterior samplers combine a learned prior with an explicit forward operator that they assume to be accurate. In ECGI this operator is only an estimate, because the body changes with respiration and posture, and body composition such as subcutaneous fat is rarely known for an individual patient. The resulting operator discrepancy is structured and depends on the heart signal. We introduce OpDis-PS, a diffusion posterior sampler that models this discrepancy instead of treating it as signal-independent noise. OpDis-PS learns how the discrepancy depends on the signal, folds this into a corrected forward operator, and reconstructs with a fixed prior across all operator conditions. We study two realistic sources of discrepancy, changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer. Across both, OpDis-PS reconstructs more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors, with its largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.

title: Is Framer built on React? Getting React code from a Framer site
description:
Yes. Published Framer sites are rendered with React, Framer's code components are React components, and its animation library started life as Framer Motion, now published as Motion. But Framer doesn't give you the React source of your site. To get React code, you either rebuild the design in React, or convert the published site with a tool such as Deframer, which writes React 19 components in TypeScript inside a Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite project.

What you get from a conversion is real React, with a few particulars worth knowing before you plan to reuse it.

How React shows up in Framer

  • Published sites. Each page you publish is made of modules that Framer's runtime renders with React, on the server and then in the browser. That's why a converter can read a published site as components rather than as flat HTML.
  • Code components and overrides. When you write code in Framer, you write React: a code component is a React component, and an override is a function that changes a layer's props. Framer's developer documentation covers both.
  • Motion. The animation library many React developers know as Framer Motion is now published as motion, imported from motion/react (Motion). Framer's springs, transitions and gestures are built on it.

None of that means Framer is "a React app you can open". The editor stores your design in its own format, and the published output is built for Framer's runtime, the framer package, not for a React project of your own.

Your options for getting React code

Rebuild in React

Use your Framer site as the reference and build the components yourself. You get exactly the structure you want, at the cost of matching every breakpoint, variant and animation by hand.

Export components from the editor

Framer's marketplace lists plugins aimed at this, such as React Export, whose listing describes it as bridging "Framer's intuitive design environment and your production-ready React codebase" (Framer Marketplace). Plugins work on components inside your project; check what each one covers before relying on it for a whole site.

Convert the whole published site

Deframer converts the entire published site into a Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite project: every page, layout, component, style, CMS collection, form and animation. It reads only the public files the site serves, so it needs no access to your Framer account. See how to export a Framer site to Next.js for the steps.

What the React code looks like after converting

A converted project is a standard React 19 app in the framework you picked (Next.js 16 by default), where every file is .ts or .tsx (plus .astro pages in Astro). The components are the same in all four:

  • Design components in src/components/, in the designer's own folders, each with a CSS module. Their props use human names: variants are called what the designer called them, such as "Desktop" or "D / Light", not Framer's internal ids.
  • Pages as components in src/views/, wired to the framework's routes (src/app/ in Next.js, src/routes/ or src/pages/ in the others).
  • Your own code components and overrides in src/code/; marketplace code in src/vendor/.
  • Styles in src/styles/: color styles as CSS variables, shared text styles as classes, fonts as @font-face rules.

Two details matter if you want to use these components outside the project.

They're client components. Every generated module starts with "use client", because the design components use state, effects and animation. Your route files stay server components and render them.

They use the project's kit. Instead of the framer package, the code imports a small helper kit that ships in the project at src/lib/deframer/, imported as @/deframer. The kit reproduces what Framer's runtime does for published sites: variants, breakpoints, effects, routing, CMS, forms. The project's tsconfig.json also points JSX at it:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "jsxImportSource": "@/deframer",
    "paths": {
      "@/deframer": ["./src/lib/deframer"],
      "@/deframer/*": ["./src/lib/deframer/*"],
      "@/*": ["./src/*"]
    }
  }
}

That JSX runtime applies defaultProps to function components as React 18 did, which code written for Framer relies on, and passes DOM elements only the props they can render.

Reusing components in another React app

The simplest path is to keep working in the converted project and build new features there, since it's an ordinary React app. If you do want to move a component into another codebase, bring what it depends on:

  1. the component's .tsx file and its .module.css;
  2. the components it imports, and their CSS modules;
  3. the styles it uses from src/styles/ (color tokens, text styles, fonts);
  4. the kit, src/lib/deframer/, plus the @/deframer path alias and jsxImportSource setting in your tsconfig.json.

Then render the component inside a client boundary and check it at each breakpoint. Deframer's terms let you use, change and distribute the kit as part of the project and its derivatives; read the terms for the exact wording.

For a component you'll maintain long-term, it can be cleaner to treat the converted version as the reference and rewrite it in your app's own conventions. Framer code components and overrides in a Next.js project covers the code you wrote in Framer, and what you get in a converted Next.js project tours every folder.

Types and strictness

Framer's editor never type-checks code components, so code you wrote there can contain real type errors. A project that contains such code builds with typescript: { ignoreBuildErrors: true } in next.config.ts, with a comment saying why. npx tsc --noEmit still lists the errors, so you can fix them file by file and then remove the setting. Generated components get explicit prop and ref types where TypeScript can't infer them.

Cost and ownership

Converting is free; downloading a converted project uses one credit: $10 for one, $25 for five or $100 for thirty, on the pricing page. You own the converted code of your own site. Deframer is an independent tool, not affiliated with Framer, and gives the code only of sites you own or have the owner's permission to download.

FAQ

Is Framer made with React?

Yes. Published Framer sites are rendered with React, code components are React components, and Framer's animations build on the library now called Motion. The editor itself stores designs in Framer's own format.

Can I export React code from Framer?

Not natively. Marketplace plugins can export some components, and Deframer converts a whole published site into a Next.js, TanStack Start, Astro, React Router or Vite project with React 19 components in TypeScript (Framer to React).

Is Framer Motion the same as Framer?

No. Framer is the website builder. Framer Motion was its open-source animation library for React and is now published as motion, imported from motion/react. You can use it in any React project, and converted Framer sites use it for their animations.

Can I use converted Framer components in my existing Next.js app?

Yes, if you bring their dependencies: the CSS modules, the styles they use and the project's @/deframer kit with its tsconfig settings. Building inside the converted project is simpler, and if your app uses Next.js, convert to Next.js so the routes match.

Do converted components need the Framer runtime?

No. The project contains no Framer runtime. A small, readable helper kit in src/lib/deframer/ replaces it, and you can read and change it like the rest of your code. See the FAQ.

Originally published on the Deframer blog. Deframer converts a published Framer site into Next.js, Astro, React Router, TanStack Start, Vite, Nuxt or static HTML code.

title: Market Analysis: Structural Liquidity Risks and Institutional Vulnerabilities in the Crypto-Asset Ecosystem
description:
The recent decline of XRP to its lowest price point in two years is not merely an isolated bearish event for a single digital asset; rather, it serves as a critical leading indicator of structural fragility within the maturing crypto-asset market. As the market transitions from a retail-driven speculative landscape to one dominated by institutional-grade instruments, such as Spot Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs, a new paradigm of systemic risk has emerged. The very mechanisms designed to provide institutional access—ETFs—have introduced a "negative feedback loop" where capital outflows trigger profound liquidity dislocations.
The Paradigm Shift: From Speculation to Institutional Dependency
Historically, crypto-asset price discovery was driven by retail sentiment, technological milestones, and speculative demand. However, the integration of Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) has fundamentally altered the market's DNA. Market dynamics are now increasingly tethered to traditional financial mechanisms, specifically institutional portfolio rebalancing and net ETF flows. While inflows provide much-needed legitimacy, the "reverse trigger" of outflows presents a systemic threat. The current volatility suggests that the market is becoming hypersensitive to institutional capital movements, where the withdrawal of liquidity through regulated channels can rapidly destabilize the broader ecosystem.
Technical and Structural Vulnerabilities: Liquidity Fragmentation
From a structural perspective, ETF-driven outflows exacerbate "liquidity fragmentation." The redemption process of an ETF necessitates that fund managers liquidate underlying crypto-assets to meet investor redemptions. This large-scale selling pressure absorbs on-chain liquidity, significantly widening price slippage.
This phenomenon is particularly acute for mid-cap assets like XRP. Unlike Bitcoin, which possesses deep, multi-layered liquidity, assets with specific utility profiles (such as cross-border settlement) are more susceptible to cascading sell orders triggered by algorithmic trading bots reacting to ETF-driven volatility. Furthermore, the devaluation of these assets poses a direct technical risk to the Decentralized Finance (DeFi) ecosystem, where such assets often serve as collateral. A rapid decline in value can trigger automated liquidations, creating a contagion effect that threatens the stability of smart contract-based protocols and the broader network security.
Macro-Economic Impact: The "Flight to Quality" and Market Homogenization
The business implications for the fintech and payment sectors are profound. For institutions building cross-border payment infrastructures, increased volatility directly undermines the economic viability of their solutions by complicating capital adequacy and reserve management.
We are currently observing an accelerated "Flight to Quality." Investors are migrating from high-beta altcoins toward more liquid, regulated, and "proven" assets like Bitcoin, or toward fiat-backed stablecoins. While this move toward stability is logical in the short term, it carries a long-term strategic risk: market homogenization. If capital continues to concentrate exclusively in a few dominant assets, the diversity of the crypto-ecosystem will diminish, potentially stifling the very innovation and decentralized competition that define the industry.
Strategic Governance Recommendations for Institutional Stakeholders
For organizations managing digital assets or integrating blockchain into financial services, the current volatility serves as a litmus test for IT governance and risk management frameworks. To mitigate these emerging systemic risks, I propose a three-pillar governance strategy:
1. Implementation of Real-Time Liquidity Monitoring: Organizations must move beyond simple price tracking. It is imperative to deploy advanced monitoring systems utilizing anomaly detection algorithms to track ETF net flows and significant on-chain movements. Real-time alerts regarding liquidity depletion are essential for proactive risk mitigation.
2. Advanced Scenario-Based Stress Testing: Traditional volatility modeling is no longer sufficient. Risk management departments must develop sophisticated stress-testing models that specifically simulate "liquidity exhaustion" scenarios resulting from massive ETF redemptions. These tests should quantitatively assess the impact of asset devaluation on the firm’s solvency, collateral ratios, and regulatory compliance.
3. Multi-Layered Asset Custody and Diversification: To eliminate "Single Points of Failure," institutions must adopt a multi-layered approach to asset governance. This involves technical and operational diversification of the underlying networks and assets used in settlement processes. Reducing dependency on any single asset or network is critical to maintaining operational resilience during periods of extreme market fragmentation.
In conclusion, the current market volatility is a symptom of a structural transition. As the boundary between traditional finance and crypto-assets blurs, the ability to manage the complexities of institutional liquidity will define the winners in the next era of digital finance.

title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
description:
arXiv:2611.17786v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS for readers' free use.

title: Fix "findDOMNode is not a function" with react-transition-group on React 19
description:
If you upgraded a project to React 19 and an animation now crashes the moment it starts, you have probably seen one of these:

TypeError: _reactDom.default.findDOMNode is not a function

TypeError: (0 , a.findDOMNode) is not a function

TypeError: react_dom__WEBPACK_IMPORTED_MODULE_1__.findDOMNode is not a function

They are the same error with different bundler names in front. Often the stack trace mentions Transition, CSSTransition, performEnter or onTransitionEnd. It usually happens when something opens, closes, fades or collapses, not on first render. That is why it can slip past a quick smoke test.

Why it happens

React 19 removed ReactDOM.findDOMNode (see the React 19 upgrade guide). It had been deprecated in StrictMode for years.

react-transition-group needs the real DOM node to add classes and listen for transitionend. When you don't give it that node, it falls back to findDOMNode(this). On React 19 that function no longer exists, so the transition throws.

Verified on npm, 2026-11-16 (Asia/Shanghai):

  • react-transition-group 4.4.5, published 2022-08-01, still the latest version.
  • react / react-dom 19.3.1.

The library already has the fix built in. Since 4.4.0 (May 2020), every transition component accepts a nodeRef prop. When you pass it, react-transition-group never calls findDOMNode.

Many thanks to the react-transition-group authors and maintainers, including Jason Quense, Matija Marohnić and the reactjs community contributors. This library has quietly animated a huge part of the React ecosystem for years. The nodeRef escape hatch they added in 2020 is exactly what makes React 19 work today.

Fix 1: pass nodeRef (your own code)

Create a ref, pass it as nodeRef, and attach the same ref to the element you are animating.

CSSTransition 

import { useRef } from "react";
import { CSSTransition } from "react-transition-group";

export function FadeBox({ show }: { show: boolean }) {
  const nodeRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  return (
    <CSSTransition in={show} timeout={200} classNames="fade" nodeRef={nodeRef} unmountOnExit>
      <div ref={nodeRef}>Hello</div>
    </CSSTransition>
  );
}

Transition (render-prop style) 

import { useRef } from "react";
import { Transition } from "react-transition-group";

export function Slide({ open }: { open: boolean }) {
  const nodeRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  return (
    <Transition in={open} timeout={300} nodeRef={nodeRef} onEnter={(isAppearing: boolean) => console.log("enter", isAppearing)}>
      {(state) => <div ref={nodeRef} className={`slide slide-${state}`}>Panel</div>}
    </Transition>
  );
}

Watch the callback signatures. With nodeRef, the callbacks no longer receive the DOM node as their first argument:

  • onEnter(node, isAppearing) becomes onEnter(isAppearing). The same goes for onEntering, onEntered, onExit, onExiting and onExited.
  • addEndListener(node, done) becomes addEndListener(done).

If you used the node inside a callback, read nodeRef.current instead. Code that still expects (node, isAppearing) won't crash, but it will quietly get a boolean where it expected an element.

The ref has to end up on a DOM element. If the child is your own component, forward the ref to its root element. In React 19 you can accept ref as a normal prop; on older versions, use forwardRef.

SwitchTransition: one ref per key

SwitchTransition keeps the old child mounted while the new one enters. If both children share one ref, the transition reads the wrong element. Give each key its own ref:

import { useRef, useState } from "react";
import { CSSTransition, SwitchTransition } from "react-transition-group";

export function Toggle() {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false);
  const onRef = useRef<HTMLButtonElement>(null);
  const offRef = useRef<HTMLButtonElement>(null);
  const nodeRef = on ? onRef : offRef;
  return (
    <SwitchTransition>
      <CSSTransition key={on ? "on" : "off"} nodeRef={nodeRef} timeout={150} classNames="fade">
        <button ref={nodeRef} onClick={() => setOn((v) => !v)}>{on ? "On" : "Off"}</button>
      </CSSTransition>
    </SwitchTransition>
  );
}

TransitionGroup: one ref per item

In a list, every item needs its own ref, and that ref must stay stable while the item is leaving. Hooks can't be called inside .map(), so a simple pattern is to create the ref together with the item and keep it in your state:

import { createRef, useState, type RefObject } from "react";
import { CSSTransition, TransitionGroup } from "react-transition-group";

type Item = { id: string; text: string; nodeRef: RefObject<HTMLLIElement | null> };

export function TodoList() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([
    { id: "1", text: "Buy milk", nodeRef: createRef<HTMLLIElement>() },
  ]);
  const add = () =>
    setItems((xs) => [...xs, { id: String(Date.now()), text: "New", nodeRef: createRef<HTMLLIElement>() }]);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={add}>Add</button>
      <TransitionGroup component="ul">
        {items.map(({ id, text, nodeRef }) => (
          <CSSTransition key={id} nodeRef={nodeRef} timeout={200} classNames="item">
            <li ref={nodeRef} onClick={() => setItems((xs) => xs.filter((x) => x.id !== id))}>{text}</li>
          </CSSTransition>
        ))}
      </TransitionGroup>
    </>
  );
}

ReplaceTransition works the same way: put a nodeRef on each of its children.

I ran all four snippets with React 19.3.1, react-dom 19.3.1 and react-transition-group 4.4.5 (in jsdom): they mount, enter and exit with no error. They also type-check with @types/react 19 and @types/react-transition-group 4.4.12. The same components without nodeRef throw findDOMNode is not a function.

Fix 2: when the crash comes from a UI library

If the stack trace points into node_modules/<some-ui-library>, you can't add nodeRef yourself. The library has to do it. Here is what I tested with React 19.3.1. Each component was rendered, opened and closed once:

Library (version tested) Result on React 19
@material-ui/core 4.12.4 (MUI v4) Crashes (Collapse, Fade)
react-bootstrap 1.6.8 Crashes (Collapse, Fade)
react-bootstrap 2.10.10 OK (Collapse, Fade, Modal)
@mui/material 9.5.0 OK (Collapse, Fade)
reactstrap 9.2.3 OK (Collapse, Fade, Alert, Modal, Toast)
@blueprintjs/core 6.23.0 OK (Overlay2, Collapse)
react-select 5.10.2 (react-select/animated) OK

So the fixes are:

  • MUI v4 (@material-ui/core): v4 only declares support for React 16 and 17. Move to @mui/material (v5 and later declare React 19 support; 9.5.0 tested above) with the official v4 → v5 migration guide.
  • react-bootstrap 1.x: upgrade to react-bootstrap 2.x (2.10.10 tested above; migration notes).
  • Any other library: check its React 19 notes or changelog for "findDOMNode" or "nodeRef". Your other option is to keep that part of the app on React 18.3 until the library ships a fix.

To find out which package actually pulls in react-transition-group:

npm ls react-transition-group
# or
pnpm why react-transition-group

Fix 3: stay on React 18 for now

If an important dependency hasn't caught up and you can't replace it yet, stay on React 18.3. There findDOMNode still exists and only warns in StrictMode. It's a stopgap, not a fix.

Alternatives, if you are rewriting animations anyway

You don't have to drop react-transition-group: with nodeRef it works fine on React 19. If you are rewriting your animations anyway, these are common choices:

  • Plain CSS transitions plus a mounted/unmounted state. Often enough for simple fades and slides.
  • motion (formerly Framer Motion), for AnimatePresence-style enter/exit animations.
  • react-transition-state, a small hook-based state machine with an API that resembles react-transition-group.

Summary

  • findDOMNode is not a function with react-transition-group on React 19 means a transition has no nodeRef.
  • In your own code: add nodeRef and put the same ref on the DOM element. Use one ref per key in SwitchTransition and one per item in TransitionGroup. Callbacks then no longer get the node as an argument.
  • From a UI library: upgrade it (MUI v4 → @mui/material, react-bootstrap 1 → 2), or stay on React 18.3 until it's fixed.

title: Agent-as-a-Judge
description:
arXiv:2611.18067v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence has progressed from task-specific systems toward general models spanning perception, generation, reasoning, and autonomous interaction, making reliable evaluation essential for comparison, deployment, and post-training feedback. At scale, modern evaluation pipelines increasingly rely on LLM-as-a-Judge to produce scores, preferences, and critiques; in its fixed-context setting, the judge relies on the supplied evaluand and evaluation materials. Yet a reliable verdict may require evidence beyond the supplied evaluand and context---either because critical environmental states remain unrecorded in the static execution log, or because controversial factual claims require external verification. Passive judges cannot obtain that missing evidence before deciding, especially when evaluating agent trajectories, executable artifacts, or domain-specific reports. Recent work therefore develops active evaluators that seek missing evidence and update their grounds for judgment before deciding. We bring these advances together through Agent-as-a-Judge, focusing on how evaluators construct and control checking processes within the broader LLM-based judging landscape. We define the scope through evaluation-directed checks and the use of their results, covering both structured workflows and observation-driven control. We organize the design space by multi-agent collaboration, tool integration, memory, and planning, and show how these mechanisms supply the checks and evidence on which a verdict rests. We consolidate published scores and reproduce missing entries for key agentic judges; the comparison reveals uneven agentic gains and motivates dedicated agentic evaluation. We conclude by characterizing application demands and open challenges in cost, reliability, safety, and governance that condition trusted deployment of agentic judges at scale.
