title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
description:
arXiv:2611.17472v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.

title: Go Token Expiry UX in Live Stock Watchlists: Deterministic Session Tests
description:
Short answer: keep the watchlist token short-lived, make expiry an explicit state transition, and test that transition with a fake clock and a replayable event log. The client should never infer authorization from whether a socket happens to be open.

In a stock trading watchlist, a live poll is a deceptively small feature. Prices arrive while a user edits symbols, the session token expires, and the UI must say what is still trustworthy. A stale quote is annoying; a stale permission boundary is a ledger problem waiting to happen.

Start with the bill, then decide what to retain

The largest recurring term is usually event delivery, not token issuance. A useful first estimate is subscribers × updates per second × encoded bytes per update; it gives the team a concrete number to measure before debating transports. Token minting and refresh calls are comparatively sparse, while retaining every transient quote event for replay can quietly turn a UX feature into a storage and compliance obligation.

For a watchlist, I retain an append-only audit record of authorization decisions, symbol changes, and the final session state. I do not retain every duplicate price tick by default. That choice reduces replay fidelity, so the recovery path uses a timestamped snapshot plus a sequence number; an operator can prove which quote version was displayed without preserving an unlimited stream of ephemeral values.

The catch is operational. If a regulator or incident responder needs tick-level reconstruction, dropping those events is not suitable. In that case, route the raw feed to a separately governed market-data archive and keep the product's audit log focused on user-visible decisions. Mixing the two retention policies makes deletion, access reviews, and cost attribution harder.

A simple budget worksheet should include fan-out bandwidth, connection counts, refresh traffic, and retained bytes. Cost is a constraint, not a selection criterion: a cheaper transport that makes expiry ambiguous creates more support work and a larger reconciliation surface.

Measure first.

How should token expiry shape a trusted watchlist session?

Treat authorization as a state machine shared by server and client: active, expiring, expired, and reconnecting. The server validates the token on connection and on privileged actions; the client displays quotes as provisional once the lease ends, stops submitting symbol mutations, and offers a deliberate re-authentication action. An open WebRTC data channel, WebSocket, or long poll is only a delivery mechanism. It is not proof that the lease remains valid.

Use an absolute expiry timestamp issued by the server, plus a small safety margin for clock skew. Do not schedule a single browser timer and call the job done. Background tabs throttle timers, laptops sleep, and a reconnect can race with a refresh response. On every message and before every mutation, compare the server-derived deadline with the current monotonic clock.

The UX should make the boundary legible: show “updates paused; sign in to continue,” preserve the last known quote with its age, and never silently re-submit a queued edit after a new token arrives. A fresh token starts a new authorization epoch. The epoch and the last accepted event sequence belong in the audit trail so duplicate callbacks remain harmless.

That is the trust boundary.

Here is the core of a deterministic test harness in Go. The production adapter can use a real clock; tests inject the fake one and advance it explicitly.

package session

import "time"

type Clock interface {
    Now() time.Time
}

type FakeClock struct{ current time.Time }

func (c *FakeClock) Now() time.Time { return c.current }
func (c *FakeClock) Advance(d time.Duration) { c.current = c.current.Add(d) }

type Lease struct {
    Epoch     uint64
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

type State int

const (
    Active State = iota
    Expiring
    Expired
)

func SessionState(clock Clock, lease Lease, margin time.Duration) State {
    remaining := lease.ExpiresAt.Sub(clock.Now())
    if remaining <= 0 {
        return Expired
    }
    if remaining <= margin {
        return Expiring
    }
    return Active
}

The test should assert observable transitions, not sleep for five minutes. Advance to one second before expiry, verify that mutations are blocked in Expiring, then advance one second and verify that delivery is marked stale in Expired. Include a duplicate event with the same sequence number and assert that the audit writer records it once. This is an exactly-once mindset applied at the boundary where it matters; the network itself will not provide exactly-once delivery.

Testing reconnects without flaky timing

Build tests around a scripted event log. Each record contains epoch, sequence, received_at, and kind (quote, authorization, or mutation result). Feed the same log through a state reducer in unit tests, then run a smaller set of browser tests for rendering and focus behavior. The reducer gives you deterministic coverage for races such as “expiry arrives while a quote is buffered” and “refresh completes after reconnect.”

type Event struct {
    Epoch uint64
    Seq   uint64
    Kind  string
}

type Reducer struct {
    Epoch      uint64
    LastSeq    uint64
    Authorized bool
}

func (r *Reducer) Apply(e Event) bool {
    if e.Epoch != r.Epoch || e.Seq <= r.LastSeq {
        return false
    }
    r.LastSeq = e.Seq
    if e.Kind == "authorized" {
        r.Authorized = true
    }
    if e.Kind == "expired" {
        r.Authorized = false
    }
    return true
}

The important assertion is not “the reconnect finished within 200 ms.” It is “an event from epoch 4 cannot mutate state in epoch 5.” For example, imagine a trader's token expires just after sequence 881 carries a quote for NVDA, while the browser has already sent a symbol-removal request and the refresh endpoint is waiting behind a sleeping mobile radio. When the device wakes, the feed may deliver sequence 882, the refresh may complete, and the old mutation response may arrive in either order; the reducer must reject any record from the old epoch, retain the age of the last quote, and require the user to repeat the edit under the new lease. Add property tests that randomize event order, duplicate delivery, and reconnect count while keeping the clock fixed. Your mileage may vary with browser scheduling, but the authorization and ordering rules should remain invariant.

For integration tests, put the feed behind a controllable test server that can close the channel, delay a refresh response, and replay a sequence. Avoid monkey-patching wall-clock APIs in the browser; it often hides the exact race you are trying to expose. A short end-to-end suite can then verify accessible status text, disabled controls, and focus returning to the sign-in action.

Delivery choices and explicit limits

WebRTC data channels, WebSockets, and server-sent events each solve delivery, not authorization. WebRTC adds ICE and connection-state concerns; WebSockets offer a familiar bidirectional stream but still need application-level sequencing; server-sent events simplify one-way updates and browser reconnection while leaving mutations on ordinary HTTPS. The standards document for WebRTC describes its connection and data-channel states, which are useful signals for transport health, but none of them extend a token's lifetime.

Pick the least complex transport that matches the direction of traffic. For a read-heavy watchlist with separate HTTPS mutations, one-way events may be sufficient. Stay with a bidirectional channel when the session genuinely needs low-latency commands and you can operate its reconnect and backpressure behavior. Do not choose based on a benchmark that omits token refresh, audit writes, and mobile sleep.

I initially treated expiry as a timer concern. That was the wrong boundary. The durable boundary is an authorization epoch recorded beside the user's intent, because that is what reconciliation can explain after a reconnect or a disputed order. Keep transport telemetry (connect, close, retry, buffered bytes) separate from financial audit events, and sample high-volume quote metrics without sampling security decisions.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449

title: How to make a pivot table in Excel in five steps (no formulas)
description:
To make a pivot table in Excel, click any cell inside your data, open Insert, choose PivotTable, and drag one text field into Rows and one number field into Values. The summary appears in seconds, and you never write a formula to get it.

When a pivot misbehaves, the source data is almost always the culprit. The steps below assume one header row, no blank rows and one kind of value per column. Menu names come from the Microsoft 365 desktop app on Windows, so expect small differences in other versions. Work on a copy of the workbook while you learn, so a misplaced drag never touches the original file.

Clean the source before you click anything

A pivot wants a database-style layout. Every column needs a unique, non-blank header, every row is one record, and every column holds one type of value. Merged cells are the classic trap. A region typed once with empty cells beneath it breaks the grouping, and dollar amounts pasted from an email often arrive as text, which Excel quietly skips in a sum.

Next, select the data and press Ctrl+T to turn it into an Excel Table. A pivot built on a plain range remembers the exact cells you selected, so rows pasted underneath later get ignored. A Table grows with the data, and the pivot can follow it.

Build the first pivot in five steps

Imagine a small sales table with six rows and the columns date, region, rep, product, units and sales. Click one cell, go to Insert, click PivotTable, confirm the range, and choose New Worksheet. Then drag Region into Rows and Sales into Values.

The result should read East at 3,900 dollars, South at 1,200 and West at 3,300, with a grand total of 8,400. Right-click a value, apply a currency format, and the sheet starts to look like a report someone would actually read.

Now drag Product into Columns. Laptops come to 6,000 and monitors to 2,400, and those two add back up to the same 8,400. Two different cuts agreeing on the grand total is the cheapest check you have, so run it every time.

Good to read before you audit totals:

Change the math and group the dates

Click a value field and open Value Field Settings to change the calculation. The same Sales column answers three questions. Sum tells you revenue, Count tells you how many orders, and Average tells you how large a typical order is. In the sample, East leads on revenue while West has the bigger average order, which you would miss if you only looked at totals.

Dates need extra care. Right-click any date in the pivot, choose Group, and pick Months, Quarters or Years. If your data spans more than one year, select Years along with Months, or January 2026 and January 2027 collapse into a single January row. If Group is greyed out, the date column still contains text or blanks.

When something breaks along the way, the symptom fix table in the original post lists the common errors with a cause and a fix for each one. I would bookmark that part before anything else.

Refresh, slice and trust the numbers

A pivot is a snapshot. Editing the source changes nothing until you choose PivotTable Analyze and then Refresh, or Refresh All when a workbook holds several pivots. If you want fresh numbers every time the file opens, switch that on under PivotTable Options.

Slicers replace dropdowns with buttons that anyone can click. Insert one from PivotTable Analyze, and if a second pivot should respond to the same buttons, open Report Connections and tick it. That single step is what turns a pivot into a tool a manager will actually use.

Pivots never alter the underlying numbers, so experimenting is safe. Drag fields around until the report answers your question, then check the grand total once more against a plain SUM of the source column. If the two disagree, the source is the place to look first.

One habit saves a lot of confusion. Name the pivot sheet something clear, such as Sales by Region, and keep the source on its own tab. A pivot pointing at a moving target is hard to debug, while a clean layout makes refreshes predictable.

The original post lists seven symptoms, each with a fix and its cause:

See the symptom fix table on daylongs.com

title: Learning Word-Level Explanations of Text Reuse in Latin Literature with Little Annotation
description:
arXiv:2611.18319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detecting an intertextual reference is only the first step; philologists also need to know how a later author reworked the source. We explain a reuse pair word by word: each word of the reusing passage is first aligned to its source word, then labeled with the operation that transformed it, such as a copy, a change of inflection, or a substitution. Such word-level operations are expensive to annotate, and only a few corpora annotated at this level exist for text reuse in Latin literature. We describe a procedure that needs only a limited number of annotations: synthetic pairs, built by applying known operations to Latin text, train a first model, and active learning chooses the pairs an annotator corrects. Among several architectures, a model that links and labels together performs best: a pointer network that, for every reuse word, chooses a source word and names the operation in the same step. We show that with active learning, 200 pairs chosen by uncertainty are enough for the model to match one trained on every annotated pair of the 1,490 references of the Loci Similes benchmark. We release our code, word-level predictions for all references, and an interactive demo.

title: NER-D: A cross-domain benchmark for German NER
description:
arXiv:2611.18257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present NER-D, a cross-domain benchmark for German NER comprising 13 datasets spanning 9 domains, including General/Politics, Wikipedia, Legal, Medical, Historical, Financial, Agriculture and Archaeology. We examine the performance of both proprietary LLMs and state-of-the-art small open-source models using normal prompting and further examine the performance gains achievable via in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning. Our results show that without any sort of optimization a proprietary model (GPT-5.4 mini) outperforms the smaller open-source models on 6 out of 13 datasets, but LoRA fine-tuning enables the smaller models to substantially outperform the proprietary baseline. We further analyze the influence of the domain and the tagset used in each task on the performance achieved in the different evaluation settings. Our benchmark will be available as a resource for the development of future German NER methods on both general and specialized domains.\footnote{We make our code, data, and models publicly available upon acceptance of this paper.

title: DySENSE: Dynamic Spatiotemporal ENergy Synthesis and Emulation with Satellite Imagery
description:
arXiv:2611.17878v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions. City energy is essential for achieving the 2050 net-zero target and the UN's Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 11. Although existing studies have made progress, they are limited by data and methodological gaps. Existing studies are largely predictive for existing cities rather than generative for future cities; fine-grained, aligned monthly dynamic energy data are scarce; and existing GenAI models struggle to generate dynamic urban functional monthly energy. We present DySENSE, a joint multimodal GenAI framework that synthesizes static urban satellite imagery together with spatially aligned, dynamic monthly building energy consumption maps. We decouple long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption. By conditioning on static urban land use, DySENSE can generate realistic, diverse and new static urban imagery with aligned energy maps. By conditioning on dynamic monthly and climate prompts, DySENSE can jointly generate dynamic, monthly energy consumption maps while keeping the urban morphology static. Experiments across four cities (New York, Washington, Norfolk, Busan) demonstrated that DySENSE can generate annotated high-fidelity synthetic energy data using less than 25% labelled data, boosting downstream prediction performance by 8% mIoU, and achieving strong energy dynamic consistency. Compared to existing methods, DySENSE significantly improved prediction performance (8.7% accuracy) and reduced prediction error (9%-18% CVRMSE, ASHRAE). DySENSE offers an effective foundation for energy-efficient cities, peak-load analysis, building performance simulation and dynamic demand response for city, energy, and building science. The data and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/skl24/MUSE2 and https://github.com/kailaisun/DySENSE

title: PF-Exec: Large-Scale UAV Relay Load Balancing with an Anchored Potential Direction Decider and a Per-Dimension Gain-Learning Executor
description:
arXiv:2611.17492v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Relay load balancing in large-scale UAV networks requires joint decisions on association, bandwidth, power and hovering position, while the dimension grows with the number of UAVs and each UAV sees only its local state. This paper splits the decision into two layers. An anchored potential direction decider emits a closed-form target at every instant and returns its direction only. A gain-learning executor maps a local observation into a positive gain per dimension, composes gain and target, and clips the action against the physical single-step bound; the two layers form PF-Exec. The unit gain is the default start, so the executor reduces to the pure potential policy before training. The load is first-order homogeneous in bandwidth, making the bandwidth target closed form, and the position target is the demand-weighted centroid of the served users. The system uses a two-hop access and millimetre-wave backhaul link with soft association, a 3GPP UMa-AV channel with two shadowing layers, an OU-type social-force crowd and a quadrotor physical layer. Evaluation spans all fleet sizes, two crowd scenarios, independent seeds, the published baselines in their own settings and a degraded-information line. In the highest-pressure burst setting the fixed-step comparison breaks down on part of the seeds, losing fairness and mean load at once, while PF-Exec holds fairness near one. Among the ten comparison methods only the greedy heuristic survives that setting; its load variance stays far higher. Under stale global state and position noise the fairness index stays high at both largest-scale scenarios. Flight energy is nearly identical between the learned and the fixed-step executor, and three constants are fixed once across all settings. The convergence properties of both layers, from the truncated gain iteration to the perturbed tracking bound, are proved in the companion analysis.

title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
description:
arXiv:2611.17495v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.

title: We looked up our new hostname four minutes too early and our resolver remembered that it did not exist
description:
In October we moved our stock service behind a new internal name, stock.internal, in a Route 53 private hosted zone. The cutover plan had two parts. The platform team's Terraform would create the record pointing at the new load balancer, and the client teams would deploy configuration that switched their services to the new name. The change window was ten o'clock.

The client deploys went out at five to ten. Terraform created the record at one minute past. For the next fifteen minutes, eleven of our nineteen client services, in two of our three VPCs, failed every call to stock with name not found, while the other eight worked perfectly against the same record.

Each client deploy had run a readiness check that resolved stock.internal before the record existed. The VPC resolver answered that the name did not exist and, as resolvers are supposed to, it cached that answer. How long a resolver keeps a negative answer is set by the zone's SOA record: the smaller of the SOA record's own TTL and its minimum field. In Route 53's default SOA the TTL is nine hundred seconds, so the resolver kept saying the name did not exist for fifteen minutes after it did. The eight that worked ran in a VPC where nothing had asked for the name before it existed, so its resolver had nothing to remember.

Nothing was broken, and every resolver in the path was doing what the standard tells it to do. Our plan had simply never considered that asking a question early is also an answer that gets remembered.

Records for a cutover are now created at least a day ahead, pointing at the old target, and the cutover itself changes the value of a record that already exists. A positive answer is cached for the record's own TTL, which we lower to sixty seconds the day before, so the switch lands in a minute. We also lowered the TTL on our private zones' SOA records to sixty seconds, so a negative answer that slips through costs a minute rather than fifteen. The cutover checklist begins with a lookup of every new name from inside the network, and it must succeed before any client deploy starts.

The plan asked whether the record would exist by ten. It never asked who would look for it before then.

– Sergey Shinder

title: Building a WhatsApp-First Booking Flow Without a Backend
description:
Why WhatsApp

In Morocco, WhatsApp is the universal messaging app. Our guests are tourists arriving at Marrakech Menara airport, and they already have WhatsApp open. A traditional booking form with login, payment gateway, and confirmation emails adds friction. WhatsApp adds none.

The Implementation

Every "Book Now" button on our site is a pre-filled WhatsApp link. The helper function is straightforward:

export function whatsappHref(text: string) {
  return `https://wa.me/${site.whatsapp}?text=${encodeURIComponent(tagged(text))}`;
}

The tagged() wrapper prepends a source tag so the office knows which site the message came from (we operate multiple domains):

const SOURCE_TAG = `[navetteforyou.com \u00b7 Marrakech Transport]`;
const tagged = (s: string) =>
  s.startsWith(SOURCE_TAG) ? s : `${SOURCE_TAG}\n${s}`;

Pre-Filling the Message

Each route page composes a booking message with the transfer details already filled in: route, date placeholder, number of passengers, vehicle class, and quoted price. When the guest taps the button, WhatsApp opens with a message like:

[navetteforyou.com \u00b7 Marrakech Transport]
Transfer: Marrakech Airport \u2192 Medina
Vehicle: Mercedes E-Class (3 pax)
Price: 300 MAD
Date: [your arrival date]
Flight: [your flight number]

The guest fills in two blanks and hits send. The office responds within minutes.

Email Fallback

For guests who prefer email, we use the same pattern with mailto: links:

export function mailHref(subject: string, body: string) {
  const subj = `[navetteforyou.com] ${subject}`;
  return `mailto:${site.email}?subject=${encodeURIComponent(subj)}&body=${encodeURIComponent(tagged(body))}`;
}

Zero Backend

There is no server, no database, no payment processing. The entire booking flow is a static site generating deep links into WhatsApp and email. The operator's office handles confirmations, payments (cash or bank transfer), and driver dispatch. This architecture costs nothing to run and has zero downtime risk.

Tradeoffs

The obvious gap: no automated scheduling, no calendar integration, no payment capture. For a small transfer operator handling 10-30 bookings per day, a WhatsApp thread with context is faster than any dashboard. At scale, you would add a backend. We are not at that scale, and premature infrastructure is a cost, not a feature.

Operated by Serenity Morocco Tours. Visit navetteforyou.com or WhatsApp +212 701 664 704.

title: Learn React by reading your own Framer site's code
description:
The fastest way for a Framer designer to learn React is to read a React project whose design you already know: your own site. Convert your published Framer site to code, run it locally, and trace each thing you built on the canvas (a component, a variant, a breakpoint, a CMS list) to the file that renders it. Because you know what every part should look like, you can focus on how the code expresses it, and every change you make shows up in the browser straight away.

This guide uses Deframer, which converts a published Framer site into a TypeScript project. Deframer is an independent tool and is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by Framer. Use it on your own site, or one whose owner allows it.

Why your own site beats a tutorial

Tutorials teach React with to-do lists. That works, but the gap between a to-do list and a real website is wide. Your own site closes the gap from the other side:

  • You know the intent. You know the hero should stack on phones and the card should lift on hover, so you can tell whether you understand the code.
  • Framer already taught you the concepts. Components, variants, props (Framer's property controls), breakpoints and CMS collections all exist in React too, under similar names.
  • It's real. The project is a standard React app, so what you learn carries over to any React job.

Step 1: get the code running

  1. Convert your site with Deframer: paste the published address and keep the default framework, Next.js. Converting is free.
  2. To download, verify the site is yours by publishing a one-line meta tag in Framer's Site Settings, Custom Code. A verified download uses 1 credit ($10 as a single pack). See verifying Framer site ownership.
  3. Install Node.js (20.9 or later), unzip the project and run: 
npm install
npm run dev
  1. Open http://localhost:3000. That's your site, running from code on your machine.

Open the folder in an editor such as VS Code. Keep the browser and the editor side by side.

Step 2: learn the map

The project's README has a "Where to edit" table. These are the folders that matter while learning:

Framer concept Where it is in code
A page src/views/<page>.tsx plus <page>.module.css
The URL of a page src/app/<path>/page.tsx (a few lines that render the view)
Layout templates (nav, footer) src/layouts/
A design component src/components/<your folders>/
Color styles src/styles/tokens.ts, as CSS variables
Text styles src/styles/text/
CMS collections src/cms/<collection>.json
Code components you wrote src/code/

Components keep the folder names you used in Framer, and props and variants keep the names you gave them. A variant you called "Hover" or "Mobile Open" is called that in the code. What you get in a converted Next.js project tours every folder.

Step 3: five small exercises

Do these in order. Each one teaches a core React idea using something you designed.

1. Change some text (JSX)

Open the view for your home page and find a headline you wrote. Change the words and save; the browser updates. You've just edited JSX, React's HTML-like syntax. Notice how text sits inside elements, and how elements nest the way layers nest in Framer.

2. Change a color everywhere (CSS variables)

Open src/styles/tokens.ts and change one of your color styles. Every component that uses it changes. This is the same idea as a Framer color style, expressed as a CSS variable such as --token-....

3. Follow a component's props

Pick a component you reuse, such as a button. Find where a page uses it and look at what it passes in: a label, a link, a variant. Then open the component file and find where it reads those values. That's props: data passed from the parent, like property controls in Framer.

4. Read a variant

In the same component, look for its variants by name, such as variant === "Primary". Variants in React are usually just a prop that picks different styles or content. Hover and press states are written with motion/react, the animation library Framer's own animations grew from. Framer variants and hover states as React code explains the patterns.

5. Add a CMS item

Open a collection's JSON in src/cms/, copy one record, change its fields and give it a new slug. Restart the dev server if needed and visit its URL. You've just seen how data drives a list and a detail page: a component maps over records and renders one card per item.

Step 4: learn the concepts behind what you saw

Once the exercises feel natural, read the official React docs at react.dev with your project open. The sections on components, props, rendering lists, conditional rendering and state will each map to something you've already touched. When the docs show an example, find the equivalent in your site.

For routing and pages, read the Next.js docs on the App Router. Each folder in src/app is a URL, and each page.tsx is what that URL renders.

What to skip at first

Some parts of the project are there to reproduce Framer's runtime, and they're not where a beginner should start:

  • src/lib/deframer/: the small kit that replaces Framer's runtime. Useful later, distracting now.
  • src/vendor/: marketplace components as source, written by other people.
  • src/proxy.ts and next.config.ts: redirects and URL forms.

Treat them like a car's engine bay: know it's there, don't start learning to drive by opening it.

Use AI as a tutor, not a replacement

Tools like Cursor or Claude Code can explain any file in plain language. Ask "explain what this component does and which props it takes" rather than "change this for me". When you do let a tool edit, read the diff before you accept it. Editing a Framer site with Cursor or Claude Code has prompts and guardrails.

Keep designing in Framer if you like

Learning React doesn't mean leaving Framer. Many designers keep designing there and use the code to understand what developers will build, to prototype ideas faster in code, or to hand cleaner work to a team. If you want to understand the differences in depth, is Framer built on React? is a good next read, and which framework should your Framer site use? explains the other export options.

FAQ

Do I need to know JavaScript before starting?

It helps to know the basics, such as variables, functions and arrays, but you can learn them alongside. Your site gives you real examples of each.

Is the code readable for a beginner?

It's generated code, but it is formatted, uses human names for props and variants, and keeps your folders. Some parts are dense; start with views and components.

Will I break my live Framer site?

No. The code is a copy on your computer. Nothing you do in it changes the site Framer hosts.

Which framework should a beginner pick?

Next.js, the default. It has the most learning material and is what most React jobs use.

How much does it cost?

Converting and reviewing are free. Downloading your own site's code uses 1 credit with verification; a single credit costs $10. See pricing.

Originally published on the Deframer blog. Deframer converts a published Framer site into Next.js, Astro, React Router, TanStack Start, Vite, Nuxt or static HTML code.

title: RSSA: Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner for Collaborative Perception
description:
arXiv:2611.18023v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: V2X collaborative perception improves single-vehicle perception by aggregating multi-view features from collaborative agents. However, existing methods typically rely on simple spatial warping to align the collaborative features, which can cause semantic misalignment during fusion. Meanwhile, these deterministic warping-based methods are highly sensitive to the positional noises. In this paper, we propose a plug-in module called Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner (RSSA), which performs semantic and probabilistic spatial transformations for robust feature alignment. Specifically, a Semantic Transformation (SemT) block modulates feature channels based on the observed relative pose to correct semantic inconsistencies. Subsequently, a Probabilistic Spatial Transformation (P-SpaT) block performs probabilistic warping by sampling from the Gaussian-modeled relative pose space. A Relative Transformation Augmentation (RT-Aug) strategy is further introduced to augment the relative poses and facilitate the training of the RSSA. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that RSSA improves the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin under the configuration of both clean and noisy positions.

title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
description:
arXiv:2611.17784v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning.
