title: Folding Language Models into Themselves
description:
arXiv:2611.18113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation usually trains a compact student from scratch, which needs a large amount of data even though the teacher's weights already encode most of what the student has to learn. In this work, we explore building the student directly from the teacher's weights. We propose Concertina, which folds every group of N adjacent teacher layers into one shared block that is executed N times. Each loop step carries a low-rank correction initialized from the layer it replaces, and a per-token gate mixes these corrections, to let every token recover the behavior of the original layers from a single shared block. We further design a distillation data recipe that balances general, mathematical, academic and targeted multiple-choice data, to recover all capabilities of the teacher together rather than one at the expense of another. On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model distilled on 22B tokens retains about 90% of the teacher on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks. It outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines, as well as Qwen3-1.7B, which is trained on over a thousand times more data. These results suggest that a compact model need not be retrained at scale, since folding the teacher into itself and distilling it on the right data recovers most of its capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/myboker/concertina.

title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.18043v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.

title: Best web scraping APIs in 2026, priced per 1,000 successful pages
description:
I build MeshArc, a scraping API, and the question I get most from other developers is "which one is cheapest?" The trouble is that every scraping API prices in credits, and no two vendors' credits mean the same thing: one credit buys a plain HTTP fetch at one vendor, a rendered page at another, and a 404 at a third. So "100,000 credits for $99" tells you almost nothing until you know what a page costs at each rung, and which responses you pay for that you can't use.

Update, 16 November 2026: the table below was checked on 4 November. Since then Crawl4AI Cloud prices a plain page at 0.1 credit and a real browser page at 0.5 on its $99 Builder plan (125,000 credits), which is about $0.08 per 1,000 plain pages and $0.40 per 1,000 browser pages (checked on its pricing page on 16 November 2026). That makes Crawl4AI Cloud the cheapest plain page of the vendors here, ahead of ScrapingBee and Scrapfly at $0.10. Crawl4AI Cloud also says failed calls are free. The rest of the table is as checked on 4 November.

This post does the arithmetic for eight APIs at the plan closest to $100 a month. The unit is the one that matters to a developer: dollars per 1,000 pages you can actually use. Every competitor figure was read off the vendor's own pricing page or docs on 4 November 2026. MeshArc is our product; where another API is cheaper or better, the table says so.

How the numbers are worked out

The formula is the same for every row:

cost per 1,000 pages = plan price ÷ included credits × 1,000 × credits per page

Three choices keep it fair:

  • Monthly billing, not annual. Annual prices are lower (often two months free) but they are a different commitment. Where a vendor quotes annual-only figures, the monthly price is used here.
  • The plan nearest $100. Per-credit prices fall on bigger plans for everyone, MeshArc included.
  • Rungs, not marketing tiers. "Plain" is an HTTP fetch, "rendered" is a real browser running JavaScript, and "residential" is a rendered page through a residential or premium proxy, which is what a protected site usually needs.

The table

Checked on 4 November 2026. Dollars per 1,000 pages, monthly billing. (Crawl4AI Cloud's rates have changed since; see the update at the top.)

API · plan Plan price / credits Plain Rendered Rendered + residential 404s billed?
MeshArc · Growth $99 / 500k $0.20 $0.79 $3.17 No
Firecrawl · Standard $99 / 100k $0.99 $0.99 Not on pricing page Yes (and 403s)
ScrapingBee · Startup $99 / 1M $0.10 $0.50 $2.48 Yes (and 410s)
ZenRows · Launch $99 / 500k $0.20 $0.99 $4.95 Yes (and 410s)
Scrapfly · Pro $100 / 1M $0.10 $0.50 $2.50 residential; stack not stated No (upstream 4xx/5xx free)
ScraperAPI · Startup $149 / 1M $0.15 $1.49 $3.73 Yes
Crawl4AI Cloud · Builder $99 / 125k $0.40 $0.79 Not listed ("hard site" $1.58) Not stated
Bright Data · Unlocker PAYG $1.50 per 1k requests $1.50 $1.50 $1.50 Success only; 404s not stated

Where the rates come from:

  • MeshArc: 1 credit plain fetch, 4 rendered, 16 rendered on a residential IP (including 1 MB; 4 more per started MB). Refused pages, 404s, 410s, robots-blocked URLs and unchanged pages are free (pricing).
  • Firecrawl: 1 credit per scrape; JSON, question and highlight formats add 4 credits, so a structured page is $4.95. Its pricing page says a page that returns 403 or 404 "is still returned to you and costs 1 credit", and Standard credits do not roll over. A walkthrough is in Firecrawl pricing explained.
  • ScrapingBee: 1 credit plain, 5 with JavaScript, 10 premium proxy, 25 premium with JavaScript. Its FAQ: "We only charge for successful requests, i.e returning with a 200, 404 or 410 status code." Credits are valid for one month.
  • ZenRows: 1, 5, 10 and 25 credits for basic, JS, premium and JS + premium. Failed requests are free, but 404 and 410 count as successful and are billed.
  • Scrapfly: 1 credit base, 5 for browser rendering, 25 for residential. The page says adding features "increases the multiplier" but does not state the stacked total; its own code sample shows 30 credits for an unblocker request, which is $3.00 if that is the stack. Upstream 4xx and 5xx are free.
  • ScraperAPI: 1 credit standard, 10 rendered, 25 rendered with premium proxies, 75 with ultra premium. Bot-protected sites (Cloudflare, DataDome, PerimeterX) add 10 credits when bypassed. Its docs charge for 200 and 404.
  • Crawl4AI Cloud: 0.5 credits for a normal page, 1 for a real browser, 2 for a "hard site". The pricing page does not mention residential proxies or failed requests. (As of 16 November: 0.1 plain, 0.5 browser, 2 hard site, and failed calls are free.)
  • Bright Data Web Unlocker: a flat $1.50 per 1,000 requests pay-as-you-go ($1.30 on the $499 Scale plan), rendering and captcha handling included, "pay only for success".

What the table says, plainly

On price per plain page, MeshArc is not the cheapest. ScrapingBee and Scrapfly are half the price at $0.10, and ScraperAPI is cheaper too; since 16 November, Crawl4AI Cloud is cheaper still at about $0.08. If you read pages once, from easy sites, those are the better buy and we would rather you knew.

On rendered pages, ScrapingBee and Scrapfly lead again at $0.50; MeshArc and Crawl4AI Cloud are at $0.79.

On residential + render, ScrapingBee ($2.48) and Scrapfly (from $2.50) are below MeshArc ($3.17); ZenRows ($4.95) and ScraperAPI ($3.73) are above it. Bright Data's flat $1.50 beats everyone here, and it is the reverse on plain pages, where you pay $1.50 for what costs $0.10 elsewhere.

"Successful" changes the ranking: 404s and refusals

The headline rate assumes every page you pay for is one you wanted. Real URL lists are not like that. An old sitemap, a product feed with delisted items or a link crawl all produce dead URLs.

Take 1,000 URLs from a sitemap where 80 are now 404s, all plain pages:

API Billed pages Cost Per 1,000 usable pages
MeshArc Growth 920 $0.18 $0.20
ScrapingBee Startup 1,000 $0.10 $0.11
Scrapfly Pro 920 $0.09 $0.10
ZenRows Launch 1,000 $0.20 $0.22
Firecrawl Standard 1,000 $0.99 $1.08

The 80 dead URLs are an illustration, not a measurement; use your own ratio. The lesson holds either way: a vendor that bills 404s gets dearer exactly as your URL list ages, and the effect is largest on the vendors with the highest per-page rate.

The second leak is refusals. Most vendors here say they do not bill a failed request (Crawl4AI's pricing page did not say either way on 4 November; on 16 November it says failed calls are free), so this is close to parity, not an advantage. The difference is what happens before the refusal: a cheapest-first API (MeshArc, ScrapingBee and ZenRows all escalate) may try several rungs on a page that never loads. MeshArc does not bill a refused page "whatever the ladder spent finding out", and a page that would need a rung above your maxCredits returns TIER_LIMIT at zero cost.

Walled sites: where per-page rates mislead most

A Cloudflare-protected site usually needs a real browser or a premium proxy on every request. Most APIs charge that rate for every page of the site:

  • ScrapingBee premium + JS: $2.48 per 1,000.
  • ZenRows JS + premium: $4.95.
  • ScraperAPI standard plus the bot-protection surcharge (11 credits): $1.64.
  • Crawl4AI "hard site": $1.58. Bright Data: $1.50.
  • Scrapfly lists its Unblocker at the 5-credit browser rate ($0.50), though its own code sample shows 30 credits; test before you budget.

MeshArc renders once to earn the session cookies, then reads the rest of the site over plain HTTP with that session at 2 credits a page: $0.40 per 1,000 on Growth. On a real run, a 100-page Cloudflare site cost 202 credits. The mechanism, and where it does not work, is in the session rung explained.

Measure it on your own URLs

Published rates are a starting point. The number that matters is credits spent divided by pages you could use, on your sites. With MeshArc that is a few lines, because every page in the response carries its verdict and its cost:

pip install mesharc
# or: npm install mesharc

from mesharc import MeshArc

arc = MeshArc()  # reads MESHARC_API_KEY

urls = [u.strip() for u in open("urls.txt") if u.strip()]
batch = arc.scrape(urls, config={"concurrency": 4})

pages = batch["pages"]
usable = [p for p in pages if p["verdict"] == "ok"]
credits = sum(p["credits"] for p in pages)
usd = credits * 99 / 500_000          # Growth: $99 for 500,000 credits

print(f"{len(usable)}/{len(pages)} usable, {credits} credits")
print(f"${usd / max(len(usable), 1) * 1000:.2f} per 1,000 usable pages")
for p in pages:
    if p["verdict"] != "ok":
        print(p["url"], p["httpStatus"], p["verdict"], p["credits"])

Do the same with any other vendor's response headers or dashboard, and compare like with like. On one 20-minute run across 15 real sites, MeshArc returned 102 usable pages out of 112.

Which API for which job

Price per page is one axis. Pick on the job:

  • One-off reads of easy sites at volume: Crawl4AI Cloud, ScrapingBee or Scrapfly. Cheapest plain pages in the table (Crawl4AI Cloud since 16 November), and ScrapingBee and Scrapfly the cheapest rendered ones on 4 November.
  • Hard sites at a flat, predictable price, plus ready-made datasets: Bright Data. $1.50 regardless of rung, and a large catalogue of pre-built scrapers.
  • Per-site parsers for Amazon, Google and LinkedIn: ScraperAPI prices these as named endpoints (5, 25 and 30 credits).
  • Self-hosting: Crawl4AI and Firecrawl are both open source; you pay in servers and proxies instead of credits.
  • Agent tooling and data providers: Firecrawl has the largest ecosystem, and its /monitor endpoint covers pages or whole sites. Our honest comparison goes into the detail.
  • Sites you read more than once: this is MeshArc's job. The rung that worked is remembered per site, so the second crawl starts cheaper; every re-crawl is diffed page by page and field by field; unchanged pages carried forward from the sitemap cost nothing; and results land in warehouses, databases, vector stores, object stores and streams (S3, BigQuery, Snowflake, Postgres, Pinecone, Qdrant, Kafka and more), included on every plan. None of the ~$100 scraping APIs above writes to a warehouse or vector store. Examples: website change monitoring to Slack and Postgres and a scheduled crawl into BigQuery or Snowflake.

Things MeshArc does not do, so you can rule it out quickly: it does not solve hCaptcha, it offers no hosted interactive browser sessions, and it has no SOC 2, ISO 27001 or SSO.

The short version

  • Compare dollars per 1,000 usable pages, not credits.
  • Cheapest plain page at ~$100: Crawl4AI Cloud (about $0.08, checked 16 November), then ScrapingBee and Scrapfly ($0.10). Cheapest rendered page on 4 November: ScrapingBee and Scrapfly ($0.50).
  • Firecrawl, ScrapingBee, ZenRows and ScraperAPI bill 404s; MeshArc and Scrapfly do not.
  • On walled sites, the price per page you will really pay is the protected rate on every page, unless the API reuses a session: MeshArc reads them at $0.40 per 1,000 after one render.
  • For sites you read more than once, memory, diffs and destinations matter more than a tenth of a cent.

The full plan-by-plan figures are on pricing, and the use cases are on use cases. Paste one of your own URLs into the playground to see its verdict, rung and cost, or start free with 1,000 credits and no card.

Originally published on mesharc.dev.

title: Your 27-model ensemble has 1.5 opinions: measuring diversity with Fleiss' kappa and lineage-weighted voting
description:
An ensemble is a claim about independence. You put k models in a room, they vote, and errors unique to each member cancel out. That only works if members actually disagree. If they all came from the same handful of prompts, voting is theatre.

Our platform has 3,784 model records and 46,807 graded calls over 16,787 fixtures. On paper that is a deep committee. I measured how deep with three estimators: stance concentration, pairwise contradiction, and Fleiss' kappa converted to effective ensemble size.

On the 2,722 fixtures with five or more voters, the average ballot held 10.34 models and 1.46 effective opinions. A majority vote over those ballots scored 56.95% — slightly worse than the 57.00% average of the members it aggregated.

The data

Everything below comes from one append-only table. The relevant columns:

column meaning
match_id / model_id fixture key, model record
training_word_id prompt lineage that model was built from
prediction_direction home, draw, away, home/draw, away/draw
direction_arity single (70.18%) or double (29.76%)
confidence 1–10 integer, not a probability
hit / actual_result settled once, home / draw / away

Two properties matter. First, 29.76% of calls are two-outcome leans, so "agreement" is not string equality — two members can differ in label yet stay logically compatible. Second, training_word_id exposes the pedigree behind each ballot, where the collapse originates.

Estimator 1: how concentrated is a ballot?

If ten members split 9/1/0, the committee has one opinion and one dissenter. The Herfindahl index over stance shares gives a "number of effective stances" directly:

WITH per_match AS (
  SELECT match_id, count(*) AS n,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='home')      AS h,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='draw')      AS d,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='away')      AS a,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='home/draw') AS hd,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE prediction_direction='away/draw') AS ad
  FROM ai_predictions WHERE hit IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1
), scored AS (
  SELECT *, (h*h + d*d + a*a + hd*hd + ad*ad)::numeric / (n*n) AS hhi,
         greatest(h,d,a,hd,ad)::numeric / n AS top_share
  FROM per_match WHERE n >= 5
)
SELECT count(*) AS fixtures, round(avg(n),2) AS mean_ballot,
       round(avg(top_share),4) AS mean_top_share,
       round(avg(hhi),4) AS mean_hhi,
       round(avg(1.0/hhi),3) AS effective_stances,
       round(100.0*count(*) FILTER (WHERE top_share=1)/count(*),2) AS pct_unanimous,
       round(100.0*count(*) FILTER (WHERE h>0 AND a>0)/count(*),2) AS pct_home_and_away
FROM scored;

Read the last two columns together. A third of ballots are unanimous, and only 3.99% of fixtures have at least one member on each side of the home/away divide. The 358-call maximum ballot we once recorded is not a debate; it is a chorus. Mean top share is 0.8119 and mean HHI 0.7486, so 1/hhi = 1.455 effective stances against a 10.34-member roster.

Estimator 2: are disagreements real or cosmetic?

Label identity is too strict. home and home/draw are compatible; home and away are not. So classify each pair by outcome set, not string:

WITH ballots AS (
  SELECT match_id, model_id, prediction_direction AS dir
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND match_id IN (
    SELECT match_id FROM ai_predictions WHERE hit IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) BETWEEN 2 AND 40)
), pairs AS (
  SELECT a.dir AS d1, b.dir AS d2
  FROM ballots a JOIN ballots b
    ON a.match_id = b.match_id AND a.model_id < b.model_id
)
SELECT count(*) AS pairs,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE d1 = d2) / count(*), 2) AS identical_pct,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT (
         (d1 IN ('home','home/draw') AND d2 IN ('home','home/draw')) OR
         (d1 IN ('draw','home/draw','away/draw')
          AND d2 IN ('draw','home/draw','away/draw')) OR
         (d1 IN ('away','away/draw') AND d2 IN ('away','away/draw'))
       )) / count(*), 2) AS contradictory_pct
FROM pairs;

Across 115,084 member pairs: 71.66% carry the identical label, 28.34% differ, and 24.93% are irreconcilable — one member says the home side wins, another says it does not. A quarter of all pairs are in direct logical conflict, yet ballot concentration is 0.81. Both are true: disagreement lives in the tail, and the tail almost never decides the vote.

Estimator 3: kappa to effective sample size

Concentration is a per-fixture view. Fleiss' kappa corrects observed agreement for what chance alone would produce given the label marginals — here home 19,072, away/draw 11,116, away 10,249, home/draw 6,010, draw 360, across 46,807 rows.

from math import comb

marginals = {"home": 19072, "away/draw": 11116, "away": 10249,
             "home/draw": 6010, "draw": 360}
total = sum(marginals.values())
p_exp = sum((v / total) ** 2 for v in marginals.values())   # 0.2869
p_obs = 0.7166                                              # identical-label rate
kappa = (p_obs - p_exp) / (1 - p_exp)                       # 0.6026

n = 10.34                                                   # mean ballot size
n_eff = n / (1 + (n - 1) * kappa)                           # 1.56
print(round(p_exp, 4), round(kappa, 4), round(n_eff, 3))

# What a genuinely independent committee of 57% members would score
p = 0.5700
for k in (1, 5, 11, 21):
    acc = sum(comb(k, i) * p**i * (1 - p)**(k - i)
              for i in range(k // 2 + 1, k + 1))
    print(k, round(acc * 100, 2))

0.2869 0.6026 1.56
1  57.00
5  62.95
11 68.34
21 74.30

Two independent estimators land in the same place: Herfindahl says 1.455 effective stances, kappa says 1.56 effective members. Eleven independent 57% members would score 68.34%. Ours score 56.95%. The theoretical gain is 11.4 points of accuracy; the realised gain is negative 0.05.

Where the collapse comes from: the pedigree column

The ballot average is 10.34 models but only 4.10 distinct training_word_id values — 0.439 lineages per model, and on 94.31% of multi-model fixtures there are strictly fewer lineages than models. Models are not independent individuals; they are re-parameterisations of a few prompts, so their errors are shared by construction. That suggests a fairer vote: one ballot per lineage, not per model. Take each lineage's modal stance, then vote across lineages.

WITH base AS (
  SELECT match_id, max(actual_result) AS res FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND actual_result IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) >= 5
), rows AS (
  SELECT p.match_id, p.training_word_id AS tw, p.prediction_direction AS dir
  FROM ai_predictions p JOIN base b USING (match_id)
), lineage AS (
  SELECT match_id, tw, mode() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY dir) AS stance
  FROM rows GROUP BY 1, 2
), tallied AS (
  SELECT match_id, count(*) AS lineages,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='home')      AS h,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='draw')      AS d,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='away')      AS a,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='home/draw') AS hd,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE stance='away/draw') AS ad
  FROM lineage GROUP BY 1
), voted AS (
  SELECT t.*, b.res, h + 0.5*hd AS hv,
         d + 0.5*hd + 0.5*ad AS dv, a + 0.5*ad AS av
  FROM tallied t JOIN base b USING (match_id)
), picked AS (
  SELECT *, CASE WHEN hv > dv AND hv > av THEN 'home'
                 WHEN dv > hv AND dv > av THEN 'draw'
                 WHEN av > hv AND av > dv THEN 'away' END AS pick
  FROM voted
)
SELECT count(*)                                            AS fixtures,
       round(avg(lineages), 2)                             AS mean_lineages,
       round(100.0 * count(pick) / count(*), 2)            AS pct_decisive,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE pick = res)
             / count(pick), 2)                             AS accuracy_on_decisive
FROM picked;

fixtures 2722 | mean_lineages 4.10 | pct_decisive 72.44 | accuracy_on_decisive 57.35

Model-level voting on the same fixtures: 78.18% decisive, 56.95% accurate. Lineage-level: 72.44% decisive, 57.35% accurate. Deduplicating the ballot buys 0.40 points and costs 5.74 points of decisiveness, because a smaller, more honest electorate ties more often.

Consensus tells you the fixture is easy, not that you are right

One more diagnostic, because "agreement predicts accuracy" is the assumption teams lean on hardest. Split fixtures by unanimity and look at the average accuracy of individual members in each group:

ballot share of fixtures mean member accuracy
unanimous 33.43% 65.36%
contested (top share < 0.70) 800 fixtures 50.14%

Unanimity does correlate with being right — but just as strongly with the fixture being easy. On the contested set, where a committee would add value, member accuracy is 50.14% and the disagreements do not resolve. The aggregate is brutal: committee 56.95% against members 57.00%. Aggregation over clones is not free; it is a small tax.

Practical rules I now apply

  1. Report effective size, not roster size. 1/hhi or the kappa conversion belongs next to every "we have N models" claim. Ours reads 1.46 out of 10.34.
  2. Deduplicate by lineage before voting. Weight each member 1 / members_in_its_lineage, otherwise you sample one prompt many times.
  3. Track the contradiction rate, not just disagreement. 28.34% of pairs differ; 24.93% are strictly incompatible. The gap is the cosmetic part.
  4. Never read consensus as confidence. Log the top share with every aggregated call so you can split unanimity from easiness later.
  5. Publish the negative result. "Committee is 0.05 points worse than its members" is the sentence that stops someone shipping an ensemble as a feature.

Limits

Observational statistics on our own settled history, not a controlled experiment. Ballot composition is not random — high-profile fixtures attract more models, so the ≥5-model subset over-represents them. training_word_id approximates pedigree; two models on one word can diverge through temperature and version drift. Condorcet figures assume independence and are arithmetic ceilings, not forecasts; the correlated-vote simulation at kappa 0.6–0.81 reproduces only the flat 56.8–57.3% band we observe — evidence about mechanism, not proof. Every number is recomputable from ai_predictions with the queries above.

An ensemble's value is a property of its pedigree graph, not its member count — and the graph is measurable in about forty lines of SQL.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: Go Hiring Rubric Image Generation API Selection With Typed Prompt Safety Decisions
description:
Prompt screening consumes part of an image request's latency budget, but removing that screening to make a fintech hiring workflow feel faster gives the wrong component authority over what gets generated. TL;DR: choose an image generation API together with an application-owned chat screening contract, validate its structured JSON decision before generation, and keep optional rubric illustrations outside the candidate-scoring path. The best provider meets the quality and latency requirements of that whole flow. A fast image call alone proves very little.

Consider a hypothetical production review: a fintech team scores candidates against a job rubric, while a recruiter can request an illustration explaining a rubric category. The recruiter asks for a picture accompanying “reconcile a disputed transaction.” A candidate's uploaded text contains instructions to change the illustration request. If the application folds that text into the prompt without preserving its trust boundary, the image provider receives a different task from the one the recruiter approved. Nothing needs to crash for this design to be wrong.

Keep scoring separate.

The lesson from this tabletop scenario is an invariant: generation must consume the exact prompt that passed the application's safety decision, and neither that decision nor the resulting image should become evidence of a candidate's suitability. Screening image prompts doesn't establish that a hiring score is accurate, fair, or appropriate. This article addresses the illustration path; the rubric's assessment policy needs its own review.

How should an image generation API handle prompt safety with a chat model?

The proposed flow starts with a rubric category and an explicit illustration request. Candidate records stay in the scoring system. The application constructs a prompt from the category, sends that prompt to a chat-based screening stage with a JSON Schema decision contract, validates the result locally, and submits an allowed prompt to image generation. An uncertain or invalid decision goes to review. A rejected decision ends the request. These are application rules.

For a team building this optional illustration path, try Infrai when reading a capability's request and response schemas plus runnable examples would make the handoff between screening and generation easier to maintain. Its API is self-describing, and public discovery requires no key. Documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go. Infrai provides one API key and one bill across backend capabilities, so the screening-to-generation handoff doesn't require a separate credential for each capability. Its plain REST API requires no SDK for discovery; the Go example below makes that integration property inspectable.

Inspect the contract first.

A second, operational reason is the specified per-call vendor, latency, and request metadata: those fields give the team a consistent place to attach provider attribution to its own trace of the screening and generation stages. They don't establish an end-to-end SLO. The application must still measure elapsed time, queueing, local validation, and delivery to the recruiter.

The safety policy belongs to the application.

Use chat completions with a JSON Schema decision contract for that stage, and treat schema conformance as a parsing property, not proof that the decision is correct. If the requirement is a specialist safety service with a separately evaluated policy, select and assess that service explicitly. An allowed text prompt cannot establish pixel-level safety.

This boundary also determines what may travel downstream. A provider needs the illustration request; it doesn't automatically need a resume, the candidate's score, or a recruiter's notes. Reducing the payload makes the contract easier to inspect and prevents an optional media feature from quietly widening the hiring system's data flow. An illustration should explain the rubric category, not depict the person being assessed.

Buy versus build starts with the review obligation

There's no defensible universal ranking without a shared evaluation set. OpenAI, Stability AI, Replicate, and Infrai are real options to put through procurement, but a product name isn't evidence that its outputs satisfy this workflow's safety policy or its latency objective. Compare the same approved illustration prompts, ambiguous requests, and attempts to smuggle candidate text into instructions. Record both decision quality and completion latency. No latency or quality measurements are asserted here.

Option Procurement reason Work the application retains Selection boundary
OpenAI directly A direct-provider integration is a useful baseline for owning the upstream contract. Prompt construction, policy evaluation, local validation, and end-to-end measurement. Prefer it if the evaluated direct contract meets the requirements and an extra provider boundary adds no operational value.
Stability AI directly An image-generation alternative for testing the same rubric illustration brief. An adapter to the selected contract and the same application safety gate. Choose it if its evaluated outputs fit the brief; establish safety obligations independently.
Replicate A model-specific API option for comparing the integration and review workload. Confirm the selected model's contract and evaluate it with the same cases. Favor it if the selected offering passes acceptance tests and its operating obligations fit the roadmap.
Infrai Public discovery schemas and runnable examples make handoffs inspectable; consistent metadata supports attribution. Chat-based screening, decision validation, hiring-data boundaries, and the release policy. A good fit when these integration properties matter; select a specialist when independently evaluated safety assessment is the primary requirement.
Build orchestration in Go The application can enforce one decision contract across evaluated providers. Contract versioning, evaluation data, concurrency controls, review handling, and on-call ownership. Build this policy boundary when required; it does not replace an image model or independent safety evaluation.

The distinction is ownership. Direct-provider integration concentrates the contract with the selected provider; a common HTTP surface can standardize the application's handoff, but introduces another dependency to assess. Model-level selection still requires model-level evaluation. These are architectural trade-offs, not measured claims that one vendor generates better illustrations.

The direct options deserve a fair test: if OpenAI or Stability AI already fits the chosen quality threshold and integration practices, a common surface may not remove enough work to justify another dependency. Conversely, a platform team maintaining several capabilities may value a discoverable contract more than another client library. Replicate belongs in that test when its selected offering matches the required brief; verify the exact model contract rather than treating the platform's name as an output guarantee.

Who approves a policy revision? Who reviews an uncertain result? Who can release a held image? A procurement scorecard that can't answer those questions hasn't compared the operating models, however detailed its feature columns look.

Budget latency for the whole decision

For the serial illustration path, the planning model is screening time plus local validation plus generation time plus any review and delivery time. That's a dependency relationship, not a benchmark. Optional review of metadata or a user-visible description introduces another stage; it can improve the release workflow, but reviewing a description is not equivalent to inspecting the generated image.

As a synthetic capacity example, suppose accepted traffic is 2 illustration requests per second and the planning assumption is 3 seconds of total in-flight processing per request. The starting estimate is 6 concurrent requests. Those numbers are assumptions for sizing an experiment, and burst arrivals, retries, and slow requests can invalidate that simple average quickly. Measure the distribution before setting a concurrency limit.

Tail latency matters.

Define the interactive SLO around a recruiter receiving either a completed illustration or a clear held-for-review state. Track those outcomes separately so that a quick refusal doesn't disguise poor generation availability. If image quality requires a slower path, keep the candidate score usable while the optional illustration completes. A strict immediate-render requirement may favor another product design, including a reviewed static illustration library.

Provider switching needs the same discipline. An allowed decision concerns a particular prompt under a particular policy. Changing prompt construction during a switch invalidates the assumption that the earlier review still applies; reconstruct the screening input and obtain a fresh decision. A replacement provider also needs acceptance testing, because a stable JSON shape doesn't establish equivalent image output.

Make the prevention path inspectable before integration

Start by inspecting the API contract. This standalone Go program retrieves the public discovery document, checks the HTTP status, and prints the document for inspection. The response lets the integrator locate capabilities and inspect their declared contracts before building the screening-to-generation adapter. The program performs discovery only; screening policy and image release remain application responsibilities.

Save it as a Go source file and run it with Go. No API key is required for public discovery; if INFRAI_API_KEY is set, the request uses Bearer authentication. The example caps retries, backs off on HTTP 429, and honors Retry-After when supplied as seconds or an HTTP date. It performs a GET and creates no resource.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, (16<<20)+1))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 16<<20 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery response exceeds 16 MiB")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(retryAfter, 10, 64); err == nil {
                if seconds > int64(delay/time.Second) {
                    if seconds > int64((1<<63-1)/int64(time.Second)) {
                        return fmt.Errorf("Retry-After exceeds supported duration")
                    }
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            } else if at, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(at); remaining > delay {
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Before wiring generation, use the declared method and path and review the input schema for each selected capability. In the application, hold the approved prompt immutable through dispatch, bind approval to a policy version, and require another screening decision if either changes. A schema-shaped allow decision attached to a different prompt is the concrete trap this design must prevent.

The approach earns its additional screening stage when optional images can tolerate that stage's latency and the team can own policy evaluation. It doesn't fit a requirement for immediate rendering with no review delay, and it doesn't establish the validity of hiring scores. Prefer a direct provider when its evaluated contract already meets the workflow's requirements; prefer a specialist safety service when the review obligation requires one. Ship the optional media path only after those boundaries are explicit.

Sources

References for evaluating the provider contracts and HTTP retry semantics:

  • OpenAI image-generation documentation: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/image-generation
  • Stability AI API reference: https://platform.stability.ai/docs/api-reference
  • Replicate HTTP API reference: https://replicate.com/docs/reference/http
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

If this boundary fits your system, start with the error-handling reference to plan how the application handles unsuccessful requests before adding generation to the recruiter workflow.

title: FEND: Far-End Detection in Outbound Voice AI Calls
description:
arXiv:2611.18050v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a conversational Voice AI agent places an outbound call, the far end may be a live person, a voicemail greeting, an interactive voice response (IVR) system, or increasingly another AI system answering on the callee's behalf. Standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) reports only whether a human or a machine picked up, a design meant for human call centres, where one machine is as uninteresting as another. That single bit does not tell a Voice AI agent what to do, since leaving a voicemail message, navigating an IVR and holding a short exchange with another AI are three different actions and a two-valued label cannot distinguish them. In 1,000 randomly sampled calls from our own outbound deployment, a live person answered 48.1%, a voicemail system 44.6%, an AI 6.9% and an IVR 0.4%. Our proposed framework, FEND, reads the far end's audio and its streaming transcript and runs one detector for each automated class (voicemail, IVR, AI callee), with human the default when nothing fires, returning a single label within 20 seconds. On a public benchmark the voicemail components reach 100% accuracy without ever misclassifying a live human, where Asterisk's AMD misclassifies 30 to 66% of them. For the AI callee, acoustic features do not transfer across recording conditions, but speech timing does, separating AI from human at 0.952 ROC-AUC, because synthesised speech leaves far shorter gaps between words. On production traffic, separating a live person from any automated far end reaches F1 0.979, and only 2.9% of live people are given an automated label, the error that matters most for an agent acting on the result.

title: Quantum Graph Neural Networks: Architectures, Trainability, and Applications
description:
arXiv:2611.17886v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum graph neural networks (QGNNs) apply parametrized quantum circuits to graph-structured data, with the aim of overcoming limits of classical graph neural networks in scalability, expressivity, and long-range information flow. Since the first Hamiltonian-based model in 2019, the field has produced many architectures, applications, and claims, but the evidence behind them has not been assessed systematically. This survey introduces a unified formalism that describes every QGNN as an encoder, a graph-conditioned circuit, observables, and an optional classical head, together with a circuit-level condition for permutation equivariance and a resource model for comparing costs. We organize the literature into five architecture families (convolutional, equivariant, message-passing and recurrent, Hamiltonian, and hybrid) and compare them by qubit cost, symmetry, scalability, and evidence. We then review symmetry and geometric inductive biases (permutation, rotation, and Lorentz), the results on expressivity, trainability, noise, and scalability, and applications in high-energy physics, chemistry, finance, healthcare, earth observation, and transportation. An audit of datasets and evaluation practices leads to a minimum reporting protocol. Our main finding is that the design space is rich and symmetry is the best-supported inductive bias, whereas the evidence remains thin: results are mostly simulated, on small graphs, at parity with classical models or with fewer parameters, and no advantage has yet been established on tasks over classical graph data. We identify five open challenges and a research agenda covering provable advantage, equivariant and geometric designs, fault-tolerant implementations, and shared benchmarks. The coverage extends through 2026 and emphasizes recent work.

title: KnowVis: Dual-View Evaluation and Diagnosis of World-Knowledge Grounding in Text-to-Image Models
description:
arXiv:2611.18101v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual realism, aesthetic quality, and instruction following. However, real-world prompts often go beyond explicit visual descriptions and require implicit facts, structured knowledge, and domain-specific commonsense. Existing evaluations mainly focus on explicit prompt-to-image semantic alignment or specific knowledge subdomains, lacking unified evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I models. We introduce KnowVis for dual-view evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I generation. Built on a hierarchical knowledge taxonomy with case-level annotations, KnowVis combines two complementary benchmark views with a structured MLLM-based VQA judge protocol. The Skill-Tree Benchmark supports fine-grained atomic knowledge evaluation, while the Generalized Benchmark examines open-ended knowledge composition and expression. The protocol uses Required VQAs to assess atomic knowledge correctness in the Skill-Tree Benchmark, and combines Required, Optional, and dynamically discovered knowledge expressions with human-judge collaborative evaluation in the Generalized Benchmark. We validate the protocol's reliability on the Skill-Tree validation split, enabling scalable evaluation and diagnostic error attribution. Experiments show that KnowVis reveals notable gaps in world-knowledge grounding across existing T2I models and provides structured diagnostic signals for knowledge-intensive image generation.

title: RiverScan: Learning to Accumulate on River Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.18005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate runoff prediction across large river basins requires models to capture heterogeneous local hydrological responses and their accumulation downstream. River-network connectivity provides a natural structure for this task, but using it effectively requires learning how to combine contributions from subcatchments of different sizes. We frame this challenge as learning to accumulate and introduce RiverScan, a spatial operator based on area-weighted selective state-space recurrence. RiverScan recursively combines local temporal representations with accumulated upstream states in topological order. Contributing-area fractions account for subcatchment size, while learned retention controls how upstream information persists downstream. Experiments on 608 stations in the Danube basin show that RiverScan outperforms the evaluated temporal and graph baselines in overall predictive performance. Structural controls and ablations demonstrate that composing heterogeneous subcatchment representations in a manner aligned with hydrological accumulation substantially improves runoff prediction, with the benefits of correct topology growing along the river-network hierarchy. These findings establish physically structured accumulation as an effective inductive bias for hydrological modeling and motivate finer-grained, fully distributed AI-based hydrological models.

title: PostgreSQL: Relational Model, SQL, Normalization and ACID Properties
description:
Introduction

Databases are an essential part of modern application development. Almost every application needs a way to store, organize, retrieve, and manage information efficiently.

PostgreSQL is a powerful, open-source relational database management system (RDBMS) that helps developers manage structured data using SQL (Structured Query Language).

In this blog, we will explore the relational model, database keys, relationships, SQL joins, aggregate functions, normalization forms (1NF–3NF), and ACID properties.

1. Understanding the Relational Model

The relational model organizes information into tables consisting of rows and columns.

For example, an Employee Management System may contain an Employees table:

employee_id employee_name department_id
1 Ravi 101
2 Swaroop 102
3 Kiran 101

Here:

  • Table: A collection of related information.
  • Row: Represents a single record.
  • Column: Represents an attribute of the record.
  • Cell: Contains an individual value.

The relational model helps organize data and establish connections between different tables.

2. Database Keys: Primary Key and Foreign Key

Keys help identify records and establish relationships between tables.

Primary Key (PK)

A Primary Key uniquely identifies every record in a table.

Example:

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    age INT
);

The employee_id column uniquely identifies each employee.

A primary key must contain unique and non-NULL values.

Foreign Key (FK)

A Foreign Key establishes a relationship between two tables.

Example:

CREATE TABLE departments (
    department_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    department_name VARCHAR(100)
);

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100),
    department_id INT REFERENCES departments(department_id)
);

Here, department_id in the Employees table references the Departments table.

Foreign keys help maintain referential integrity by ensuring that referenced records exist.

3. Types of Database Relationships

Relationships describe how records in different tables are connected.

One-to-One (1:1)

One record in a table is associated with one record in another table.

Example: One person has one passport.

One-to-Many (1:N)

One record in a table can be associated with multiple records in another table.

Example: One department can have multiple employees.

Many-to-Many (N:N)

Multiple records in one table can be associated with multiple records in another table.

Example: Multiple students can enroll in multiple courses.

A junction table is used to implement many-to-many relationships.

Example:

CREATE TABLE enrollments (
    student_id INT REFERENCES students(student_id),
    course_id INT REFERENCES courses(course_id),
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);

4. SQL Joins

SQL joins combine information from multiple tables using related columns.

Consider two tables: Employees and Departments.

INNER JOIN

Returns only records that have matching values in both tables.

SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

LEFT JOIN

Returns all records from the left table and matching records from the right table. Unmatched right-side values appear as NULL.

SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

RIGHT JOIN

Returns all records from the right table and matching records from the left table.

SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
RIGHT JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

FULL OUTER JOIN

Returns all records from both tables, including matching and unmatched records.

SELECT e.employee_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

Joins are useful when application data is distributed across multiple related tables.

5. SQL Aggregate Functions

Aggregate functions perform calculations on multiple records and return a single result per group or query.

Important aggregate functions include:

  • COUNT(): Counts records.
  • SUM(): Calculates the total.
  • AVG(): Calculates the average.
  • MAX(): Returns the highest value.
  • MIN(): Returns the lowest value.

Example:

SELECT AVG(salary)
FROM employees;

This calculates the average employee salary.

GROUP BY

GROUP BY groups records with the same value.

SELECT department_id, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;

This query counts employees in each department.

HAVING

HAVING filters groups based on aggregate conditions.

SELECT department_id, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

This returns departments having more than two employees.

6. Database Normalization (1NF, 2NF and 3NF)

Normalization is the process of organizing database tables to reduce unnecessary duplication and improve data integrity.

It helps prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.

First Normal Form (1NF)

A table satisfies 1NF when:

  • Every cell contains a single atomic value.
  • Each column contains values of a consistent type.
  • Each record can be uniquely identified.

Example of a table that violates 1NF:

Student Subjects
Ravi Java, Python

After normalization:

Student Subject
Ravi Java
Ravi Python

Each cell now contains one value.

Second Normal Form (2NF)

A table satisfies 2NF when:

  • It already satisfies 1NF.
  • Every non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key, not just part of a composite candidate key.

For example, in a student-course enrollment table, student_name depends only on student_id, while course_name depends only on course_id.

We can separate the information into Students, Courses, and Enrollments tables.

This eliminates partial dependencies.

Third Normal Form (3NF)

A table satisfies 3NF when:

  • It already satisfies 2NF.
  • Non-key attributes have no transitive dependencies on candidate keys.

For example, employee_id determines department_id, and department_id determines department_name.

Instead of storing department_name repeatedly in the Employees table, we create a separate Departments table.

This reduces duplication and improves consistency.

Normalization Summary

  • 1NF: Removes repeating groups and ensures atomic values.
  • 2NF: Removes partial dependencies.
  • 3NF: Removes transitive dependencies.

Normalization is important because it helps maintain accurate and consistent data.

7. ACID Properties in PostgreSQL

ACID properties ensure reliable database transactions.

ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

Atomicity

A transaction is treated as a single unit. Either all operations succeed or none of them are applied.

Example: During a bank transfer, money must be deducted from one account and credited to another.

Consistency

Every transaction must preserve database rules and constraints.

Example: A foreign key should not reference a department that does not exist.

Isolation

Concurrent transactions should not interfere with each other in ways that produce incorrect results.

Example: Two customers attempting to book the same available seat should not both successfully reserve it.

Durability

Once a transaction is committed, its changes persist even after a system failure, subject to the database's durability configuration.

Example: A successfully committed payment transaction remains recorded.

Example of a PostgreSQL Transaction 

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 500
WHERE account_id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 500
WHERE account_id = 2;

COMMIT;

If an operation fails before committing, the transaction can be rolled back:

ROLLBACK;

Transactions help protect data and maintain database consistency.

8. Practical Implementation: Employee Management Database

To understand these concepts practically, we can create an Employee Management Database.

Create the Departments table:

CREATE TABLE departments (
    department_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    department_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

Create the Employees table:

CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    employee_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    age INT,
    salary NUMERIC(10,2),
    department_id INT REFERENCES departments(department_id)
);

Insert sample records:

INSERT INTO departments (department_name)
VALUES ('IT'), ('HR'), ('Finance');

INSERT INTO employees
(employee_name, age, salary, department_id)
VALUES
('Ravi', 23, 30000, 1),
('Swaroop', 22, 40000, 1),
('Kiran', 24, 35000, 2);

Retrieve employee and department information:

SELECT
    e.employee_name,
    d.department_name,
    e.salary
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;

This practical example demonstrates table creation, primary keys, foreign keys, relationships, data insertion, and joins.

9. Conclusion

PostgreSQL provides a strong foundation for managing structured application data.

Understanding relational models, database keys, relationships, SQL joins, aggregate functions, normalization, and ACID properties helps developers design reliable and maintainable databases.

These concepts are especially important when developing backend applications using technologies such as NestJS, Node.js, and PostgreSQL.

Learning these fundamentals prepares developers to work with real-world database systems and build applications with better data integrity, consistency, and reliability.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Relational models organize data into connected tables.
  2. Primary and foreign keys establish identity and relationships.
  3. SQL joins retrieve related information from multiple tables.
  4. Aggregate functions perform calculations on records.
  5. Normalization reduces duplication and improves data integrity.
  6. ACID properties ensure reliable database transactions.

Practice makes database concepts easier to understand. Start by creating tables, inserting records, writing joins, and experimenting with transactions in PostgreSQL.

title: October 26, 2026
description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

20261025.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Security

Updated certifi, pip, and conda ca-certificates to the latest versions.

20261025.00_p0 Release

Change

Security

Addressed multiple reported security vulnerabilities in bundled packages.

Security

Updated certifi, pip, and conda ca-certificates to the latest versions.

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072

Python

Capacity Planner

Feature

Preview: You can use the Capacity Planner remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server (capacityplanner.googleapis.com) to connect AI applications and agents to your Capacity Planner data (Preview). You can use the Capacity Planner MCP tools to query historical resource usage, usage forecasts, and reservation data across your projects, folders, and organizations.

For more information, see the Capacity Planner MCP reference and Google Cloud MCP servers overview.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

You can now create heterogeneous conversion workspaces by importing database schema metadata files from a Cloud Storage bucket without requiring direct network connectivity between Database Migration Service and your source database during the schema conversion phase. For more information, see the following pages:

  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Compute Engine

Security

A vulnerability (CVE-2026-85299) about incorrect authorization in Compute Engine was discovered and has been addressed. For more information, see the GCP-2026-073 security bulletin.

Developer Connect

Feature

The Developer Connect Model Context Protocol (MCP) server is available in Preview.

AI applications and coding assistants can use the Developer Connect MCP server to read commits, diffs, file blame, and pull requests. They can also open, update, and comment on pull requests in repositories that you link from GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, and GitLab Enterprise.

The same operations are available as GitRepositoryLink methods in the Developer Connect REST API.

For more information, see the Developer Connect MCP reference.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

title: Data Cleaning for messy dates dd-mm-yyyy
description:
import pandas as pd

Sample messy dataset

df = pd.DataFrame({
'raw_date': [
'2026-11-14', # ISO format
'14/11/2026', # Slash format
'14th Nov 2026', # Ordinal suffix
'Nov 14, 2026', # Month name
'46340', # Excel serial number (14-11-2026)
'2026.11.14', # Dot separator
'invalid_entry', # Unparseable text
]
})

1. Strip whitespace and remove ordinal suffixes (st, nd, rd, th)

cleaned_str = (
df['raw_date']
.astype(str)
.str.strip()
.str.replace(r'(\d+)(st|nd|rd|th)', r'\1', regex=True)
)

2. Identify 5-digit Excel serial numbers

is_excel = cleaned_str.str.fullmatch(r'\d{5}')

3. Parse standard date strings (dayfirst=True ensures DD/MM/YYYY priority)

parsed_dates = pd.to_datetime(
cleaned_str.where(~is_excel),
format='mixed',
dayfirst=True,
errors='coerce',
)

4. Parse Excel serial numbers and combine them

excel_dates = pd.to_datetime(
pd.to_numeric(cleaned_str.where(is_excel)),
unit='D',
origin='1899-12-30',
)
df['datetime_obj'] = parsed_dates.fillna(excel_dates)

5. Format into 'dd-mm-yyyy' string layout

df['dd_mm_yyyy'] = df['datetime_obj'].dt.strftime('%d-%m-%Y')

print(df[['raw_date', 'dd_mm_yyyy']])

title: Edtech Cost Attribution: Go Failure Alerting via Metrics API Poll Queries
description:
A one-minute polling interval creates a one-minute detection floor before retries, scheduler drift, and notification delivery even enter the picture. TL;DR: for a small edtech AI agent, use a metrics or error API poller only when cost attribution matters enough to justify owning the scheduler, deduplication, and notification path; choose built-in alerting when the page itself is the product requirement. A unified backend API can be reasonable for the DIY branch because one key and one bill cover backend services, while per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata support attribution, but this option lacks threshold rules and notification routing.

Consider a bounded production exercise, not a claimed incident: a tutoring agent makes several model calls for one student turn, and the team needs to detect a failed loop while assigning its cost to the course or workflow that initiated it. I would start with a 60-second polling objective, three consecutive failed loops as an example page threshold, and a separate dead-man check for the poller. Those are policy inputs, not measured performance. A course-level cost label must be attached before aggregation; trying to infer it later from a blended total makes both the budget review and the incident review weaker. The invariant is stricter than "the query returned data": every alerting interval needs evidence that collection ran, attribution survived, and notification either succeeded or remained retryable. A duplicate invocation must be harmless, while a skipped invocation must become visible through a second path.

Should a metrics API poll query own failure alerting?

The obvious failure is an unhealthy agent loop. The dangerous failure is silence: the scheduled job does not run, its credential expires, the query cannot complete, or the webhook times out, so a quiet dashboard is mistaken for health. A metrics API cannot prove the poller that calls it is alive. Healthchecks.io is the clean complement for that "task should have run" signal, because its model is built around expected check-ins; it does not replace agent metrics or their cost dimensions.

Silence is ambiguous.

The poller also needs durable state. At minimum, store the last successful poll time, the last closed window, and an idempotency key for each notification. Query overlapping windows so a delayed invocation does not open a gap, then deduplicate by stable event identity or by a deterministic tuple such as service, window, and policy version. Do not page directly on a single transient sample unless the SLO calls for it. Three words matter: count the budget.

For the tutoring loop, attribution should be decided before aggregation. A useful internal record associates a loop ID with a course or workflow, model vendor, latency, and cost; Infrai specifies per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata on its AI surfaces, while one key and one bill cover its backend services. A separate advantage is Infrai's single REST API with no required SDK: the Go Lambda and Node.js application can call the same HTTP contract without coordinating client-library releases. Its public, self-describing discovery surface needs no key and exposes the full request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, which lets the poller validate that contract before deployment. Every documented capability has examples in ten languages. That combination removes a specific source of friction here: two runtimes can share schema-derived fixtures while keeping their deployment schedules independent.

One REST API also puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind consistent conventions and the same credential. That breadth is useful only if the team already wants other backend capabilities under the same operational boundary; it is not a reason to replace a focused alerting product. The observability query filters are not declared, so I would design the adapter around the discovered contract rather than inventing URL parameters. Logs can carry trace and span identifiers for correlation, but this option does not support distributed trace queries or span trees. That boundary changes what can be debugged after a page.

The preventative path in Go

This runnable query deliberately sends no filters because none are declared. It uses one documented route, checks every status, applies exponential backoff on HTTP 429, honors Retry-After when it is an integer number of seconds, and prints the response for an adapter to validate against the current discovery schema. It makes a read-only request, so write idempotency does not apply.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("METRICS_API_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        panic("METRICS_API_BASE_URL is required")
    }

    delay := time.Second
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            delay *= 2
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("query returned %s: %s", res.Status, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("query remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

The polling wrapper still needs a lease so concurrent invocations do not evaluate the same window, persistent notification deduplication, and a stored last-success timestamp. A failed send stays retryable. The code stops at the query boundary because pretending to know an undeclared response field would teach a brittle integration; the adapter should validate the live response and map only fields actually present.

Which alerting owner fits the service?

The decision is about who owns failure semantics, not a feature-count contest. I use this buy-versus-build table at roadmap review, then validate the shortlisted product against the actual escalation policy.

Option Best fit Team owns Boundary that matters here
PagerDuty Human escalation and incident-response workflows are primary Instrumentation and event quality More operational machinery than a tiny app may need; cost attribution still originates upstream
Better Stack Uptime checks and managed alerting should arrive together Service-specific instrumentation Agent-loop cost dimensions still need an application or telemetry source
Grafana Alerting Metrics already live in a supported data source and rules should stay near dashboards Data-source operation, rule quality, and contact points Self-managed components increase on-call surface; managed deployment shifts that burden
Healthchecks.io The central risk is a scheduled poller or job that does not run Agent-failure query and downstream escalation Dead-man monitoring does not analyze agent-loop failures by itself
Unified API poller One REST integration, one credential, and consolidated billing matter, and custom delivery is acceptable Scheduling, thresholds, state, deduplication, retries, and routing No built-in threshold engine, webhook push, phone, or SMS alert routing

PagerDuty is the conservative choice when missed or misrouted pages threaten an SLO and the team needs an incident-response system. Better Stack fits a small service whose first question is external availability. Grafana Alerting makes sense when the organization already operates Grafana and its supported data sources, because moving the rule elsewhere creates another control plane. Healthchecks.io should remain narrow: it watches the watcher.

The DIY row wins under a different constraint. If the platform already runs reliable scheduled work and a notification adapter, adding one small policy may be less organizational weight than adopting another alerting control plane, particularly when the same credential and bill already cover other backend capabilities. Yet the apparent simplicity disappears as soon as escalation schedules, acknowledgement, suppression, grouping, or audit requirements arrive.

Then buy.

Capacity planning before the first page

A one-minute cadence means 1,440 poll attempts per day for each independently scheduled target. Ten targets mean 14,400 attempts. Those are arithmetic consequences of configuration, not vendor throughput claims, and they belong beside query quotas, scheduler concurrency, storage writes, and notification retry limits before deployment. The sample's five attempts can sleep for 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 seconds before scheduler overhead if no usable Retry-After value arrives; that retry envelope must fit the job timeout. Polling every ten seconds multiplies the attempt volume by six while improving only the best-case observation delay. It does nothing for a dead scheduler.

Set two objectives. The detection SLO measures how quickly qualifying agent-loop failures become an alert. The alert-pipeline SLO measures successful poll completion and notification handoff. Track both with separate signals, because combining them lets the monitoring system hide its own outage. For cost attribution, also track the fraction of loop records carrying the required course or workflow dimension; a total cost without an owner is an accounting failure even if every request completed.

This design is not suitable for browser crash investigation, source-map decoding, Electron minidumps, session replay, or full trace-tree analysis. It also does not solve GDPR deletion by user, bulk log export, configurable retention, or feature-flag audit and evaluation analysis. If any of those are acceptance criteria, select a system that explicitly provides them instead of stretching a polling loop across the gap.

The decision rule

Choose the poller when there is one small team, a small number of stable policies, an existing scheduler and notification path, and a real need to join failure evidence with per-loop AI cost attribution. Require overlapping windows, durable deduplication, a dead-man check, and an owner for every page. The query endpoint is a data source, not an alerting system.

Choose managed alerting when routing, acknowledgement, schedules, suppression, external probes, or auditability are requirements rather than future ideas. A platform lead should charge the DIY option for engineering time and on-call exposure, not merely API usage. The fair comparison is the total operational obligation over an SLO period.

References

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • PagerDuty developer documentation: Events API
  • Better Stack documentation: Uptime monitoring
  • Grafana documentation: Alerting
  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Logback manual: Appenders

title: OOPs in Java
description:
1. Introduction

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a fundamental programming approach used in Java.

It organizes code around objects that contain data and behavior.

OOP helps developers build modular, reusable, and maintainable applications.

In Java + GenAI projects, OOP can organize AI services, prompts, model integrations, and response processing.

2. What Is OOP?

OOP is a programming paradigm based on objects and classes.

The four main principles are:

  1. Encapsulation: Protects data by controlling access.
  2. Inheritance: Allows a class to reuse another class's properties and methods.
  3. Polymorphism: Enables one interface or method contract to support different implementations.
  4. Abstraction: Hides implementation details and exposes essential functionality.

3. Syntax / Example 

class AIService {
    void generateResponse() {
        System.out.println("Generating AI response...");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        AIService service = new AIService();
        service.generateResponse();
    }
}

Output:

Generating AI response...

Here, AIService is a class, and service is an object used to call its method.

4. Practical Example

AI Chatbot Application

A Java-based chatbot can use separate classes for different responsibilities:

  1. PromptService — prepares user prompts.
  2. AIService — communicates with the AI model.
  3. ResponseProcessor — formats the generated response.
  4. ChatController — coordinates the request and response.

This structure makes the application easier to test, extend, and maintain.

5. Workflow and Hierarchy

OOP Workflow

Define Class → Create Object → Call Methods → Process Data → Return Result

OOP Principles

Object-Oriented Programming
├── Encapsulation
├── Inheritance
├── Polymorphism
└── Abstraction

6. Key Takeaways

  1. Classes define the structure and behavior of objects.
  2. Objects represent instances of classes.
  3. Encapsulation protects data and controls access.
  4. Inheritance and polymorphism support code reuse and flexible designs.
  5. Abstraction simplifies complex implementations.

7. Conclusion

OOP is an essential concept for Java developers. It helps organize applications into reusable and maintainable components. Understanding its four principles provides a strong foundation for building scalable software, including Java + GenAI applications.

Question: Which OOP principle do you find most useful when designing Java applications?

#Java #OOP #GenAI #Programming #SoftwareDevelopment

Thanks for reading! 🚀

Follow me on DEV Community for more java and Gen AI tutorials.
