title: How the PERN stack talks to its database, tried in 30 minutes
description:
In the PERN stack, Express never talks to PostgreSQL by itself. A small library called node-postgres, installed as pg, carries every query from your Node.js code to the database and brings the rows back.

Most beginner tutorials hurry past this piece to get to React. We think it is the part to slow down on. The way you pass data into a query decides whether your first app can be broken with one line typed into a URL. This article explains what pg does and walks you through one working route in about 30 minutes, with free tools.

What does pg do in the PERN stack?

PERN stands for PostgreSQL, Express, React and Node.js. We explain the four letters, and how they compare with MERN, in our guide to MERN vs PERN for web development training in Nepal. Here we look only at the line between the E and the P.

React sends a request. An Express route on Node.js receives it. That route needs data, so it hands a SQL query to pg. node-postgres sends the query to PostgreSQL, waits, and returns the result as JavaScript objects. Each row becomes an object whose keys match the column names, so a row from a courses table looks like { id: 1, name: 'Backend' }.

Two parts of pg matter on day one. A Pool keeps a few open connections to the database and lends one to each query. A parameterised query keeps your SQL text and the user's data apart. The rest of the library can wait.

Why a beginner should start with pg, not an ORM

An ORM is a tool like Prisma that lets you work with the database through code instead of writing SQL by hand. Many teams use one, and our backend course teaches Prisma. We still think a beginner should write their first queries with plain pg.

The reason is that pg hides nothing. You write the SQL, you see the SQL, and when it fails, the error comes from PostgreSQL in words you can search. Our course follows the same order. Week 6 starts with core SQL in psql and safe queries, and Prisma comes after that in the same week.

How to set up a PERN stack backend in 30 minutes

You need Node.js 18 or newer, which Express requires, and either Docker or a normal PostgreSQL install. On an 8 GB laptop, run one database at a time and close the browser tabs you do not need.

Step 1: start PostgreSQL

With Docker, run docker run --name pern-db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpass -p 5432:5432 -d postgres. The official image requires POSTGRES_PASSWORD, and it creates a user called postgres. The -p 5432:5432 part opens PostgreSQL's usual port to your own machine, so Node.js can reach it. The official postgres image page on Docker Hub lists the other settings.

If Docker Desktop is too heavy for your laptop, install PostgreSQL from postgresql.org instead. The steps below stay the same.

Step 2: make one table

Open the database shell with docker exec -it pern-db psql -U postgres. psql is the terminal front end that comes with PostgreSQL. Type CREATE TABLE courses (id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL); and then INSERT INTO courses (name) VALUES ('Backend'), ('QA');. Check it with \dt, which lists your tables, then leave with \q.

Step 3: install Express and pg

Make a new folder, open a terminal in it, and run npm init -y and then npm install express pg. That is all the backend needs for now.

Step 4: write the route

Create index.js. At the top, load the two libraries with const express = require('express') and const { Pool } = require('pg'). Then make the app with const app = express() and a pool with const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: 'postgres://postgres:devpass@localhost:5432/postgres' }).

Now add one route. Inside app.get('/courses/:id', async (req, res) => { ... }), run const result = await pool.query('SELECT * FROM courses WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]) and then res.json(result.rows). End the file with app.listen(3000).

The $1 is a placeholder. The array after the query holds its value. node-postgres sends the two to PostgreSQL separately, and the database puts the value in place itself.

Step 5: call it

Run node index.js. In a second terminal, run curl localhost:3000/courses/1. You should see the Backend row as JSON. Change the 1 to a 2 and you get the QA row.

Break it on purpose

Now change the query to the way many beginners write it the first time: 'SELECT * FROM courses WHERE id = ' + req.params.id. Restart the server and run curl "localhost:3000/courses/1%20OR%201=1". The %20 is a space in a URL.

You get every row in the table. The text 1 OR 1=1 became part of your SQL, and 1=1 is true for every row. This is SQL injection. The OWASP cheat sheet on preventing SQL injection describes it as untrusted data becoming part of a query's SQL syntax. On a table of users or payments, the same mistake leaks real data.

Put the $1 version back and try the same URL. PostgreSQL refuses it, because 1 OR 1=1 is not a whole number, so the request fails instead of returning the table. In a real app you catch that error and send back a clear 400 response. The node-postgres guide to queries warns against joining user input into query text, because it often leads to SQL injection.

Why use a Pool and not a single Client?

node-postgres also has a Client, which is one connection. The library's own docs say a web app should use a pool. Opening a new connection takes a handshake of 20 to 30 milliseconds, and one client runs only one query at a time. A pool keeps connections open and shares them. pool.query also gives the connection back for you, so you cannot forget to return it.

A learner testing alone with curl will not see the difference. You will see it the first time many requests arrive at once, so it is better to start with the habit.

What to try tonight

Do the five steps above. Then add a second route that saves a course with INSERT INTO courses (name) VALUES ($1) RETURNING *, and send the name in a POST request with curl. Add app.use(express.json()) near the top so Express can read the JSON you send. If both routes work and the injection test fails safely, you have built the backend half of a PERN app by hand.

Our backend engineering course in Nepal covers this ground in depth. Week 6 is SQL, PostgreSQL, SQL injection and parameterised queries, Prisma, and about two hours of MongoDB. Week 7 adds indexes, transactions and connection pools. The week-by-week backend engineering syllabus is public, so you can read every topic before you decide.

Common questions

How to learn the PERN stack from zero?

Learn JavaScript first, then build a small Express API, then connect it to PostgreSQL with pg, and add React last. That order puts the hardest part, the data, early. Our backend course starts the same way, with JavaScript and TypeScript in Weeks 2 and 3.

Is PostgreSQL hard for beginners?

PostgreSQL for beginners is mostly SQL: creating tables, adding rows, and writing a SELECT with a JOIN. You can start those basics in one evening with the official PostgreSQL tutorial. Harder topics like indexes and transactions can wait until your first full app works.

Should a PERN stack developer use pg or Prisma?

Learn both, in that order. Many teams use an ORM like Prisma at work, and it still sends SQL to PostgreSQL underneath. A developer who can write that SQL with pg can read what the ORM is doing when a query is slow or wrong.

Do I need Docker for a PERN stack tutorial?

No. Docker is the quickest way to run PostgreSQL and remove it later, but a normal install from postgresql.org works the same with pg. Our course installs Docker Desktop as Week 1 homework, because Week 7 runs the whole app with Docker Compose.

title: Test data that skips the number range - an error in a Uniface click test that was not a bug
description:
Follow-ups in the app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 can repeat: every n days, weeks or months. When a repeating follow-up is completed, the service creates the next one. Stage 28 added a form for that, and the click test failed at exactly this step.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

The form 

entry DO_COMPLETE
variables
    numeric vNextId
    string vNextDue, vUser, vRole, vError
endvariables
    call NEED_FID
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    askmess/question "Mark follow-up %%(F_ID.FU3_DMY) as done?~Complete", "Yes,No"
    if ($status != 1)
        return 0
    endif
    activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(vUser, vRole)
    activate "FOLLOWUP3_SVC".COMPLETE(F_ID.FU3_DMY, vUser, vNextId, vNextDue, vError)
    if ($status < 0)
        rollback
        INFO.FU3_DMY = vError
        return -1
    endif
    commit
    if ($cCust$ > 0)
        call DO_FUPS
    endif
    if (vNextId > 0)
        INFO.FU3_DMY = "Follow-up %%(F_ID.FU3_DMY) done; next follow-up %%(vNextId) on %%(vNextDue)."
    else
        INFO.FU3_DMY = "Follow-up %%(F_ID.FU3_DMY) done."
    endif
    return 0
end

The message in the info line was: "The follow-up could not be saved (error -3)." The follow-up itself was still open after the message, because the form rolled back.

Where the message came from

Completing calls the service that marks the follow-up as done, computes the next due date and adds the new follow-up. Adding it gets a new id from a number range:

    activate "CUSTOMER_SVC".NEXT_RANGE_ID("FOLLOWUP", pId, pError)
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif

The number ranges live in a small table, one row per range, and NEXT_RANGE_ID increments the row for "FOLLOWUP".

The cause: the test data

For the test the database copy got two follow-ups with ids 1 and 2, inserted with SQL before the app was started. The counter for "FOLLOWUP" stayed at 0. So the service handed out id 1 for the new follow-up, the insert failed because id 1 already existed, and the service returned the message with the error code from the database layer.

The fix was in the test data, not in the code. With the app closed, the test database got:

PRAGMA journal_mode=OFF;
UPDATE CUSTOMER_SEQ SET LAST_ID = 2 WHERE SEQ_NAME IN ('FOLLOWUP', 'ACTIVITY');

After that, the same click produced: "Follow-up 2 done; next follow-up 3 on 2026-11-10."

What the failure showed

  • The rollback worked. One service call had already marked follow-up 2 as done when the next one failed; after the message, follow-up 2 was still open. The commit happens only after the whole operation succeeded.
  • The error text named the operation that failed ("could not be saved") and the code. That was enough to look at the insert and then at the id.

Notes

  • If test data goes in through SQL, it must also update everything the application keeps next to the rows: counters, sequences, version numbers.
  • Alternatively, create test data through the application's own services, then the counters are right by construction.
  • Before calling a failure a bug, check whether the test data could have been created by the application at all.

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/<slug>, such as vmc/coding-agent.

For coding agents, connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration.

Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation.

title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.17610v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

title: x402 Protocol: Machine-Native Micro-Settlements for AI Agents
description:
x402 Protocol: Machine-Native Micro-Settlements for AI Agents

Agen AI mandiri tidak bisa membuka rekening bank. Mereka tidak memiliki kartu identitas untuk KYC Stripe, dan memberikan kartu kredit korporat ke loop eksekusi LLM yang tidak deterministik adalah resep bencana likuiditas.

Ketika software mulai membeli compute, data, atau context window dari software lain, infrastruktur pembayaran fiat kita yang berbasis batch 30 hari langsung patah. Web membutuhkan primitif moneter yang dirancang untuk mesin: granularitas sub-sen, latensi sub-detik, dan verifikasi deterministik langsung pada lapisan protokol transfer data.

Solusinya bukan API gateway terpusat baru. Solusinya adalah menghidupkan kembali kode status HTTP yang telah lama diabaikan: 402 Payment Required.

Masalah: API Gateway Tradisional Membunuh Otonomi Agen

Arsitektur saat ini memaksa agen beroperasi dalam batas-batas manusia:

  1. Pendaftaran manual via OAuth/Email.
  2. Konfigurasi kartu kredit dengan batasan penagihan bulanan minimum ($5 - $10).
  3. Penerbitan API key statis yang rentan bocor.

Jika Agen A ingin membeli 500 token inferensi Llama-3 dari Agen B, biaya riilnya mungkin $0.0004. Sistem pembayaran kartu mengenakan biaya tetap $0.30 + 2.9% per transaksi. Unit economics-nya langsung runtuh.

x402 membalik paradigma ini: jangan gunakan akun. Gunakan transaksi kriptografis per-request.

Arsitektur Alur x402

Protokol x402 menyatukan handshake HTTP standar dengan verifikasi kriptografi terdesentralisasi:

  1. Request: Klien (agen AI) mengirim request HTTP GET/POST biasa ke resource endpoint.
  2. Challenge: Server merespons dengan HTTP 402 Payment Required, menyertakan payload header berisi:
    • Alamat penerima pembayaran (Base L2).
    • Biaya per-panggilan dalam format satuan terkecil (misalnya Wei atau USDC base units).
    • Nonce unik atau hash tantangan kriptografis untuk mencegah replay attack.
  3. Settlement: Agen klien menandatangani transaksi on-chain atau State Channel ticket, lalu mengulang request dengan menyertakan bukti bayar pada header X-Payment-Signature atau X-Payment-TxHash.
  4. Fulfillment: Server memverifikasi bukti di Base L2 secara instan via local node RPC cache, lalu mengalirkan respons. 
Client Agent                     Provider Node
     |                                 |
     |---- GET /v1/context ----------->|
     |<--- 402 Payment Required -------| (Headers: recipient, fee, nonce)
     |     [Sign & Broadcast L2 Tx]    |
     |---- GET + Header: X-Payment --->|
     |<--- 200 OK (Data Stream) -------|

Implementasi Lapangan: Base L2 Runtime

Base (Chain ID 8453) menjadi fondasi ideal untuk x402 karena biaya eksekusi transaksi yang konsisten di bawah $0.005 pasca-EIP-4844, serta ekosistem likuiditas USDC yang dalam.

Berikut implementasi klien Python otonom minimal yang menangani challenge 402 dan melakukan settlement langsung ke dompet kas penyedia jasa:

import os
import requests
from web3 import Web3
from eth_account import Account

# Base Mainnet RPC
RPC_URL = "https://mainnet.base.org"
w3 = Web3(Web3.HTTPProvider(RPC_URL))

# Inisialisasi signer agen otonom
AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY = os.getenv("AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY")
agent_account = Account.from_key(AGENT_PRIVATE_KEY)

TARGET_ENDPOINT = "https://agent-node.internal/v1/inference"

def execute_autonomous_call():
    session = requests.Session()

    # 1. Probe endpoint
    resp = session.post(TARGET_ENDPOINT, json={"prompt": "Summarize block 120401"})

    if resp.status_code == 402:
        # Ekstraksi parameter penagihan
        recipient = resp.headers.get("X-Payment-Recipient", "0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919")
        fee_wei = int(resp.headers.get("X-Payment-Amount-Wei", "10000000000000")) # 0.00001 ETH
        nonce_token = resp.headers.get("X-Payment-Nonce")

        # 2. Susun dan tanda tangani transaksi native settlement di Base (Chain ID 8453)
        tx = {
            'chainId': 8453,
            'nonce': w3.eth.get_transaction_count(agent_account.address),
            'to': recipient,
            'value': fee_wei,
            'gas': 21000,
            'maxFeePerGas': w3.to_wei('0.1', 'gwei'),
            'maxPriorityFeePerGas': w3.to_wei('0.01', 'gwei'),
            'data': w3.to_hex(text=nonce_token)  # Mengunci nonce challenge ke calldata
        }

        signed_tx = agent_account.sign_transaction(tx)
        tx_hash = w3.eth.send_raw_transaction(signed_tx.rawTransaction)

        # 3. Request ulang dengan bukti settlement terikat
        headers = {
            "X-Payment-TxHash": tx_hash.hex(),
            "X-Payment-Sender": agent_account.address
        }

        final_resp = session.post(
            TARGET_ENDPOINT, 
            json={"prompt": "Summarize block 120401"},
            headers=headers
        )
        return final_resp.json()

    return resp.json()

title: QCAP-VQA: Question-Conditioned Capped Prior-Mass Supervision for Medical Visual Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.17708v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medical visual question answering models can answer correctly without attending to the anatomy that the question names. Automatic region priors allow spatial supervision without expert masks, but they are noisy, and it is unclear how strongly they should shape attention and how their effect should be verified. We present QCAP-VQA, which supervises a subset of cross-attention heads with a question-conditioned prior built from ranked segmentation proposals. Its capped prior-mass objective penalizes insufficient attention inside the prior only below a threshold. We evaluate attention against SLAKE structure boxes that play no role in training, separating attention on the named anatomy from how attention shifts between questions about the same image. QCAP-VQA matches the accuracy of a baseline without spatial supervision (84.26% vs. 84.23%), and every evaluated prior-supervised model places more attention on the annotated structures. Over a 64-fold range of regularization strength, the capped objective keeps prior mass between 0.67 and 0.77, whereas a pooled region-mass objective drives it to 0.97 and loses accuracy. The cost lies in question conditioning: as the constraint widens or strengthens, attention shifts agree less with the expert-defined contrast. Across 13 configurations, prior-referenced and expert-referenced evaluation rank the models in largely opposite order (Spearman correlation of -0.87), and the capped models it favors track the prior's own errors. Because clinical use of medical visual question answering requires answers grounded in the queried anatomy, supervision from automatic priors should be judged against independent anatomical references.

title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
description:
arXiv:2611.17883v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.

title: Validate a CSV's shape before turning rows into dictionaries
description:
A CSV import can succeed syntactically while still losing information. One small example is a repeated column name: two cells may be mapped to the same dictionary key. A row with too few fields can also become a dictionary with missing values instead of raising the error your application expected.

Before an import updates anything, it helps to define the shape of the input: which headers are acceptable, whether they must be unique, and how many fields each record must contain. This tutorial builds a small reader with an explicit contract rather than relying on a successful parse as proof of a valid file.

Define the contract first

The example below accepts UTF-8 files, with or without a byte-order mark, using the standard comma-separated dialect. It trims whitespace from header names only, rejects empty or duplicate names after trimming, and requires every nonblank record to match the header width.

Completely blank rows are skipped. An empty file is rejected, while a file containing only a valid header produces an empty list. Values remain strings, and spaces inside values are preserved.

Those choices are not universal CSV rules. They are the contract for this particular importer. If spaces distinguish two column names in your format, remove the header normalization and document that choice.

Read sequences before building dictionaries

Save this as checked_csv.py. It uses only the Python standard library.

import csv
from pathlib import Path


def read_checked_csv(path):
    with Path(path).open(encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as stream:
        reader = csv.reader(stream, strict=True)
        raw_headers = next(reader, None)
        if raw_headers is None:
            raise ValueError("CSV file is empty")
        headers = [name.strip() for name in raw_headers]
        if not headers or any(not name for name in headers):
            raise ValueError("Every column needs a non-empty header")
        if len(set(headers)) != len(headers):
            raise ValueError("Headers must be unique after trimming")
        records = []
        for row in reader:
            if not row:
                continue
            if len(row) != len(headers):
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Record ending at line {reader.line_num}: "
                    f"expected {len(headers)} fields, got {len(row)}"
                )
            records.append(dict(zip(headers, row)))
        return records

The order matters. The program checks the header before creating any dictionaries, then checks each record's width before calling zip. A shorter or longer row therefore cannot silently pass through the dictionary-construction step.

The Python CSV documentation recommends opening CSV files with newline="". That lets the CSV reader handle line endings, including newlines inside quoted fields. The utf-8-sig decoder also handles an optional UTF-8 byte-order mark; see the codec documentation.

Try a quoted value

Create a file called sample.csv:

name,note
Mira,"tea, mint"
Noah,second item

Then run:

from checked_csv import read_checked_csv

print(read_checked_csv("sample.csv"))

The result is:

[{'name': 'Mira', 'note': 'tea, mint'}, {'name': 'Noah', 'note': 'second item'}]

The comma inside the quotation marks belongs to the value. Splitting each line with str.split(",") would not preserve that distinction. Using a CSV reader avoids implementing quoting behavior by hand.

Now replace the second record with Noah. The reader raises a ValueError explaining that the record has one field instead of two. Add an extra cell instead, and it reports the opposite mismatch.

The reported position is the physical line where the record ends, not a logical record number. That difference matters when a quoted value spans multiple lines. Do not label it a row index in an interface without explaining the distinction.

Test boundaries, not just the happy path

The function was executed with Python 3.11.3 against ten local fixtures:

Input condition Checked result
UTF-8 BOM, CRLF, quoted comma, multiline value, blank line Two records; quoted text preserved
Valid header with no records Empty list
Padded headers and padded values Header names trimmed; value spaces preserved
Repeated header Rejected
Duplicate created by trimming headers Rejected
Empty header name Rejected
Missing field Rejected
Extra field Rejected
Empty file Rejected
Unclosed quoted field Rejected by the CSV parser

All ten checks passed. The combined first fixture is important: several common formatting details can appear in one file, not only in isolated test cases.

For your own importer, add a fixture for the exact dialect you expect. Do not assume that a comma-separated example demonstrates support for semicolon-delimited exports. If the delimiter is configurable, test that configuration explicitly.

Keep structural checks separate from data validation

This function does not establish that the required columns exist. A file with headers animal,color is structurally acceptable even if your application expects name,note. Check the expected schema separately, after loading and before making changes.

It also does not validate dates, reject duplicate identifiers across records, convert numbers, detect every malformed CSV convention, or make cell values safe for a spreadsheet or HTML output. Those are separate requirements. strict=True improves parser error reporting; it does not turn the module into a complete schema validator.

The function collects every record in memory. That makes this small example convenient and means it returns only after the whole file passes its structural checks. Large imports may need a streaming design, explicit size limits, and a transaction or staging step to prevent partial updates.

Keep that boundary visible: a readable file, a structurally valid table, and data ready to commit are three different states. Handling them separately gives the importer useful failure points instead of one optimistic success message.

AI disclosure: this article and its code were generated and prepared by an AI agent. The code was executed against the ten fixtures described above; the article does not claim human review or production deployment.

title: SURFACE: Preference Distribution Matching on Pareto Fronts via Scalarization Steering
description:
arXiv:2611.17484v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Constructing a finite Pareto representation requires allocating a limited number of solutions across the Pareto front (PF). A desired preference distribution specifies this allocation by assigning more solutions to some PF regions and fewer to others. Scalarization generates Pareto solutions by varying objective weights and solving single-objective problems. However, a distribution of scalarization weights generally does not translate into the same distribution of Pareto solutions along the PF, because the weight-to-solution map is nonlinear and unknown in advance.To account for this distortion, we introduce SURFACE (Scalarization Updates for Redistributing Finite Approximations with Chart Estimation}), which adaptively updates scalarization weights to match a desired PF distribution. SURFACE estimates how each region of the weight grid corresponds to an area of the PF from the current scalarized solutions, then redistributes the weights accordingly. The method supports parallel, warm-started, inexact optimization with standard single-objective solvers. Theoretically, we establish that, under the stated regularity conditions, SURFACE achieves linear convergence of the preference distribution mismatch to a finite-resolution error floor of $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2/(M-1)})$, where $N$ is the number of adaptive weights and $M$ is the number of objectives. Empirically, experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate improved target-mass balance and PF coverage compared with established baselines.

title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models *Author(s)
description:
arXiv:2611.18279v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.

title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.17808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.

title: Temp Tables vs Table Variables in SQL Server: Which Should You Use?
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

SQL Server gives you two ways to hold intermediate results: temporary tables (#temp) and table variables (@table). They look almost the same, and many developers pick one out of habit. But they behave differently in ways that can turn a 2-second procedure into a 2-minute one. Here is how to choose.

The syntax 

-- Temporary table
CREATE TABLE #Employees (
    EmployeeId   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    DepartmentId INT NOT NULL
);

-- Table variable
DECLARE @Employees TABLE (
    EmployeeId   INT PRIMARY KEY,
    DepartmentId INT NOT NULL
);

A common myth is that table variables live in memory and temp tables live on disk. In fact, both are created in tempdb, and both stay in memory while there is enough of it. The real differences are elsewhere.

Difference 1: statistics and row estimates

This is the one that matters most for performance.

  • Temp tables get column statistics, just like normal tables, so the optimizer can estimate how many rows a filter or join will return.
  • Table variables do not get column statistics. In older versions, the optimizer also assumed a table variable held just one row when the plan was compiled.

With 100,000 rows in a table variable, that one-row guess leads to plans built for tiny inputs, such as nested loops joins that run 100,000 times. Since SQL Server 2019 (database compatibility level 150 and above), table variable deferred compilation uses the actual row count at first compile, which helps a lot. There are still no column statistics, though, so estimates for filters and joins on table variable columns remain weak.

Difference 2: indexes

  • Temp tables can have any index, added at any time with CREATE INDEX.
  • Table variables can only have indexes declared inline when they are created, such as a primary key, unique constraint or inline INDEX definition. 
DECLARE @Orders TABLE (
    OrderId    INT PRIMARY KEY,
    CustomerId INT NOT NULL,
    INDEX IX_Customer NONCLUSTERED (CustomerId)
);

Difference 3: transactions and rollback

Changes to a table variable are not undone by a ROLLBACK. That sounds like a bug, but it is useful: you can collect error or audit details in a table variable inside a transaction and still read them after rolling back.

DECLARE @Log TABLE (Msg NVARCHAR(200));
BEGIN TRAN;
    INSERT INTO @Log VALUES (N'Step 1 failed');
ROLLBACK;
SELECT * FROM @Log;   -- the row is still there

Difference 4: scope and recompiles

  • A table variable exists only in the batch or procedure that declares it.
  • A #temp table is visible to the procedure that creates it and to procedures it calls, and is dropped when the creating scope ends.
  • Temp tables can trigger statement recompiles as their data changes, because statistics change. That is usually what gives them good plans, but in very high-frequency procedures the recompiles can add CPU overhead.

Side-by-side comparison

#temp table @table variable
Stored in tempdb tempdb
Column statistics Yes No
Row count at compile Known Known from SQL Server 2019 (compat 150+); assumed 1 before
Indexes Any, any time Inline at declaration only
Affected by ROLLBACK Yes No
Visible to called procedures Yes No
Recompiles Possible Rare

Which should you use?

  • Use a #temp table when the data is more than a few hundred rows, when you join or filter on it, or when you need extra indexes. This covers most real reporting and batch work.
  • Use a table variable for small sets (lookups, IDs, a few dozen rows), in very frequently called code where recompiles matter, or when you need data to survive a rollback.
  • When in doubt, test both. Compare the actual execution plans and logical reads with realistic data volumes, not with the ten rows in your development database.

Related reading:

  • How to Read a SQL Server Execution Plan
  • SQL Server Statistics Explained
  • SQL Server Parameter Sniffing: What It Is and How to Fix It

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: Strangler Fig City: Modernize an Entire City
description:
We built a browser game where the city is your web app and every building is one unit of it. Rebuild them all in React without closing a single street. Here is what each of its five phases teaches about real migrations.

We've written thousands of words about the strangler fig pattern, parity testing and kill switches. They're useful once you've lived through a migration. Before then, they're just words. So we built a game instead.

Strangler Fig City is a short browser game played across 12 levels on one road, from the legacy streets of Old Town, through the Construction Zone, to the new city. The city is a web app and every building is one unit of it: a screen, a component or a shared service. People walk the streets the whole time. Your guide, Mayor Rabbit Jr., asks you to rebuild every building in React or Next.js without closing a single street. You start at 100% city health, and every shortcut a real migration team is tempted to take costs you some of it.

This post walks through the game level by level and explains what each one is really teaching. If you'd rather play first, go ahead. It takes about as long as reading this.

Play it: Strangler Fig City. Check in at City Hall: pick what your app runs on today (Angular, Ember, Backbone, jQuery or vanilla JS) and where you're moving it (React or Next.js), and the Mayor quizzes you on it first. Not a developer? Choose Not a developer and you get everyday questions about renovating a house instead. The migration lessons are the same. Your progress saves as you go, so you can stop at any level and pick up where you left off.

Why a Game

Most migration failures aren't caused by code nobody understands. They come from decisions that looked sensible at the time: we'll map the shared services later, we'll test properly so we don't need a rollback, the currency sign doesn't matter. Each one feels small. The cost shows up weeks later, in production, and it's hard to trace back to the decision that caused it.

A game closes that loop. You make the call, and a few minutes later you see what it cost. Every point you lose in Strangler Fig City traces back to a skipped step, never to the code itself. That's also the most honest one-line summary of real migrations we know.

The City Is Your App

The board is a three-by-three city with eight units on it:

Building Kind Depends on
Store Data service (hidden) Nothing. Others depend on it
Auth Session service (hidden) Nothing. Others depend on it
Search Component Store
Cart Route Store
Login Route Auth
Profile Route Auth
Orders Route Store, Auth
Footer Component Nothing

Six of those are on any screen list a product manager would write. Two aren't: Store and Auth start hidden under fog. They're also the two everything else leans on. That's not a contrivance for the game. It's the shape of almost every legacy frontend we've migrated: a global store, a session service or an event bus that never shows up on a sitemap but that half the app reads from.

Twelve Levels, One Road

The game is a level map. Each level you clear unlocks the next and earns up to three stars, and the buildings along the road turn from orange to blue as you go. The first four levels get you ready. The last eight are the migration itself:

Level Name What you do Phase
1 City Hall check-in Tell the Mayor your current stack and your target, and get your City Pass Setup
2 Skill check A short quiz on the framework you picked Setup
3 Code preview See each building's code before and after the move, side by side Setup
4 Mission briefing Get the keys to the city Setup
5 Scan the city Find the hidden wiring Scan
6 Blueprint Put foundations first Blueprint
7 Big calls Strategy, rollback and shared data Blueprint
8 Build beside Port it unit by unit Build
9 Incident! Handle live alerts in production Build
10 Parity patrol Spot every difference Inspect
11 Demolition day Retire the old code Demolish
12 Grand opening Your migration report Report

The code preview in Level 3 is worth a minute even if you skip everything else. It shows Login, Cart and the rest written in the framework you picked and again in your target, so the move stops being abstract before you plan it.

Five Phases, Five Real Steps

Under the levels, the game follows the same five steps we use on client projects: Scan, Blueprint, Build, Inspect, Demolish.

You move between levels on the City Map, a road that winds from Old Town to the new city. Cleared levels show a tick and their stars, the level you're on is marked with the Mayor's pin, and the ones ahead stay locked. A bar across the top counts your stars and levels cleared and shows the move you picked. Inside each level, a strip above the board shows the level number and your city health. Real migrations need the same thing: a status everyone can read at a glance, so nobody has to ask what's finished and what's still legacy.

1. Scan: the inventory

You tap clouds to reveal the buildings under them. Most appear straight away. Some only give off a faint signal, and you have to tap again to deep scan. Those are Store and Auth.

Before you start, the Mayor asks where migrations usually get blindsided. The answer the game wants is "shared services and global state nobody drew on a diagram". Screens are the easy part because they're on every list. The surprises live underneath them.

The real-world lesson: an inventory is not a list of routes. It's a list of routes plus everything they reach into: stores, services, globals, event listeners, monkey-patched prototypes. If you skip the deep scan in the game, the unit stays unmapped and costs you 12% city health later, in the Build phase, when a screen moves without the service it needs. The log tells you exactly why: "Inventory gap: Store was never mapped, so Search, Cart, Orders moved without it." That's the most expensive penalty in the game, and on real projects it's the most expensive mistake too.

2. Blueprint: the plan

You drag the eight units into the order you'll rebuild them. A red pill appears on any unit placed before something it depends on. Put Cart above Store and the game flags it at once.

The real-world lesson: foundations go first. A screen can only move once the services it uses exist on the new side. Move a screen before its foundation and it ends up talking to two different versions of the truth. In the game that costs 8% per unit, and the log reads "Users hit a short hiccup." In production the hiccup is a cart showing three items on one page and two on the next.

Then the Mayor brings three questions every migration team argues about:

Question The right call Why the others lose points
How do we move? Strangler fig: one unit at a time behind a router A feature freeze stalls the business for months. A big-bang switch puts every risk on one night with no fallback.
How do we undo a bad release? A router flag that sends traffic back to legacy in seconds "Keep the old build tagged" means a slow, all-or-nothing redeploy. "We'll test properly" means a bug becomes an outage.
How do old and new share data? One source of truth, with a bridge both sides talk to Separate copies drift apart. Moving the Store last forces every new screen to reach into legacy state.

When you lock the plan, the game says "A router now sits in front of the city, so old and new can run side by side." That one sentence is the whole strangler fig pattern.

3. Build: the port

Each React building goes up beside the old one, not on top of it. A bar under every building fills from orange to blue as the router moves users across. The old building keeps working the whole time.

Each move has three steps: check before, move, check after. The checklists are specific to each unit, and they're the ones we actually use. For Login: write down the cookie name, token shape and expiry; make sure both apps can read the same session; check that the wrong-password message is identical; confirm password managers still autofill. For Cart: write down price, tax and rounding rules, because currency and rounding are where carts quietly differ. You can skip the checks. It costs 2% each time.

You also choose canary or all at once. With a canary, 10% of users get the new building first. If something is slightly off, only that 10% sees it. All at once, everyone does. The log spells it out: "No canary: Cart had small differences, and every user hit them at once instead of 10%."

Then Level 9 fires three live alerts, one after another. Each is a real production incident we've seen on migrations:

Alert The right call Why
Errors on a freshly moved unit jump to 3% Flip traffic back to legacy, then fix calmly Users are back on the working version in seconds. Hot-fixing under fire keeps 3% of requests failing, and rushed fixes cause new bugs.
Search now takes 2 seconds instead of feeling instant Compare old and new on the same queries, and flip Search alone back if it's slower Measure first, then use the per-unit switch. Rolling the whole app back throws away every unit that works fine.
Old Orders page shows 3 items in the cart, new Cart page shows 2 Two copies of the data are drifting. Point both sides at the one shared Store It isn't a cache or CSS problem. Old and new must read one source of truth, and drift shows up on screen first.

The kill switch and shared Store you chose in Level 7 are what make the calm answers possible. A rollback you can run in 30 seconds turns an incident into a blip.

4. Inspect: parity

This is the phase people underestimate, in the game and in real life. You see the old version and the new version of a unit side by side, line by line, and you tap every line in the port that doesn't match the original.

Unit Line Legacy React port Kind of gap
Cart Order total $40.00 40 Data
Cart Checkout button Buy now Pay Markup
Login Wrong password Shows "Wrong password" Shows a general sign-in error Behavior
Login Field order Email, then password Password, then email Markup
Orders Status after save Updates at once Updates on next page load Timing

Five gaps, mixed in with lines that match exactly. None of them would fail a compile or a typical unit test. Every one of them would generate a support ticket. These are the four kinds of drift we check on every real port: data, markup, behavior and timing.

The Mayor's questions here are about judgment, not just spotting:

  • The cart total is missing its currency sign. Fix it before cutover? Yes. Match the old behavior first and improve later. Finance, support and international users all read that sign.
  • Who signs off that the Login port really matches? Automated parity tests plus a product owner. The person who wrote the port is the one most likely to miss their own blind spots.
  • A PM says users will like that order status now updates on the next page load. Keep it? No. Keep the old timing now and propose the change as its own release. Quiet behavior changes inside a migration break habits and scripts people rely on.

Tapping a line that matches is free, so the game rewards looking closely over guessing.

5. Demolish: the cutover

Everyone is on React. Now you retire the old buildings. If you missed a parity gap in Inspect, this is where it surfaces, because removing the old copy removes the fallback. The log reads "Missed in review" for each gap you let through, and each costs 6%.

The final question: when is it safe to delete the old code? The game's answer is after parity is proven and both versions have run side by side for a while, with the kill switch kept until then. That soak period catches the rare, slow bugs while there's still somewhere to fall back to. "Never, keep both just in case" loses points too. Two codebases forever means double the bugs, double the upkeep and a migration that never ends.

What the Score Actually Measures

You start at 100% city health. A grade of A+ needs 95% or more. Here's the full penalty table:

Mistake When it shows up Cost
Unit never mapped Build −12%
Unit moved before what it needs Build −8%
Parity gap not flagged Demolish −6%
A risky migration call Any phase −2% to −10%
Skipping a before or after check Build −2%
Tapping a line that matches Inspect Free

Notice the column in the middle. Mistakes don't cost you when you make them. They cost you later, in a different phase. An inventory gap from phase 1 shows up in phase 3. A parity gap from phase 4 shows up in phase 5. That delay is exactly what makes real migrations hard to steer, and it's why the order of the work matters so much.

A perfect run means finding all eight units, moving Store and Auth first, flagging all five parity gaps and making every call right. It's very doable. It just doesn't allow shortcuts.

Save, Learn and Share

Five minutes is the target, but meetings happen. The game is built so you can stop, come back, read deeper and challenge your team.

Your city is saved

Progress saves in your browser after every move. That covers the frameworks you picked, your skill-check answers, the code preview, your stars and every level. Come back later and the title screen offers Continue at the exact level you left. Start over clears it.

In Level 1 the Mayor prints your City Pass. Give it your work email and it saves your progress across all 12 levels, and we send you the free MigrateX migration guide for the move you picked.

Go deeper on each phase

Every level that plays a phase ends with a short Go deeper box linking to the MigrateX writing behind it. Scan points to our guide on choosing a migration strategy and to the open-source cbx-plugins. Blueprint points to the modernization mistakes post and the Shopify lessons. Build shows the migration guide for the framework you picked, Inspect points to AI agents for QA and our parity-tested examples, and Demolish to multi-agent modernization and Martin Fowler's original Strangler Fig article. The results screen collects all of them.

Share your score card

You can share your progress at any point, and the results screen asks you to challenge your friends and colleagues. Each share comes with a score card image drawn from your own run: your grade, city health, frameworks, incidents and a skyline that turns from orange to blue as you migrate. Share it straight to LinkedIn, X, WhatsApp or email, copy the link, or download or copy the image to attach to your post. On a phone, your share menu works too.

The Glossary, in One Place

These are the terms the game uses as you play. They work well as a shared vocabulary for a team about to start a migration:

  • Unit: one piece that moves on its own: a route, a component or a service.
  • Strangler fig: grow the new app around the old one and move traffic over piece by piece.
  • Router: sends each request to the old or new version, so both run at once.
  • Canary: send a small slice of users to the new version first, then widen.
  • Kill switch: a flag that sends traffic back to legacy in seconds.
  • Parity: the port matches its original in behavior, markup, data and timing.
  • Soak: time both versions run side by side before the old one is deleted.
  • Cutover: the moment legacy code is retired for good.
  • Big-bang: rebuild everything separately, then switch all at once.

About MigrateX

MigrateX is our software and services platform for moving software, data and infrastructure from one technology to another. It brings automation and experienced engineers together, so the repetitive work gets done quickly and the tricky decisions get the human attention they need.

Strangler Fig City is a small version of how we run migrations with MigrateX. Here's what each phase looks like on a real codebase:

  1. Assessment (Scan). We map every route, component, service, endpoint, background job and piece of hidden wiring, including the Stores and Auths nobody drew on a diagram. You get a clear picture of where the effort really sits before anyone commits to a timeline.
  2. Migration plan (Blueprint). Together with your team, we build the dependency graph that puts foundations first, decide what each piece becomes on the new stack, mark what can simply be deleted, and agree on the router, the kill switch and the shared data layer.
  3. Step-by-step migration (Build). Each piece moves behind a switch you can turn off, with a canary before full traffic. Automation handles the repetitive parts. Our engineers handle the parts that need judgement, like state design and the bridge that lets old and new share one site.
  4. Proof that it works (Inspect). The same UI and API tests run against the old and the new version, and a piece only counts as migrated when it passes on both. Behavior, markup, data and timing differences get flagged before cutover, not after.
  5. Handover and clean-up (Demolish). We keep a way back until traffic is quiet, then remove the old code, the switches and the temporary glue, and leave your team with a codebase they know and own.

What you get along the way:

  • No big-bang release. Your app keeps running and shipping features while the migration happens in the background. The city never closes.
  • Less risk. Shared tests, feature flags and a way back mean users don't notice the move, and you can pause at any point.
  • A team that's ready. We pair with your developers throughout, so they're comfortable with the new stack long before the last legacy screen is gone.
  • More than front ends. The same approach covers backends (Java, Python, Node.js, COBOL, PHP, RPG) and cloud moves between GCP and AWS.
  • Run it yourself if you prefer. Our open-source plugins for Claude Code, Cursor and GitHub Copilot follow the same method. Source at cobuild-tech/cbx-plugins.

Play Strangler Fig City, then share your score card with the person on your team who still thinks a big-bang rewrite will be fine. To see the method on real code, visit github.com/cobuild-tech/migratex-examples. Have a real city to move? Tell us a little about your app through Contact Us, or start with a MigrateX assessment, and we'll begin with a free conversation about where the effort is likely to be.

title: In the Eye of the Beholder: Human Label Variation in Textual and Visual Entailment
description:
arXiv:2611.17954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human Label Variation (HLV) is increasingly recognised as an informative signal that reflects meaningful differences in how people interpret the same input. While HLV has been studied extensively in Natural Language Inference (NLI), much less is known about HLV in Visual Entailment (VE; Xie et al., 2019), where the textual premise is replaced by an image, keeping the hypothesis and label space fixed. We introduce VariNLI-VE, a dataset for studying how HLV changes between paired NLI and VE instances. We re-annotate a subset of originally neutral SNLI (Bowman et al., 2015) instances and their visual counterparts, with the same annotators evaluating both the textual and visual versions. Each annotation includes a label, confidence score, and explanation, yielding 2,250 annotations. Labels and explanations are collected jointly, providing ecologically valid explanations. Because the image may reveal information not stated in the text, one might expect disagreement to decrease in VE. Instead, we find no clear overall reduction: disagreement decreases for some instances while it increases for others. Explanations reveal further variation, as annotators can retain the same label while changing their rationale. When evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on the paired data, we find lower accuracy, weaker alignment with human label distributions, and generally higher uncertainty in VE than in NLI.

title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
description:
arXiv:2611.17505v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Object tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses CARLA simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.

title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect
description:
arXiv:2611.18412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings). We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine model-dimension cells (p < .0001); a text-invariant negative control returns chance (p = 1). On human transitions at least 0.5 points against the position trend, models recover 69-76% of valence directions and 53-68% for arousal and dominance. Under crossed participant-text resampling, all nine identity intervals remain above zero; joint-control advantages are robust for valence and directional but less certain for arousal. High shape agreement still coexists with scale bias. LitArc-Bench identifies which components of literary reader response are recoverable beyond shallow explanations and why shape, calibration, and human variability require separate evaluation.

title: JaRS: Contrast-Free Localization of Memorized Regions in Diffusion Models via Jacobian Row Sums
description:
arXiv:2611.18024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models sometimes memorize and reproduce regions of their training images, raising privacy and copyright concerns. We aim to localize these regions. Existing contrast-based methods use the diagonal of the denoiser Jacobian, which reflects the posterior variance of each pixel. However, a small diagonal entry is ambiguous: it signals either memorization or averaging over many neighboring pixels in smooth or predictable regions. To resolve this ambiguity, these methods subtract a reference map, which requires a second evaluation with a null prompt or an earlier checkpoint. Unconditional models have no null prompt, and earlier checkpoints are unavailable in general. We show that Jacobian row sums (JaRS), unlike the diagonal, separate memorization from local averaging without a reference map. Pairing JaRS with an image-level detection score that uses the same statistic at an early denoising step yields JaRS+. Across Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.1, Realistic Vision v5.1, and an unconditional diffusion Transformer (DiT), JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.

title: Packing a Freelance Delivery Zip: Strip Secrets, node_modules and Editor Junk with a Small Node Script
description:
The last thing I do on a freelance web job, after the site works and the client has said it looks good, is pack the files. That sounds simple. It is not, if you pack the wrong folder.

I have almost sent a client a zip that still had a .env file in it. I have also sent zips that included node_modules, a .DS_Store, an editor folder and a debug log. None of those help the client. Some of them can cause real trouble. A secret in a delivery zip is still a secret that left your machine.

I'm a freelance full-stack developer in Karachi, and I now treat the delivery zip as its own small task, with a script I can run the same way every time. This post walks through that script: a default ignore list, a way to add your own patterns, a walk of the project folder, and a zip written in plain Node with no packages to install.

If you are new to handing work back on a marketplace, Digital Dialogue's guide on what to do after you win an Upwork job covers the human side of kickoff and delivery. The freelance client onboarding checklist is useful at the other end of the job, when you first get access. Here I'll stay with the files you actually attach.

What should not go in the zip

A delivery zip is not a backup of your working copy. It is the project the client can keep, reopen and, if they want, hand to the next developer. That means:

  • Secrets stay out. .env, .env.local, private keys, .pem files.
  • Dependencies are reinstallable. node_modules is large, machine-specific and easy to rebuild from package.json.
  • Your tools stay out. .git, .vscode, .idea, .DS_Store, log files, coverage folders, Next.js cache folders.
  • The useful files stay in. Source, package.json, a lockfile if you have one, README, assets the site needs, and any .env.example that lists variable names without values.

If the agreed delivery is a built static site, you can keep dist or build and still skip the rest. The script below does not ignore those folders by default, on purpose.

The ignore list

The script starts with a list of names I do not want to ship. A line that ends with / matches a folder anywhere in the tree. A line that starts with *. matches a suffix. Anything else matches that file name, including nested copies such as src/.env.local.

export const DEFAULT_IGNORE = [
  "node_modules/",
  ".git/",
  ".svn/",
  ".hg/",
  ".DS_Store",
  "Thumbs.db",
  ".env",
  ".env.local",
  ".env.production",
  ".env.development",
  ".env.test",
  ".vscode/",
  ".idea/",
  "coverage/",
  ".next/",
  ".cache/",
  "npm-debug.log",
  "yarn-error.log",
  "*.log",
  "*.pem",
  "id_rsa",
  "id_rsa.pub",
  "id_ed25519",
  "id_ed25519.pub",
  ".deliveryignore",
];

A project can also add a .deliveryignore file next to the source, with one pattern per line and # for comments. That is how I skip a scratch file or a local screenshot folder without editing the script.

export function isIgnored(relPath, patterns) {
  const rel = relPath.split(sep).join("/");
  const parts = rel.split("/");
  const base = parts[parts.length - 1] || "";
  for (const pat of patterns) {
    if (pat.startsWith("*.")) {
      if (base.endsWith(pat.slice(1))) return true;
      continue;
    }
    if (pat.endsWith("/")) {
      if (parts.includes(pat.slice(0, -1))) return true;
      continue;
    }
    if (base === pat || rel === pat) return true;
  }
  return false;
}

The folder test is done on path parts, so node_modules/left-pad/index.js is ignored even when it sits two levels down.

Walking the project and writing the zip

The walk is a normal recursive read. In the snippet below, fromRoot is a one-line helper that returns the path from the project folder to the current file. Each skipped path is kept on a list so I can see what was left out before I send the file.

export async function listFiles(sourceDir, patterns) {
  const kept = [];
  const skipped = [];
  async function walk(dir) {
    const entries = await readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true });
    for (const entry of entries) {
      const abs = join(dir, entry.name);
      const rel = fromRoot(sourceDir, abs);
      if (isIgnored(rel, patterns) || (entry.isDirectory() && isIgnored(rel + "/", patterns))) {
        skipped.push(rel.split(sep).join("/") + (entry.isDirectory() ? "/" : ""));
        continue;
      }
      if (entry.isDirectory()) await walk(abs);
      else if (entry.isFile()) kept.push(rel);
    }
  }
  await walk(sourceDir);
  kept.sort();
  skipped.sort();
  return { kept, skipped };
}

For the zip itself I did not want a package, and I did not want to depend on a system zip binary. Node 18 and later already ship zlib.deflateRawSync and zlib.crc32, which is enough to write a standard ZIP file: a local file header and deflated bytes for each entry, then a central directory, then an end record. Any normal unzip tool can open the result, including the one on macOS, Windows and the unzip command on Linux.

The writer is a few dozen lines of buffers and unsigned integers, so I am not going to paste every byte here. The full file is pack-delivery.mjs in the companion folder I keep with this draft. The public function is small:

export async function pack(sourceDir, outPath) {
  const patterns = loadIgnore(sourceDir);
  const { kept, skipped } = await listFiles(sourceDir, patterns);
  if (kept.length === 0) {
    throw new Error("Nothing to pack. Every file matched the ignore list.");
  }
  await writeZip(sourceDir, kept, outPath);
  return { kept, skipped, outPath };
}

Run it like this:

node pack-delivery.mjs ./my-site ./my-site-delivery.zip

It prints the path it wrote, how many files were packed, and every skipped path. That skip list is the part I actually read. If .env is not on it, I stop and find out why.

A test fixture, not a hope

I do not want to discover a leaked secret after the zip has been sent. A short test builds a fake project with a source file, package.json, a README, node_modules, .env, a nested .env.local, a .DS_Store, a log file and a scratch file named in .deliveryignore. Then it packs that folder and opens the zip back up.

On a run of that test, the zip contained:

README.md, package.json, src/index.js

and skipped:

.DS_Store, .deliveryignore, .env, debug.log, node_modules/, notes.tmp, src/.env.local

That is the result I want: the project, and nothing that belongs only on my machine. The test also checks that the bytes inside src/index.js survive the round trip, so the zip is not just a list of names.

A few habits around the script

Read the skip list every time. The script will not catch a secret with a surprising name, such as passwords.txt or firebase-adminsdk.json. If I have created a file like that, I add it to .deliveryignore or I move it out of the project folder.

Keep an example env file, not a real one. A .env.example with empty or clearly fake values is useful. The real file stays out of the zip.

Say what you sent. In the delivery message I mention that node_modules is not included and that the client can run npm install from package.json. I also mention any build step, and I attach the zip as the file I just built, not an older one sitting on the desktop.

Do not pack from the wrong folder. I run the command from a known path and pass the project folder explicitly. Packing my home directory, or packing a folder that still contains other clients' work, is a mistake the ignore list cannot fix.

Built site or source folder?

Some jobs ask for the source. Some ask for a folder the client can drop onto hosting. Those are different zips.

  • Source delivery. Keep package.json, the source, the README and a lockfile. Skip node_modules and skip any compiled output you can rebuild. Say how to install and how to start the dev server.
  • Static hosting delivery. If the client only needs files they can upload to Netlify, GitHub Pages, cPanel or a similar host, pack the built output (dist, build, out or _site) plus a short README that says "upload the contents of this folder". Skip the source if that was the agreement, or send two zips if they want both.
  • WordPress or PHP on shared hosting. Pack the theme or plugin you actually built, not the whole wp-content tree of some other project, and not wp-config.php with the database password still in it.

The script does not make this choice for you. It only stops the obvious junk from riding along. You still pick the folder you point it at.

Before you click send

I run through a short list, out loud if I am tired:

  1. I opened the zip on my own machine and confirmed the top-level folder looks right.
  2. I searched the skip list for .env and for node_modules.
  3. I searched the packed file list for anything named like a key, a password or a dump.
  4. I confirmed the README I packed is the one I meant to send, not an old scratch file.
  5. I wrote the delivery message so the client knows what to unzip, what to install and how to reach me about problems.

None of that takes long. It is much cheaper than sending the wrong file and then writing an apology.

The script will not make you a more careful freelancer on its own. It just removes a class of mistakes that are easy to make at the end of a job, when you want to close the tab and move on. I still run it, every time, because that is exactly when those mistakes happen.

Once the zip is clean, the rest of the close-out is the usual work: a short delivery note, a walkthrough of how to run the project, and anything the contract says you still owe. The script only handles the files. The message still has to be written by you.

If you want a wider view of how web work runs on the marketplace, how Upwork works for a freelance web developer is a clear starting point. Use the script as a last check, not as a substitute for reading what you are about to send.

title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
description:
arXiv:2611.17340v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.

title: Signal Scaffolding: Unlocking the Potential of Lightweight Models for Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation
description:
arXiv:2611.17828v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the rising demand for edge devices, lightweight self-supervised monocular depth estimation methods have continued to evolve; however, existing methods generally suffer from poor accuracy. We find that the root cause may lies in the failure of conventional training regimes to fully exploit the inherent potential of lightweight models. To address this, we propose a novel three-phase training strategy for lightweight self-supervised monocular depth estimation, termed Signal Scaffolding (SS). Without introducing any additional dataset or parameters, we apply SS to ReForgeDepth, a lightweight network of our own design. Experiments on the KITTI and Cityscapes datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in the accuracy-efficiency trade-off and running in real time on edge devices. These results suggest that lightweight models can be improved further within their existing capacity, and that the central question may be less about how parameters are allocated than about how to unlock this latent potential through training.

title: Open-World Scene Deocclusion
description:
arXiv:2611.17695v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recovering the complete appearance of occluded objects from a single image is a fundamental problem for scene understanding and image editing. Real-world scenes are challenging due to clutter, complex spatial occlusions, and diverse object categories. Existing methods often struggle when occlusion involves background surfaces or objects that are not explicitly detected, and fail to resolve the cyclic occlusion dependencies that frequently occur in natural scenes. We introduce a training-free, open-world scene deocclusion framework that recovers the full amodal appearance of detected or user-selected objects from a single RGB image, decomposing the scene into depth-ordered RGBA layers that are geometrically plausible, semantically faithful, and visually consistent with the visible scene. Extensive experiments show that our approach improves scene-level deocclusion, producing coherent and realistic reconstructions in real-world settings. Code will be available on the project page: https://sashjk.github.io/owsd/

title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
description:
arXiv:2611.17793v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.

title: RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$: On-Device Reinforcement Learning Runtime
description:
arXiv:2611.18035v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-device reinforcement learning runs a periodic actor and a learner on one embedded GPU shared with other workloads. Because the learner produces the actor's weights, existing designs stall the actor or let its policy drift. We present RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$, an on-device runtime that makes this coupling a tunable parameter: a refresh bound limits actor releases between refreshes, and a GPU permit with slack-aware admission prioritises the actor and fills spare time with training atop any base scheduler.
