title: How to Pick Cron or Message Queue Delivery for Scheduled Cleanup
description:
Short answer: for scheduled data cleanup, use cron to run a recurring database scan until one batch can no longer finish comfortably inside its interval; add a message queue when you need bounded worker concurrency, independent retries, or isolation from slow downstream work. In either design, make the Postgres cleanup transition conditional and safe to repeat. The delivery mechanism can wake the work up, but the database must decide whether a held reservation is still eligible to expire.

For a customer-support system, the job is narrow: release reservations whose fixed hold window has ended. Don't begin with permanent deletion. Mark a row expired first, preserve enough information to audit the transition, and run physical retention as a separate policy. I've been paged for both missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, and the useful lesson is plain: a timer is not a completion guarantee, while a delivered message is not proof that the handler committed.

Start with the failure signal, not the scheduler

Define the invariant before choosing infrastructure: a reservation in held state may become expired after hold_expires_at, and repeating that attempt must not produce another business transition. That gives the operator something stronger than “cron ran at 02:00.” It gives a queryable outcome.

Track the age of the oldest overdue held reservation. Also track rows claimed, rows changed, batch duration, retry count, and the gap between hold_expires_at and expired_at. A run that reports success after changing zero rows can be healthy; a steadily growing overdue age cannot. Alert on the business lag, with the threshold tied to the support workflow's tolerance, rather than alerting merely because one trigger was late.

Duplicates deserve equal attention. A queue consumer may receive a message again after its visibility timeout, so the handler has to tolerate another delivery. Extending visibility can give long-running work more time, but it doesn't remove the need for an idempotent state change. If a handler calls a rate-limited downstream HTTP service, treat 429 Too Many Requests as backpressure and honor Retry-After when it is present; don't turn that response into a tight retry loop.

One detail changes the whole design: expiring the reservation and sending a customer notification are two separate effects. Commit the expiry in Postgres first. Represent any notification as durable follow-up work, preferably in the same transaction through an outbox record, so a process exit can't leave an untraceable gap between database commit and message publication.

Should scheduled data cleanup jobs use cron or a message queue?

Cron is the smaller operational system when a bounded query can find all overdue rows, each transition is quick, and a later run can catch anything missed by an earlier trigger. It is often the cheapest option in that situation because it reuses the database and scheduler already being operated. The catch is that a single scanning process becomes a poor fit when work duration is highly variable, downstream calls dominate runtime, or one batch needs more parallelism than the database should absorb at once.

A message queue earns its place when each reservation needs independently paced work, consumers need explicit concurrency limits, or retries must be isolated per item. It also adds moving parts: publication has to be durable, consumers need visibility-timeout discipline, poison work needs a terminal policy, and operators must watch both queue age and database lag. A queue is therefore not automatically the safer or cheaper choice. It shifts the failure boundary.

For this reservation case, the practical default is a hybrid only when scale requires it: a periodic scanner discovers eligible IDs and records outbox work, then queue workers perform bounded follow-up. The database transition remains conditional. Stick with the direct scanner when expiry is only a local row update and batches stay well within the operating window; choose queued workers when measured lag or downstream latency proves that isolation is needed.

I'm not sure where that boundary sits for your workload. Query plans, row counts, hold-window clustering, and downstream latency will resolve it; a vendor price table won't.

Make the reservation transition safe to repeat

The following Go program runs a bounded scan. It uses row locks with SKIP LOCKED, so overlapping workers can take different eligible rows, and the WHERE status = 'held' predicate makes a repeated attempt a no-op after the first commit. Set DATABASE_URL in the process environment and run it from the scheduler you already trust.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "os"
    "time"

    "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
)

const expireBatchSQL = `
WITH eligible AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM reservations
    WHERE status = 'held'
      AND hold_expires_at <= $1
    ORDER BY hold_expires_at, id
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    LIMIT $2
)
UPDATE reservations AS r
SET status = 'expired',
    expired_at = $1
FROM eligible
WHERE r.id = eligible.id
  AND r.status = 'held'
RETURNING r.id`

func expireBatch(ctx context.Context, db *pgxpool.Pool, now time.Time, limit int) (int, error) {
    rows, err := db.Query(ctx, expireBatchSQL, now, limit)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    changed := 0
    for rows.Next() {
        var reservationID string
        if err := rows.Scan(&reservationID); err != nil {
            return changed, err
        }
        changed++
    }
    return changed, rows.Err()
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    db, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()

    started := time.Now()
    changed, err := expireBatch(ctx, db, time.Now().UTC(), 500)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("reservation_expiry changed=%d duration=%s\n", changed, time.Since(started))
}

Keep the transaction short. The code does no network I/O while locks are held, and its batch limit is a guardrail rather than a throughput promise. If more than 500 rows are overdue, the next invocation can claim another batch. If the cleanup interval is too slow to drain the backlog, first confirm the query plan and index for the eligibility predicate, then increase invocation frequency or worker count carefully while watching database lock time and lag. For queued follow-up, use the same reflex in the consumer: pass a stable reservation ID, attempt a conditional transition, acknowledge only after the database commit, and treat “zero rows changed” as an already-completed delivery rather than an error. Make the outbox identifier unique so retrying the scanner does not publish an unbounded number of logical copies. Consider the ugly timing window: worker A commits the expiry, loses its lease before acknowledgement, and worker B receives the same reservation. Worker B's conditional update changes zero rows, checks that the current state is already expired, and acknowledges. No second notification is implied merely by that duplicate delivery, because notification work has its own unique outbox key. If worker A instead loses its lease before commit, its transaction ends without a committed transition and worker B can perform the update. This distinction belongs in the runbook because an operator staring at two delivery log lines needs to know whether they represent two attempts or two customer-visible effects. Exactly-once language hides that question; an observable, repeatable state transition answers it.

Attempts are not effects.

Verify deployment and keep rollback boring

Before enabling writes, run the eligibility query in read-only mode against production-shaped data. Inspect its plan, estimate the largest expiry wave, and verify that rows with a future hold_expires_at, a non-held status, or an already populated expired_at remain untouched. Then enable a small batch and compare three counts: eligible before, changed during the run, and eligible after. Re-run the same IDs. The second transition count should be zero.

Deploy with a kill switch that prevents new claims without terminating in-flight database commits. During rollout, watch oldest-overdue age and batch duration together. Falling lag with stable database latency is the desired signal. Rising lag means capacity is inadequate; rising database latency means the cleanup is competing too aggressively. Pause, reduce the batch or concurrency, and reassess the plan.

Rollback is operational, not magical. Disable new claims first. Let current transactions finish, then verify the invariant and preserve the transition log. Automatically changing expired rows back to held can reopen reservations that support agents have already replaced, so restoration should be a reviewed business action based on recorded IDs and timestamps. This is why soft expiry belongs ahead of irreversible deletion.

Test the awkward boundaries too: two workers selecting at once, a retry after commit but before acknowledgement, a reservation updated by an agent at the cutoff, and a clock value exactly equal to hold_expires_at. Use a database-controlled or explicitly passed UTC timestamp consistently. Short test. Big payoff.

Use a decision rule the on-call can explain

Choose the direct scheduled scan when the work is a local conditional update, overdue rows are efficiently discoverable, missed triggers are recovered by the next scan, and the measured batch duration has comfortable headroom. It minimizes coordination and keeps diagnosis in one place.

Choose scanner-plus-queue when per-item work varies widely, downstream rate limits require pacing, independent retries matter, or database lag cannot be controlled with short batches. It is not suitable as a substitute for idempotency, nor does it repair an unsafe publish-after-commit gap by itself. Use a transactional outbox or another atomic handoff pattern for that boundary.

The cheapest architecture is the one that meets the delivery objective with the fewest failure modes your team must operate. For stale customer-support reservations, start with the conditional Postgres scan, measure business lag, and introduce queued delivery only in response to evidence. Keep the invariant unchanged across both designs. That makes migration dull — which is exactly what an expiry runbook should aim for.

References

  • AWS, “Amazon SQS visibility timeout”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • MDN, “429 Too Many Requests”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429

Further reading

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429

title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts
description:
arXiv:2611.17735v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.

title: How to Audit Go Image Purchases Before Expiring Downloads Trigger Pages
description:
The useful page identifies the purchased original that a buyer cannot retrieve and the purchase that authorized its link. Start with a private original, a short presigned download window, and a durable purchase-to-link record. A green delivery dashboard cannot explain a missing entitlement.

Short answer: In a Node.js Express application, verify the purchase, presign the private original for a short window, record which purchase the link belongs to before returning it, and re-issue after checking entitlement when another download is needed. Keep that application contract stable when changing the provider behind the signing capability. The Go example below checks the image lookup boundary without pretending that a metadata response is a download credential.

Consider a hypothetical fintech media library that auto-tags licensed illustrations for search and sells their originals. Quality versus bandwidth is two decisions here: test whether a smaller tagging input preserves useful search detail, and fulfill a purchase with its original regardless of the derivative chosen for search. No accuracy or transfer savings are assumed.

What should an expiring download link record for a purchased original?

Use this exercise page: the original associated with purchase-1042 cannot be downloaded. That identifier is a fixture, not a customer story. The responder needs the purchase ID, original object reference, issuance ID, issuance time, and expiration time; otherwise the alert describes a symptom without identifying the access grant that needs investigation.

Ask what fired.

A page about expiry alone is suspect because expiration is intended behavior. A page about an issuance with no matching purchase record is different: support has lost the evidence needed to explain why access was granted. Work backwards from that distinction, through credential delivery and the audit commit, to the earlier signal that should have fired when the mapping could not be persisted. An aggregate success chart can remain reassuring while the purchase under investigation has no usable record.

Require the authenticated buyer to own the purchase, resolve the original on the server, and obtain a presigned URL for that private object. Persist the issuance mapping before returning the credential. If that commit fails, decline to deliver the credential and surface the failed issuance to the operator. This is an application policy; it does not assume a distributed transaction with the storage provider.

For the exercise, use a 300-second window. That is a design input, not a measured recommendation or a provider default. Choose the real window from legitimate download behavior and the sensitivity of the originals. Record a new issuance when reissuing; do not reinterpret an old audit record as an extension.

Keep originals private.

The audit mapping can reference an issuance ID without copying a live bearer URL into routine logs. Retain the purchase, object, and expiry relationship in access-controlled records after the credential expires. The access window and the support record serve different purposes.

2. Check the lookup boundary before trusting the delivery chart

Save the complete program below as main.go and execute it with the Go toolchain. Set INFRAI_API_KEY from your secret store, MEDIA_ORIGIN to the documented HTTPS API origin without a path, and IMAGE_ID to an image your application has already resolved from an authorized purchase. The origin is configuration so the example contains no vendor URL. Do not point this client at a returned presigned download URL: its bearer authorization belongs to the API request only.

This is a runnable image lookup check, not a complete Express handler or a signing implementation. It uses the verified lookup route, surfaces unsuccessful response bodies, and does not invent a presign request schema. A successful lookup is evidence about the media API boundary; it proves neither entitlement nor completed delivery.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    imageID := os.Getenv("IMAGE_ID")
    origin, err := url.Parse(os.Getenv("MEDIA_ORIGIN"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if key == "" || imageID == "" || origin.Scheme != "https" ||
        origin.Host == "" || origin.User != nil ||
        (origin.Path != "" && origin.Path != "/") ||
        origin.RawQuery != "" || origin.Fragment != "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set the key, image ID, and a trusted HTTPS API origin")
    }
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(strings.TrimRight(origin.String(), "/") +
        "/v1/image/get/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(imageID))
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 60 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry later after %d seconds", seconds)
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if at, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(at); wait > 0 {
                    if wait > time.Minute {
                        return fmt.Errorf("retry later at %s", at.Format(time.RFC3339))
                    }
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("media lookup status %d: %s",
                resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(data)))
        }
        fmt.Println("image lookup accepted; purchase and issuance checks still required")
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("lookup retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The retry budget is four attempts, with a 20s timeout per request and a 1 MiB response read limit. These are example limits, not provider guarantees. An explicit rate-limit delay longer than a minute returns control to the caller for later scheduling rather than sleeping indefinitely; a usable shorter delay is honored, and otherwise the client backs off exponentially. This example performs a read. It neither creates a link nor retries a purchase write.

Now apply the instrumentation change to the real issuance handler: distinguish lookup rejection, entitlement denial, failed audit persistence, and expected expiry. Count those decisions and attach the issuance reference to access-controlled events. Test that an audit commit failure prevents credential delivery. Also test the exact expiration boundary and a reissue by a buyer who no longer qualifies; a successful image lookup must not bypass either check.

The integration still needs its chosen signer's documented schema and durable storage. Do not turn a guessed JSON field into a production access boundary. Keep the signed URL out of the lookup client's authorization path, and let the buyer use the returned credential through the intended download flow.

For tagging, evaluate a derivative against a labeled sample before accepting lower bandwidth. Fine text or a small visual distinction in a fintech illustration might matter to search; that is a hypothesis to test, not a claimed model defect. Preserve the derivative-to-original relationship so a search hit resolves to the purchased original. MDN's format guide helps frame format selection, but it cannot establish search quality for this dataset.

3. Compare providers against the same purchase evidence

Infrai offers one key, one wallet, one bill and a single REST API with no SDK to install. Its unified API keeps the capability contract stable when swapping the vendor behind a capability, so the application code does not change with that swap. For the tagging and original-delivery workflow, the supporting advantage is a single API key across media and storage rather than separate credentials. The Go client above uses plain HTTP through the standard library. Buyer authorization and audit persistence still belong to the application; a common contract still needs provider-specific verification of the actual signed access.

The trade-off is another integration boundary to qualify. For a service that only needs to sign originals already stored in S3, direct S3 presigning is a better fit if avoiding that boundary matters more than a shared capability contract. The limitation of either choice is that signing alone cannot establish purchase ownership. A 20-second client timeout also limits each lookup attempt; it isn't a promise about end-to-end download time.

There are credible alternatives. Evaluate their access controls against the same purchase and reissuance tests instead of ranking a transformation demo as though it proves private-original fulfillment.

Option Where it merits evaluation Boundary to verify
Cloudinary A media workflow centered on image management and delivery. Check its documented private asset delivery mechanism, expiration behavior, and original-versus-derived resource selection.
imgix A workflow centered on image rendering and delivery from a source. Verify source protection and distinguish request signing from the purchase-specific expiration policy the application needs.
ImageKit A workflow combining image optimization and delivery. Evaluate its documented private-file and signed-URL configuration against the application's entitlement and reissuance rules.
Amazon S3 Originals already live in object storage and a direct presigned download meets the need. Verify effective expiry with the signing credentials, and keep purchase mapping in the application.

The first three deserve consideration where image handling is a substantial part of the application; a storage signer deserves consideration where controlled original delivery is the narrow requirement. None of these choices, by itself, records which purchase authorized a credential. Test that separately.

An existing Express handler can retain its purchase check, issuance record, and response responsibilities while delegating the provider call through an adapter. The Go check above makes one boundary observable; production acceptance needs an actual signed download test too. Refusing to conflate those two results makes the comparison less flashy and more useful to whoever receives the page.

4. Make the threshold pay for its false positives

Return to the exercise page. A broken purchase mapping is actionable at issuance time; ordinary expiry belongs in a buyer recovery flow that checks entitlement and issues a fresh link. A failed lookup needs its own diagnosis. Production paging thresholds require traffic context, and no measured incident rate is available here.

Do not page on every expired link.

The false-positive cost is responder attention: expected expirations generate noise, noise invites suppression, and suppression makes the missing audit commit harder to notice. The opposite mistake matters too, because returning a credential without its purchase mapping leaves support unable to explain that issuance. Decide which condition warrants a page by asking what the responder can repair, then review the threshold against legitimate reissues and mapping failures separately. A dashboard total that mixes them is a poor substitute for that decision.

Further reading

References for format selection and the provider-specific access boundaries discussed above:

  • MDN image file type and format guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Media/Formats/Image_types
  • Amazon S3 presigned URL documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudinary media access control documentation: https://cloudinary.com/documentation/control_access_to_media
  • imgix securing assets documentation: https://docs.imgix.com/setup/securing-assets
  • ImageKit delivery URL security documentation: https://imagekit.io/docs/media-delivery-basic-security

title: What size_of could not tell me about a protobuf optimization
description:
While investigating Temporal Rust SDK issue #1653, I measured an enum that occupied 624 bytes inline. Boxing every variant brought a mirror of it down to 16 bytes.

That was an attractive number. It was also far from enough evidence to call the change a performance improvement.

The investigation became draft PR #1781. It contains a descriptor-driven boxing experiment and a runnable allocation probe. As of November 16, 2026, it remains open and incomplete. Here is what the measurements actually establish.

The handwritten enum, UpdateMsg, carries three generated protobuf message types: Acceptance, Rejection, and Response. My initial measurements used Rust 1.95.0 on aarch64-apple-darwin:

Representation Inline bytes
Original enum mirror 624
Only Rejection boxed 352
All three variants boxed 16

These are size_of results for that compiler, target, and resolved dependencies. They are not stable Rust ABI promises.

The enum needs enough inline space for its largest variant. Boxing the 624-byte Rejection removes that large inline value, but leaves the 352-byte Response. Boxing every variant leaves pointers and the enum's discriminant.

The missing part of the 16-byte result is the pointee. With every variant boxed, an acceptance needs a 320-byte heap object, a rejection 624 bytes, and a response 352 bytes. Adding the 16-byte enum gives nominal live storage of 336, 640, or 368 bytes respectively, before allocator overhead and separately allocated contents.

A rejection can therefore occupy more nominal storage than the original 624-byte enum slot. The smaller slot may still matter in some contexts, but the allocation has not disappeared. Neither have the backing allocations of strings, vectors, and maps; size_of does not include their contents.

Next I investigated selecting boxes from protobuf descriptors instead of maintaining a field-name list. This is a different experiment from manually boxing enum variants.

An early selector considered large message-valued oneof arms. It shrank Outcome from 304 to 24 bytes but left the UpdateMsg mirror at 624. The large rejection contained ordinary singular message fields, so optimizing only oneof arms did not remove the controlling size.

The later experiment also considers ordinary fields when the enclosing message exceeds a budget. Its approximate model uses estimated field sizes, minimum estimated savings, and an enclosing-message budget. The thresholds are experimental choices, not tuned defaults or an exact Rust layout model.

In the full protos pipeline, that version reduced the unchanged UpdateMsg mirror from 624 to 328 inline bytes. That result must stay separate from the manual 624-to-352 and 624-to-16 comparisons: each changes a different representation.

The public investigation document records those distinctions and the reproduction commands.

To look beyond layout, the standalone probe generates baseline and selected types from the same real proto import closure. It checks wire equality for four populated branches and measures construction plus Any encoding separately from decoding.

In those samples, rejection and failed-response paths gained an allocation; acceptance and successful-response paths did not. The measured allocation belongs to a selected field inside the generated structure. It is not the same operation as allocating an entire 624-byte Rejection in the initial manual experiment.

Even those allocation counts do not tell me the production outcome. I do not have production branch frequencies, payload distributions, replay measurements, or peak-memory data. A synthetic frequency table can show sensitivity to assumptions; it cannot supply the missing workload.

There was another important correction to the original intuition: Core immediately serializes UpdateMsg. Its outbox contains encoded protocol messages with Any bytes. A smaller temporary enum does not establish that the resident queue becomes smaller. That would require measuring the representation the queue actually holds.

Compatibility also remains work. Boxing changes generated Rust field types, which changes construction and conversion code. Focused checks and sample round trips passed, but the recorded all-feature lint attempt still had 45 Core type/conversion errors. Full workspace, server integration, and cross-platform validation remain incomplete.

The probe README also distinguishes its generation settings from the full SDK pipeline. A passing standalone experiment cannot substitute for those unfinished checks.

I can report a smaller inline representation and sample-specific allocation costs. I cannot yet report a runtime win. The next decision is about which generated API changes are acceptable and which real workload to measure—not how prominently to display the 16-byte number.

title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.18397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

title: How I handle ~1M requests a day on 1 vCPU and 2GB RAM (and keep bots out without user accounts)
description:
I run a Tempgbox : free temporary email service on one vCPU and 2GB of RAM. Django, PostgreSQL, Redis, Celery. It serves around a 1 million+ requests a day. Still i notice that backend use only 500 Mb ram and 1.5 GB ram free.

Four changes made the biggest difference for such a small server.

Cloudflare in front. I put Cloudflare in front of everything as a proxy. Most requests are for frontend pages, and Cloudflare caches those, so they never reach my server. That alone took a lot of load off it.

DRF to Django Ninja. I migrated the API from Django REST Framework to Django Ninja, which has built-in async support. I’m still learning how much that gives me, but it was the right direction for an API that does a lot of waiting.

Cleaning up guest users. Most of my users are guests, so guest accounts pile up fast. Now I delete a guest user as soon as their token expires. The database stays small, and I stopped paying to store people who were gone anyway.

Redis, with regular cleanup. I use Redis for short-lived data, and I clean it up on a schedule instead of letting it grow. With only 2GB of RAM, Redis can quietly eat memory that the rest of the stack needs, so I treat it like a cache that must stay small, not a place to dump things.

I’m curious what other people with tiny servers did first. Caching, cleanup, or something else?

title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
description:
arXiv:2611.17539v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

title: Vercel Security Review no longer requires a linked Vercel project
description:
You can now scan code changes for vulnerabilities with Vercel Security Review in GitHub repositories that have not yet been linked to a Vercel project.

By default, Security Review covers all unlinked repositories the Vercel GitHub App can access in a connected GitHub account. You can limit coverage to selected connected accounts or individual repositories in Agent settings. Once enabled, each push to a covered repository automatically triggers a review of its code changes.

Security Review checks commits directly in repositories with Security Review enabled, without requiring a Vercel project or deployment. When a push creates a deployment for a linked project with Security Review enabled, the review uses the additional project and deployment context.

Connect the account in your team’s Git settings, then enable Security Review in Vercel Agent settings.

title: Small Open-Weight Language Models for Crowd Decision-Making: Capabilities and Limits of Output-Level Fusion and Linguistic Aggregation
description:
arXiv:2611.17589v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Small open-weight language models can run crowd decision-making (CDM) on an institution's own infrastructure, which keeps the checkpoint, the inference settings and the opinions under its control. Their judgements vary across repeated queries; whether repeating and aggregating them, often through the 2-tuple linguistic representation, settles the decision rather than the labels is untested. Five open-weight models of 8-36B total parameters on one consumer GPU and a hosted reference classify 474 TripAdvisor reviews of four London restaurants ten times each; three open-weight models repeat the protocol on 600 reviews of twelve Madrid restaurants. Continuous evaluations preserve resolution: snapping each review leaves 5 distinct values against 21-65, and snapping at every level at most two collective values. Sensitivity to the participants persists once run-to-run variability is reduced: in London, redrawing the reviewers keeps the winner on 47-81% of replicas against 86-100% for redrawing the runs. With simultaneous intervals over every pair of alternatives under crowd resampling, no system on either corpus names a single winner: in London every system keeps all four restaurants as candidates, and in Madrid the candidate sets hold five to eight of the twelve. Extra runs and output-level fusion stabilize the winner but do not remove that sensitivity, and the fusion does not beat its best member. The three larger open-weight models name the hosted reference's London winner and at least match its per-review correlation with the reviewers' stars, so small open-weight models can support local CDM, reported as candidate sets with margins rather than forced rankings.

title: Building Northstar Files: an experimental Rust file manager for Windows
description:
Why build another file manager?

Northstar Files is an early attempt to combine familiar folder browsing with a few storage and organization tools that usually send you to separate apps. It is a Windows desktop app written in Rust, with an egui interface. Version 0.1.0 is experimental; this is a request for useful criticism, not a claim that the app is ready to replace Explorer.

What is in the current build

The app has tabs and an optional dual pane for moving between two locations. For organizing a disk, it can scan folder sizes, find duplicate files by content hash, and compare directory contents. Search filters can be saved; there is also local text search, a batch-rename preview, and Rhai action scripts. The uninstaller view launches the uninstall command registered by each installed application.

That last feature has a limitation worth being clear about: launching an app’s registered uninstaller does not prove that every leftover file or registry entry was removed. Large transfer queue controls, universal previews, NTFS permission editing, and file version history are not implemented.

A small Rust workspace

The source is split into a desktop app and a file-engine crate. Directory listing uses Tokio’s asynchronous filesystem APIs. Recursive scans use walkdir; duplicate detection hashes file contents with BLAKE3. The UI runs longer scans on blocking worker tasks so those jobs do not run directly on the immediate-mode UI thread. The Windows installer is built with Inno Setup.

The code is MIT-licensed and available on GitHub. I’d like the project to stay approachable for ordinary users while keeping the core easy for developers to inspect and extend.

Please test carefully

This is an experimental first release and may contain bugs or unfinished behavior. Back up important files before trying file operations. The Windows executables are unsigned, so SmartScreen may show a warning.

  • Source: https://github.com/D4nix1/Northstar-Files
  • Website and downloads: https://d4nix1.github.io/Northstar-Files/
  • Report bugs or suggest features: https://github.com/D4nix1/Northstar-Files/issues

If you try it, please share your Windows version, steps to reproduce, what you expected, and what happened. I’m especially interested in usability feedback from both new and advanced file-manager users. Please remove personal information from screenshots and logs.

AI disclosure: AI tools assisted with parts of the code, documentation, and artwork.

title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
description:
arXiv:2611.17583v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs.
  In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better.
  These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

title: TechInventory: cómo comprobar la recuperación de CouchDB con Docker, GitHub Actions y Azure
description:
Autor: Gabriela Estefania Cohaila Alvarado

El problema: conservar datos no demuestra que podamos recuperarlos

En la primera etapa de TechInventory usamos un volumen de Docker para que el inventario sobreviviera al reemplazo de contenedores. Esa persistencia depende del almacenamiento original: si desaparece la máquina o el volumen, también podemos perder la información.

Por eso esta continuación incorpora un respaldo físico cifrado y un ensayo de restauración. El criterio de aceptación es concreto: recuperar en otro volumen y comprobar que los documentos, sus revisiones y los permisos coincidan.

Los recursos públicos de esta construcción son:

  • Repositorio de la aplicación.
  • Script de respaldo y recuperación.
  • Prueba automatizada de recuperación exitosa.
  • Aprovisionamiento y despliegue automatizado en Azure.
  • Resultados de la demostración en Azure.
  • Video público de la construcción, con narración femenina en español y duración aproximada de 3:03.

Una decisión adecuada para nuestro alcance

El laboratorio utiliza un nodo de CouchDB y pocos datos sintéticos. Elegimos una copia física en frío: pausamos las escrituras de Express, obtenemos una referencia del contenido y detenemos CouchDB antes de copiar su volumen y configuración.

La documentación de CouchDB permite respaldar los archivos de base y recomienda conservar la configuración necesaria para restaurar el servicio. También admite replicación; sin embargo, una réplica que recibe eliminaciones o cambios equivocados no reemplaza por sí sola una copia anterior conservada.

Nuestra pausa es una decisión de simplicidad para el laboratorio. No significa que CouchDB obligue siempre a detener la base para respaldarla, ni demuestra alta disponibilidad. Para un servicio continuo habría que evaluar la consistencia, el tiempo permitido de interrupción y el mecanismo de captura apropiado.

Del volumen a un archivo protegido

El script backup.sh exige un archivo externo con la contraseña de cifrado y utiliza flock para impedir dos respaldos simultáneos. Luego conserva los datos físicos de CouchDB, su directorio etc y las variables necesarias para reconstruir la aplicación.

Después de la captura reinicia los servicios originales. El cifrado, la transferencia y el ensayo se realizan fuera de esa pausa. El paquete se cifra con GnuPG usando AES-256; la suma SHA-256 se calcula sobre el archivo cifrado.

Estas medidas cumplen funciones diferentes. El cifrado protege la confidencialidad del paquete, que contiene configuración sensible. La suma permite detectar cambios frente a una referencia confiable. Una suma pública que puede ser reemplazada junto con su archivo no prueba quién creó el respaldo.

El destino externo es un contenedor privado de Azure Blob Storage, separado del disco de la VM. La transferencia utiliza HTTPS y una autorización SAS temporal. La clave de cifrado debe conservarse por separado: ni el repositorio público ni el mismo almacenamiento de las copias deben ser su única ubicación.

La restauración como prueba automática

El ensayo comprueba primero el SHA-256, descifra el paquete y extrae su contenido nuevamente. Esto evita aprobar una restauración usando por accidente los archivos temporales originales en lugar del respaldo cifrado.

Después crea un proyecto Compose independiente con su propia red y volumen. Arranca CouchDB con la misma imagen de la captura y recupera allí los archivos. La instancia restaurada no publica puertos ni sobrescribe el volumen original.

La comparación incluye:

  • Cantidad de documentos.
  • Identificadores y revisiones de los equipos.
  • Hash del contenido de los documentos.
  • Hash del objeto de permisos _security.

Si los resultados difieren, el comando falla. El ensayo no se limita a comprobar que un contenedor esté encendido.

Integración en GitHub Actions

El workflow backup-drill.yml levanta una instancia real de CouchDB, construye la aplicación y agrega un equipo sintético. Genera una clave efímera y ejecuta el proceso de respaldo y restauración. Se dispara ante cambios pertinentes en main y también admite ejecución manual.

La ejecución pública del 16 de noviembre de 2026 terminó con PASS, coincidencia de documentos y revisiones, coincidencia de permisos y restauración aislada. Registró dos segundos para el tramo de recuperación del pequeño conjunto de prueba.

Este dato no es un RTO de producción: no incluye recuperar toda una infraestructura, descargar desde el almacenamiento remoto ni comprobar todos los accesos de usuarios. Las evidencias del workflow tienen retención limitada; el código permanece en el repositorio.

Qué se comprobó en la nube pública

La demostración se desplegó automáticamente en una VM Ubuntu de Azure for Students mediante Azure CLI y Docker Compose, con Caddy para HTTPS. La API respondió correctamente e identificó Apache CouchDB como base de datos.

La recuperación aislada en Azure comparó tres documentos y terminó con PASS. El tramo medido tardó seis segundos. Azure Blob Storage recibió el archivo cifrado de 24 897 bytes y su suma de 108 bytes. Ambos se descargaron a Cloud Shell y la suma devolvió OK.

Es necesario distinguir las dos comprobaciones: el ensayo completo restauró el archivo cifrado local; la descarga de Blob se validó por SHA-256 por separado. No afirmamos haber ejecutado un segundo ensayo completo desde esa descarga.

Los resultados también registran acceso público de blobs deshabilitado, HTTPS obligatorio y TLS 1.2 mínimo. La infraestructura fue temporal y se retiró tras conservar las evidencias para controlar los créditos académicos.

Frecuencia y retención: objetivos de operación

Para una operación continua proponemos copias diarias y previas a cambios relevantes, siete copias diarias y cuatro semanales, con pruebas periódicas desde el almacenamiento externo. Esa política es una propuesta: el laboratorio no demuestra semanas de ejecución ni un respaldo productivo diario ya programado.

Con una copia diaria válida, el objetivo de RPO sería aproximadamente 24 horas; depende de que el proceso se ejecute y su copia sea recuperable. El RTO debe medirse con datos y condiciones representativos. También harían falta alertas, custodia de claves y pruebas de acceso posteriores a la recuperación.

La construcción tampoco demuestra una estrategia 3-2-1 completa: no contamos con una tercera copia independiente verificada. El resultado útil de esta etapa es un mecanismo reproducible que exige evidencia de recuperación antes de considerar exitoso el respaldo.

Referencias

  • Apache CouchDB: Backing up CouchDB.
  • Microsoft Learn: autorización de Azure Storage mediante SAS.
  • TechInventory: implementación y evidencias públicas.

title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination
description:
arXiv:2611.17933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.

title: eBPF Ring Buffer Backpressure in Go Services: Kernel-to-User Data Loss, Perf Event Semantics, and the Sampling Tradeoff
description:
eBPF Ring Buffer Backpressure in Go Services: Kernel-to-User Data Loss, Perf Event Semantics, and the Sampling Tradeoff

eBPF-based observability tooling—network tracing, syscall auditing, latency histograms—sits inside production Go services today not as a curiosity but as a load-bearing instrumentation layer. The appeal is real: zero application recompilation, nanosecond-accurate timestamps, kernel-side aggregation. The failure mode is subtle and almost never surfaced in vendor documentation: the ring buffer fills, the kernel drops events silently, and your dashboards look completely healthy while you are blind to entire request classes.

This article walks through the mechanics of that failure, compares the two primary kernel-to-user transport mechanisms, and proposes a concrete adaptive sampling strategy implementable in a Go consumer.

Two Transports, Two Failure Modes

Perf Event Array (BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERF_EVENT_ARRAY)

The older mechanism. Each CPU core writes to its own per-CPU ring buffer via bpf_perf_event_output. The Go side—typically cilium/ebpf or libbpf-go—opens an epoll file descriptor per CPU and drains records in a polling loop.

The critical property: when the per-CPU buffer is full, the kernel drops the event and increments a lost-samples counter accessible only by reading the perf event header's PERF_RECORD_LOST records inline with data records. If your consumer loop is not reading that header type explicitly, you never see the loss count. The buffer is sized at map creation time in pages (must be a power of two). Default tooling often uses 8–64 pages (32–256 KB per CPU). On a 32-core host tracing every syscall, that fills in under a millisecond under load.

Ring Buffer (BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF)

Introduced in kernel 5.8. A single shared ring buffer across all CPUs, avoiding the per-CPU fragmentation problem. The eBPF program reserves space atomically with bpf_ringbuf_reserve, writes, then commits. If reservation fails (buffer full), your eBPF program receives a NULL pointer—and must explicitly handle that path or silently skip the event.

The Go consumer uses a single file descriptor with epoll. Reads are lock-free via a pair of producer/consumer position counters in a shared memory region. Throughput is higher and memory utilization is better, but the single buffer means a slow Go consumer blocks all CPU cores from committing new records, not just one.

The failure modes differ:

  • Perf array: per-CPU isolation means one hot core hurts only its own queue, but loss counters are buried in stream.
  • Ring buffer: global contention, but the fd-based notification model makes watermark-driven wakeup straightforward.

Where Go Consumer Latency Causes Drops

A Go eBPF consumer is structurally a tight loop:

rd, err := ringbuf.NewReader(objs.Events)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
defer rd.Close()

for {
    record, err := rd.Read()
    if errors.Is(err, ringbuf.ErrClosed) {
        return
    }
    if err != nil {
        continue
    }
    processEvent(record.RawSample)
}

processEvent is where latency accumulates. If it does anything synchronous—a MongoDB write, a JSON marshal with allocation, a channel send to a blocked goroutine—the Read call is delayed. During that delay, the kernel continues writing. When the buffer reaches capacity, bpf_ringbuf_reserve returns NULL in your eBPF C program and the event is dropped. The kernel does expose a lost counter in the ring buffer's metadata page, but cilium/ebpf's Reader does not surface it directly; you must memory-map the consumer page yourself and read offset 24 bytes in (the lost u64 field).

The runtime scheduler compounds this. A goroutine blocked on a channel send while another goroutine holds the P can delay the consumer loop by an entire scheduler quantum (~10ms in the worst case with a saturated GOMAXPROCS). Unlike a C consumer that owns its thread, a Go consumer is subject to preemption. Pinning the consumer goroutine to an OS thread with runtime.LockOSThread() reduces jitter but does not eliminate GC stop-the-world pauses.

Adaptive Sampling: The Correct Mitigation

Buffer resizing is the blunt instrument. Doubling the ring buffer from 64 pages to 512 pages absorbs spikes but adds 1.75 MB of locked kernel memory per buffer instance and does not help if the consumer is structurally slow. The better approach is kernel-side adaptive sampling driven by a feedback signal from the user-space consumer.

The architecture:

  1. A BPF map of type BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY holds a single u32 sample_rate. The eBPF program reads it on each event and emits only when bpf_get_prandom_u32() % sample_rate == 0.
  2. The Go consumer tracks the fill ratio of the ring buffer by reading the producer and consumer position counters from the mmap'd metadata page.
  3. A control goroutine adjusts sample_rate up (more dropping) when fill ratio crosses a high-water mark, and down (more recording) when it drops below a low-water mark. 
type SamplingController struct {
    sampleRateMap *ebpf.Map
    metaPage      []byte // mmap of ring buffer consumer page
    mu            sync.Mutex
    current       uint32
}

func (sc *SamplingController) Adjust() {
    prod := atomic.LoadUint64((*uint64)(unsafe.Pointer(&sc.metaPage[0])))
    cons := atomic.LoadUint64((*uint64)(unsafe.Pointer(&sc.metaPage[8])))
    // ring size is known at construction; derive fill ratio
    inflight := prod - cons
    ratio := float64(inflight) / float64(sc.ringSize)

    sc.mu.Lock()
    defer sc.mu.Unlock()
    switch {
    case ratio > 0.75 && sc.current < 64:
        sc.current = min(sc.current*2, 64)
    case ratio < 0.25 && sc.current > 1:
        sc.current = max(sc.current/2, 1)
    }
    val := sc.current
    _ = sc.sampleRateMap.Put(uint32(0), val)
}

Run Adjust on a 500ms ticker. The convergence is coarse but sufficient: a sudden 10× traffic spike raises sample_rate to 8 within 1.5 seconds (three ticks), dropping 87.5% of events, which is far preferable to dropping 100% while the buffer saturates and losing the lost-count signal itself.

Operational Consequences

Sampling breaks rate-based alerting. If you emit events for every inbound request and drive a Prometheus counter from the Go consumer, sampling invalidates the counter without correction. The fix: maintain a total_events_seen counter in the eBPF program (a per-CPU array, summed in user space) and expose it alongside total_events_emitted. Compute effective sample rate as their ratio and apply it as a multiplier in your recording rules.

The lost counter is not a replacement for structured drop attribution. The ring buffer's metadata-page lost count tells you how many reservations failed but not which event types were dropped. Under mixed workload tracing—syscalls, network events, uprobe hits—you cannot diagnose which probe is the hot path from the aggregate. Instrument per-probe drop counters in a second BPF map keyed by probe ID.

Memory-mapping the metadata page is not documented in cilium/ebpf as a stable API. The page layout matches kernel bpf_ringbuf internals. Pin a kernel version test in CI that validates the offsets have not shifted. Alternatively, use BPF_OBJ_GET_INFO_BY_FD to retrieve ring_buffer_max_entries and correlate with the fd's seek position—noisier but kernel-API-stable.

Decision Framework

Choose your transport and mitigation path based on these axes:

Condition Recommendation
Kernel < 5.8 Perf event array; read LOST records explicitly
Single hot CPU core (e.g., network RX softirq affinity) Perf array preferred; ring buffer will serialize all cores
Mixed multi-probe workload, kernel ≥ 5.8 Ring buffer; lower total memory, single wakeup fd
Go consumer does synchronous I/O in hot path Decouple: channel → worker pool; never block Read loop
Consumer latency p99 > 5ms Add adaptive sampling controller; do not just enlarge buffer
Need event-type-level drop attribution Per-probe drop counter map; aggregate in user space
Rate-based alerting downstream Emit total-seen counter from eBPF; apply ratio correction in Prometheus rules

The ring buffer is the right default for Go services on modern kernels—its throughput and memory profile are better, and the notification model suits Go's epoll integration. But treating it as a lossless channel is the architectural mistake. Build the sampling controller, expose the drop signal, and correct derived metrics at the recording layer. Observability infrastructure that can silently lose data under its own load is not infrastructure—it is a liability dressed as insight.

title: Upgrading AG Grid from v21 to v36: Skipping 15 Major Versions, One Screen at a Time
description:
TL;DR

  • Our frontend grids (AG Grid) were a mix of v21 and v33, so we are migrating everything to v36
  • Instead of upgrading all at once, we run v21 and v36 side by side in the same app and migrate and release screen by screen
  • We turned the per-screen workflow into a fixed template (a "harness"), so an AI agent (Claude Code) or a human gets the same quality every time

Background

Where we started

Item Details
Target Web frontend of a sales-support SaaS (React 17 + TypeScript)
AG Grid usage About 40 grids across lists, detail pages, settings, and reports; about 220 files to migrate
Versions Mostly v21 (released 2019), with v33 on a few screens
License AG Grid Enterprise. Our current license covers the latest release, 36.2.0 (released September 2026)

Problems

  • Not using newer features: Although we use the Enterprise edition, we were on a version more than six years old and missed most of the features and improvements added since then
  • Two versions living together: The v21 and v33 stylesheets conflict, so the v33 screens relied on a workaround that loads their CSS only while they are displayed. Maintaining that workaround was a burden
  • Blocked on a feature we wanted: We want to expand a row in a parent list to show its related child list directly beneath it (Master/Detail). But the parent list was built on v21 and the child list on v33, and different versions can't be combined
    • Reference: AG Grid - Master / Detail

Goals

  • Standardize on AG Grid 36.2.0 and remove both the v21/v33 coexistence and the CSS workaround
  • ag-grid-react@36.2.0 supports React 16.8–19, so no React upgrade is needed

What makes it hard

  • About 220 files are affected, and the largest list is about 1,700 lines on its own
  • v21 and v36 coexist during the migration, so their CSS must not conflict
  • After migrating, infinite scrolling, sorting, row selection, range selection and copy, saving and restoring column settings, CSV export, grouping, and so on must all keep working as before

Main differences between v21 and v36

Simple renames (excerpt)

v21 v36
columnApi.xxx() api.xxx() (columnApi was removed)
cellRendererFramework cellRenderer (pass the component directly)
getRowNodeId: (data) => id getRowId: (params) => id
api.setRowData(rows) api.setGridOption('rowData', rows)
api.updateRowData(...) api.applyTransaction(...)
purgeServerSideCache() refreshServerSide({ purge: true })
stopEditingWhenGridLosesFocus stopEditingWhenCellsLoseFocus
suppressMenu suppressHeaderMenuButton
Cell editors as classes (getGui / getValue) React components (onValueChange / useGridCellEditor)

Renames that change behavior (handled with helpers)

Target If you just rename it What our helper does
Applying column state (applyColumnState) Saved column order is not restored Applies the column order as well
Getting column state (getColumnState) sort and other fields get saved, so sorting is applied twice Keeps only the fields v21 had
Resetting column state (resetColumnState) Sorting is cleared too, and the list goes empty Resets only column order, width, visibility, and pinning
getSortModel / setSortModel Removed Builds the sort model from the column state

Event and option differences

Target v21 v36 What happened
Event source for column move / resize Both uiColumnDragged Split into uiColumnMoved / uiColumnResized Column state stopped being saved
suppressSetColumnStateEvents Available Removed Applying column state through the API triggers our save logic
infiniteInitialRowCount: 0 Rows load Rows never load The list stays empty
context Later changes are reflected Only the initial value is used Updated values such as names don't reach the cells
Cell renderers returning HTML strings Rendered as HTML Shown as plain text Raw tags appear on screen
Server-side row model getRowId optional Effectively required Row selection is not kept
Line breaks in range copy \n \r\n Accepted, since pasting into Excel and similar tools works the same
Zero results Nothing shown "No Rows To Show" overlay Kept the v36 behavior

Visuals (restored to v21 in our shared wrapper)

Target v21 v36 default
Minimum column width 10px 28px
Header text 12px, system font 14px, page font
Selected row color Solid blue Translucent blue (looks different on striped rows)
Range selection color Opacity 0.3, no inner borders Opacity 0.2, with inner borders
Row selection checkbox Centered in the cell Pushed to the top left
Inline edit input 28px tall, gray border Full row height, blue border and shadow

Differences of a few pixels that CSS can't fix (such as a header that is 1px taller, or a horizontal scrollbar that now extends under pinned columns) are documented in our README with the reason, and accepted.

How we proceeded

1. Build the foundation first (not used by any screen yet)

In this phase we only prepare the parts needed to build screens on v36. Every screen still runs on v21, so users see no change. We actually start using v36 in the next phase, "Migrate screen by screen".

Step What we did
1 Upgrade TypeScript from 4.8 to 5.9 (required by v36's type definitions)
2 Install v36 under aliased package names so it can coexist with v21
3 Scope the CSS at build time so v21 and v36 styles don't conflict (explained below)
4 Build a shared wrapper, AgGridV36, with defaults and visuals aligned to v21
5 Create v36 versions of the cell renderers, cell editors, filters, and column definitions by duplicating the originals

What "scope the CSS at build time" means

v21 and v36 use the same class names (such as .ag-row), so putting both on the same page makes each version's CSS hit the other's grid. To prevent that, when webpack loads AG Grid's CSS, we automatically add a condition to every selector.

/* Original CSS */
.ag-row { ... }

/* v36 CSS: applies only inside .ag-theme-v36 */
.ag-row:where(.ag-theme-v36, .ag-theme-v36 *) { ... }

/* v21 CSS: applies only outside .ag-theme-v36 */
.ag-row:not(:where(.ag-theme-v36, .ag-theme-v36 *)) { ... }
  • Wrapping the condition in :where() keeps specificity unchanged, so our existing override styles behave the same
  • The icon fonts also share a name, so the v36 font gets a -v36 suffix
  • The library itself is left untouched; the CSS is transformed on every build

This lets us ship releases where v21 and v36 screens are mixed.

2. Migrate screen by screen (this is where v36 goes live)

  • One screen = one ticket = one PR. The first list we migrated produced the mapping tables above, and later screens just look things up in them
  • Screens with many users or shown on the home screen keep the old version behind a feature flag so we can switch back
  • Every newly found difference is added to the mapping tables in the README

3. Turn the per-screen workflow into a template (harness)

Each step has a gate, and we don't move on until it passes.

  • Investigate: List where the screen uses v21 APIs, then sort each use into "covered by the table / uses a helper / behavior difference / new"
  • Implement: Build the v36 version. Mark temporary code with a fixed TODO marker (done when typecheck and lint pass)
  • Unit tests: Extract the rewritten logic into functions and test them
  • Screen E2E: Use Playwright to test the 15 checks shared by every list plus every operation specific to that screen. First inventory the screen's features in a table, then assign a test to every row
  • Compare with v21: When something looks like a bug, switch back to v21 and repeat the same steps. Every difference is either "fixed" or "documented in the README with a reason"
  • Feed knowledge back: Update the README, the E2E tests, and our notes so the next person avoids the same traps just by reading the README

4. Remove v21 at the end (consolidation)

Once every screen is on v36, we will remove everything we kept around for the migration (planned).

  • What gets removed
    • The v21 / v33 packages
    • The originals we duplicated for v36 (v21 cell components, column definitions, shared hooks, and so on)
    • The v21 versions of high-risk screens and their feature flags
    • The build-time CSS scoping, and v33's "load CSS only while displayed" workaround
  • How we avoid missing anything
    • All temporary code added during the migration carries the same marker comment (TODO: when removing v21…), so a single grep finds all of it
    • For screens with a feature flag, the flag file states when, what, and in which order to remove things
    • The top of the shared wrapper lists the duplicated originals to delete
  • Watch out for
    • Some originals (constants and components that don't depend on v21) are also imported by the v36 versions. Move them to the v36 side instead of deleting them

Why we chose this approach

  • Ship in small pieces, one screen at a time: Changing about 220 files at once makes review and debugging hard. If something breaks, only one screen is affected
  • Duplicate instead of modifying existing parts: Screens not yet migrated stay safe. v21 is removed all at once at the end
  • Feature flags for high-risk screens: If a problem shows up in production, we can switch back to v21 without reverting code

Ideas we drew on

  • Strangler Fig: Grow the new system alongside the old one and replace it gradually Martin Fowler - StranglerFigApplication
  • Branch by Abstraction: Put an abstraction in between (here, the shared wrapper and the switch components) and swap the implementation behind it step by step Martin Fowler - BranchByAbstraction
  • Parallel Change (expand / migrate / contract): Run old and new side by side (expand), move over (migrate), then remove the old one (contract) Martin Fowler - ParallelChange

Our process follows Parallel Change directly: "build the foundation first" is expand, "migrate screen by screen" is migrate, and "remove v21 at the end" is contract.

Pitfalls

  • Many differences don't cause type errors: Differences in column state or event source pass both typecheck and unit tests, and only show up when you use the screen
  • "v36 bug" that turned out to be the same in v21: We now always repeat the steps on v21 first. Quite a few bugs had been carried over from v21
  • Comparing visuals: Comparing getComputedStyle values was more reliable than comparing screenshots

For E2E we tried both Claude in Chrome and Playwright, and chose Playwright

At first we checked screens with Claude in Chrome, where an AI operates the browser, but partway through we switched to Playwright tests.

Playwright Claude in Chrome
Setup You have to write test code first You can start right away
Speed For a fixed set of steps, many times faster than driving the browser Slow, since it looks at the screen and acts one step at a time
Repeatability Runs exactly the same steps every time Doesn't always test the same way each time
Best for Running the same checks over and over across many screens, as in a migration Quick checks after a small bug fix, or exploring how a screen is built

A migration means running the same checks many times for every screen, so Playwright paid off even after the upfront cost of writing the code.

Note: This article covers only what we verified while migrating our own project. It may contain mistakes or details that differ between versions. When you migrate, please also check the official AG Grid documentation (the upgrade guide for each version and the API reference).

title: Fair and Efficient Distributed EV Charging Coordination Using Threshold Cryptography and Machine Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17577v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distributed coordination of electric vehicle (EV) charging with the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) keeps EV constraints private but assumes that every participant follows the algorithm. This assumption fails in practice, where a biased operator or a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacker can send inconsistent signals to different EVs, and compromised EVs can deviate from their prescribed updates. We first prove that attacks by such arbitrarily malicious, i.e., Byzantine, participants do not prevent convergence and therefore remain undetected, and derive the most damaging attack in closed form. We then propose a framework that combines a threshold-signed broadcast with upload recomputation, which detects every deviation without false alarms at linear instead of quadratic communication cost. To keep the optimization running, each affected EV recovers locally with a certified, fleet-aware machine learning price forecast, and we prove that the optimization remains convergent with a recovery cost bounded by the shape of the forecast error. Simulation results with real-world load, price, and charging data show that a biased operator raises the annual cost of disadvantaged EVs by 132.7% and lowers that of advantaged EVs by 49.3% without changing the aggregate load, whereas the defense limits all cost changes to 2.6%. An external MITM attacker raises the cost of its victims by 57.6%, the peak load by 5.8%, and the grid cost by 15.8%, whereas the defense keeps them within 1.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3% of benign operation. With up to 70% of the EVs attacked, the recovery converges in at least 97.8% of the runs.

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

Read more

title: Measuring answer faithfulness in RAG: metrics that hold up
description:
Short answer: faithfulness in RAG means every claim the answer makes is supported by the retrieved context — not by what the model memorized. Three metrics hold up: a RAGAS faithfulness score for eval suites, a deterministic grounding check for CI, and a narrow LLM-as-judge for the edge cases neither catches.

The confusion I see most often: people conflate correctness and faithfulness. A correct answer can be unfaithful — the model happened to state the right fact from memory, not from the context you gave it. That's a different failure mode than getting it wrong, and it matters a lot when the retrieved context changes.

What does faithfulness actually measure — and what it doesn't?

Faithfulness answers: did the model only use what I gave it?

It says nothing about whether the retrieved context was right in the first place (that's context precision and recall), and nothing about whether the answer addressed the question well (that's answer relevancy). Three separate dimensions, easy to conflate.

The concrete definition: a faithful answer contains zero claims that require knowledge beyond the retrieved chunks to verify. If your context says "the return window is 30 days" and the model outputs "returns are accepted within 30 days" — faithful. If it outputs "returns are accepted within 30 days, free of charge" and your context says nothing about fees — the second half is unfaithful. It might even be correct. Doesn't matter.
