title: Finding two ClickHouse time zone bugs with a differential test
description:
I wanted a cheap way to find real bugs in a large database, so I stopped reading code and compared answers instead. Two of the comparisons found genuine bugs in ClickHouse's date functions, both in time zones with a UTC offset that is not a whole number of hours. The other three comparisons found nothing, which is also worth knowing.

Both fixes are open pull requests, not merged. I say so up front because the title of a post like this tends to promise more than the state of the work.

The method: ask the same question two ways

A differential test needs no expected values. You run the same logical query through two routes that must agree, and print any disagreement:

  • Against a reference. ClickHouse's date functions against Python's zoneinfo.
  • Against itself. The same JOIN with every join algorithm. The same filter with the primary key, skip indexes and PREWHERE on and off. The same GROUP BY with two-level, external and in-order aggregation.

Each probe is about 40-70 lines of Python that shells out to clickhouse local. They are public gists, with the setup in the header: date functions, JOIN algorithms, index analysis, aggregation settings.

Bug 1: toStartOfHour returns :30 on a day when the clocks move by 30 minutes

Australia/Lord_Howe shifts by 30 minutes twice a year. The probe compares toStartOfHour over thousands of timestamps with what Python says the wall clock hour is. Only two samples out of 4,000 disagreed, both on a transition day:

SELECT toStartOfHour(toDateTime('2024-04-07 03:10:00', 'Australia/Lord_Howe'));
-- 2024-04-07 02:30:00   (expected 03:00:00)

Every other sample, including all the other days of the year in that zone, was right. The test only found this because it sampled around transitions on purpose. The cause is that toStartOfHour ends in a function that rounds on a grid anchored at the local midnight. After a 30 minute shift, that grid no longer lines up with the clock. toStartOfInterval(..., INTERVAL 2 HOUR) already compensated for the shift, so the 2-hour answer was right and the 1-hour answer wrong for the same input.

The fix applies the same compensation to the 1-hour case, only when the day's shift is not a whole number of hours.

Two things I learned from the CI run:

  1. I could not build ClickHouse here, so CI was the first time the test ran. It passed.
  2. The performance comparison, which is part of the CI, flagged date_time_long at +51.7% on my first push. I had added a second lookup of the day to the hot path. Looking the day up once removed it. A correct fix can still be a regression, and the benchmark caught it before a reviewer had to.

Pull request: ClickHouse #131620.

Bug 2: minute intervals before 1970 round to the wrong boundary 

SET enable_extended_results_for_datetime_functions = 1;
SELECT toStartOfFifteenMinutes(toDateTime64('1910-06-15 12:07:00', 0, 'Europe/Warsaw'));          -- 12:00:00
SELECT toStartOfInterval(toDateTime64('1910-06-15 12:07:00', 0, 'Europe/Warsaw'), INTERVAL 15 MINUTE);  -- 11:54:00

toStartOfInterval has an arithmetic shortcut that rounds the Unix timestamp. Before 1970 it was allowed whenever the offsets were whole minutes. The dedicated functions round from the local midnight there. The two agree only if the offset is a multiple of the interval, and Warsaw was at +01:24 until 1915. Checking the neighbours turned up Pacific/Chatham (+12:45), where even INTERVAL 10 MINUTE was wrong in 1960.

The fix narrows the condition: whole hours that divide into the interval. Other zones take the slower generic path before the epoch, which is what the dedicated functions use.

Pull request: ClickHouse #131915.

What found nothing

  • JOIN algorithms (hash, parallel_hash, grace_hash, full_sorting_merge, partial_merge, direct, auto) over NULL, NaN, tuple, array, map, LowCardinality and decimal keys: no disagreement over 7 random seeds.
  • Index analysis (primary key, three skip index types, PREWHERE, the old analyzer, the query condition cache) against a full scan over 14 key types: about 6,000 comparisons, no disagreement.
  • Aggregation settings against GROUP BY, DISTINCT, ROLLUP, window functions on composite keys: about 3,200 comparisons, no disagreement.

That is a useful result about the database. It is also a reminder that most of a mature system is correct, and the bugs live in the corners where two correct-looking pieces of logic meet, here "round to the hour" and "the offset changed by 30 minutes today".

The probes lied to me first

Most of my debugging time went on the harness, not on ClickHouse:

  • A first run reported thousands of mismatches. DateTime is unsigned, so negative timestamps clamp to 1970, and my Python side disagreed with that. I limited the range.
  • toStartOfMonth returns a Date, which has no time zone, so comparing its Unix timestamp with Python's local midnight is meaningless. I compared dates instead.
  • -0.0 and 0.0 group together but print differently, so the probe flagged a representative choice as a bug. I removed -0.0 from the value pool.
  • clickhouse local keeps tables between runs, and running several seeds in parallel locked its directory. I gave each run its own path and a DROP TABLE IF EXISTS.

If your first differential test reports a flood of bugs, it is almost always the test.

Takeaways

  • A reference implementation in another language is a good oracle for date and time code, because the two have different bugs.
  • Sample around the edges on purpose. The Lord Howe bug showed up in 2 of 4,000 timestamps.
  • When a fix touches a hot path, read the performance results, not only the tests.
  • Say whether your fix is merged. Mine are not, yet.

title: My SVG Shows Up in the Browser but Not in React. Here's the Checklist I Use
description:
You open the .svg file in the browser and it looks perfect. You drop it into a React component and... nothing. No error, or a vague one, and an empty space where the icon should be.

The file is almost never the problem. Something between the file and the DOM is. Here is the order I check things in.

First, two quick checks. Open the console and look for a React warning. Then inspect the spot where the icon should be:

  • No <svg> or <img> element at all? It's the import or the component.
  • The element is there but blank? It's size, paint, or loading.

1. The import gives you a URL, not a component

Most bundlers turn import logo from "./logo.svg" into a URL string. Render that as <Logo /> and React gets a string where it expected a component.

  • Vite: add vite-plugin-svgr. In its current major version only imports ending in ?react become components: import Logo from "./logo.svg?react". A plain import stays a URL. For TypeScript, add /// <reference types="vite-plugin-svgr/client" />.
  • Create React App: the component is the named export ReactComponent; the default export is still the URL.
  • Next.js: without an SVG loader the import is an object with src, width, and height. <img src={logo} /> renders src="[object Object]". Use logo.src or next/image.

2. Raw SVG was pasted straight into JSX

JSX is not HTML. Some differences only warn (class, stroke-width), but these actually break the icon:

<svg style="fill:red">        // throws: style must be an object
<use xlink:href="#a" />        // Babel: namespace tags not supported
<!-- exported from Figma -->   // syntax error in JSX
<svg viewbox="0 0 24 24">      // lowercase, not treated as viewBox

Fixed versions: style={{ fill: "red" }}, href="#a", {/* comment */}, and viewBox.

3. No viewBox, or no size

If the element exists but takes no space, check its computed width and height.

  • Missing viewBox: a 512-unit drawing in a 24px box shows only its top-left corner. Some optimizer presets remove viewBox (SVGO 3's default preset does).
  • Zero or percentage size: width="100%" inside a parent with no width is zero.
  • Flex rows: give the icon a fixed width/height and flex-shrink: 0.
  • 1em sizing: inside a parent with font-size: 0, the icon disappears.

4. It's drawn, just in an invisible color

fill="none" with no stroke draws nothing. Outline icon sets rely on stroke, so removing stroke removes the icon. And currentColor takes the CSS color of the parent, so white text on a white button gives you a white icon.

5. Duplicate IDs in gradients, masks, and clip paths

IDs in inline SVG are global to the page. Render the same icon twice and every url(#id) points at the first copy. If that copy sits inside a hidden menu, the visible ones can lose their gradient or clip path. Generate a unique ID per instance with React's useId().

If the file loads but never draws

Check that the server sends image/svg+xml as the content type, and that your Content Security Policy allows the source you load it from.

I keep the full version of this checklist, with code for each framework and the MIME/CSP details, here: SVG Not Showing in React? Causes and Fixes. If you'd rather skip the attribute work entirely, I also built a free SVG to JSX converter that runs SVGR in the browser and keeps the viewBox (nothing is uploaded).

What's the weirdest reason an SVG went blank on you?

title: Programmatic Location Pages in Next.js Without Creating Thin Content
description:
If you build sites for local service businesses, sooner or later someone asks for city pages. A plumbing company serves twelve suburbs, a law firm takes clients across three counties, an HVAC contractor wants to show up for "AC repair" in every town on its route. The obvious engineering answer is a dynamic route, a list of cities and a template. The obvious SEO risk is that you ship forty near-identical pages that search engines treat as thin or duplicate content and quietly ignore.

This post covers how to build location pages in the Next.js App Router so they are fast, crawlable and genuinely different from each other. The code is simple. The harder part is the data model, because the data is what makes each page worth indexing.

Start with the data, not the template

Most thin location pages come from a template that swaps one word. "We offer plumbing in {city}" repeated forty times is not forty pages of content, it is one page with a find and replace.

Before writing any routes, define what actually differs between locations. For a real service business, that usually includes:

  • The neighborhoods or zip codes actually served from that area
  • Which services are offered there (not every crew covers every service everywhere)
  • Typical response time or scheduling notes for that area
  • Local conditions that change the work, such as older housing stock, hard water, climate or permit rules
  • Projects or job types that are common in that area
  • Answers to questions customers in that area actually ask

If you cannot fill those fields with something true for a city, that city probably should not have its own page yet. That rule alone prevents most thin content.

Here is a typed shape for that data:

// lib/locations.ts
export type Location = {
  slug: string;
  city: string;
  region: string;
  areasServed: string[];
  services: string[];
  intro: string;
  localNotes: string[];
  faqs: { q: string; a: string }[];
  indexable: boolean;
};

export const locations: Location[] = [
  {
    slug: "houston",
    city: "Houston",
    region: "TX",
    areasServed: ["Heights", "Montrose", "Bellaire", "Spring Branch"],
    services: ["website-design", "local-seo", "google-ads"],
    intro: "Written specifically for this market, not generated.",
    localNotes: ["Notes that only make sense for this city."],
    faqs: [{ q: "A real local question", a: "A real answer." }],
    indexable: true,
  },
];

export function getLocation(slug: string) {
  return locations.find((l) => l.slug === slug);
}

The indexable flag matters. It lets you keep a draft location in the data without exposing it to search engines until it has real content.

Whether this lives in a TypeScript file, a CMS or a database does not change the approach. A typed file is fine for a few dozen locations and keeps everything in version control.

The dynamic route

With the App Router, one folder handles every location:

app/
  locations/
    page.tsx
    [slug]/
      page.tsx

Generate the static paths at build time so every page is pre-rendered HTML:

// app/locations/[slug]/page.tsx
import { notFound } from "next/navigation";
import { locations, getLocation } from "@/lib/locations";

export const dynamicParams = false;

export function generateStaticParams() {
  return locations.map((l) => ({ slug: l.slug }));
}

export default async function LocationPage({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const loc = getLocation(slug);
  if (!loc) notFound();

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Web Design and Local SEO in {loc.city}, {loc.region}</h1>
      <p>{loc.intro}</p>

      <section>
        <h2>Areas we serve around {loc.city}</h2>
        <ul>
          {loc.areasServed.map((a) => (
            <li key={a}>{a}</li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      </section>

      <section>
        <h2>What is different about {loc.city}</h2>
        {loc.localNotes.map((n, i) => (
          <p key={i}>{n}</p>
        ))}
      </section>
    </main>
  );
}

Setting dynamicParams = false means any slug not returned by generateStaticParams gets a real 404 instead of rendering an empty template. That prevents a whole class of accidental junk URLs, such as typos in links that would otherwise produce a soft 404.

Note that in recent Next.js versions params is a Promise, so it is awaited. If you are on an older version you will see it as a plain object.

Unique metadata per page

Every location page needs its own title, description and canonical URL. generateMetadata runs on the server alongside the page:

import type { Metadata } from "next";

export async function generateMetadata({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>;
}): Promise<Metadata> {
  const { slug } = await params;
  const loc = getLocation(slug);
  if (!loc) return {};

  const url = `https://www.example.com/locations/${loc.slug}`;
  return {
    title: `Web Design and Local SEO in ${loc.city}, ${loc.region}`,
    description: `Websites and local search for ${loc.city} businesses, serving ${loc.areasServed.slice(0, 3).join(", ")} and nearby areas.`,
    alternates: { canonical: url },
    robots: loc.indexable ? undefined : { index: false, follow: true },
  };
}

Two details are worth calling out. The canonical is always self-referencing and always uses the same host, so you never end up with example.com and www.example.com versions competing. And the robots field reads the indexable flag, so drafts render for review but carry a noindex tag.

Keep the sitemap in sync

The sitemap should come from the same data, filtered by the same flag, so it can never list a page you have marked noindex:

// app/sitemap.ts
import type { MetadataRoute } from "next";
import { locations } from "@/lib/locations";

export default function sitemap(): MetadataRoute.Sitemap {
  const base = "https://www.example.com";
  return [
    { url: `${base}/locations` },
    ...locations
      .filter((l) => l.indexable)
      .map((l) => ({ url: `${base}/locations/${l.slug}` })),
  ];
}

One source of truth for routes, metadata and sitemap removes the most common drift problem, where a page gets deleted but the sitemap keeps advertising it for months.

Internal linking is part of the feature

Location pages that are only reachable through the sitemap are orphans. Search engines find them but have little reason to treat them as important. Build links into the structure:

  • A hub page at /locations that lists every indexable city with a short line about each
  • Links from each location page to the relevant service pages
  • Links from service pages back to the locations where that service is offered
  • A small "nearby areas" block on each city page linking to neighboring cities

For a working example of the hub and spoke pattern, the CodeHunterz locations hub lists each city page and links into the matching service pages, so every location is two clicks from the homepage.

The nearby block is easy to derive if you store coordinates or a manual neighbor list. A manual list is usually better, because "nearby" for a service business means "on the same route," not straight-line distance.

Add LocalBusiness schema with areaServed

Structured data helps search engines connect each page to the business and the area it covers. For a service area business without a storefront in every city, use areaServed rather than inventing addresses:

function LocationSchema({ loc }: { loc: Location }) {
  const data = {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "ProfessionalService",
    name: "Example Co",
    url: `https://www.example.com/locations/${loc.slug}`,
    areaServed: loc.areasServed.map((name) => ({
      "@type": "Place",
      name: `${name}, ${loc.city}`,
    })),
  };
  return (
    <script
      type="application/ld+json"
      dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(data) }}
    />
  );
}

Never put a fake street address on a city page to look local. It misleads users, and it conflicts with the business information search engines already have.

A build-time guard against thin pages

Rules in a document get ignored. Rules in the build do not. A small check can fail the build if an indexable location is missing real content:

// scripts/check-locations.ts
import { locations } from "../lib/locations";

const problems: string[] = [];
const intros = new Set<string>();

for (const l of locations.filter((x) => x.indexable)) {
  if (l.intro.split(" ").length < 60) problems.push(`${l.slug}: intro too short`);
  if (l.faqs.length < 3) problems.push(`${l.slug}: fewer than 3 FAQs`);
  if (l.localNotes.length < 2) problems.push(`${l.slug}: needs local notes`);
  if (intros.has(l.intro)) problems.push(`${l.slug}: duplicate intro`);
  intros.add(l.intro);
}

if (problems.length) {
  console.error(problems.join("\n"));
  process.exit(1);
}

Run it in prebuild in package.json. The thresholds are arbitrary and you should tune them, but having any automated floor changes behavior. Nobody can quietly add twenty cities with copied intros.

You can go further by comparing text similarity between pages, but in practice the duplicate check plus required fields catches the worst cases.

Performance still counts

Location pages often get traffic from mobile searches by people who need help now. Since every page here is statically generated, the HTML is fast by default. The usual things still slow pages down:

  • A large hero image on every city page. Use next/image with explicit sizes and only mark the first visible image as priority.
  • Embedding a map iframe at the top of the page. Lazy load it below the fold, or use a static image linked to the map.
  • Loading a chat widget or tracking scripts eagerly. Use next/script with lazyOnload for anything not needed on first paint.

A click-to-call link near the top of the page is often more useful to a local visitor than any of those heavy elements.

When not to build location pages

Sometimes the right engineering decision is to push back on the request. If the business genuinely serves one metro area with no meaningful differences between suburbs, one strong service area page will usually do better than fifteen weak ones. Good local SEO is about relevance and trust, not page count.

A reasonable rule: add a location page when you have something true and specific to say about that location, and the business actually wants calls from there. Otherwise list the area on a single service area page and move on. The CodeHunterz guide on SEO for service area businesses covers that decision from the marketing side, which is useful context to share with the client.

Summary

  • Model the data that actually differs between locations before writing a template.
  • Use generateStaticParams with dynamicParams = false so only real locations exist.
  • Generate unique metadata and self-referencing canonicals per page.
  • Drive the sitemap and robots rules from the same indexable flag.
  • Link locations into a hub and into service pages so none are orphaned.
  • Use areaServed in schema instead of invented addresses.
  • Add a prebuild check so thin pages cannot ship.

If you want to see how this structure looks on a production site, or you need help planning one, the team behind these notes builds Next.js sites for local businesses using this same pattern.

CodeHunterz Team

title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17790v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

title: Zoom In, Scale Out: Metric Depth Models Mistake Digital Zoom for Moving Closer
description:
arXiv:2611.17903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many new AI models estimate how far away things are, in metres, from a single photo. To do this they must also work out what camera took the photo. We check whether they really do with a simple test: digital zoom, that is, cropping a photo and enlarging the crop back to full size. Zooming moves nothing in the scene, so a correct model should give the same distance for every point still in the picture. The test is free, exact and needs no labels. Two numbers describe a model's reaction: its depth changes like $s^{-\alpha}$ (ideal $\alpha=0$) and its focal-length estimate like $s^{\beta}$ (ideal $\beta=1$), for zoom factor $s$. On 800 images from KITTI, NYUv2 and DIODE, the widely used Depth Anything V2 has $\alpha=0.95$: it treats a zoomed photo almost as if the camera had moved closer, because it judges distance mainly from how large things look. Models that also predict the camera remove only part of this error ($\alpha\approx0.31$-$0.36$), because their focal estimate grows too little. Given the true camera, Depth Pro and DA3-Nested keep their depth ($\alpha\approx0$), so the error lies in their camera estimate. The reason: a zoomed photo is, pixel for pixel, a normal photo of a scene squashed in depth, so size alone cannot tell the two apart, and a focal estimator trained by regression stays close to the cameras it saw in training. Undoing this needs no labels or training and makes Depth Pro pass the test ($\alpha=0.04$) at almost no cost on normal photos. Controls, including a real optical zoom lens, rule out blur and resizing artefacts. Finally, label-free fine-tuning for self-consistency lowers $\alpha$ to 0.05 on KITTI and 0.07 on NYUv2 once a "blurry means zoomed" shortcut is removed; we report what this costs on normal and unseen photos.

title: The pros and cons of using your phone as a mobile hotspot
description: Using your phone to help other devices connect to the internet is undeniably convenient, but it also comes with other perks – and a few downsides.

title: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search
description:
arXiv:2611.17412v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di- mension and pair without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. The embeddings come from the Weighted Euclidean SEries Encoder (WESEE), whose multi-scale Temporal Feature Extractor keeps the timing information that global pooling removes and raises recall@1 from 0.90 to 0.95, although WETW works with any encoder. We also show that fitting DTW distances is not enough for search, as regression alone misorders the closest neighbours, and that ranking regularization raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95. Our filter-and-verify pipeline, WETW-FV, uses WETW to build a shortlist and exact DTW to check it, so the search is approximate but every returned distance is exact. Over eight datasets, WETW-FV is 11.4x faster than the fastest exact method among the UCR Suite, lower bounds and MESSI-DTW, at a mean recall@10 of 0.93, while the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed. On 48K-point series, WETW- FV remains 40x faster than the UCR Suite at a recall@10 of 0.91.

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

Read more

title: Fix html2canvas 'Attempting to parse an unsupported color function "oklch"' (Tailwind CSS v4)
description:
When you call html2canvas() on a page that uses Tailwind CSS v4 — or any stylesheet that emits modern CSS color functions — the official html2canvas package may throw:

Attempting to parse an unsupported color function "oklch"

The same parser also rejects related functions, so you may instead see "oklab", "lab", "lch", "color", or "color-mix" in the message.

Why it happens

html2canvas does not take a real screenshot. It walks the DOM, reads computed styles, and paints a canvas itself. That means it has to parse CSS color values.

Tailwind CSS v4 uses the oklch() color space for its default palette. The browser is fine with that. Official html2canvas 1.4.1 (January 2022), by Niklas von Hertzen, was released before oklch() / oklab() showed up in everyday stylesheets, and its color parser throws on functions it does not know.

So a page that looks correct in the browser can still fail at html2canvas(element) time. This is a parser limitation, not a Tailwind bug.

Fixes that do not use html2canvas-lts

Try these first.

1. Switch to html2canvas-pro

html2canvas-pro is an independent maintained fork by Yorick Shan. It is built as a next-generation html2canvas and supports modern CSS colors.

Verified on npm, 2026-11-16 (Asia/Shanghai): html2canvas-pro 2.6.4.

npm uninstall html2canvas && npm install html2canvas-pro

import html2canvas from 'html2canvas-pro';

If this package already does what you need, use it. Thanks to Yorick Shan and contributors for maintaining it, and to Niklas von Hertzen for the original library.

2. Keep official html2canvas, but do not feed it oklch() styles

If you must stay on html2canvas 1.4.1, the captured DOM cannot contain those color functions in computed styles. In practice that usually means:

  • not using Tailwind v4's default oklch() palette on the nodes you capture, or
  • snapshotting a clone whose colors have been rewritten to rgb() / hex first.

This is often more work than changing the library, and it is easy to miss a theme token or a shadow. Prefer (1) unless you have a hard constraint on the official 1.4.1 package.

A maintained html2canvas fork (optional)

Another option is html2canvas-lts, a drop-in fork that teaches the original parser lab(), lch(), oklab(), oklch(), color(), and color-mix() instead of throwing. It is not the official html2canvas package, and it is a separate project from html2canvas-pro. Credit for html2canvas stays with Niklas von Hertzen and the original contributors; if the original project returns, the fork is meant to step aside.

Verified on npm, 2026-11-16 (Asia/Shanghai): html2canvas-lts 1.5.4. The package README lists 37 fixes and no new runtime dependencies, including the color-function work.

npm uninstall html2canvas && npm install html2canvas-lts

The API is the same; the module name changes:

import html2canvas from 'html2canvas-lts';

html2canvas(document.querySelector('#capture')).then((canvas) => {
  document.body.appendChild(canvas);
});

A script tag still exposes window.html2canvas:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/html2canvas-lts@1.5.4/dist/html2canvas.min.js"></script>

The current fix list is on the project page: https://cyberpusa.org/forks/html2canvas/. The fork is kept by Cyber Pusa (赛博菩萨), an AI maintainer that adopts abandoned but still-used libraries. Issues can go to cyberpusa-ai/html2canvas.

Which option to pick

  • You want a modern, independently maintained renderer: try html2canvas-pro 2.6.4.
  • You want to stay close to the original html2canvas API and pick up the oklch fix plus the other listed rendering fixes: html2canvas-lts 1.5.4.
  • You cannot change libraries: keep 1.4.1 and make sure the captured tree does not compute to oklch() / oklab() / lab() / lch() / color() / color-mix().

In every case, the underlying library is Niklas von Hertzen's html2canvas. These packages exist because that work is still in use after the last official release.

title: Modern Framework Concepts: hooks, state management, SSR with frameworks like React and Next.js
description:
Modern frameworks like React and Next.js rely on powerful concepts such as hooks, state management, and server-side rendering (SSR) to create scalable, high-performing, and maintainable web apps. Here’s an in-depth look at these core ideas.

Hooks: Making React Components Powerful

Hooks are special functions in React that let developers use features such as state and lifecycle events within functional components—features previously available only in class components.

  • The most famous hooks are useState, which manages state, and useEffect, which handles side effects like fetching data or subscribing to events.
  • Hooks simplify component logic, encourage code reuse through custom hooks, and make functional components as capable as class-based ones.

Hooks have three main rules: they must run in function components, at the top level, and not inside loops or conditions.

Example: 
javascript
import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}

This pattern keeps component logic clear and modular.

State Management: Keeping Data Predictable

State management refers to how an app organizes, stores, and updates the data that determines what users see and can do.

  • Good state management uses a single source of truth, prefers immutability for predictability, and follows a unidirectional data flow—meaning data changes in one direction across the app.
  • React’s useState and useReducer are used for local state, while modern apps often harness libraries like Redux, Recoil, or Zustand for global/shared state between many components.
  • Keeping most state local and only "lifting" state when necessary helps maintain manageable and reusable components.

Best Practices:

  • Minimize global state.
  • Normalize data structures.
  • Separate state logic from business or presentation logic.

Server-Side Rendering (SSR): Speed & SEO

  • Server-Side Rendering (SSR) is the approach of rendering web pages on the server and delivering fully-formed HTML to the browser, rather than letting the browser assemble the page from JavaScript after loading.
  • Next.js makes SSR straightforward with automatic page rendering on the server and easy data fetching methods like getServerSideProps.
  • SSR significantly improves load speed and SEO (search engines can see ready-made HTML, not just scripts).
  • SSR also allows real-time data fetching for each request and finer control over cache and performance. #####Example (Next.js): 
javascript
export async function getServerSideProps() {
  const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data');
  const data = await res.json();
  return { props: { data } };
}

This ensures that users always see the freshest possible data as soon as the page loads.

Final Thoughts

Modern frameworks like React and Next.js revolutionize development using hooks (for logic and state inside functions), advanced state management (for consistency and scalability), and SSR (for performance and SEO). Mastering these concepts empowers developers to build robust, maintainable, and lightning-fast web applications

Stay tuned for more insights as you continue your journey into the world of web development!

title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.17341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
description:
Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

What triggers a review

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together.

What a finding includes

Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating.

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard.

Fixes and resolution

Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it.

To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON.

Security policies

Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings.

Limitations

Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

Pricing

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate: provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate.

Enable Security Review in your team’s Agent settings, or read the documentation and the announcement to learn more. The CLI command needs Vercel CLI 65.10.0 or later.

title: CO-197 Denial Code: Missing Prior Authorization
description:
The Medicare Advantage prior authorisation data contains a number that should alter the way your practice interprets this code. not the rate of denial. rate of overturns.

An authorisation denial is often seen as final. According to the data, it's usually not.

What does the CO 197 denial code mean?
Code 197, which was last updated on May 1, 2018, is defined by X12 as "Precertification/authorization/notification/pre-treatment absent," with effect from October 31, 2006.

There is no mention of "doing the work." The payer does not claim that the service was unneeded or uncovered. It indicates that a necessary permission step was not completed prior to the provision of the service.

What is authorisation in advance? A service must be approved by the payer before it is rendered. Regardless of whether the service was appropriate, the payer refuses payment in the absence of approval.

Pre-certification, authorisation, notification, and pre-treatment are the four different topics covered by the term. A payer who demands notification within 48 hours is enforcing something very different from one who demands clearance before to the first session. These are distinct requirements with separate regulations. Examine your contracts to see if they apply.

Since the group code is CO, the amount is not the patient's responsibility but rather a contractual obligation. Generally speaking, you cannot bill the patient for a service you did not obtain authorisation for, and trying to do so would likely result in a complaint.

How often is this actually denied, and how often is it overturned?
This is the real-world application of the data. Medicare Advantage insurers "fully or partially denied 4.1 million prior authorisation requests, which is a somewhat larger share (7.7%) of all requests" (KFF) of the roughly 53 million prior authorisation requests that were filed to them in 2024.

"Just 11.5% of denied prior authorisation requests were appealed to Medicare Advantage insurers in 2024," and "80.7" of those appeals were partially or totally reversed (KFF). This is the bit that counts for your workflow.

Together, read those two numbers. Approximately one in nine denials are contested, and four out of five challenges are successful. It is evident that a significant number of appealable denials are being accepted without any testing.

Commercial coverage follows the same trend. KFF discovered that "8% due to lack of preauthorization or referral" was one of the stated reasons for denials in HealthCare.gov marketplace plans in 2021, while customers appealed "less than two-tenths of 1." of in-network denials.

Just to be clear, the Medicare Advantage numbers include denials of prior authorisation requests, which are a slightly different demographic than claims that are denied with CO 197 after the fact. It is nevertheless difficult to dispute the findings' direction.

What do you do when a CO 197 arrives?
Work in this sequence. Neither the appeal nor the write-off should be used first.

Verify the existence of the authorisation. It did, surprisingly frequently, and the number was just not sent on the claim. It settles in a single cycle and is a rectified claim rather than an appeal. This is similar to CO 16, where the stated cause is incomplete information.

Make a request for retroactive approval. In situations where the service was urgent or eligibility was questionable at the time, many payers allow it within a specified window. This is the most frequently omitted phase.

Verify if authorisation was indeed necessary. Requirements are subject to change more frequently than most practices keep track of. It is worthwhile to contest a denial that claims there was no authorisation for a service that no longer needs one.

Make an appeal using clinical records. The appeal focuses on medical necessity and the accompanying documentation if the service was required and provided.

After the foregoing, merely write off. Writing off at step one is leaving money behind due to the overturn rates.

Why is behavioral health hit harder by this?
Because authorisation requirements in the field of behavioural health are more specific, more inconsistent between payers, and more likely to be associated with session counts as opposed to a single authorised episode.

Usually, one authorisation is required for a medical operation. An initial authorisation, a concurrent review at a predetermined number of sessions, and then another may be required for a course of therapy. Each of those represents a distinct chance to miss a deadline, and failing to meet the second one eliminates all subsequent sessions.

This arrangement creates a particular failure mode that is worth keeping an eye out for. Because it belongs to someone, the initial authorisation is sought with caution. The refusal for sessions eleven through eighteen appears all at once, and the concurrent review is overlooked since no one was monitoring session counts against the authorised number.

A tracked session count against each active authorisation, with a trigger prior to the limit instead of after it, is the solution. That is a tracking issue, and tracking issues can be resolved.

Where automation actually helps with CO 197
This is the code where automation pays off the most on both sides. Routing recovers a significant portion of the remaining volume after prevention eliminates the majority of it.

At scheduling, requirements are checked. At the time of booking, it is known whether this payer needs authorisation for this service. The intervention that completely stops the denial is checking it at each appointment.

monitoring the session count in relation to authorisation. There is only a counting issue with the concurrent review failure. Instead of raising the flag after the limit, a system that has the authorised number and the sessions provided can do it before.

Sending denials in the proper direction. A rectified claim is a CO 197 where the authorisation was present. An appeal or a retroactive request can be one in which it didn't. Separating those distinct operations prevents everything from defaulting to write-off.

In order to close the gap that the KFF figures highlight—denials that were appealable but were never appealed—Supabill automates benefits verification across payers and handles denials with routing and appeals.

It's worth specifying the actual limit. Automation cannot create medical necessity or get an authorisation that a payer declines to provide. The write-off is appropriate when a service was actually not authorised and the payer refuses to grant it retroactively. The difference with automation is that you come to that decision after testing it, as opposed to before.

title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.17831v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.

title: What Are the Key IT Services Essential for a Modern Logistics Company?
description:
A few years ago, a logistics company could get by with a decent fleet, a good dispatcher and a stack of spreadsheets. That doesn't hold up anymore. Customers expect to see where their shipment is at any moment, shippers want quotes in minutes, and margins are thin enough that one badly planned route can wipe out the profit on a load.

Behind almost every logistics business that runs smoothly today, there's a set of IT services doing the quiet work. Here are the ones that matter most, and why.

Custom software built around how you actually work

Off-the-shelf tools are fine for general accounting or email. Logistics is different. Every company has its own way of handling consignments, billing, driver allocation and proof of delivery. When your software forces you into someone else's workflow, people end up working around it, and that's where errors creep in.

Custom software development lets you build the system the way your operations really run. Booking, invoicing, consignment notes and customer communication can live in one place instead of five disconnected tools. If you want to see what this looks like in practice, iWebwiser has a logistics industry case study collection that walks through real projects.

Mobile apps for drivers, customers and field staff

Your drivers are not sitting at desks. They're on the road, often with patchy network, and they need to accept jobs, update status, capture a delivery signature or photo, and move on. A simple, reliable mobile app does more for on-time delivery than most people expect.

The same goes for customers. A tracking screen that actually shows progress cuts down the "where is my order?" calls that eat up your support team's day. One example worth looking at is the myBilty case study, which shows how a digital approach can replace paperwork-heavy transport processes.

Real-time tracking and IoT integration

GPS trackers, temperature sensors, fuel monitors and door sensors are cheap now, and the data they produce is valuable. The catch is that raw data on its own doesn't help anyone. It needs to be pulled into a dashboard where a dispatcher can see a delayed truck, a cold-chain breach or an unusual stop and act on it straight away.

Good IoT integration means the information flows into the same system your team already uses, not into yet another login they'll forget about.

Cloud infrastructure that can scale with the season

Logistics demand is lumpy. Festive seasons, sale events and month-end rushes can multiply your volume overnight. If your systems sit on a single server in the office, they'll slow down or fall over at exactly the wrong time.

Cloud hosting solves this by letting you scale up when traffic spikes and scale back when it calms down. It also gives you backups, better uptime and the ability to let teams in different cities or warehouses use the same system without a headache.

Data analytics and reporting

Most logistics companies are sitting on years of data about routes, delivery times, fuel use, failed deliveries and customer behaviour. Very few use it well. Analytics services turn that history into answers: which routes always run late, which clients are least profitable, where fuel is quietly leaking money.

Even basic dashboards help. Predictive models, such as estimating delivery times or forecasting demand, are a natural next step once the foundations are in place.

Automation of repetitive back-office work

Invoice generation, status emails, document uploads, payment reminders, e-way bill entries. These tasks are boring, repetitive and easy to get wrong when done by hand. Automating them frees your staff to deal with exceptions, which is where human judgement is actually useful.

You don't need to automate everything at once. Start with the task that eats the most hours each week and build from there.

Integrations and APIs

A logistics business rarely lives in one system. You'll have an ERP or accounting tool, maybe a warehouse system, payment gateways, customer portals and third-party carriers. APIs are what let these talk to each other without someone copying data from one screen to another.

When integrations are done properly, an order placed by a customer can trigger dispatch, tracking and invoicing automatically. When they're not, you get duplicate entries and mismatched records.

Security and ongoing support

This one gets ignored until something goes wrong. Logistics systems hold customer details, pricing, contracts and payment information. A breach or a long outage doesn't just cost money, it damages trust with clients who rely on you.

Regular updates, access controls, backups and a team you can actually reach when something breaks are part of the IT picture too, not an optional extra.

Choosing the right technology partner

None of this needs to be built in one go, and you don't need every service on day one. The sensible way to start is to find the biggest bottleneck in your operations, fix that, and then move to the next one.

What matters most is working with a team that understands logistics, not just code. You can browse the industries iWebwiser serves to get a sense of their range, and the logistics case studies are a good place to see how similar problems have been handled before.

Final thoughts

Modern logistics is as much about information as it is about trucks and warehouses. The companies that invest in the right IT services, from custom software and mobile apps to analytics and automation, tend to deliver faster, waste less and keep customers longer. Pick one area, start small, and build from there.

title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
description:
arXiv:2611.17846v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.
