title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes
description:
arXiv:2611.17556v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.

title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
description: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

title: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
description:
arXiv:2611.17767v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256$\times$256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.

title: "What If Your CSS Compiler Could Catch Accessibility Bugs Before Production?"
description:
Modern frontend development has become increasingly sophisticated.

We have component-driven architectures, server components, powerful build tools, automated testing, design systems, and AI coding assistants.

Yet one problem remains surprisingly common:

We still discover many styling and accessibility problems too late.

A color combination fails contrast requirements. A component introduces duplicated CSS. A dark theme needs additional overrides. An RTL layout breaks because physical spacing properties were used. A styling engine adds work to the browser that could have been completed during the build.

What if your styling system could prevent these problems before your application ships?

That is the idea behind "traceless-style" (https://traceless-style.dev/).

It is an open-source, MIT-licensed, build-time atomic CSS library designed around three principles:

  • Zero-runtime styling for compiled style declarations.
  • Automated accessibility validation.
  • Intelligent styling diagnostics and transformations.

Let's explore what this approach looks like in practice.

  1. Move CSS work from runtime to build time

Traditional runtime CSS-in-JS approaches can involve generating class names, processing styles, maintaining caches, or inserting CSS rules while an application runs.

These operations are not necessarily expensive in every application, but they introduce work that may be avoidable.

traceless-style takes a different approach.

Instead of processing compiled styles in the browser, it transforms "tl.create()" calls during the build process into ordinary class-name strings.

For example:

import { tl } from "traceless-style";

const $ = tl.create({
card: {
padding: "1.5rem",
background: "#ffffff",
color: "#0f172a",
borderRadius: "12px",

_hover: {
  transform: "translateY(-2px)",
},

_dark: {
  background: "#13131a",
},

},
});

export function Card() {
return (


Build faster. Ship cleaner.

);
}

During compilation, the styling declaration is transformed into generated class names, while the corresponding atomic CSS rules are emitted into a static stylesheet.

The result:

  • No runtime styling engine for transformed declarations.
  • No runtime style injection for compiled styles.
  • Reusable atomic CSS rules.
  • Automatic deduplication of identical property-value combinations.
  • A stylesheet generated before production deployment.

The browser receives the compiled output rather than having to interpret the original styling object.

The central idea is simple: do the styling work before the user visits the application.

Technical explanation:
https://traceless-style.dev/docs/learn/01-introduction

  1. Accessibility should be part of the build process

This is where the project takes an interesting direction.

Accessibility is often handled through manual reviews, separate testing tools, or checks performed late in development.

But color contrast problems can be introduced by something as simple as changing a text color or background.

traceless-style includes build-time contrast validation based on WCAG requirements.

It checks relevant contrast requirements, including:

  • WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for normal text.
  • WCAG AAA: 7:1 for normal text.
  • UI component contrast requirements.
  • Focus-indicator contrast requirements.

It also provides APCA Lc readings as an additional perception-oriented measurement.

Consider this diagnostic example:

traceless-style build

✘ TLS0301 app/Button.tsx:24:7

WCAG 2.1 §1.4.3
AA 4.5:1 not met.

Foreground: #94a3b8
Background: #ffffff

Contrast ratio: 2.85:1

Suggested replacement: #475569
Contrast ratio: 7.55:1

Run with --fix-contrast to apply.

Instead of discovering the issue after deployment, developers can receive actionable feedback during the build process.

The interactive contrast-fixing workflow can also suggest alternative colors.

This changes the role of accessibility from a final checklist into part of the development workflow.

Important: automated contrast checks do not replace complete accessibility testing, keyboard testing, screen-reader testing, or evaluation with real users.

Documentation:
https://traceless-style.dev/docs

  1. Automatic dark mode without duplicating every color

Dark mode is easy to demonstrate and surprisingly easy to implement inconsistently.

A typical application may contain hundreds of components, each with different backgrounds, text colors, borders, and interactive states.

Maintaining all those variations manually can become difficult.

traceless-style can derive dark variants for colors during compilation, while allowing explicit overrides when necessary.

For example:

const $ = tl.create({
panel: {
background: "#ffffff",
color: "#0f172a",
borderRadius: "12px",

_dark: {
  background: "#13131a",
},

},
});

You can retain control over individual dark-mode decisions without manually duplicating every declaration.

The goal is to make theme support part of the styling architecture rather than a separate layer of repetitive CSS.

  1. RTL support built into the styling workflow

Global applications need more than English interfaces.

Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, and other right-to-left languages introduce additional layout requirements.

Developers frequently encounter problems when using physical CSS properties such as:

margin-left: 16px;
padding-right: 12px;

A layout designed around physical directions can become difficult to maintain across LTR and RTL interfaces.

traceless-style supports automatic RTL transformations by rewriting physical properties into logical CSS equivalents during compilation.

For example, a left-side margin can be transformed into its logical inline-start equivalent.

This is particularly useful for teams building multilingual applications and shared design systems.

One styling architecture can serve different writing directions without requiring developers to maintain separate copies of every component.

  1. Atomic CSS and stylesheet deduplication

Large applications often contain repeated styling declarations across many components.

Atomic CSS addresses this by representing individual CSS property-value combinations as reusable classes.

Imagine hundreds of components using:

display: flex;

Rather than repeatedly emitting identical declarations, the compiler can reuse the corresponding generated atomic rule.

traceless-style also provides:

  • "tl.defineTokens()" for design tokens.
  • "tl.createTheme()" for theme creation.
  • "tl.merge()" for style composition.
  • "tl.cx()" for class composition.
  • "tl.extend()" for reusable style extensions.
  • "tl.keyframes()" for animations.

This creates a more structured styling environment as an application grows.

  1. More than a CSS library: a developer tooling ecosystem

A modern developer tool should fit into the workflow developers already use.

The traceless-style ecosystem includes:

Compiler

Transforms styling declarations into generated atomic CSS during the build.

CLI

Provides commands for initialization, extraction, development, production builds, auditing, and inspection.

VS Code extension

Provides features including autocomplete, color swatches, hover documentation, and inline diagnostics.

Browser DevTools extension

Helps inspect generated styling classes in the browser.

Framework integrations

Supports environments including:

  • Next.js
  • Vite
  • Remix
  • Astro
  • SvelteKit
  • Qwik
  • Solid
  • Webpack
  • Rollup
  • esbuild

The objective is not simply to introduce another way to write CSS.

It is to create a connected workflow covering styling, compilation, validation, and debugging.

  1. Install it and try it in a real project

You can install traceless-style using npm:

npm install traceless-style

Or pnpm:

pnpm add traceless-style

Then initialize your project:

npx traceless-style init

Start the development workflow:

npx traceless-style dev

For production:

npx traceless-style build

You can also run the contrast-fixing workflow:

npx traceless-style --fix-contrast

The initialization command detects supported project frameworks and helps configure the integration.

No complicated setup process is required for the standard supported configurations.

Start with a small component, inspect the generated CSS, and evaluate the workflow in your own project.

  1. Why this approach matters as AI-assisted development grows

AI coding tools are changing how frontend applications are created.

Developers can now generate components, layouts, themes, and entire application interfaces much faster than before.

But generating code is not the same as generating reliable production-ready code.

AI-generated interfaces can still contain:

  • Poor color contrast.
  • Inconsistent design tokens.
  • Duplicated styling declarations.
  • Incorrect RTL behavior.
  • Unnecessary runtime styling work.

A build-time styling system with automated validation offers another layer of engineering discipline.

Instead of relying entirely on developers or AI assistants to remember every styling rule, the compiler can enforce defined constraints.

This is an interesting direction for the future of frontend infrastructure.

  1. Open source and developer contributions

traceless-style is released under the MIT license.

Developers can explore the implementation, evaluate its architecture, use it in their projects, and contribute improvements.

The project is actively documented through its official documentation and source repository.

Useful resources:

  • Official website: https://traceless-style.dev/
  • Documentation: https://traceless-style.dev/docs
  • Installation guide: https://traceless-style.dev/docs/learn/02-installation
  • npm package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/traceless-style
  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/sparkgoldentech/traceless-style
  • VS Code extension: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=SparkGoldenTech.traceless-style-vscode
  1. Let's discuss the future of CSS tooling

I would love to hear from frontend engineers, open-source maintainers, and developers working on large applications.

A few questions:

  1. Do you prefer build-time CSS compilation over runtime CSS-in-JS?
  2. Should accessibility validation be a mandatory part of every production build?
  3. Would automatic dark-mode and RTL transformations simplify your design system?
  4. How should CSS tooling evolve to support AI-generated interfaces?
  5. What would you improve in a zero-runtime styling architecture?

If you are interested in modern CSS architecture, frontend performance, accessibility engineering, or developer tooling, give traceless-style a try.

Install it. Test it against a real component. Inspect the generated output. Share your feedback.

Explore the project:

https://traceless-style.dev/

GitHub:
https://github.com/sparkgoldentech/traceless-style

npm:
https://www.npmjs.com/package/traceless-style

title: Agentic induction of common data elements and information extraction from sarcoma case report abstracts
description:
arXiv:2611.18506v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Common data elements (CDEs) support clinical data comparability but are usually defined manually. We investigated whether large language model agents could derive a CDE schema from sarcoma case report abstracts and apply it at scale. An agent proposed 72,909 candidate CDEs from 24,588 PubMed abstracts; agentic consolidation yielded 1,570 CDEs. We retained 53 supported by at least 50 abstracts and attempted evidence-linked extraction across the corpus. Processing succeeded for all retained CDEs in 79.2% of abstracts, including responses indicating non-mention. Two human reviewers approved 83.0% of retained CDEs for relevance, 67.9% for clarity, and 56.6% for correctness. In 100 sampled abstracts, exact agreement with the value extracted by the LLM was 94.9% among 1,116 pairs with a non-empty answer (abstract-level bootstrap 95% CI, 93.0-96.4%). Errors concentrated in anatomical and temporal fields. These findings support agent-assisted schema drafting followed by expert curation before large-scale extraction.

title: MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.17931v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.

title: Understanding the MERN Stack: A Complete Guide to Modern Full-Stack Web Development
description:
Introduction
Modern web development requires powerful, scalable, and efficient technologies to build interactive web applications. One of the most popular technology stacks used by developers today is the MERN Stack.

MERN is an acronym for four powerful JavaScript-based technologies: MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js. Together, these technologies provide a complete environment for developing full-stack web applications using JavaScript across both the frontend and backend.

The MERN Stack has gained popularity because of its flexibility, developer-friendly ecosystem, reusable components, and ability to build scalable applications.
What Is the MERN Stack?
The MERN Stack is a full-stack JavaScript technology stack consisting of four major technologies:

  1. MongoDB – Database Layer

MongoDB is a NoSQL document-oriented database that stores application data in flexible, JSON-like documents called BSON documents.

Unlike traditional relational databases, MongoDB does not require a fixed table structure. This makes it easier to manage dynamic application data.

Key features:

  • Flexible document-based data storage.
  • High scalability.
  • Efficient data retrieval.
  • Support for complex data structures.
  • Easy integration with Node.js.
  • Express.js – Backend Framework

Express.js is a lightweight and flexible web application framework built on top of Node.js.

It simplifies backend development by providing tools for handling HTTP requests, managing routes, implementing middleware, and building RESTful APIs.

Key features:

  • Routing and request handling.
  • Middleware integration.
  • REST API development.
  • Error-handling mechanisms.
  • Simplified server-side development.
  • React.js – Frontend Library

React.js is a JavaScript library used to build interactive and dynamic user interfaces.

It follows a component-based architecture, allowing developers to divide an application into smaller, reusable components.

Key features:

  • Component-based architecture.
  • Virtual DOM.
  • Reusable UI components.
  • State management.
  • Efficient rendering.
  • Node.js – Runtime Environment

Node.js is a JavaScript runtime environment that allows developers to execute JavaScript outside the browser.

It uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model, making it suitable for building scalable network applications.

Key features:

  • Asynchronous programming.
  • Non-blocking I/O.
  • Large npm package ecosystem.
  • Cross-platform compatibility.
  • Efficient server-side execution. How Does the MERN Stack Work? The four technologies work together to create a complete web application.

The general application workflow is:

  1. A user interacts with the React.js frontend.
  2. React sends an HTTP request to the backend API.
  3. Express.js receives and processes the request.
  4. Node.js executes the backend JavaScript code.
  5. The backend communicates with MongoDB when database operations are required.
  6. MongoDB returns the requested data.
  7. The backend sends a response to React.
  8. React updates the user interface with the received information. Advantages of the MERN Stack
  9. Single programming language: JavaScript can be used throughout the application.
  10. Open-source technologies: All four technologies have strong open-source ecosystems.
  11. Reusable components: React improves development efficiency through reusable UI components.
  12. Scalability: MongoDB and Node.js support applications with growing requirements.
  13. Large community: Developers can access extensive documentation, tutorials, and community support.
  14. Cost-effective development: The stack offers many free tools and libraries. Applications Built Using MERN The MERN Stack can be used to develop various types of applications, including:
  15. E-commerce platforms.
  16. Social networking applications.
  17. Learning management systems.
  18. Food delivery applications.
  19. Real-time chat applications.
  20. Content management systems.
  21. Portfolio websites.
  22. Business management dashboards. Conclusion The MERN Stack is a powerful choice for modern full-stack web development. Its JavaScript-based architecture, flexibility, scalability, and extensive ecosystem make it suitable for beginners as well as experienced developers.

By mastering MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js, developers can build complete web applications, from interactive user interfaces to secure backend systems and database management.

title: AI-aided Decision-Making in Education - Uncertainty, Explainability, and Human Responsibility
description:
arXiv:2611.17858v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based systems have become increasingly integrated into various aspects of everyday life, including education, understanding how these systems make decisions is of paramount importance. AI holds significant potential to enhance educational practices through the facilitation of personalized and adaptive learning, automation of assessment procedures, and assistance with administrative tasks. However, the opacity of AI-based decision-making in education (especially with deep learning and generative AI models) can hamper decision-making, especially when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect. In this chapter, we argue that three key principles (uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility) are essential for the legitimate use of AI in educational settings. Acknowledging the inherent uncertainties in AI-based decisions, analogous to those in human decision-making, is fundamental. Explainability is critical for ensuring that the functioning and outcomes of AI applications are transparent and comprehensible to both educators and learners. Furthermore, human responsibility is crucial, particularly in human decision-making, which remains indispensable across all stages of AI development and deployment. By examining these three principles, this chapter provides a comprehensive guide for stakeholders seeking to integrate AI thoughtfully and effectively into the educational system.

title: IP geolocation now covers more visitors at higher resolution
description:
IP geolocation on Vercel now resolves visitor locations with finer network granularity, delivering city-level data for nearly all requests and postal-code data for 90% of traffic.

Geolocation data is now refreshed more often, so locations keep up as IP ranges are reassigned and routing changes. This is enabled for all projects with no code or configuration changes required. Existing geolocation headers along with the geolocation() helper in @vercel/functions, return the same fields for Vercel Functions and Routing Middleware.

If you use geolocation for access controls, localization, or compliance, some visitors will now resolve to a different city or country, most often traffic from VPNs, hosting providers, and leased IP ranges:

  • Physical termination location:

    Subnets announced from a hosting provider in a different country than their regional internet registry (RIR) record now resolve to the data center where the traffic actually terminates.

  • Testing geo-dependent routes:

    Verify access rules against an IP's active network location rather than its static registry allocation.

Read the request headers documentation for all available geolocation headers and fields.

title: MamaReason: Unfinished Reasoning and Answer Recovery in Clinical Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.18264v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Answer continuation often returns a diagnosis already stated in unfinished clinical reasoning. We study this behavior in MamaReason, adapted from dense Gemma 4 31B, on MamaBench's 217 paired maternal and child-health presentations. An explicit-commitment extractor identifies a diagnosis in 75 of 94 failed RL first passes and 75 of 93 failed SFT first passes. The continuation matches that diagnosis in 67/75 RL cases and 58/75 SFT cases, using diagnosis strings alone. Reading these commitments without additional generation recovers 30 of the 40 RL pairs restored by continuation under the archived correctness labels. Recurrence controls distinguish routine mentions from repeated answer selection. An offline second-commitment trigger measures the tradeoff between earlier readout and paired accuracy. The resulting decomposition separates diagnostic content already present in a trace, completion of an accepted answer, and paired diagnostic correctness. For clinical language-model evaluation, these are distinct outcomes that become visible when the same reasoning trace is examined through multiple readouts.

title: Provable Cross-Modal Transfer of Hierarchical Concept Structure in CLIP Embeddings
description:
arXiv:2611.17671v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP are trained to align images and text, not to represent taxonomies. Yet empirical studies show that CLIP embeddings exhibit hierarchical structure aligned with the hierarchy of semantic concepts. A theoretical characterization of why such hierarchy emerges from a non-hierarchical objective remains open. In this paper, we formalize this phenomenon as Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), a geometric property whereby each non-leaf concept embedding is more similar to its descendants than to off-branch concepts. Empirically, we show that HAS holds approximately in raw images and randomly initialized CLIP image embeddings, while in text embeddings it holds approximately only after contrastive learning. To theoretically explain this asymmetry, we analyze an unconstrained features model in which the image embeddings are fixed and only the text embeddings are trained. At the global minimizer, the text-side HAS violation percentage at each node is at most the image-side HAS violation and near-violation percentage. The key mechanism is the hierarchical co-occurrence structure of image-text pairs, which biases text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes. For a linear contrastive loss, we derive a closed-form solution that makes this mechanism explicit. We extend the analysis to the InfoNCE loss and establish analogous guarantees under sufficient regularization. Synthetic experiments validate the theory and show that HAS is transferred even beyond the regimes covered by our analysis.

title: OpenTelemetry Java Agent 3.0 Migration: Kafka Dashboards
description:
Short answer: upgrading to the OpenTelemetry Java agent 3.0 can silently break Spring Boot Kafka dashboards and alerts, because Kafka spans move to new verb-style names such as poll orders. To migrate safely, inventory every query that depends on span names, emit old and new telemetry side by side, remap names in the Collector, canary one consumer group and lint alert queries in CI.

The incidents that cost me the most sleep made no noise at all. No crash, no page. One panel on a wall dashboard drew a flat line, and the first person to notice was a customer.

Swapping an observability agent version can produce exactly that. The OpenTelemetry Java agent 3.0 changes several telemetry defaults, including how Kafka work is named. I treat a major agent bump as a production change with its own inventory, canary and diff, the same way a schema migration would be handled, and not as a line in pom.xml.

Start here: what the agent actually does

Some vocabulary, kept short, since the rest of the post leans on it.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the CNCF project that standardises how applications emit traces, metrics and logs. A span is one timed unit of work, say a Kafka poll or an HTTP handler. A trace strings together the spans of one request as it crosses services. In Kafka, producers write to a named topic and consumers in a consumer group read from it.

The Java agent is a JAR passed with -javaagent at JVM start. It rewrites library classes as they load, so Spring MVC, Kafka clients and JDBC drivers emit spans with zero source changes. The convenience has a price: you never chose those span names, so you may not know how many dashboards quietly depend on them.

Every span carries a name and attributes (key-value facts such as topic or consumer group). Dashboards, alerts and sampling rules filter on those. Rename one and the filter matches nothing, with no error anywhere.

What changes in 3.0, and why Kafka is the loudest case

The agent follows the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions, the project's naming spec for spans, metrics and attributes. As the conventions evolve, the agent's output follows. In the 3.0 line, Kafka spans move to verb-first names: what used to appear as orders receive or orders process is now poll orders or process orders. Attribute keys move too. The kind of change to expect, based on the messaging conventions, looks like this:

Old shape (example) New shape (example)
span orders receive span poll orders
span orders process span process orders
messaging.kafka.consumer.group messaging.consumer.group.name
messaging.kafka.destination.partition messaging.destination.partition.id

Treat that table as an illustration of the pattern, not the authoritative list. I have not verified every row against the 3.0 build you will run, and the exact set depends on your instrumentation versions, so diff real spans (Step 4) and read the release notes before you write anything into a runbook.

Why Kafka hurts most, in practice:

  1. Event-driven systems are watched through message-path spans, which are the ones renamed. A Grafana Tempo query like { name = "orders process" && resource.service.name = "orders-consumer" } simply returns an empty set after the upgrade.
  2. Lag and processing-time alerts are frequently built from span-derived metrics (a spanmetrics connector, for instance), such as duration_milliseconds_bucket{span_name="orders process"}. The series stops being written under that label, and the alert expression evaluates to nothing.
  3. A consumer has no user waiting on it, so nobody complains when its alert goes blind. The silence can last days.

Kafka share groups will reshape consumer topology again; I covered that in Kafka share groups in Spring Boot payment pipelines. Whatever contract file you build below should survive that change as well.

On an airline platform handling roughly 130 million requests a day, I once watched a latency chart that had not broken at all. A refactor had changed what its query matched, so it was now averaging a smaller, calmer population of spans, and a retry storm sat unnoticed for most of a weekend. In payments work under PSD2 the stakes are sharper. Regulators do not mandate alerting on span names, but if your fraud or settlement alert depended on one and silently stopped, you would struggle to explain your monitoring story afterwards. If the pipeline moves money, treat telemetry names as an interface. The tracing setup underneath is in distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry in Spring Boot; this post covers what happens when the agent changes beneath it.

The failure modes, ordered by how often they bite

After a rename like this, these are the things that break:

  • Dashboards filtered by span name. A panel plotting p95 of orders process drops to zero or "no data".
  • Alert rules on span-derived metrics or trace queries. They fail open: most alert engines treat "no data" as healthy unless told otherwise.
  • Trace-based SLOs. An SLO of "good spans over total spans" with a name filter returns 100 percent on an empty set, or divides by zero, depending on the tool.
  • Tail-sampling policies. A rule that keeps every trace containing an error span with a given name stops matching. Or the catch-all keeps everything and your storage bill climbs.
  • Recording rules and exemplars that derive labels from span names.
  • Saved searches that the on-call engineer opens at 3 a.m.

The last one gets missed every time, because nobody tracks saved searches in a repo. The same name-dependency applies to AI-service dashboards, which my notes on observability and guardrails for agentic AI backends discuss.

The migration playbook

This is the sequence I would run for a Spring Boot 4 fleet on Kubernetes.

Step 1: Inventory everything that depends on names or attributes

Before changing a version, extract the list from source rather than from memory.

  • Export dashboards as JSON and grep for span names, attribute keys and metric names.
  • Export alert rules, recording rules and SLO definitions.
  • Pull tail-sampling and filter configs from the Collector repo.
  • Search application code for hand-written span names and for code that reads attributes (some teams branch on messaging.destination.name).
  • Ask on-call engineers for their saved searches.

Per item, note what it matches, who owns it, and what happens when it matches nothing. The last column is the useful one: "pages the on-call" and "feeds a weekly report" deserve very different urgency.

A rough script gets you most of the way:

# Find every dashboard/alert artefact that mentions Kafka-derived span names or attributes
grep -rEn "(\b(receive|process|publish)\b orders|messaging\.(kafka|destination|operation)|kafka\.)" \
  observability/dashboards observability/alerts observability/slo collector/ \
  | sort | tee inventory-kafka-names.txt
wc -l inventory-kafka-names.txt

It is crude, but a crude list you actually have beats a careful plan with no list.

Step 2: Prefer dual-emit or an opt-in flag over a hard cutover

OpenTelemetry has a convention for these transitions: a stability opt-in that keeps the old shape, emits the new one, or emits both for a while. For HTTP and database conventions this is the OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN environment variable, which has a duplicate-emit value. Whether the Kafka and messaging spans in 3.0 sit behind that same switch or an agent-specific property is something to confirm in the release notes for your exact version.

What matters is the goal: old and new telemetry present together, in the same backend, for the same requests. That turns the migration into a comparison.

I set it in the Deployment so the change is reviewable and revertable like any other config:

env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar"
  - name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
    value: "orders-consumer"
  # Confirm the exact opt-in value for messaging in the 3.0 release notes
  - name: OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN
    value: "<dual-emit value from release notes>"
  - name: OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES
    value: "agent.rollout=canary-v3"

The rollout attribute is deliberate. Tagging telemetry with its cohort lets every query and diff split canary from baseline.

If there is no dual mode for a particular rename, the next step covers it.

Step 3: Remap names in the Collector during the transition

The OpenTelemetry Collector is a standalone service that receives telemetry, processes it and forwards it. Its transform processor rewrites span names and attributes with OTTL (OpenTelemetry Transformation Language).

Choose a direction. I remap new to old first, so existing dashboards work on day one, then migrate dashboards at a calm pace and delete the remap last. Going old to new would force every query to change before the upgrade, which is the cutover we are avoiding.

processors:
  transform/kafka_compat:
    error_mode: ignore
    trace_statements:
      - context: span
        statements:
          # "poll orders" -> "orders receive" ; "$$" escapes "$" in Collector config
          - replace_pattern(name, "^poll (.+)$", "$$1 receive") where attributes["agent.rollout"] == "canary-v3"
          # "process orders" -> "orders process"
          - replace_pattern(name, "^process (.+)$", "$$1 process") where attributes["agent.rollout"] == "canary-v3"
          # Keep a breadcrumb so we can query what was remapped
          - set(attributes["compat.remapped"], true) where attributes["agent.rollout"] == "canary-v3"

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, transform/kafka_compat, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp]

Three lessons from getting burned. Test OTTL against recorded spans before deploying, because error_mode: ignore turns a typo into the same silent failure we are fighting. Add the compat.remapped breadcrumb and graph it, so you can watch it fall to zero as dashboards migrate. And do the remap in the Collector, not in the app, so a rollback needs no application redeploy.

Metrics need care too. If span names feed a span-metrics connector, the remap must run before that connector sees them. Otherwise your derived metrics carry new names while your alerts still ask for the old ones.

Step 4: Canary with diffed span output

Most teams skip this step, and it is the one that pays off.

Run the new agent on a small slice of one consumer group, for example one pod in twelve on a non-critical topic, with the others on the old agent. Kafka partitions are shared across the pods of a group, so canary and baseline process comparable work in the same window. You get a natural experiment for free.

Then compare mechanically:

  1. Export a few thousand spans per cohort (a Collector file exporter or a backend query).
  2. Normalise: drop trace IDs, timestamps and durations.
  3. Group by (span name, kind, sorted attribute keys) and count.
  4. Diff the two sets. 
import json, collections, sys

def shape(path):
    c = collections.Counter()
    for line in open(path):
        s = json.loads(line)
        key = (s["name"], s["kind"], tuple(sorted(s["attributes"].keys())))
        c[key] += 1
    return c

old, new = shape(sys.argv[1]), shape(sys.argv[2])
for k in sorted(set(old) | set(new)):
    if (k in old) != (k in new):
        side = "ONLY-OLD" if k in old else "ONLY-NEW"
        print(side, k)

Every line of output is either an expected rename from your inventory or a surprise, and the surprises are the point. This is how I would catch renamed attributes, dropped attributes and extra spans that skimming a changelog would never surface.

Compare behaviour as well as shape: error rate, spans per message and consumer lag across cohorts. An agent upgrade can change overhead or how context travels in message headers. If a trace that used to cover producer and consumer now splits into two unrelated traces, find out before 100 percent of traffic is on it. Propagation matters even more through an outbox; see transactional outbox and idempotent consumers.

Let the canary live through a peak, not a quiet afternoon. On the live market-data systems I run, behaviour at the open looks nothing like midday, and an observability change deserves judging under the load you fear. The same reasoning drives my deterministic market-data replay engine on QuestDB.

Step 5: Lint alert queries in CI

Manual diligence decays, so make the pipeline refuse alert rules that reference telemetry nobody emits.

Keep a contract file listing the span names, metric names and attribute keys your rules may use. Generate it from the Step 4 diff or from staging. A CI job then parses every dashboard and alert definition and fails on anything outside the contract.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/lint-alert-names.sh: fail if any alert references a name outside the telemetry contract
set -euo pipefail
allowed=$(cat observability/telemetry-contract.txt)
status=0
for f in observability/alerts/*.yaml; do
  # pull quoted tokens that look like span or metric names
  for name in $(grep -oE '"[a-z_.]+ [a-z_.-]+"|span_name="[^"]+"' "$f" | tr -d '"' ); do
    if ! grep -qxF "$name" <<<"$allowed"; then
      echo "UNKNOWN TELEMETRY NAME in $f: $name"; status=1
    fi
  done
done
exit $status

A production version should parse PromQL properly instead of grepping, but even this blunt tool catches the common case. Add a synthetic canary alert too: push one message through staging and assert the expected alert condition becomes reachable. That tests the whole chain, not only the strings.

Last, check how each alert treats "no data". Making critical rules fire on absence is a cheap guard against the flat-line failure this post opened with.

A rollout timeline I would use

Phase Action Exit condition
Week 0 Inventory, contract file, CI lint added on the old agent Lint passes; inventory owners assigned
Week 1 Canary one non-critical consumer with dual-emit and Collector shim Span diff has zero unexplained entries
Week 2 Widen canary to one critical service during peak Alerts, SLO values and lag match baseline
Weeks 3 to 4 Roll out service by service, migrate dashboards to new names compat.remapped count trending to zero
Week 5 Remove shim and dual-emit; update contract CI lint passes on new names only

The upgrade itself is one row's worth of work. Everything else is the scaffolding around it.

Spring Boot 4 specifics worth checking

Spring Boot 4 ships Micrometer-based observability of its own. If you run both the Java agent and Spring's native instrumentation, confirm which one produces the Kafka spans, because duplicates or clashing names after an upgrade are common. Pick one owner per library and disable the other. If a framework upgrade also moved your HTTP clients, the notes in my RestClient migration guide apply: outbound span names can shift when the client does.

Also check resource attributes such as service.name and k8s.* metadata. They are outside the Kafka rename, but bumping the agent and the Collector together can alter them, and every dashboard variable depends on them.

What I would tell a team lead

The playbook costs roughly a week of part-time work for one engineer. Discovering mid-incident that an alert has been blind since the upgrade costs customer trust and, in regulated finance, audit findings. Under DORA and NIS2 a monitoring gap is something an assessor will ask about, which is why I file the contract file under compliance evidence as code for Spring Boot and Kubernetes. I would spend the week every time. More of the systems I have run are on my experience page, and the projects section shows the live market-data work where observability choices get tested daily.

The short version

  • Inventory every query, alert, SLO and sampling rule that depends on span names or attributes.
  • Prefer dual-emit or the documented stability opt-in so old and new telemetry coexist.
  • Use the Collector transform processor to remap new names to old while consumers migrate.
  • Canary one cohort, diff span shapes and compare behaviour under peak load.
  • Lint alert queries against a telemetry contract in CI, and treat "no data" as a failure state.

Do the first one today: run the Step 1 grep against your dashboards and alerts repository, open the output file, and assign an owner to every line before anyone bumps the agent version. If you want a second pair of hands designing the canary for your own fleet, reach me through the contact section.

FAQ

Will OpenTelemetry Java agent 3.0 break my Kafka dashboards?

It can. Kafka spans move to verb-style names such as poll orders and process orders, so any panel, alert or SLO filtering on the old names may return no data. Check the 3.0 release notes for your instrumentation versions and run the inventory before upgrading.

How do I keep old span names while migrating?

Use the documented stability opt-in to emit both shapes if it covers messaging, and add a Collector transform processor that remaps new names back to old ones. Remove the shim once every dashboard and alert uses the new names.

How do I test an agent upgrade in Kubernetes?

Canary one pod of a consumer group on the new agent, tag its telemetry with a rollout attribute, export spans from both cohorts and diff the span shapes. Run it through a peak period before widening.

How do I stop alerts from silently going blind?

Keep a telemetry contract file, lint every alert query against it in CI, and set critical alerts to fire on missing data instead of treating absence as healthy.

Related Articles

  • Distributed Tracing with OpenTelemetry in Spring Boot Production
  • Transactional Outbox and Idempotent Consumers for Spring Boot Payment Systems
  • Spring Boot 4.2 RestTemplate Deprecation: Migrating to RestClient and HTTP Interface Clients

title: Is robots.txt enough to let AI crawlers in? (Usually not)
description:
More sites now ask a simple question: can ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity actually read my pages? Most people open robots.txt, see nothing scary, and stop there. That check is not enough.

Two layers can block an AI crawler

  1. robots.txt. A Disallow rule for a user agent like GPTBot or PerplexityBot. Polite crawlers respect it.
  2. The firewall or CDN. Cloudflare's "Block AI bots" toggle, a host's bot protection, or a WordPress security plugin. These return a 403 to the crawler no matter what robots.txt says.

The second layer is invisible if you only read robots.txt. Your file says "allowed", the bot gets blocked anyway, and you never find out.

Training bots vs search bots

Blocking every AI crawler is rarely what people actually want. The user agents fall into three groups:

Type Examples Block it and...
Training GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, CCBot your pages aren't used to train models. You can still appear in AI answers.
AI search OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot you usually disappear from that tool's answers.
User request ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, Perplexity-User the AI can't open your page when a user asks it to.

So a common setup is "search yes, training no": allow the search and user-request bots, disallow the training bots.

User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
User-agent: ChatGPT-User
User-agent: Claude-SearchBot
User-agent: PerplexityBot
Allow: /

User-agent: GPTBot
User-agent: ClaudeBot
User-agent: Google-Extended
User-agent: CCBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: *
Allow: /

I keep the full list of 20 user agents and three ready-made templates in a small open repo: ai-crawlers-robots-txt on GitHub.

Testing the firewall layer yourself

You can fake a crawler's request with curl and look at the status code:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -A "Mozilla/5.0 AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko; compatible; GPTBot/1.2; +https://openai.com/gptbot)" \
  https://yoursite.com/

A 200 means the request got through. A 403 or a challenge page means something in front of your site is blocking that user agent. Repeat with OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot and ClaudeBot.

One caveat: some CDNs verify real crawlers by IP, so a spoofed user agent can be treated differently from the real bot. It's still a quick way to catch the most common problem, a blanket "block AI bots" rule.

What two big sites look like

On 16 Nov 2026 I ran both layers against two well-known sites:

  • nytimes.com: only 4 of 20 AI bots allowed in robots.txt, and only 2 of 9 live test requests got through. A deliberate choice for a publisher.
  • hubspot.com: all 20 allowed and all 9 live requests got through.

If you're a business that wants to be recommended by AI tools, your result should look like the second one.

A faster check

If you don't want to script it, we built a free checker at CodedSEO that does both layers for 20 bots and also looks for llms.txt: AI Visibility Checker. No sign-up.

Either way, check the firewall, not just the file.

title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
description:
arXiv:2611.17461v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.

title: Ten Uniface forms without painting a single field - generating the XML instead
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 had grown to more than a hundred services for sales: products, prices, quotes, orders, invoices, payments, dunning, deliveries, subscriptions, bank statements. None of it had a user interface yet. The next stage was ten new forms with between 11 and 58 fields each - 310 fields in total - plus one new button in the existing main menu.

Painting 310 fields one by one in the form painter is slow, and it is hard to keep a consistent layout. The IDE can export and import repository objects as XML, so the forms were generated as XML and imported instead. This article shows how that worked, what the form picture inside the XML looks like, and the one mistake that crashed the IDE.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. Paths are shortened to C:\Projects\CustomerApp\.

Start from a real export

The safest template is a form that already works. In the IDE, the menu at the top right (≡) has Export and Import XML.... Exporting one existing modal form gave a file with three tables:

Table Content
UFORM one occurrence: the form itself, with USCRIPT (the ProcScript), UDECLARATIONS (component variables), window size and FORMPIC
UXGROUP one occurrence per entity painted on the form
UXFIELD one occurrence per field: widget type, label, initial value, field script

The forms in this app all follow the same pattern: a non-database dummy entity (PRD_DMY.NOMODEL, DOC_DMY.NOMODEL, ...), labels as non-editable fields, single-line and multi-line edit boxes, and command buttons whose detail trigger calls an entry in the form script:

trigger detail
    call DO_SAVE
end

So the generator only needs four field kinds. It takes one field occurrence of each kind from the exported template and changes the name, the label, and for buttons the trigger script.

The form picture is text

The interesting part is FORMPIC. It is not binary; it is a text picture of the form, one line per row, and every painted object is a token. The entity token looks like this:

&uFRM;TYP=E&uSEP;NAM=PRD_DMY.NOMODEL&uSEP;WID=96&uSEP;HEI=32&uSEP;HOC=96&uSEP;VOC=32&uFRM;

and a field token like this:

&uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_SAVE&uSEP;WID=16&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;

The position of a token is its column in the line. WID and HEI are the size in characters and rows. In the template, line 0 was empty, line 1 started with six spaces and the entity token, and the fields followed in the lines below.

The generator builds that picture from a list of rows. This is the code that was used for all ten forms (Python):

def token_e(name, wid, hei):
    return '&uFRM;TYP=E&uSEP;NAM=%s&uSEP;WID=%d&uSEP;HEI=%d&uSEP;HOC=%d&uSEP;VOC=%d&uFRM;' % (name, wid, hei, wid, hei)
def token_f(name, wid, hei):
    return '&uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=%s&uSEP;WID=%d&uSEP;HEI=%d&uFRM;' % (name, wid, hei)
def formpic(ent, ewid, ehei, fields):
    rows = {}
    for f in fields:
        rows.setdefault(f['row'], []).append(f)
    lines = ['', '      ' + token_e(ent + '.NOMODEL', ewid, ehei)]
    maxrow = max(f['row'] + f['h'] - 1 for f in fields)
    for r in range(1, maxrow + 1):
        line = ''
        cur = 0
        for f in sorted(rows.get(r, []), key=lambda x: x['col']):
            c = f['col'] + 6
            assert c >= cur, (f['name'], c, cur)
            line += ' ' * (c - cur) + token_f(f['name'], f['w'], f['h'])
            cur = c + f['w']
        lines.append(line)

(The function ends by joining the lines with line breaks; the XML writer escapes & and writes the file as UTF-8 with BOM and CRLF, like the export.)

A layout is then just a list. This is the first block of the product form:

build('PRODUCT_FRM', 'PRD_DMY', [
 (1, [('LBL_SEARCH', L, 14), ('SEARCH', E, 30), ('BTN_SEARCH', B, 12), ('BTN_SEARCH_ALL', B, 24)]),
 (2, [('RESULT', M, 92, 8)]),
 ...

The + 6 that crashed the IDE

The first version did not have + 6. It placed the first field of each row at column 2 - which looked right, because in the painter the fields start just inside the entity frame.

The import reported success. Opening the form in the IDE did not:

Unhandled Exception
Error code  -100000   Description  Coding error
ERROR -10104  <UINTERNALERROR>  Internal error
COMPONENT UC_CPT   PROCNAME 109\GETPAINT   PROCLINE interrupt 22, FORMPIC.UFORM

The details pointed straight at FORMPIC. Comparing the generated picture with the template showed the difference: the entity token starts at column 6, and in the template the fields start at column 8. Column 2 put every field to the left of its own entity frame. The IDE does not validate that on import; it fails later, when it paints the form.

The dialog offers Exit and Ignore. Exit plus a restart of the IDE was the clean way out. After the fix (field columns relative to the entity, + 6), the corrected XML was imported over the broken form and opened normally.

Two lessons from this:

  • An import that succeeds is not a form that works. Always open and compile the imported object straight away.
  • Check the generator against a real export, not against your idea of the format.

A round-trip test for the generator

The second lesson became a test. A small parser reads the FORMPIC of the exported template back into a field list (name, row, column, width, height). Feeding that list into formpic() must give the original picture back, character for character. After the column fix, the round trip for the template form was identical. If the generator ever drifts from what the IDE writes, this test notices before the IDE does.

What else needed care

  • Button labels. The template's buttons all had the initial value "Button text". The forms set their labels in an entry SET_LABELS called from exec, so the XML did not need a label per button.
  • Default field triggers. Edit fields in the template carried a default onEdit trigger script. The generator drops it; the forms don't need it.
  • The import dialog. It sometimes closed itself after an import and sometimes stayed open. Typing the next file name without checking the dialog first sent the text into whatever had focus - once the open script editor. Check the dialog before typing.
  • Compile every form after import. Each of the ten forms (and the changed main menu) compiled with 0 errors and one warning: 1016, the dummy entity is not in the application model. That warning is expected for non-database entities.

Result

Ten forms, 310 fields, all generated from layout lists and the ProcScript source files. When a form needed a change - a label, a new button, a bug fix in the script - the source file changed, the XML was generated again and imported over the old form. After every import, the script in the repository was compared with the source file; all of them were identical.

The XML route does not replace the painter for a form that needs careful visual design. For many similar forms with a fixed pattern, it turned a lot of clicking into a list per form, and it made the layout reviewable as text.

title: Building an Offline-First Field App That Survives Weak Connectivity
description:
A field application should not stop working when the network disappears.

That sounds obvious. Yet many mobile apps still depend on a successful API response for every inspection, delivery update, equipment reading, photo, and customer signature.

This approach may work in an office. It fails inside warehouses, mechanical rooms, industrial sites, loading yards, and remote service areas.

Houston companies in logistics, construction, energy, maintenance, and field services face this problem regularly. Their teams need to complete work wherever the job takes them, not only where a stable connection is available.

This article explains a practical offline-first architecture for that situation.

Start With the Failure Scenario

Consider a technician completing an equipment inspection.

The technician selects a work order, enters measurements, adds notes, takes three photos, records a customer signature, and taps Complete.

At that moment, the connection drops.

A network-dependent app may show an error and ask the technician to repeat the process. A poorly designed app may lose the inspection entirely.

An offline-first app handles the same event differently. It saves the inspection on the device immediately, marks it as waiting for synchronization, and uploads it when a suitable connection becomes available.

The user can move to the next job without waiting.

Treat the Local Database as the Immediate Source of Truth

The interface should read from a local database instead of waiting for the server every time a screen opens.

SQLite is a practical option for structured mobile data. Depending on the platform, teams may use Room on Android, Core Data or SwiftData on iOS, Drift in Flutter, or another persistence layer.

A simplified work-order record could look like this:

CREATE TABLE work_orders (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    notes TEXT,
    version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    sync_status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'synced',
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

When the technician updates a work order, the application writes the change locally first.

async function completeWorkOrder(
  workOrderId: string,
  notes: string
): Promise<void> {
  await database.transaction(async tx => {
    await tx.execute(
      `UPDATE work_orders
       SET status = ?,
           notes = ?,
           sync_status = ?,
           updated_at = ?
       WHERE id = ?`,
      [
        "completed",
        notes,
        "pending",
        new Date().toISOString(),
        workOrderId
      ]
    );

    await tx.execute(
      `INSERT INTO sync_outbox
       (id, entity_type, entity_id, operation, created_at)
       VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)`,
      [
        crypto.randomUUID(),
        "work_order",
        workOrderId,
        "update",
        new Date().toISOString()
      ]
    );
  });
}

The transaction matters. It prevents the app from updating the work order without also recording the operation that must reach the server.

Use an Outbox for Pending Changes

A single isSynced field may work for a small prototype. It becomes difficult to manage when users create, update, and delete several records while offline.

An outbox stores every pending operation explicitly.

CREATE TABLE sync_outbox (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    entity_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    entity_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    operation TEXT NOT NULL,
    attempt_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    last_error TEXT,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    processed_at TEXT
);

The synchronization worker reads unprocessed operations in order and sends them to the backend.

This design makes failed requests visible. It also allows the app to retry one operation without resending every local record.

Make API Requests Idempotent

Mobile clients cannot always determine whether a request failed before or after the server processed it.

Imagine that the server saves an inspection, but the connection drops before the app receives the response. The app retries the request and accidentally creates a duplicate.

An idempotency key prevents this.

POST /api/inspections
Idempotency-Key: 7d80b65c-99af-4e95-a107-936fa748d302
Content-Type: application/json

The backend stores the key with the completed operation.

async function createInspection(request, response) {
  const key = request.headers["idempotency-key"];

  const previousResult = await idempotencyStore.find(key);

  if (previousResult) {
    return response.status(200).json(previousResult);
  }

  const inspection = await inspectionService.create(request.body);

  await idempotencyStore.save(key, inspection);

  return response.status(201).json(inspection);
}

If the client sends the same request again, the server returns the original result instead of creating another inspection.

Use Client-Generated IDs

Waiting for the server to generate an ID creates unnecessary dependence on connectivity.

The mobile app can generate a UUID when a record is created locally.

const inspection = {
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  workOrderId,
  status: "draft",
  createdAt: new Date().toISOString()
};

That ID can be used immediately by related notes, photos, checklist responses, and signatures.

When synchronization begins, the backend accepts the existing identifier.

Handle Conflicts Deliberately

Offline work creates an important question: what happens if two people edit the same record?

There is no universal conflict strategy. The correct choice depends on the data.

For ordinary notes, the system may accept the most recent edit. For inventory quantities, blindly accepting the last update could produce an incorrect count. For regulated inspections, both versions may need to be preserved.

Version numbers provide a simple way to detect conflicts.

PATCH /api/work-orders/WO-1048
If-Match: 12

If the server still has version 12, it accepts the update and returns version 13. If another user has already created version 13, the server returns a conflict.

{
  "error": "version_conflict",
  "serverVersion": 13,
  "clientVersion": 12
}

The app can then refresh the record, merge safe fields, or ask the user to review the conflict.

The important point is that conflict behavior must be defined before development. It should not be left to whichever API response happens to arrive last.

Separate Record Sync From File Uploads

Photos, videos, documents, and signatures need a different synchronization path from ordinary JSON data.

A field app should save the file locally, create a file record, and upload the binary content separately. The work order should not remain blocked while a large photo uploads over a weak connection.

A common flow is:

Capture file
    ↓
Save encrypted local copy
    ↓
Create upload record
    ↓
Request signed upload URL
    ↓
Upload file in resumable chunks
    ↓
Confirm upload with backend
    ↓
Attach uploaded asset to work order

The interface should show whether each file is saved locally, uploading, failed, or synchronized.

Compression also matters. Uploading a full-resolution image from a modern phone may waste time and mobile data when the business only needs a readable inspection photo.

Schedule Background Synchronization Carefully

On Android, persistent synchronization can use WorkManager. Google recommends it for work that should continue reliably after the app leaves the visible state, exits, or the device restarts. It also supports network constraints and exponential retry policies. See the official Android background-task documentation.

val constraints = Constraints.Builder()
    .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED)
    .build()

val syncRequest = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
    .setConstraints(constraints)
    .setBackoffCriteria(
        BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL,
        30,
        TimeUnit.SECONDS
    )
    .build()

WorkManager.getInstance(context)
    .enqueueUniqueWork(
        "field-data-sync",
        ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP,
        syncRequest
    )

Apple provides Background Tasks APIs for scheduling eligible background work on iOS. The operating system decides when that work may run, so the application should never assume that background synchronization will begin immediately. See Apple’s BGTaskScheduler documentation.

Flutter’s official offline-first architecture guide also recommends combining local and remote data behind a repository. This keeps connectivity decisions away from the user interface.

The app should attempt synchronization after a local change, when connectivity returns, when the app becomes active, and through platform-approved background work. It should also provide a manual Sync action for urgent field situations.

Retry Without Overloading the Server

A failed operation should not retry continuously.

Use exponential backoff with jitter:

function retryDelay(attempt: number): number {
  const maximum = 15 * 60 * 1000;
  const exponential = Math.min(1000 * 2 ** attempt, maximum);
  const jitter = Math.random() * 1000;

  return exponential + jitter;
}

This produces longer delays after repeated failures and prevents thousands of devices from reconnecting at exactly the same moment after an outage.

Permanent errors must be separated from temporary ones. A timeout may be retried. An invalid record or expired authorization token needs a different recovery path.

Make Synchronization Visible

Do not hide every synchronization detail from the user.

A field employee should be able to see whether a job is saved, waiting to sync, currently uploading, synchronized, or blocked by an error.

Useful interface states include:

Saved on this device
Waiting for connection
Syncing 3 changes
Last synced at 2:14 PM
Action required: customer record was updated elsewhere

These messages build trust. A generic spinner does not.

Measure the Sync System

Application monitoring should include more than API response time and crash rate.

Track the age of the oldest pending operation, the number of queued operations per device, successful sync duration, retry counts, conflict frequency, upload failure rate, and records that remain unsynchronized beyond an expected period.

These measurements reveal problems that ordinary backend dashboards miss.

A healthy API can still support an unhealthy field application if devices are carrying hours of unsynchronized work.

Protect Data Stored on the Device

Offline capability increases the amount of business information stored locally.

Store only the data a worker needs. Encrypt sensitive records and files. Keep authentication tokens in platform-protected storage. Remove completed jobs after the required retention period. Clear company data when a managed session is revoked.

Healthcare, financial, and regulated field applications may require stronger controls, including audit trails, role-based access, remote session termination, and restrictions on screenshots or file sharing.

Security should be designed with the offline workflow, not added after synchronization is complete.

Test the Network Conditions Users Actually Face

A successful test on office Wi-Fi proves very little.

Test airplane mode, unstable cellular service, slow uploads, interrupted file transfers, expired sessions, process termination, device restarts, low storage, duplicate submissions, clock differences, and two users editing the same job.

Also test older devices. A field application may run on rugged tablets and mid-range Android phones rather than the newest hardware used by the development team.

The most valuable test is simple: begin a real workflow online, lose the connection halfway through, finish the task, close the application, restart the device, reconnect, and verify that every record reaches the server exactly once.

A Practical Architecture for Houston Field Operations

Offline-first development is not about adding a cache to an otherwise online application. It changes how the mobile client, database, API, background workers, file storage, authentication, and user interface cooperate.

For Houston logistics carriers, energy contractors, warehouse operators, maintenance teams, and field-service businesses, that difference determines whether an app supports operations or interrupts them.

At AppVerticals, we apply these patterns when planning custom app development for products that must keep working beyond reliable office networks. Teams evaluating mobile app development in Houston should define offline workflows, conflict rules, retry behavior, and recovery requirements before choosing a framework.

The framework matters. The failure model matters more.

title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
description:
arXiv:2611.17620v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
description:
arXiv:2611.17532v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.17681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.
