Each cycle improves both the technical interface and the confidence of adopters.

For a robotics company, contributing an interface developed internally can also reduce long-term integration burden. If customers, partners, fleet platforms, and other robot manufacturers adopt compatible contracts, fewer custom adapters are required. The company can continue differentiating through hardware, autonomy, AI, performance, and application capability while using common interfaces for functions that provide little competitive value when implemented differently.

The broader lesson is that open-source API standardization is not simply code publication. It combines domain modeling, precise semantics, machine-readable schemas, reference implementations, security and safety boundaries, version governance, conformance testing, documentation, licensing, and community collaboration. The quality of the ecosystem depends on how consistently these elements are maintained after initial release.

A mature contribution creates a stable interoperability layer between heterogeneous robots and the software systems that coordinate them. Robots from different generations and vendors can expose common operational concepts, while specialized capabilities remain available through controlled extensions. This balance between a stable core and extensibility allows the standard to grow without forcing every robot into an identical architecture.

When maintained through transparent governance and real deployment feedback, an open robot API can evolve from a company-specific interface into shared infrastructure for the robotics ecosystem. The result is lower integration cost, more portable fleet software, clearer compatibility expectations, faster development of multi-vendor applications, and a stronger foundation for scalable robotic systems that must operate across organizations, technologies, and product generations.

12.10 Future Robot API Standardization and Strategy

Future robot API standardization must evolve from simple message interoperability toward a shared operational architecture for heterogeneous autonomous systems. Robots are increasingly connected to fleet managers, AI services, digital twins, enterprise platforms, smart infrastructure, and cloud-edge environments. Future standards must therefore describe not only how data is exchanged, but also how capabilities, missions, states, policies, security, and lifecycle information are interpreted consistently across systems.

A central strategy is to separate stable semantic models from rapidly changing communication technologies. REST, gRPC, MQTT, WebSocket, DDS, and future protocols may coexist or change over time, while concepts such as robot identity, mission, task, action, pose, capability, energy state, fault, and execution result should remain comparatively stable. Standardization should focus first on shared meaning and then provide multiple protocol bindings for different deployment environments.

The future API model should adopt a layered structure rather than attempting to create one universal interface for every robotic function. A stable core can define common robot resources, mission lifecycle, state reporting, diagnostics, capabilities, and security metadata. Domain profiles can extend this foundation for mobile robots, manipulators, drones, inspection systems, healthcare robots, construction equipment, and other specialized platforms without fragmenting the common ecosystem.

Capability-driven interaction will become increasingly important as fleets become heterogeneous. Applications should not assume functionality from a manufacturer name or robot model. A robot should advertise supported actions, payload limits, sensors, mobility modes, docking interfaces, manipulation functions, localization technologies, AI services, and optional extensions through machine-readable capability descriptions. Clients can then construct missions according to actual available functions.

Mission APIs will also need to evolve from simple destination commands toward composable task models. Future missions may combine navigation, manipulation, perception, inspection, human interaction, charging, waiting, data collection, and conditional execution. Standard task primitives can provide interoperability, while vendors retain freedom to implement planning, control, optimization, and autonomy internally. This preserves innovation beneath a stable operational contract.

The boundary between robot APIs and fleet APIs should remain explicit. A robot interface describes the capabilities and state of an individual machine, while a fleet interface manages assignment, traffic, scheduling, shared resources, and coordination among many robots. Standardization should define how these layers interact without forcing every manufacturer to expose internal planning algorithms or adopt an identical fleet architecture.

Multi-vendor fleet interoperability will remain a major strategic requirement. Warehouses, hospitals, factories, airports, campuses, and smart cities may operate robots from several suppliers over long service periods. Common mission semantics, capability discovery, state models, traffic coordination interfaces, and conformance profiles can reduce dependence on proprietary integrations and allow fleet systems to coordinate heterogeneous machines more predictably.

Cloud-edge hybrid operation should become a first-class part of API standards. Real-time safety and motion remain onboard, site-level coordination and low-latency services operate at the edge, while cloud systems provide cross-site analytics, model management, long-term storage, and global administration. Standard APIs should define how missions, telemetry, events, configurations, software, and AI models move across these boundaries while preserving local operation during network disruption.

Offline and degraded operation therefore require standardized semantics. APIs should distinguish unavailable, disconnected, degraded, paused, failed, and safely operating states rather than representing every communication problem as a generic error. Store-and-forward behavior, command expiration, synchronization, conflict resolution, and data ownership should be defined so that distributed robotic systems can reconnect without creating ambiguous operational states.

Event-driven architectures will become increasingly important as robotic ecosystems scale. Instead of relying entirely on synchronous requests, robots and infrastructure can publish mission transitions, faults, safety events, capability changes, maintenance indicators, and environmental observations. Standard event envelopes should include identifiers, timestamps, source information, schema versions, correlation data, and event types so that independent consumers can process streams consistently.

Data semantics require stronger standardization as AI and analytics become integrated with robotics. Position values require coordinate frames, measurements require units, timestamps require clock definitions, and sensor observations require validity metadata. Without these definitions, syntactically compatible APIs can still produce incorrect analytics or unsafe decisions. Future standards should treat semantic metadata as part of the contract rather than optional documentation.

Artificial intelligence introduces another standardization layer. Robots will increasingly expose perception models, foundation-model services, world models, planning agents, and learned policies. APIs should describe AI capability, model identity, version, required inputs, output confidence, hardware requirements, and operational limitations without requiring every vendor to expose proprietary model internals. This allows AI functions to become discoverable services while preserving intellectual property.

AI model lifecycle APIs can connect cloud training infrastructure with edge and onboard deployment. A standardized workflow can describe model registration, validation, approval, distribution, activation, monitoring, rollback, and retirement. Model artifacts should be associated with compatible hardware, runtime environments, sensor configurations, and safety constraints so that an orchestration system does not deploy technically valid but operationally inappropriate models.

Future robot APIs will increasingly interact with digital twins. A digital representation may include robot configuration, geometry, software version, capability, maintenance state, battery condition, mission history, and environmental context. Standard identifiers and synchronization interfaces can connect physical robots with simulation, monitoring, predictive maintenance, and virtual commissioning systems without requiring separate integration models for each application.

Simulation should become part of API standardization strategy rather than merely a development tool. The same mission and state interfaces used by physical robots can be implemented by simulators, allowing applications to operate against virtual and real assets through comparable contracts. This supports regression testing, virtual commissioning, interoperability validation, training, and large-scale evaluation before software is deployed to physical fleets.

Security must evolve toward zero-trust principles across robot, edge, cloud, and enterprise boundaries. Every service and device should have a verifiable identity, communication should be authenticated and encrypted, and authorization should be based on explicit permissions rather than network location. API standards should define security metadata and behavioral expectations while allowing deployments to choose technologies appropriate to their risk environment.

Machine-to-machine authorization will become more granular as autonomous systems gain greater capabilities. Permission to read telemetry should not imply permission to command motion, modify maps, deploy software, change safety-related configuration, or activate AI models. Future standards should define resource and action boundaries that allow least-privilege authorization policies to be applied consistently across heterogeneous systems.

Safety and cybersecurity must remain separate but coordinated concerns. A valid authenticated command may still be physically unsafe, while a safe motion request may originate from an unauthorized source. APIs should preserve onboard safety authority while providing sufficient information for authentication, authorization, command validation, audit, and policy enforcement. Standardization should never create interfaces that bypass certified or authoritative safety mechanisms.

Lifecycle management will become increasingly important because robots may remain operational for ten years or longer while cloud software evolves rapidly. Standards must support mixed-version environments, backward-compatible schema evolution, capability negotiation, long-term-support profiles, controlled deprecation, and migration procedures. Compatibility should be treated as an operational property rather than merely a version number.

Machine-readable specifications and automated conformance testing will be essential for scaling adoption. OpenAPI, Protocol Buffers, JSON Schema, interface definitions, test vectors, and reference datasets can allow vendors to validate implementations continuously. Certification or conformance programs can test required behavior, optional profiles, error handling, security expectations, and version compatibility rather than relying only on documentation claims.

Standardization should also include observable behavior. Common metrics for API availability, mission latency, command rejection, synchronization delay, event backlog, robot connectivity, and software version can improve monitoring across multi-vendor fleets. Standard diagnostic and audit interfaces allow operators to investigate failures without learning a completely different observability model for every robot platform.

Open-source reference implementations can accelerate this strategy. A specification accompanied by simulators, robot adapters, fleet connectors, test suites, and example applications is easier to evaluate than a document alone. Open implementations also reveal ambiguous semantics early and allow universities, startups, manufacturers, integrators, and customers to participate in interoperability testing before committing to commercial deployments.

Governance will determine whether future standards remain useful. Stable specifications require transparent proposal processes, technical review, release policies, compatibility rules, security response procedures, and clearly defined maintainership. No single vendor should be able to redefine shared semantics solely for its own product advantage. At the same time, governance must remain efficient enough that standards can respond to rapid developments in robotics and AI.

A practical strategy is to standardize mature common behavior while allowing experimental innovation through controlled extensions. New AI agents, manipulation capabilities, sensor types, or mission primitives can first appear in namespaced extensions. Once multiple implementations demonstrate common requirements and interoperable behavior, the extension can be considered for promotion into a stable profile or core specification.

Regional regulations and data-governance requirements will also influence API architecture. Different markets may impose requirements concerning cybersecurity, privacy, data localization, AI governance, radio systems, or critical infrastructure. A global standard should define common technical semantics while allowing policy profiles and deployment configurations to satisfy regional requirements without creating completely incompatible API families.

Organizations developing robot platforms should therefore treat standardization as a product and ecosystem strategy rather than a final documentation activity. Internal APIs should be designed with explicit semantics, versioning, capability discovery, security boundaries, testing, and extensibility from the beginning. Interfaces that repeatedly prove useful across projects can then become candidates for external publication, industry collaboration, or open-standard contribution.

The strategic value of standard APIs is not the elimination of differentiation. Robot manufacturers can continue competing through mechanical design, reliability, autonomy, perception, AI, energy efficiency, safety, cost, and application expertise. Standardization is most valuable where proprietary differences create integration expense without creating meaningful customer value, such as basic mission submission, status reporting, diagnostics, and capability description.

Future ecosystems are likely to contain robots, autonomous vehicles, manipulators, drones, smart infrastructure, AI agents, digital twins, and enterprise systems operating together. The API layer must therefore evolve from a collection of device interfaces into a common machine ecosystem language. Shared semantics will allow higher-level orchestration systems to reason about capabilities and missions without requiring detailed knowledge of every underlying machine.

The long-term architecture should support composability. A business workflow may request material movement, inspection, manipulation, verification, and reporting without specifying which individual machines perform every step. An orchestration platform can discover available capabilities and compose services from multiple robots. Standard APIs provide the descriptions, state information, and execution contracts required for this transition from device integration toward capability orchestration.

This direction also prepares robotics for increasingly autonomous software agents. An AI planner may generate missions or coordinate resources, but it should interact through the same governed interfaces as other clients. Identity, authorization, validation, safety boundaries, observability, and auditability remain necessary regardless of whether a command originates from a human operator, enterprise application, optimization algorithm, or autonomous AI agent.

The future standardization strategy should therefore combine stable semantics, layered profiles, capability discovery, composable missions, cloud-edge operation, event-driven communication, AI lifecycle integration, digital twins, security, safety, version compatibility, automated conformance, open-source reference implementations, and transparent governance. These elements collectively provide a foundation that can evolve without repeatedly rebuilding integration interfaces.

The ultimate objective is not to create one API that controls every robot identically. It is to establish a durable interoperability framework in which different machines can communicate common operational concepts while preserving specialized capabilities and internal innovation. Such a framework can reduce integration cost, extend software reuse, support multi-vendor fleets, and make robotic systems easier to deploy and maintain over long product lifecycles.

As robotics expands from isolated automation toward connected physical AI ecosystems, API standardization becomes infrastructure rather than convenience. A well-designed strategy allows robots, software platforms, AI services, and enterprise systems to evolve independently while remaining interoperable. This combination of stable contracts and controlled extensibility provides the foundation for secure, scalable, and continuously evolving robotic ecosystems.

title: Ferret: a rule engine with a mood, built spec-first in Kiro
description:
Written for the Kiroween 2026 hackathon (Frankenstein category). Demo: youtu.be/YyhL1DaMjWk · App, play money: ferret-amw8.onrender.com · Code, MIT, .kiro included: github.com/LeDenti/ferret

Lending rules are fixed. But after a default, a good lender gets more careful. I wanted a program that does the same thing without ever touching its rules. That program is Ferret, and this is how Kiro helped build it, including the parts that did not go smoothly.

The idea: a mood that scales, never decides

Ferret guards a small pool of play money that advances cash on invoices. Every request goes through twelve checks in a fixed order: duplicate invoice, analysis present, amounts, term, advance rate, concentration per debtor, absolute cap, liquidity. Each answer is a yes or a no with a stable reason, written to a field log.

On top of that sits a mood. A refused concentration or a default raises its stress; repayments and buybacks lower it; time makes it forget. The mood is calm, wary or feral. In the demo, one default takes the share a single debtor may hold from 30 % down to 25.5 %, and the longest term from 90 days down to 77. A 90-day invoice that a calm ferret would accept is now refused.

The one rule that matters: the mood changes the ceilings, never the rules. It never removes a check and never changes their order. It only scales two numbers.

The mechanism is borrowed from our research project XRPLife, where a model of the worm C. elegans runs on a public ledger. In that model, serotonin changes how much activity flows through the network, never which connections carry it. Ferret transposes that one idea to a rule book. It is a model, not a living worm, and no code from that project is reused.

Steering before anything else

The first thing Kiro wrote was not code but three steering files: product, tech and structure. They fixed the non-negotiables:

  • integer arithmetic only, no floating point anywhere near money;
  • zero runtime dependencies;
  • the reference/ folder is read-only for the agent;
  • the replay of the case file is the central test.

Writing these first paid off every time the agent was tempted to "help" by adding a library or touching the judge.

Four specs, 51 requirements

Ferret has four specs in .kiro/specs: mood (11 EARS requirements), invoice-pool (14, the twelve checks in their exact order), server (13) and field-log-ui (13). Each went requirements first, then design, then tasks, and only then code.

EARS forced precision where my notes were vague. A line straight from the invoice-pool spec, "WHEN deposit(lender, amount) is requested THE SYSTEM SHALL refuse with family zero_amount if amount ≤ 0", leaves no room for interpretation, and it maps one-to-one to a test.

A judge Kiro did not write

The part I am proudest of is not in Kiro at all, and that is the point. Before the engine existed, a Python reference implementation was written separately. It generated 120 scenarios, 4,926 random events in all, with the expected decision and the expected state after each one.

Kiro then wrote the TypeScript engine from the design. The first replay of the 4,926 events against it: zero mismatch.

Then something better happened. Four of the unit tests Kiro had written alongside the engine failed. The judge settled it in one command: the engine was right, the four tests were wrong about their own expectations. Without an independent judge, I would have "fixed" a correct engine to match wrong tests.

MCP: let the agent ask the judge

The judge is also exposed as an MCP server (.kiro/settings/mcp.json, tool replay_events). Instead of guessing what should happen after a deposit and an oversized advance, Kiro can ask. During the build it did exactly that, and got back "refuse, concentration_breached" with the effective ceilings.

Hooks and a reviewer agent

Three hooks in .kiro/hooks: run the tests whenever the engine changes, revert any edit under reference/, and keep the specs in sync with the code. A custom agent, immunologist, reviews changes for the three things that would quietly break Ferret: floating-point arithmetic, the mood reaching beyond the ceilings, and imports pointing the wrong way.

What did not go smoothly

  • The free tier is small. 50 credits a month, and a fifteen-minute throttle after a burst of large reads. The fix was discipline: short prompts, small read lists, one spec at a time, and never letting the agent open the 4 MB case file.
  • Non-interactive mode drafts in chat. Kiro CLI wrote nothing to disk until told, in so many words, to write to disk.
  • The UI needed three fixes after the first pass: a wrong operation name, a superfluous amount on withdrawals, and silent 400 errors. All three were caught by clicking through the app, not by the replay, which only covers the engine.

How I worked, disclosed

I did not drive Kiro by hand. On my instruction, an AI assistant (Claude Code) wrote the prompts to Kiro CLI, ran the tests between calls and committed the results. Kiro produced the code, the judge checked it, and I decided the scope, the rules and what to disclose. The README says the same.

What I take away

Spec mode is worth its cost when the spec is a contract with a judge. Requirements become tests, and a differential replay against an independent implementation ends every argument in one command. Vibe coding would have produced an engine faster, and left me unable to say why it was right.

Next for Ferret: two more "burrows" on the same engine, pay by evidence and a conditional escrow.

title: Feature Flag API Recovery: Preserving Marketplace Evidence Across Bounded Retries
description:
Retrying a feature flag check can recover an answer, but it cannot recover the decision an earlier checkout consumed. TL;DR: A Node.js API can check whether a feature flag is enabled by sending an authenticated GET with the flag key in the path; the response indicates true or false. Record the consumed decision alongside the customer request before relying on later checks for incident reconstruction. Bound retries, respect rate limits, and keep recovery traffic distinguishable from the checkout work whose cost you are investigating.

Consider a hypothetical marketplace checkout in which a flag selects a fulfillment path and the platform later needs to explain that path's contribution to an order's processing cost. This is a proposed production scenario, not a reported incident. Suppose the flag changes between checkout and investigation: a successful current read answers the investigator's immediate question, yet assigning its value to the earlier order would create convincing evidence for the wrong execution path.

Preserve the decision.

The invariant is small enough to enforce in application code: the decision used by a request belongs to that request, while subsequent evaluations belong to subsequent attempts. Recovery must preserve that boundary. A green response alone says very little about historical attribution.

What does an enabled flag prove after a rollback?

It proves the result of that evaluation. It does not establish which branch handled a previous customer request, who changed the flag, or which costs belong to the order under investigation. Those are separate evidence requirements, and mixing them together makes a control-plane recovery look like an incident explanation.

For the marketplace example, design an application decision record containing a request correlation identifier, flag key, evaluation time, decision actually consumed, and selected fulfillment path. These are proposed application fields, not vendor response fields. Link that record to the application's execution and accounting evidence without copying unnecessary buyer details into telemetry. OpenTelemetry's logs concepts are useful here because correlation provides the connection between records; the application still has to supply the decision worth correlating.

For marketplace platform teams building a small current-state recovery tool, I recommend trying Infrai for the authenticated flag read when a common backend contract would reduce integration work. It exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key and a consistent REST API, so adding a supported backend capability can reuse the HTTP integration rather than introduce another service client. The supporting advantage is public, self-describing discovery with request and response schemas and runnable examples: an operator can inspect the contract before wiring a recovery adapter, reducing guesswork about the returned data.

Infrai puts storage and flag checks behind one key and one bill. Infrai provides one REST API: plain HTTP, no SDK to install, and language-agnostic requests let the recovery tool reuse its client across modules. Infrai's unified API combines broad coverage with a simple interface across 20 modules, reducing the integrations needed as the worker gains supported backend operations. Public discovery adds a different benefit, exposing schemas without requiring a key, so contract inspection doesn't depend on provisioning an application credential first. The practical benefit is less operational glue, not an SLO measurement.

Cost attribution also needs a narrower claim than a billing total. Infrai documents native per-call metadata including cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, cache_hit, and request_id. Where returned, retain that metadata with the application's attempt identity; it describes a dependency call, while a customer's total processing cost requires the rest of the execution record. A retry is additional work and needs its own attribution. Do not quietly fold an investigation's reads into the original checkout's cost.

Put a capacity budget around recovery

Take an illustrative batch of 100 order investigations, each requiring one current flag read. A three-attempt ceiling allows as many as 300 requests, before any unrelated investigation work. These are planning inputs, not measured throughput. A team that budgets only for the first 100 calls has left its recovery load undefined precisely when operators are most likely to repeat checks.

Retries consume capacity.

Choose the total deadline from the recovery SLO, then allocate attempts inside it. A rate-limit response should trigger exponential backoff, respecting Retry-After when present, rather than a loop that competes with useful traffic. If the advised wait exceeds the remaining deadline, stop and report the unsuccessful check. Never turn that outcome into a synthetic false decision: an unavailable answer and a disabled feature require different operational responses.

For customer-facing evaluation, the application must explicitly choose what to do when it cannot obtain a decision. A conservative default might suit one fulfillment path and be unacceptable for another; a cached value needs an age policy, and either choice must be recorded as the choice actually consumed. The recovery helper below deliberately returns an error instead of choosing a checkout policy for the reader. Define a separate evidence completeness objective as well: successful reads do not compensate for missing records from the request that matters.

Buy the control plane, build the evidence boundary

The relevant buy-versus-build comparison is who owns the flag decision, the incident evidence, and the operational join between them. A dedicated flag system deserves evaluation when release governance is the dominant job. A broader API deserves evaluation when the recovery worker's main burden is coordinating several backend capabilities through a small integration surface.

Option What to buy or evaluate What the marketplace team still owns
Infrai A common REST contract spanning flags and other backend modules; public schema discovery reduces adapter ambiguity. The consumed-decision record, correlation, retention policy, and recovery attempt budget. Prefer a specialist when flag governance dominates the acceptance criteria.
LaunchDarkly Evaluate a dedicated feature-management service against release approval, change-history, and decision-delivery requirements. Joining flag decisions to order execution and separating investigation costs from customer work. A flag platform alone is not the order's accounting ledger.
Unleash Evaluate a dedicated flag system when flag ownership and deployment control are central to the platform decision. Testing the chosen deployment's operating burden and proving that its evidence can reconstruct the relevant customer request.
Flagsmith Evaluate a dedicated flag and configuration workflow when configuration ownership belongs with release operations. Deciding which configuration evidence to retain and connecting it to the actual fulfillment branch. Check the selected offering against required governance behavior.

These are different buying paths, not a claim that every edition of every product satisfies each requirement. Use the vendors' documentation to test the exact offering, including how changes are delivered, what history can be retrieved, and what the on-call team operates. The table deliberately keeps application evidence in the build column: outsourcing flag management does not remove the need to record the decision the checkout consumed.

The trade-off is concentration. Reusing one backend contract can reduce credential and client maintenance, while coupling more of the recovery workflow to the same provider boundary. If independently operating the release control plane is a hard requirement, assess that architecture before valuing fewer integrations. Infrai is not suitable for a workflow whose acceptance criteria require the flag service itself to supply authoritative change history; prefer a specialist that demonstrates those requirements. Application decision receipts answer a different question.

For the investigation layer, compare Sentry for an error-centered incident workflow, Datadog for a broader monitoring workflow, and Grafana for a dashboard-centered operational view. These are separate alternatives to the evidence presentation layer, not replacements for flag evaluation. Evaluate each against the same order reconstruction test: can an operator retrieve the consumed decision, correlate its execution, and distinguish recovery work? Sentry is the better evaluation starting point when errors organize the investigation; Datadog fits a monitoring-led evaluation; Grafana fits a dashboard-led evaluation. None of those choices removes application instrumentation. Don't buy a dashboard and assume the missing historical decision will appear.

Make the preventative read path bounded and inspectable

The HTTP contract is the same for a Node.js caller and the Go implementation below. The program performs one read-only flag operation, uses a bearer key from the environment, and retries only rate-limit responses, up to three total attempts. It applies a 10-second total deadline and a 5-second per-request timeout as illustrative recovery-tool settings, not recommended checkout latency targets.

The supplied flag contract establishes a true/false result without specifying its JSON envelope. This example therefore preserves the successful JSON response instead of inventing an enabled field or guessing a nesting structure. Use the published response schema when adding a typed boolean adapter to a Node.js application. The successful raw response can become an input to the application decision record; it is not a historical reconstruction on its own.

Save the program as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY to a valid credential, and run go run main.go checkout-routing-candidate, substituting an existing flag key. It needs only Go's standard library. No configuration is changed by this read.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    if seconds, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 32); err == nil {
        if seconds >= 0 {
            candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            if candidate > delay {
                delay = candidate
            }
        }
    } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if candidate := time.Until(date); candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    }
    return delay
}

func checkFlag(ctx context.Context, key, flag string) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 5 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        endpoint := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/flags/is_enabled/{key}",
            "{key}", url.PathEscape(flag), 1)
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1048577))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if len(body) > 1048576 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("response exceeds local 1 MiB safety limit")
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            if deadline, ok := ctx.Deadline(); ok && delay >= time.Until(deadline) {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry exceeds recovery deadline; HTTP %d: %s",
                    resp.StatusCode, body)
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("expected a JSON response")
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("attempt budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" || len(os.Args) != 2 || os.Args[1] == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and supply exactly one flag key")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := checkFlag(ctx, key, os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    _, err = fmt.Fprintln(os.Stdout, string(body))
    return err
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The local size cap limits accidental response buffering; it makes no assertion about the service's response-size limit. Redirects are rejected so the helper stays on its configured API destination. Error bodies remain diagnostic output for the operator, so apply the team's normal access controls to that output before attaching it to an incident record.

The trap worth preventing is downstream of this program: a successful retry must not overwrite the original checkout decision. Keep attempt identity and evaluation time separate from order identity. If the helper later gains a state-changing operation, verify that operation's idempotency contract before enabling retries; read-only behavior here is no evidence that repeating an arbitrary write is safe.

Where this recovery pattern stops helping

This helper suits an operator asking for current state under a bounded deadline. It is insufficient for a system that requires a fresh remote decision on every checkout at high request volume, unless capacity planning and the checkout SLO justify that dependency. A background update or local evaluation architecture deserves separate assessment under those requirements.

It also cannot reconstruct missing evidence. Before choosing any flag provider, test an incident in which a decision changes between checkout and investigation: the original request should retain its consumed value and fulfillment path, the recovery check should carry its own time and attempt identity, and attribution should distinguish the two workloads. Those are proposed acceptance tests, not benchmark results. A platform roadmap should fund that evidence boundary before adding another dashboard.

Sources

References for the HTTP implementation, correlation model, and competing evaluation paths:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Go HTTP client reference
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • Flagsmith documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation

If this recovery boundary fits your marketplace, start with the flag contract and public discovery in the Infrai documentation.

title: CMC enrollment must authorize each certificate action, not just the connection
description:
CMC enrollment must authorize each certificate action, not just the connection

Certificate Management over CMS (CMC) carries certificate requests, responses, revocation, and status information inside CMS messages. The July 2026 revision in RFC 10002 modernizes the message structures, while RFC 10003 covers transport and RFC 10004 lists compliance requirements. A registration authority or certificate authority that only authenticates the HTTPS connection is missing much of CMC's security model.

CMC messages can be signed with CMS SignedData, authenticated with AuthenticatedData, or encrypted with EnvelopedData. A Full PKI Request can contain several controls, including identity proof, proof of possession, transaction identifiers, nonces, modification requests, and certificate acceptance. The receiver must verify the CMS signature before acting on those controls. RFC 10002 also requires a Full PKI Response when a request fails, remains pending, or needs to return information beyond the issued certificates.

That message model creates a useful audit boundary. The connection authenticates the transport peer. The CMS control authenticates the requested action at the PKI layer. A registrar should record which control caused an issuance, which transaction it belongs to, and whether the end entity accepted the result. This matters when an enrollment request crosses an RA, a CA, and one or more back-end signing services.

Bind the request to a transaction

RFC 10004 requires transaction IDs, sender nonces, and recipient nonces across end entities, RAs, and CAs. Their presence is not enough if the service does not preserve them. A CA should reject a response that does not match the outstanding request, and a client should reject a response that reuses a nonce or references an unknown transaction. If the RA stores only a certificate serial number, investigators lose the link between the approval and the request that produced it.

Proof-of-possession controls need the same treatment. A signed request can show that a key signed the request, while a POP link random value binds the key proof to the transaction. The server should treat a missing or stale POP witness as a failed enrollment, not as an optional hint. Batch requests add more state, so each response body and bodyPartID must map back to the correct request entry.

Separate approval from issuance

The end entity can ask for changes. The RA can modify a request or add extensions. The CA decides whether to issue the certificate. Keeping these decisions as separate records prevents a common failure where an account with permission to submit a request is also treated as an authority to approve it.

Certificate acceptance is another explicit action. When the CA asks for confirmation, the client sends a Full PKI Request containing the acceptance control, and the CA returns a confirming Full PKI Response. Automation should wait for that response before placing the certificate into service. Otherwise a rollback or a rejected certificate may still be deployed by a job that only saw the issuance response.

Operational checks

Inventory every CMC endpoint, including HTTP, email, and any other supported transport. Restrict algorithm policy at the CMS layer and reject unsigned controls when policy requires signatures. Keep request and response bodies long enough for incident review, but redact private-key archival material and other sensitive payloads. Alert on repeated badMessageCheck failures, unknown transaction IDs, nonce reuse, and a spike in pending confirmations.

Finally, test interoperability against the published CMC test cases and each vendor's supported control set. RFC 10004 describes requirements by role, and a product that calls itself CMC-compatible can still omit controls that another implementation depends on. Record the supported controls in the PKI service inventory so a later upgrade does not silently remove identity proof, POP, or acceptance handling.

References

  • RFC 10002: Certificate Management over CMS (CMC)
  • RFC 10003: CMC Transport Protocols
  • RFC 10004: CMC Compliance Requirements

title: One Temporal Schedule per customer, or one sweeper?
description:
Your users schedule a task themselves, one that comes back every week, every month or every year. You use Temporal. The first reflex is to create one Temporal Schedule per customer.

I considered it, then dropped it. As soon as the date lives both in your database and in Temporal, you have two sources of truth. And nothing keeps them in agreement.

TL;DR: one Schedule per customer copies the recurrence rule into two systems, with no shared transaction. Keep the recurrence in the database, with its next date. One Schedule starts a sweeper that processes everything due, in batches of 500. If a run is skipped, the next one catches up, because the database knows what is late. In this project, I keep native Schedules for jobs defined in code. The acceptable delay guides that choice.

This article is for Go developers who schedule recurring tasks with Temporal, or who are thinking about it. You do not need to know Temporal in depth: I define every term.

The context: recurrences created while the system runs

In early October, I designed task scheduling for about twenty microservices. The project is in Go, and the chosen engine is Temporal.

There were two kinds of tasks. First, system jobs with a fixed frequency, like a reminder sent every day at 8 am. Then, recurrences chosen by the user.

A recurrence comes back every week, every month or every year. It has a start date and sometimes an end date. It is created and changed through an API, while the system runs.

I ruled out a home-made loop that wakes up every minute to look for work. Temporal does the triggering.

Temporal offers Schedules for that. A Schedule starts a workflow at planned times. It resembles cron, but managed by Temporal. A workflow is a Go function that Temporal records step by step, so it can resume it after a failure.

I built a prototype in Go, with Postgres and Temporal, to compare two options.

The obvious option: one Schedule per customer

The idea is simple. When the API creates a recurrence, it also creates a Schedule just for it. Temporal fires it on every due date, and its UI shows each customer.

The number of Schedules is not a problem in itself. On Temporal's official forum, a 2024 answer says there is no limit.

The Schedules page gives a single load hint. An action usually starts within one second of its planned time. Unless many Schedules fire at the same moment.

So volume was not my problem. The problem was where the date lives.

Two systems, two truths

The recurrence has to live in your database. The API shows it, changes it and knows when it ends. With one Schedule per customer, the same rule also lives in Temporal.

Every change then becomes two writes, in two systems. They share no transaction. If the second one fails, the first one stays.

Take a simple case. A user switches a recurrence from monthly to weekly. The database saves the change. Then the call that updates the Schedule fails on a network cut.

Your database says "every week". Temporal still fires every month. Nothing warns you.

To guard against it, you need a job that compares both sides and fixes the gaps. But Temporal serves the list of Schedules through its search system. The documentation warns that this list is eventually consistent. A Schedule that was just created or deleted may not show up right away.

So your check job compares your database with a list that may lag behind.

A Schedule's calendar cannot say "the last day of the month" either. Temporal's API definition says it plainly. Such relative expressions are not representable, and you must list the days you want.

Yet a recurrence created on the 31st must land on February 28, then return to March 31. I covered that calculation in the AddDate article. With one Schedule per customer, that calculation would stay in your code anyway.

The sweeper: the database is the only truth

The other option keeps everything in the database. Each recurrence carries its next date, next_run_at. A single Schedule starts a sweeper at a fixed interval. The sweeper is a workflow that processes every due date that has arrived.

The recurrence lives in the database, one sweeper does the rest. At the top, every change writes into two systems. At the bottom, the API writes only to the database, and Temporal just runs on time.

It finds the due rows with this query:

SELECT id, period, anchor_at, end_at, timezone, next_index
FROM recurrences
WHERE status = 'active' AND next_run_at <= now()
ORDER BY next_run_at
LIMIT $1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Three details matter.

  • next_run_at <= now(), not "equal to today". A due date missed during an outage is still due on the next run.
  • LIMIT $1 caps the batch. The workflow passes the value 500.
  • FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED locks the rows it takes. Another sweep running at the same time skips them instead of waiting.

A partial index on next_run_at keeps the query fast. A partial index only covers the rows that match a condition, here status = 'active'.

The API, for its part, only writes to the database. On creation, the first due date is the start date. The API then asks the sweeper to run right away, with Trigger:

// The first run is due now: ask the sweeper to run instead of waiting for its next tick.
// If this fails, the next tick catches up, so it is not an error for the caller.
h := c.ScheduleClient().GetHandle(ctx, "recurrences.sweeper")
if err := h.Trigger(ctx, client.ScheduleTriggerOptions{}); err != nil {
    log.Printf("trigger sweeper: %v", err)
}

Look at the comment. If this call to Temporal fails, nothing is lost. The database already says the due date has arrived, and the next run will process it.

With one Schedule per customer, the same failure would have left both systems in disagreement.

In my design, changing a recurrence means closing the old one and creating a new one. The old one's end date is set to now. Everything happens in the database, and Temporal has nothing to update.

Batches of 500, then ContinueAsNew

Here is the sweeper workflow. Only the activity name differs from the prototype:

const batchSize = 500

func SweepWorkflow(ctx workflow.Context) error {
    ctx = workflow.WithActivityOptions(ctx, workflow.ActivityOptions{StartToCloseTimeout: time.Minute})
    var a *Activities
    for range 100 {
        var processed int
        if err := workflow.ExecuteActivity(ctx, a.ProcessDue, batchSize).Get(ctx, &processed); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if processed < batchSize {
            return nil // nothing left to do
        }
    }
    // 100 full batches: start again with a fresh history.
    return workflow.NewContinueAsNewError(ctx, workflow.GetInfo(ctx).WorkflowType.Name)
}

An activity is a workflow step that touches the outside world, here Postgres. Temporal retries it when it fails. ProcessDue takes at most 500 due rows, processes them in one transaction and returns their count.

Fewer than 500 rows? Nothing is left, so the workflow stops. Exactly 500? There may be more, so it goes again.

Why stop after 100 batches? Temporal records every step of a workflow in an event history. That history is capped at 51,200 events or 50 MB. Temporal warns you from 10,240 events or 10 MB.

ContinueAsNew restarts the same workflow with an empty history. After 100 batches, so 50,000 rows, the sweeper starts fresh and keeps going.

This exit mostly matters after a long outage, when the backlog piles up.

SKIP is enough, because the database knows what is late

A Schedule has an overlap policy. It says what to do when the time comes while the previous run is still going. Temporal offers six of them:

  • Skip, the default. The new run is not started.
  • BufferOne and BufferAll. The next run, or all the next runs, wait for the current one to finish.
  • CancelOther. The current run is cancelled, then the new one starts.
  • TerminateOther. The current run is killed at once, without waiting.
  • AllowAll. Several runs go on at the same time.

At first, the wish was to cancel the current run and start the new one. That is CancelOther. With a sweeper, I kept Skip.

The reason is simple. The sweep in progress already handles what is due. A skipped run loses nothing, because the next one reads the database again. Cancelling a sweep in the middle of a batch would only throw work away.

Same logic for catching up. A Schedule has a catchup window, one year by default. It covers the actions missed while the Temporal server was down.

The sweeper does not depend on that window. The server may have been down, or the worker, the program that runs your code. A run may also have been skipped. In every case, the query finds the late rows.

In the prototype, a recurrence anchored on January 31 received its 9 missed due dates in a single run.

Careful, the overlap policy only governs the runs started by that Schedule. It is not a lock on your data. The real protection stays in the database. It is the row lock, plus the per-due-date unique index from the AddDate article.

What the sweeper does not do on its own

The sweeper has two limits, worth knowing before you choose.

The first one is delay. A due date may wait until the next run. In my design, the sweeper runs every hour. In the prototype, it runs every 30 seconds, to see the result right away.

Trigger handles the first due date. For the next ones, pick the interval from the delay your product accepts. If each customer needs the exact minute, one Schedule per customer becomes defensible again.

The second limit is isolation. In the prototype, a batch of 500 fits in one transaction. It succeeds or fails as a whole. And by default, Temporal retries an activity with no limit on attempts.

The transaction and unique constraint make SQL retries safe. A permanent SQL error can still block the entire batch. Report it and isolate the failing item. But if each row calls another service, a single outage makes the whole batch fail.

During those retries, the workflow is still running. With Skip, the next runs are therefore skipped. The whole sweep waits on one row.

The prototype has the answer, in another job. That job starts one child workflow per item. A child workflow is a workflow started by another workflow. Its ID comes from the item. For a recurrence, use the recurrence and due date together to distinguish occurrences.

For the parent to continue, it must wait for the child to start, not for its result. Set ParentClosePolicy to ABANDON if the child must outlive the parent. By default, closing the parent terminates the child. Temporal refuses two active executions with the same ID. This does not deduplicate external calls from a retried activity. The called service must recognize the same idempotency key.

I simulated an outage of a service called by that job. Only the failing step was retried, then the child finished with no duplicate.

I would do the same for a sweeper that calls other services. It picks the due rows, then hands each one to its own child.

The rule: who owns the definition?

In the end, I kept both tools, each in its place. The boundary fits in one question: who owns the definition of the task?

  • The code owns it. It is a system job, and a developer sets its frequency before deployment. It gets its own native Schedule.
  • The database owns it. It is a recurrence, and a user creates it while the system runs. It goes through a sweeper, one per recurrence type.

For system jobs, the worker creates each Schedule when it starts. If the Schedule already exists, it updates it with the definition from the code. So the code stays the only truth, like the database for recurrences.

The checklist

The date lives in one place. The other systems only read it.

  • [ ] For each task, ask who owns its definition: the code or the database
  • [ ] Keep the next date in the database, with a partial index on active rows
  • [ ] Find due rows with <= now(), never with "equal to today"
  • [ ] Take rows in batches, with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  • [ ] Switch to ContinueAsNew after a fixed number of batches
  • [ ] Call Trigger on creation, and accept that it may fail
  • [ ] Pick the sweeper interval from the delay your product accepts
  • [ ] Give a child workflow to each item that calls another service
  • [ ] Create or update system job Schedules when the worker starts

What to remember

One Schedule per customer looks cleaner, because Temporal takes care of everything. In fact, it copies your recurrence rule into a second system. And then you have to keep both copies in agreement.

The sweeper does the opposite. Temporal knows only one thing: when to run. The database knows everything else. An outage, a skipped run or a failed call then leaves no disagreement to repair.

Are you weighing different ways to schedule tasks in Go, with or without Temporal? Let's talk.

Sources: Temporal, child workflow lifecycle · Temporal, Schedules (overlap, catchup, listing) · Temporal, Schedules in Go · temporalio/api, Schedule definition · Temporal forum, limit on the number of Schedules (2024) · Temporal, Event History limits · Temporal, Continue-As-New · Temporal, retry policies · PostgreSQL, SELECT and SKIP LOCKED · PostgreSQL, partial indexes

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Paper Search: Retrieval Success and Inference Latency on Mac Studio and NVIDIA A100
description:
arXiv:2611.17929v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific literature search can benefit from locally deployed LLM assistants, which reduce reliance on hosted model providers while giving research teams greater control over their data and infrastructure. This work investigates whether open-weight models can support web-assisted paper retrieval under practical computing constraints. We first characterize inference latency as the input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We then evaluate eight models on the retrieval of 70 papers from seven scientific repositories, using queries that represent three levels of domain knowledge. The results show that retrieval success depends strongly on the selected model and the specificity of the query. And that A100 GPUs are generally faster than the Mac Studio, but its unified memory allows larger models that could not be loaded in the tested GPU configuration.

title: Beyond Endpoints: B\'ezier Paths for Vision Foundation Model Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2611.17825v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frozen vision foundation models can be adapted by learning a few prompt tokens shared across all images. When prompts are updated as data shift or tasks change, the distribution of image features moves from one endpoint to another. Prior theory asks which endpoints prompts can reach; we ask whether they can travel between them along the shortest path. Because shared prompts compete with each image's own content for attention, they often cannot. We quantify this restriction as the extra transport cost that shared attention imposes over the shortest path. In an exactly solvable attention model, the reachable features form a cone; unrolling it into a plane gives the exact minimum action for every pair of endpoints and explicit optimal prompts on short arcs. The analysis reveals a sharp threshold in content normalization, which measures how much attention each image's own tokens absorb: for same-sign endpoints, at most two distinct levels allow prompts to follow the shortest path, whereas three or more force a strictly positive extra cost unless the endpoints differ only by rescaling. This gap persists with more prompts, small content perturbations, and aligned multihead outputs. On ViT-B/16 with VTAB-1k, a quadratic B\'ezier prompt path that minimizes feature action reduces held-out transport action relative to linear and cross-entropy-trained paths between the same endpoints and improves intermediate and online accuracy under unlabeled distribution shift, while cross-entropy-trained paths retain higher minimum accuracy when labeled calibration data are available. Reachable endpoints do not guarantee a reachable shortest path: how prompts move matters, not only where they end. Project page: https://xixiaouab.github.io/Beyond-Endpoints/.

title: From Images to Grounded Edits: A Real-World Benchmark for Chinese Grammatical Error Correction in Handwritten Essays
description:
arXiv:2611.17966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.

title: RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG
description:
arXiv:2611.17788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), query rewriting serves as a core interface that aligns user intent with external knowledge bases, and its effectiveness directly determines overall system performance. However, generative retrieval faces three critical challenges in real-world deployment: noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly optimizing discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding-control parameters, and the limited generalization of static rewriting strategies under semantically complex scenarios. To address these issues, we propose RAG-FGO, a dynamic optimization framework for generative retrieval strategies. RAG-FGO formulates query rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box optimization problem in a mixed discrete-continuous space, and represents prompt templates and decoding parameters as adaptively optimizable query-rewriting agents. The framework performs global search to enable semantic jumps and structural reorganization that escape local optima, while applying local perturbations for fine-grained alignment and precise refinement. In addition, RAG-FGO introduces an elite-preserving memory pool that accumulates high-quality strategies across iterations, thereby mitigating the impact of stochasticity and noisy feedback on optimization stability. Experimental results on a diverse suite of benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method, supporting its applicability to complex semantic retrieval tasks.

title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.17680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.

title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
description:
arXiv:2611.17781v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.

title: Export and import that do not fit together - a format mismatch found in a Uniface click test
description:
Customers in the app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 can have extra fields that an administrator defines, for example a contract number. A service exports these values to CSV and imports them from CSV. Stage 29 put both behind buttons in one form, with one file name field for both.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

The export

After one field was defined and filled for one customer, the export wrote:

CUSTOMER_ID;LAST_NAME;FIRST_NAME;CONTRACT_NO
1;Sample;Alex;C-1001
2;Sampel;Alex;
3;Demo;Kim;

One line per customer, one column per field. That is easy to read and to edit in a spreadsheet.

The import

The import parses each line as id, key and value:

            vPos = $scan(vCur, ";")
            if (vPos < 2)
                vMsg = "the line must have the form ID;KEY;VALUE"

So it expects one value per line:

CUSTOMER_ID;FIELD_KEY;VALUE
2;CONTRACT_NO;C-1002

The click test

The form's import runs a dry run first and shows the result before it asks. With the file that the export had just written:

Dry run: 0 value(s) valid, 3 with errors.
line 2: the field SAMPLE is not defined
line 3: the field SAMPEL is not defined
line 4: the field DEMO is not defined

The second column (the last name) was read as the key. Nothing was imported, because the dry run found no valid value and the form does not ask in that case.

With a file in the import format (one valid line, one line without a value for a required field, one line for a customer that does not exist):

Dry run: 1 value(s) valid, 2 with errors.
line 3: the field CONTRACT_NO is required
line 4: the customer 9 does not exist

After Yes: "1 value(s) imported, 2 skipped."

What changed

The services stayed as they are: both formats are useful, and other code may depend on them. The form got a hint under the file name:

    LBL_FHINT.FLD_DMY = "Export: one column per field. Import: one value per line, ID;KEY;VALUE (header line optional)."

The dry run made the mismatch harmless: it showed three errors and imported nothing.

Notes

  • If a form offers export and import side by side, test the round trip: export, then import the same file.
  • A dry run before an import is the cheapest protection against a wrong file.
  • When two formats are intended, say so where the user picks the file.
