title: Choosing Between Python and Go for CLI Development: Balancing Familiarity and Structure
description:
Architectural Transition Mechanics: Event-Driven Loops versus Sequential Execution Flow

For the hobbyist transitioning from the Godot engine runtime, the departure from an implicit game loop—which natively orchestrates state updates, rendering frames, and event propagation—catalyzes an immediate architectural crisis. Stripped of the host engine environment, writing a standalone CLI or TUI application eliminates external scaffolding. The internal process demands a radical shift: instead of registering asynchronous callback methods (such as _process or _input) with an external scheduler, the programmer must explicitly engineer a deterministic, linear entry-to-exit execution pipeline. The observable effect is an acute architectural vacuum, where developers frequently falter in structuring main entry points, control flow loops, or state lifecycles because the application lifecycle is no longer handled implicitly by an external framework. This psychological shock exposes the fragility of engine-dependent mental models.

Type Systems and Compilation Overhead: Dynamic Interpretation versus Static Verification

The choice between languages encapsulates a fundamental tension between frictionless creative momentum and structural discipline. Python provides dynamic runtime interpretation and duck typing, maintaining high syntactic proximity to GDScript. The immediate impact is minimal cognitive friction when writing raw logic, allowing creative momentum to surge while type safety is deferred to runtime. Conversely, Go enforces a strict static compilation pipeline, demanding explicit type declarations, rigorous compile-time type checking, and mandatory error-handling structures (such as if err != nil). The observable consequence is stark: while Python permits immediate script execution, it insidiously masks architectural errors until runtime execution strikes a failure path. Go, by contrast, forces early type resolution at the distinct cost of upfront compilation overhead and unyielding syntax enforcement, testing whether a hobbyist can endure rigorous technical constraints.

Composition Logic: Inheritance Hierarchies versus Struct Embedding and Interfaces

Scaling software architecture requires confronting deep-seated habits formed within Godot's reliance on deep class inheritance hierarchies, which notoriously cultivate rigid object coupling and severe refactoring bottlenecks. When hobbyists encounter these structural limitations trying to scale game object logic in new environments, Go offers an epistemological break by replacing traditional class inheritance with structural composition. Through structs, method receivers, interface satisfaction, and embedding, Go replaces rigid parent-child class trees with decoupled behaviors. Types satisfy interfaces implicitly, fundamentally altering how modular components interact within system memory and forcing the developer to master a more flexible, decoupled paradigm of object design.

Pedagogical Resource Friction: Exhaustive Hand-Holding versus Independent Documentation Synthesis

The emotional and intellectual trajectory of the learner is profoundly shaped by the available pedagogical landscape. Python features an expansive ecosystem of beginner-focused literature, tutorials, and step-by-step guides, ensuring low friction in finding syntactic explanations and task-based walkthroughs. In sharp contrast, Go educational material exhibits a structural polarization, split between infantile introductions and advanced references that brazenly assume prior systems programming knowledge and direct manual consultation. The observable effect of this scarcity of intermediate-tier guided resources in Go forces developers to parse raw standard library documentation independently. This abrupt transition produces acute cognitive load and temporary operational paralysis, acting as a crucible that separates casual hobbyists from dedicated systems engineers.

Systemic Instabilities and Failure Modes

  • Engine-Callback Hangover: The persistence of event-driven mental models prevents the construction of linear command-line logic flows, resulting in structural gridlock.
  • Documentation Paralysis: The scarcity of intermediate-tier guided resources in Go induces stall states during standard library exploration.
  • Cognitive Overload: Distributing mental bandwidth between learning low-level memory pointers, strict type systems, and software architecture simultaneously destabilizes the development process.
  • Over-Modeling Composition: Paralyzing iteration cycles spent engineering perfect struct embeddings and interfaces before establishing functional baseline execution code.

Architectural Realities and Resource Gaps: Navigating Boilerplate versus Dynamic Abstraction

Transition from Engine-Driven Lifecycle to Standalone Execution Pipelines: Shifting from GDScript within Godot to standalone CLI/TUI development forces a structural paradigm shift from reactive, framework-managed event loops (_process, _input) to explicit, linear entry-to-exit execution flows. In Godot, the external engine scheduler handles frame rendering, state updates, and asynchronous callback propagation. When an engine-trained hobbyist attempts to build a standalone application, the absence of an overarching framework scaffolding causes structural gridlock, as the developer lacks a mental model for managing sequential initialization, blocking reads, and clean program termination. Analytically, this reveals the psychological vulnerability of losing framework safety rails, turning a technical migration into a disorienting trial of architectural survival.

Type Systems and Cognitive Load in Compilation: Python utilizes runtime interpretation and duck typing, eliminating upfront syntactic friction but deferring type safety and structural errors to execution time. Conversely, Go enforces a strict compilation pipeline with explicit type declarations, compile-time type checking, and mandatory error handling structures (if err != nil). For a beginner transitioning from a scripting environment, Go's strict syntax increases initial cognitive load, splitting mental bandwidth between learning low-level memory concepts (pointers, explicit allocation) and designing application logic. The consequence is a severe operational risk: the emotional thrill of low-level technical rigor frequently gives way to cognitive exhaustion and burnout.

Component Composition Mechanics versus Inheritance: Godot relies on deep class trees, which cultivate rigid object coupling and create severe refactoring bottlenecks when hierarchies are misdesigned. Go replaces parent-child class trees with structs, method receivers, explicit embedding, and implicit interface satisfaction. This compositional model allows behaviors to be decoupled and modularized without inheritance overhead. However, hobbyists frequently enter an over-modeling failure mode, spending excessive cognitive cycles trying to design "perfect" struct embeddings and interfaces before establishing baseline functional execution. This misplaced pursuit of architectural purity paralyzes momentum long before code ever runs.

Pedagogical Friction and Documentation Asymmetry: The stark disparity in learning resources creates distinct operational failure modes. Python offers continuous, low-friction, hand-held beginner literature. Go features a polarized ecosystem split between infantile introductions and advanced systems references that assume deep prior systems knowledge. This resource gap induces documentation paralysis: learners attempting Go are forced to independently parse the standard library documentation, resulting in operational stall states, uncertainty regarding capability limits, and trial-and-error dependency resolution. Ultimately, choosing between Python and Go for the transitioning hobbyist represents a critical trade-off between frictionless creative momentum and structural discipline, establishing Python as the more pragmatic vehicle for mastering standalone architecture without extinguishing enthusiasm.

Execution Lifecycle Transition Mechanics

Impact: Disconnecting application logic from the Godot game engine eliminates the underlying asynchronous scheduler.

Internal Process: The Godot runtime implicitly handles frame rendering, state updates, and event propagation via reactive hooks like _process and _input. A standalone CLI or TUI environment lacks this framework scaffolding, requiring explicit, deterministic, linear entry-to-exit execution pipelines, manual lifecycle initialization, blocking standard I/O reads, and explicit termination routines.

Observable Effect: Retention of engine-driven callback mental models forces structural gridlock, manifesting as execution halts when attempting to map sequential command-line execution onto non-existent event loops.

Type Systems and Compilation Overhead

Impact: Enforcing static compilation and explicit memory management versus runtime interpretation alters developer bandwidth distribution.

Internal Process: Python defers type checking to runtime via duck typing, eliminating upfront syntax overhead. Go enforces strict compilation pipelines, explicit type declarations, compile-time checks, mandatory error handling constructs (if err != nil), and direct pointer-based memory manipulation.

Observable Effect: The simultaneous processing of low-level memory addressing, strict type rules, and unfamiliar architectural patterns induces cognitive overload, splitting mental bandwidth between syntax enforcement and structural logic implementation.

Architectural Composition Dynamics

Impact: Replacing rigid class hierarchies with Go's structural composition modifies object coupling and modularity.

Internal Process: Traditional game engines rely on deep parent-child inheritance trees that create refactoring bottlenecks. Go substitutes inheritance with structs, method receivers, explicit embedding, and implicit interface satisfaction, decoupling behaviors at the memory level.

Observable Effect: In the absence of prior standalone architecture experience, the system enters a premature optimization loop where complex struct embeddings and interfaces are modeled before establishing baseline operational code, producing architectural paralysis.

Pedagogical Resource Asymmetry and Documentation Friction

Impact: The structural polarization of learning resources forces independent parsing of standard library specifications.

Internal Process: While Python provides continuous, low-friction hand-held beginner literature, Go's literature is divided between infantile overviews and advanced systems references. Developers must navigate standard library documentation directly without intermediate-tier guided scaffolding.

Observable Effect: This asymmetry produces operational stall states and trial-and-error dependency resolution cycles, destabilizing development velocity until intrinsic motivation drives the construction of independent mental models.

title: Process Mining-Enabled Federated Anomaly Detection for the Industrial IoT
description:
arXiv:2611.17869v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While federated anomaly detection enables the integration of local data insights across diverse nodes to reduce false positives, it inherently struggles with non-IID data. In practice, industrial IoT plants often operate under varying conditions and experience diverse environmental phenomena, resulting in significant heterogeneity in the monitored time series. In such settings, standard federated learning approaches fail to perform nuanced aggregation that accounts for these cross-node differences, ultimately leading to increased false positive rates. In this paper, we propose a process mining approach to evaluate the similarity of local node data against a reference provided by a global node. The global node utilizes these similarity metrics to dynamically weight local models during aggregation, producing personalized updates distributed across the network. We evaluate our approach using industrial IoT time-series data collected from manufacturing plants operating under distinct conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our process mining-enabled federated anomaly detection pipeline achieves superior performance, yielding a 46.52% and 11.99% relative improvement in F1-score compared to isolated local training baselines and standard FedAvg, respectively, alongside a 51.24% relative reduction in false positives over standard federated aggregation.

title: How to Ace Minimalistic UI Designs for Apps in the UK
description:
Mastering the art of minimalistic user interface (UI) design can be a game-changer for app developers looking to make a mark in the market. This design approach, characterised by its clean lines, simple aesthetics, and focus on functionality, provides users with an intuitive and clutter-free experience.

If you are looking to develop apps that will offer an enjoyable and efficient user experience, this a detailed guide on perfecting minimalistic UI designs.

What Does Minimal UI Design Mean in App Development?

Minimal UI design in app development means keeping things simple and clear. Think of this as when you look at a clean and organised room - it is easy to find what you need, and it feels comfortable.

In an app with minimal design, you will not see too many fancy decorations or lots of different colours. Instead, you will see a neat layout with just the important stuff your users need to use the app.

Buttons and menus will be easy to find and use, and everything will look clean and uncluttered.

Elements of Minimalistic UI Design in App Development to Keep in Mind

1. Make Functionality a Priority

A hallmark of minimalistic UI design is its unwavering focus on functionality and user-centred design. Identify the core features and functionalities that your app must offer and ensure they are easily accessible. Use intuitive navigation patterns and interactive elements that guide users seamlessly through the app's interface. Always prioritise user needs and convenience in every design decision.

2. Curate a Thoughtful Colour Palette

Selecting an appropriate colour palette is crucial in minimalistic design. Muted tones, soft pastels, and neutral hues are often well-received. Choose a limited set of colours that not only align with your brand identity but also evoke the desired emotional response from users. Maintain consistency in colour usage to create a cohesive and visually pleasing experience.

3. Balancing Style and Readability

Typography is pivotal in conveying information and establishing the app's visual identity. Opt for clean, legible fonts that complement your brand's personality. Consider using a combination of fonts for headings, body text, and buttons to establish visual hierarchy. Pay careful attention to font sizes and spacing to ensure optimal readability on various device screens.

4. Leverage White Space Strategically

White space, often called negative space, is a fundamental element in minimalistic UI design. It serves to reduce visual clutter and direct focus towards essential elements. Ensure that there is ample breathing room around buttons, text, and images, allowing the interface to feel balanced and harmonious. Strategic use of white space enhances overall user comprehension and engagement.

5. Intuitive Navigation to Guide Users Seamlessly

Efficient navigation is the backbone of any successful app. In a minimalistic UI, navigation should be intuitive and unobtrusive. Employ familiar navigation patterns like tab bars, hamburger menus, and clearly labeled buttons. Prioritise user flow, ensuring that users can effortlessly transition between different app sections.

6. Uphold Design Consistency Across Elements

Consistency in design elements and interactions is paramount in a minimalistic UI. Maintain a unified style for buttons, icons, and other UI components throughout the app. This consistency fosters a sense of familiarity and predictability for users, ultimately enhancing usability and user satisfaction.

7. Test, Iterate, and Incorporate User Feedback

After developing a working UI design, conduct rigorous usability testing with real users. Gather feedback on the user experience, identifying any pain points or areas for improvement. This feedback is invaluable in refining the UI to ensure it aligns with the evolving needs and preferences of your audience. Iterate on the design based on user insights to achieve an optimal user interface.

Characteristics of Minimal App Design

Minimal app design is characterised by several key features that set it apart from more complex or ornate design styles. Here are the key characteristics of minimal app design:

1. Simplicity

At its core, minimal app design is all about simplicity. It embraces a "less is more" philosophy, focusing on the essential elements and functionality without unnecessary embellishments or distractions.

2. Clean Lines and Shapes

Minimalist designs often feature clean lines, geometric shapes, and straightforward layouts. This creates a visually uncluttered and organised appearance.

3. Limited Colour Palette

A minimal app design typically employs a limited colour palette with muted tones, neutral hues, and subtle contrasts. This restrained use of colour contributes to a clean and harmonious visual experience.

4. High-Quality Imagery

When images are used, they are of high quality and relevance. They are often employed sparingly to complement the overall design without overwhelming the user.

5. Mobile-Friendly

Given the prevalence of mobile devices, minimal app designs are typically optimised for smaller screens. They prioritise responsive layouts and ensure that content remains accessible and legible on various devices.

6. Timeless Aesthetics

Minimalist designs often have a timeless quality. They can age well and are less likely to become dated than designs heavily relying on trends or complex visual elements.

Benefits of Minimal Design in Apps

Minimalistic UI designs go beyond just looking fancy and provide the following advantages:

1. Enhanced User Experience

A clutter-free, minimalistic UI reduces cognitive load for users. It allows them to focus on the core functionality of the app without distractions. This leads to a smoother and more enjoyable user experience.

2. Faster Load Times

Simple UIs typically require fewer resources to render, resulting in faster loading times. This is crucial for retaining user engagement, especially in today's fast-paced digital environment, where attention spans are limited.

3. Improved Readability and Comprehension

Minimalistic designs often feature clean typography, well-spaced elements, and legible fonts. This makes content easier to read and understand, enhancing user interaction with the app.

4. Increased Accessibility

A minimalist approach to UI design can lead to better accessibility. Clear visual hierarchies, larger font sizes, and simplified navigation contribute to a more inclusive experience for users with varying abilities.

5. Consistency and Branding

A minimalistic UI can help maintain a consistent brand identity. It allows for a unified design language that extends across different screens and platforms, reinforcing brand recognition.

6. Reduced User Frustration

Cluttered interfaces can confuse and frustrate users. A clean, minimalistic UI reduces the likelihood of users getting lost or overwhelmed, leading to a more positive overall experience.

7. Mobile-Friendly Design

With the increasing use of mobile devices, minimalistic UIs are particularly effective. They ensure that content and functionality are easily accessible and legible on smaller screens.

8. Faster Learning Curve

Intuitive design patterns in a minimalistic UI reduce the learning curve for new users. They can quickly grasp how to navigate and interact with the app, leading to faster onboarding.

9. Adaptability to Trends and Updates

Minimalistic designs tend to age well and are more adaptable to evolving design trends. They can be easily updated without overhauling the entire UI, providing longevity to the app's visual appeal.

10. Focus on Core Functionality

By removing unnecessary elements and features, a minimalistic UI puts the spotlight on the core functionalities of the app. This ensures that users can easily access and utilise the app's primary purpose.

title: SWAM: Saliency-Weighted Asymmetric Merging for Efficient Vision Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.18057v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong performance on image recognition tasks, yet their quadratic self-attention complexity over input tokens creates prohibitive computational costs for practical deployment. Token reduction methods offer a practical solution by progressively reducing the token sequence during the forward pass. We propose Saliency-Weighted Asymmetric Merging (SWAM), a training-based token merging framework that extends the Bipartite Soft Matching (BSM) with two saliency-aware mechanisms. We introduce a two-step matching formulation in which cosine similarity decides candidate pairs, while a multiplicative maximum saliency penalty regulates their selection for merging. We then further use asymmetric exponential saliency-weighted aggregation, which allows more salient tokens to contribute more strongly to the merged representation. A lightweight MLP-based saliency prediction module (75k parameters per stage, 1% of backbone parameters) supervised via attention rollout is trained end-to-end jointly with a DeiT-Small backbone using a composite cross-entropy, knowledge-distillation, and saliency-alignment objective. On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-100, under a conservative schedule that reduces tokens from 196 to 100 patch tokens, with the CLS token retained throughout, 27.5% FLOPs reduction and 1.35 times speedup, SWAM matches or exceeds baseline across the reported results. Under an aggressive schedule (196 to 70 tokens with the CLS token kept throughout, 33.8% FLOPs reduction, and 1.46 times speedup), accuracy gains are achieved on ImageNet-100 (+0.23%) with minimal losses on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet.

title: Adversarially Batched Online Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17500v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce adversarially batched online learning, where the learner may update its decision rule only at a restricted set of time steps. Equivalently, the time horizon is partitioned into batches, within which the learner must use a fixed policy. We study this model for four canonical problems: stochastic bandits, online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits. For stochastic bandits, we identify a universal complexity measure based on relative batch growth and establish both gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds. We show that the multiplicative penalty relative to the standard gap-dependent complexity can grow superlinearly in batch hardness. For the remaining three, we show that the optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence. The upper bound is achieved by a batch-oblivious learner who does not know the batch structure, via a generic adaptive doubling trick tailored to this complexity measure. In contrast, the lower bound holds even for batch-aware learners.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them

When you're building a payout system, ACH returns are inevitable. A user's bank account closes. Funds aren't available. The account holder disputes the transfer. Your integration needs to handle these failures gracefully—and that starts with understanding what each return code actually means.

The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) defines 85 standardized return codes (R01 through R85). Each one tells you why a debit or credit failed, and more importantly, what you should do next. Let's walk through the most common ones and how to decode them in your payout flow.

The Big Three: R01, R02, R03

R01: Insufficient Funds

The account exists and is valid, but the balance is too low. This is the most common return code—roughly 30–40% of all ACH returns in production systems.

  • When it fires: During the settlement window (typically 1–2 business days after submission).
  • What it means: The account holder has the account, but not enough money right now.
  • How to handle it: Retry after 2–3 business days, or switch to a different payout method if the user has one on file. Don't retry immediately; the funds won't magically appear.

R02: Account Closed by Institution

The bank shut down the account. This is permanent.

  • When it fires: During settlement.
  • What it means: The account is gone. Do not retry.
  • How to handle it: Flag the account as invalid, notify the user, and ask for a new bank account or alternate payout method.

R03: No Account/Unable to Locate Account

The routing number or account number doesn't exist, or the bank can't find it in their system.

  • When it fires: During settlement or early in the processing window.
  • What it means: The account details are wrong or the account was never opened.
  • How to handle it: Validate the account before the next payout attempt. Use microdeposit verification or real-time account validation (offered by some ACH providers).

Mid-Tier Returns: R04, R10, R29

R04: Reserved

This code is reserved by Nacha and rarely used in practice. If you see it, escalate to your ACH provider.

R10: Customer Advises Not Authorized

The account holder called their bank and said, "I didn't authorize this transfer."

  • When it fires: 60–90 days after settlement (this is the long tail of ACH disputes).
  • What it means: The user is disputing the payout. You may have a legitimate claim, but the burden of proof is now on you.
  • How to handle it: Log the dispute, preserve all transaction records, and prepare to provide proof of authorization (signed agreement, email consent, etc.). Some platforms flag the user as high-risk for future payouts.

R29: Corporate Account Closed

Like R02, but for business accounts.

  • When it fires: During settlement.
  • What it means: The business account is closed. Permanent.
  • How to handle it: Same as R02—ask for a new account.

Rare but Critical: R82, R83, R84

R82: Duplicate Entry

You (or your processor) submitted the same payout twice in the same batch window.

  • When it fires: During settlement.
  • What it means: The bank rejected one copy as a duplicate.
  • How to handle it: Check your idempotency logic. Use a unique transaction ID per payout and ensure your integration doesn't submit the same request twice on retry.

R83: Routing Number Check Digit Error

The routing number format is invalid or the check digit doesn't match.

  • When it fires: During validation, sometimes during settlement.
  • What it means: Bad data. The account details are wrong.
  • How to handle it: Validate routing numbers before submission using the ABA routing number database.

R84: Account Number Structure Error

The account number is malformed (wrong length, invalid characters).

  • When it fires: During validation or settlement.
  • What it means: Data quality issue.
  • How to handle it: Sanitize and validate account numbers on input.

Building Retry Logic Around Return Codes

Here's a simple decision tree for handling returns:

Return Code Retry? Timeline Alternate Action
R01 Yes 2–3 days Switch payout method
R02, R03, R29 No N/A Request new account
R10 No Dispute mode Gather proof of auth
R82, R83, R84 No Immediate Fix data, resubmit

The key insight: not all returns are retryable. R01 (insufficient funds) might resolve itself. R02 (account closed) never will.

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Amazon loses first batch of broadband satellites launched on custom rocket
description: United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan LEO didn’t reach orbit

title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.17880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simultaneously: completing the user's task (utility) and conforming to domain policies and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension -- blocking an unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other. We introduce Soteria, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajectories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.

title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.17463v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.

title: Building an Async Java REST Client with CompletableFuture, Concurrent Requests, and Virtual Threads
description:
Synchronous HTTP code is simple.

But sometimes your application needs to call several APIs at once, reduce waiting time, or avoid tying up threads while requests are in flight.

That is where asynchronous programming becomes useful.

In this tutorial, we'll build on Java's built-in HttpClient and explore:

  • sendAsync()
  • CompletableFuture
  • Running multiple HTTP requests concurrently
  • Combining several API responses
  • Handling async errors
  • Applying timeouts
  • Using Jackson with asynchronous responses
  • Comparing CompletableFuture with virtual threads
  • Understanding when async code is actually worth using

By the end, you'll have several practical patterns for building concurrent REST clients in modern Java.

1. Synchronous vs Asynchronous HTTP

A normal synchronous request looks like this:

HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(
        request,
        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
);

The current thread waits until the response arrives.

Conceptually:

Send request
    ↓
Wait
    ↓
Wait
    ↓
Receive response
    ↓
Continue

This is easy to understand.

But if you need to call three independent APIs:

API A → 2 seconds
API B → 3 seconds
API C → 1 second

and you call them one after another, the total time can be roughly:

2 + 3 + 1 = 6 seconds

That is where concurrency can help.

2. HttpClient.sendAsync()

Java's HttpClient has an asynchronous method:

sendAsync()

Instead of returning:

HttpResponse<String>

it returns:

CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>

Example:

CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> future =
        client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        );

The request starts, but the current thread does not block waiting for the result.

3. Your First Async Request

Let's create a simple example.

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;

public class AsyncExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        HttpClient client =
                HttpClient.newHttpClient();

        HttpRequest request =
                HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(URI.create(
                                "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1"
                        ))
                        .GET()
                        .build();

        CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> future =
                client.sendAsync(
                        request,
                        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
                );

        future.thenAccept(response -> {
            System.out.println(
                    response.statusCode()
            );

            System.out.println(
                    response.body()
            );
        });

        future.join();
    }
}

The important line is:

future.thenAccept(...)

This says:

When the response arrives, run this code.

4. What Does join() Do?

In the previous example, we used:

future.join();

Why?

Because this is a small console application.

Without it, the main method could finish before the asynchronous response is processed.

join() waits for the CompletableFuture to complete.

So although the HTTP operation is asynchronous, our demo waits at the end so the application stays alive.

In larger applications, you often won't call join() immediately.

5. thenApply() vs thenAccept()

These two methods are commonly used with CompletableFuture.

thenAccept()

Use it when you want to consume a result but not return another value.

future.thenAccept(response -> {
    System.out.println(
            response.body()
    );
});

thenApply()

Use it when you want to transform the result.

CompletableFuture<String> bodyFuture =
        future.thenApply(
                HttpResponse::body
        );

Now:

bodyFuture

is:

CompletableFuture<String>

rather than:

CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>

6. Transforming an HTTP Response

A common pattern is:

CompletableFuture<String> result =
        client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(
                HttpResponse::body
        );

Then:

String body = result.join();

This is much cleaner if you only care about the body.

But in production code, you should usually check the status code first.

7. Validate the Status Code

Let's create a helper:

private static HttpResponse<String> validate(
        HttpResponse<String> response
) {

    int status =
            response.statusCode();

    if (status >= 200 &&
        status < 300) {

        return response;
    }

    throw new RuntimeException(
            "HTTP " +
            status +
            ": " +
            response.body()
    );
}

Now:

CompletableFuture<String> bodyFuture =
        client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(
                AsyncExample::validate
        )
        .thenApply(
                HttpResponse::body
        );

The flow becomes:

sendAsync()
    ↓
validate()
    ↓
extract body

8. Add Jackson

Now let's combine async HTTP with Jackson.

Suppose an API returns:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Hello",
  "body": "Example",
  "userId": 1
}

Create a record:

public record Post(
        int id,
        String title,
        String body,
        int userId
) {
}

Then use Jackson:

ObjectMapper mapper =
        new ObjectMapper();

We can parse the response asynchronously.

9. Async JSON Deserialization

Example:

CompletableFuture<Post> postFuture =
        client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(
                AsyncExample::validate
        )
        .thenApply(
                HttpResponse::body
        )
        .thenApply(body -> {

            try {

                return mapper.readValue(
                        body,
                        Post.class
                );

            } catch (Exception e) {

                throw new RuntimeException(e);
            }
        });

Now:

postFuture

is:

CompletableFuture<Post>

Usage:

Post post =
        postFuture.join();

System.out.println(
        post.title()
);

10. Create a Reusable Async GET Method

Let's make the pattern reusable.

public <T> CompletableFuture<T> getAsync(
        String url,
        Class<T> responseType
) {

    HttpRequest request =
            HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(URI.create(url))
                    .header(
                            "Accept",
                            "application/json"
                    )
                    .GET()
                    .build();

    return client.sendAsync(
            request,
            HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
    )
    .thenApply(this::validate)
    .thenApply(response -> {

        try {

            return mapper.readValue(
                    response.body(),
                    responseType
            );

        } catch (IOException e) {

            throw new CompletionException(e);
        }
    });
}

Now calling an API becomes:

CompletableFuture<User> future =
        restClient.getAsync(
                "https://example.com/users/1",
                User.class
        );

11. Why CompletionException?

Inside a CompletableFuture pipeline, checked exceptions are awkward.

Jackson can throw:

IOException

but a lambda passed to thenApply() cannot simply throw it.

A common pattern is:

throw new CompletionException(e);

This wraps the checked exception inside an unchecked exception that works naturally with CompletableFuture.

12. Run Multiple Requests Concurrently

This is where async becomes especially useful.

Suppose we want:

/users/1
/posts/1
/todos/1

We can start all three requests immediately:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        client.getAsync(
                userUrl,
                User.class
        );

CompletableFuture<Post> postFuture =
        client.getAsync(
                postUrl,
                Post.class
        );

CompletableFuture<Todo> todoFuture =
        client.getAsync(
                todoUrl,
                Todo.class
        );

At this point, all three requests can be in flight at the same time.

13. Sequential vs Concurrent Timing

Sequential:

Request A
    ↓
wait
    ↓
Request B
    ↓
wait
    ↓
Request C

Concurrent:

Request A ──────────────┐
Request B ──────────┐   │
Request C ───────┐  │   │
                 ↓  ↓   ↓
               results arrive

If the requests are independent, concurrent execution can reduce total waiting time significantly.

14. Combine Two Futures with thenCombine()

Suppose we want to combine:

CompletableFuture<User>

and:

CompletableFuture<List<Post>>

We can use:

thenCombine()

Example:

CompletableFuture<UserProfile> profileFuture =
        userFuture.thenCombine(
                postsFuture,
                (user, posts) ->
                        new UserProfile(
                                user,
                                posts
                        )
        );

Now:

profileFuture

contains both results.

15. Example UserProfile 

public record UserProfile(
        User user,
        List<Post> posts
) {
}

Then:

UserProfile profile =
        profileFuture.join();

This is useful when several endpoints contribute to one final result.

16. Combine Many Futures with allOf()

thenCombine() works well for two futures.

For many futures, use:

CompletableFuture.allOf(...)

Example:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        getUser();

CompletableFuture<List<Post>> postsFuture =
        getPosts();

CompletableFuture<List<Todo>> todosFuture =
        getTodos();

Then:

CompletableFuture<Void> all =
        CompletableFuture.allOf(
                userFuture,
                postsFuture,
                todosFuture
        );

Wait for all:

all.join();

Then retrieve:

User user =
        userFuture.join();

List<Post> posts =
        postsFuture.join();

List<Todo> todos =
        todosFuture.join();

17. Build the Final Object After allOf()

A cleaner approach:

CompletableFuture<Dashboard> dashboardFuture =
        CompletableFuture.allOf(
                userFuture,
                postsFuture,
                todosFuture
        )
        .thenApply(ignored ->
                new Dashboard(
                        userFuture.join(),
                        postsFuture.join(),
                        todosFuture.join()
                )
        );

Now:

Dashboard dashboard =
        dashboardFuture.join();

18. A Helper for Lists of Futures

Suppose we have:

List<CompletableFuture<User>>

and want:

CompletableFuture<List<User>>

We can create:

public static <T>
CompletableFuture<List<T>> sequence(
        List<CompletableFuture<T>> futures
) {

    CompletableFuture<Void> all =
            CompletableFuture.allOf(
                    futures.toArray(
                            CompletableFuture[]::new
                    )
            );

    return all.thenApply(
            ignored ->
                    futures.stream()
                            .map(
                                    CompletableFuture::join
                            )
                            .toList()
    );
}

Usage:

List<CompletableFuture<User>> futures =
        ids.stream()
                .map(
                        id ->
                                client.getAsync(
                                        "/users/" + id,
                                        User.class
                                )
                )
                .toList();

CompletableFuture<List<User>> usersFuture =
        sequence(futures);

This is a very useful pattern.

19. But Don't Launch Unlimited Requests

There is an important danger.

Imagine:

10,000 user IDs

and you do:

ids.stream()
        .map(id -> getAsync(...))
        .toList();

You might launch thousands of HTTP requests at once.

That can:

  • Overload the remote API
  • Hit rate limits
  • Exhaust resources
  • Create huge memory pressure

Concurrency still needs limits.

20. Limit Concurrency

One simple approach is batching.

Instead of:

10,000 concurrent requests

do:

50 at a time

For example:

int batchSize = 50;

Then process IDs in batches.

Conceptually:

Batch 1
    → 50 requests
    → wait

Batch 2
    → 50 requests
    → wait

Batch 3
    → 50 requests

This is often safer than unlimited concurrency.

21. Async Error Handling with exceptionally()

Suppose a request fails.

You can handle it using:

exceptionally()

Example:

CompletableFuture<User> future =
        client.getAsync(
                url,
                User.class
        )
        .exceptionally(error -> {

            System.err.println(
                    error.getMessage()
            );

            return null;
        });

This converts the failed future into a successful future containing:

null

That can be useful, but be careful.

Returning null can hide failures.

22. Use handle() When You Need Both Cases

handle() receives both:

result
error

Example:

future.handle(
        (user, error) -> {

            if (error != null) {

                System.err.println(
                        "Request failed: " +
                        error.getMessage()
                );

                return fallbackUser();
            }

            return user;
        }
);

This is useful for fallback logic.

23. Use whenComplete() for Logging

Sometimes you don't want to change the result.

You just want to observe it.

Use:

whenComplete()

Example:

future.whenComplete(
        (result, error) -> {

            if (error != null) {

                System.err.println(
                        "Failed: " +
                        error.getMessage()
                );

            } else {

                System.out.println(
                        "Request completed"
                );
            }
        }
);

The original future result continues unchanged.

24. exceptionally() vs handle() vs whenComplete()

A useful rule:

exceptionally()
    → recover only from failure

handle()
    → transform success or failure

whenComplete()
    → observe success or failure

25. Add Async Timeouts

CompletableFuture provides timeout helpers.

Fail after a timeout 

future.orTimeout(
        5,
        TimeUnit.SECONDS
);

If the future does not complete in time, it fails.

Return a fallback value 

future.completeOnTimeout(
        fallbackUser,
        5,
        TimeUnit.SECONDS
);

This can be useful in applications where partial results are acceptable.

26. HTTP Timeout vs Future Timeout

These are different.

HttpRequest.timeout(...)

Controls the HTTP request.

HttpRequest.newBuilder()
        .timeout(
                Duration.ofSeconds(10)
        )

CompletableFuture.orTimeout(...)

Controls the future pipeline.

future.orTimeout(
        12,
        TimeUnit.SECONDS
);

Using both can provide stronger protection.

27. Async POST Requests

POST can also be asynchronous.

Example:

public <T, R>
CompletableFuture<R> postAsync(
        String url,
        T requestBody,
        Class<R> responseType
) {

    try {

        String json =
                mapper.writeValueAsString(
                        requestBody
                );

        HttpRequest request =
                HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(URI.create(url))
                        .header(
                                "Content-Type",
                                "application/json"
                        )
                        .POST(
                                HttpRequest.BodyPublishers
                                        .ofString(json)
                        )
                        .build();

        return client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(this::validate)
        .thenApply(response -> {

            try {

                return mapper.readValue(
                        response.body(),
                        responseType
                );

            } catch (IOException e) {

                throw new CompletionException(e);
            }
        });

    } catch (IOException e) {

        return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(
                e
        );
    }
}

28. Why failedFuture() Is Useful

Suppose serialization fails before the HTTP request starts.

We still want to return:

CompletableFuture<R>

instead of throwing immediately.

Java provides:

CompletableFuture.failedFuture(error)

So the caller sees the failure through the same async API.

29. Build an Async RestClient

Let's create a more complete version.

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.DeserializationFeature;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException;

public class AsyncRestClient {

    private final HttpClient client;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public AsyncRestClient() {

        this.client =
                HttpClient.newBuilder()
                        .connectTimeout(
                                Duration.ofSeconds(10)
                        )
                        .build();

        this.mapper =
                new ObjectMapper()
                        .configure(
                                DeserializationFeature
                                        .FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES,
                                false
                        );
    }

    public <T> CompletableFuture<T> getAsync(
            String url,
            Class<T> responseType
    ) {

        HttpRequest request =
                HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                        .uri(
                                URI.create(url)
                        )
                        .timeout(
                                Duration.ofSeconds(20)
                        )
                        .header(
                                "Accept",
                                "application/json"
                        )
                        .GET()
                        .build();

        return client.sendAsync(
                request,
                HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
        )
        .thenApply(this::validate)
        .thenApply(
                response ->
                        deserialize(
                                response.body(),
                                responseType
                        )
        );
    }

    private HttpResponse<String> validate(
            HttpResponse<String> response
    ) {

        int status =
                response.statusCode();

        if (status >= 200 &&
            status < 300) {

            return response;
        }

        throw new ApiException(
                status,
                response.body()
        );
    }

    private <T> T deserialize(
            String body,
            Class<T> responseType
    ) {

        try {

            return mapper.readValue(
                    body,
                    responseType
            );

        } catch (IOException e) {

            throw new CompletionException(e);
        }
    }
}

30. Add Authentication

We can add a bearer token:

private final String token;

Constructor:

public AsyncRestClient(
        String token
) {

    this.token = token;

    // initialize client and mapper
}

Then create a shared builder:

private HttpRequest.Builder requestBuilder(
        String url
) {

    HttpRequest.Builder builder =
            HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                    .uri(
                            URI.create(url)
                    )
                    .timeout(
                            Duration.ofSeconds(20)
                    )
                    .header(
                            "Accept",
                            "application/json"
                    );

    if (token != null &&
        !token.isBlank()) {

        builder.header(
                "Authorization",
                "Bearer " + token
        );
    }

    return builder;
}

Then:

HttpRequest request =
        requestBuilder(url)
                .GET()
                .build();

31. Async Retries

Retries can also work with async requests.

A simple recursive pattern:

private CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>
sendWithRetry(
        HttpRequest request,
        int attempt
) {

    return client.sendAsync(
            request,
            HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
    )
    .thenCompose(response -> {

        if (!isRetryableStatus(
                response.statusCode()
        )) {

            return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(
                    response
            );
        }

        if (attempt >= 3) {

            return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(
                    response
            );
        }

        return delay(
                Duration.ofSeconds(attempt)
        )
        .thenCompose(
                ignored ->
                        sendWithRetry(
                                request,
                                attempt + 1
                        )
        );
    });
}

Now we need an async delay.

32. Async Delay Without Thread.sleep()

Blocking with:

Thread.sleep(...)

inside async code defeats part of the purpose.

A better option is:

CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(...)

Example:

private CompletableFuture<Void> delay(
        Duration duration
) {

    return CompletableFuture.runAsync(
            () -> {},
            CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(
                    duration.toMillis(),
                    TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS
            )
    );
}

Now the retry delay itself does not block the request-handling thread.

33. Async Retry with Exponential Backoff

We can calculate:

private Duration retryDelay(
        int attempt
) {

    long millis =
            1000L *
            (1L << (attempt - 1));

    return Duration.ofMillis(
            millis
    );
}

Then:

return delay(
        retryDelay(attempt)
)
.thenCompose(
        ignored ->
                sendWithRetry(
                        request,
                        attempt + 1
                )
);

This produces:

1 second
2 seconds
4 seconds

34. Async Code Can Become Hard to Read

This is the main downside.

Simple synchronous code:

User user =
        client.getUser();

List<Post> posts =
        client.getPosts();

Async code:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        client.getUserAsync();

CompletableFuture<List<Post>> postsFuture =
        client.getPostsAsync();

CompletableFuture<UserProfile> profile =
        userFuture.thenCombine(
                postsFuture,
                UserProfile::new
        );

The async version can be faster for independent requests.

But it is also more complex.

So don't use async just because it looks more advanced.

35. Enter Virtual Threads

Modern Java gives us another option:

virtual threads

Virtual threads make blocking code much cheaper than traditional platform threads.

This changes how we think about HTTP concurrency.

Instead of writing async pipelines, we can often write normal blocking code while still achieving high concurrency.

36. Traditional Threads vs Virtual Threads

Traditional threads are relatively expensive.

You generally don't want:

10,000 platform threads

Virtual threads are much lighter.

So this style becomes practical:

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    // submit many blocking tasks
}

Each task can call:

client.send(...)

normally.

37. Virtual Thread Example

Suppose we want three HTTP calls.

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    Future<User> userFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getUser()
            );

    Future<List<Post>> postsFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getPosts()
            );

    Future<List<Todo>> todosFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getTodos()
            );

    User user =
            userFuture.get();

    List<Post> posts =
            postsFuture.get();

    List<Todo> todos =
            todosFuture.get();
}

These calls run concurrently.

But each method can remain synchronous internally.

38. Why Virtual Threads Are Attractive

Compare these two approaches.

CompletableFuture 

userFuture
        .thenCombine(
                postsFuture,
                UserProfile::new
        )
        .thenApply(...)
        .exceptionally(...)

Virtual threads 

User user =
        userFuture.get();

List<Post> posts =
        postsFuture.get();

return new UserProfile(
        user,
        posts
);

Virtual threads often let you keep simpler control flow.

39. Does HttpClient Work with Virtual Threads?

Yes.

You can use regular blocking:

client.send(...)

inside a virtual thread.

That is often a very clean design for applications that need high concurrency but prefer straightforward imperative code.

40. CompletableFuture vs Virtual Threads

A rough comparison:

Feature CompletableFuture Virtual Threads
Non-blocking style Yes No, logically blocking
Readability Can become complex Usually simpler
Composition Excellent Straightforward
High concurrency Yes Yes
Best for pipelines Excellent Good
Best for imperative code Okay Excellent
Error handling Functional style Traditional try/catch

Neither approach is always better.

41. When CompletableFuture Is a Good Fit

Use it when:

  • You already have an asynchronous API
  • You need to compose several asynchronous stages
  • You want non-blocking pipelines
  • You need thenCombine(), allOf(), or async transformations
  • Your framework already works heavily with futures

Example:

HTTP request
    ↓
parse response
    ↓
fetch another resource
    ↓
combine results
    ↓
transform

42. When Virtual Threads Are a Good Fit

Virtual threads are often excellent when:

  • Your code is naturally synchronous
  • You want many concurrent blocking operations
  • You want simple try/catch control flow
  • You don't want deeply nested future chains
  • Your application uses lots of I/O

Example:

User user =
        userApi.getUser(id);

List<Post> posts =
        postApi.getPosts(id);

return new Profile(
        user,
        posts
);

This style is easier to debug and understand.

43. Avoid Mixing Styles Without a Reason

You can technically combine:

CompletableFuture
virtual threads
reactive code
blocking code

in one application.

But complexity grows quickly.

Choose the simplest model that fits your needs.

A useful rule:

Simple request
    → synchronous

Many concurrent blocking tasks
    → consider virtual threads

Async pipeline composition
    → consider CompletableFuture

44. Example: Fetch 100 Users Concurrently with CompletableFuture 

List<Integer> ids =
        IntStream.rangeClosed(
                1,
                100
        )
        .boxed()
        .toList();

List<CompletableFuture<User>> futures =
        ids.stream()
                .map(
                        id ->
                                client.getAsync(
                                        baseUrl +
                                        "/users/" +
                                        id,
                                        User.class
                                )
                )
                .toList();

List<User> users =
        sequence(futures)
                .join();

This works well.

But remember: concurrency should still be bounded for large workloads.

45. Example: Fetch 100 Users with Virtual Threads 

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    List<Future<User>> futures =
            ids.stream()
                    .map(
                            id ->
                                    executor.submit(
                                            () ->
                                                    client.get(
                                                            "/users/" +
                                                            id,
                                                            User.class
                                                    )
                                    )
                    )
                    .toList();

    List<User> users =
            new ArrayList<>();

    for (Future<User> future
            : futures) {

        users.add(
                future.get()
        );
    }
}

This is very readable.

46. Partial Failure

Suppose you request:

100 users

and one request fails.

Should the entire operation fail?

Maybe.

Maybe not.

This depends on your application.

All-or-nothing 

One failure
    → entire operation fails

Best effort 

Successful responses
    → keep them

Failed responses
    → log and continue

You should decide this explicitly.

47. Best-Effort Async Example 

CompletableFuture<User> future =
        client.getAsync(
                url,
                User.class
        )
        .handle(
                (user, error) -> {

                    if (error != null) {

                        System.err.println(
                                "Failed: " +
                                url
                        );

                        return null;
                    }

                    return user;
                }
        );

Then filter:

List<User> users =
        sequence(futures)
                .join()
                .stream()
                .filter(
                        Objects::nonNull
                )
                .toList();

48. Preserve Error Information

Returning null loses useful information.

A cleaner approach is a result wrapper.

public record Result<T>(
        T value,
        Throwable error
) {

    public boolean isSuccess() {
        return error == null;
    }
}

Then:

CompletableFuture<Result<User>> future =
        client.getAsync(
                url,
                User.class
        )
        .handle(
                (user, error) ->
                        new Result<>(
                                user,
                                error
                        )
        );

Now every operation produces a result.

49. Use Cases for Concurrent REST Calls

Concurrency is especially useful when:

  • Building dashboards from several APIs
  • Aggregating microservice responses
  • Calling independent third-party services
  • Fetching multiple pages
  • Processing many independent resources
  • Enriching data from several endpoints

For example:

Customer profile
    ↓
Customer API
Orders API
Payments API
Shipping API

If those requests are independent, they can often run concurrently.

50. Don't Parallelize Dependent Requests

Suppose:

Request B needs data from Request A

Then you cannot simply run them together.

Example:

GET /users/10
    ↓
extract accountId
    ↓
GET /accounts/{accountId}

That is a dependency chain.

With CompletableFuture:

CompletableFuture<Account> accountFuture =
        getUserAsync(10)
                .thenCompose(
                        user ->
                                getAccountAsync(
                                        user.accountId()
                                )
                );

Notice:

thenCompose()

not:

thenApply()

51. thenApply() vs thenCompose()

This distinction is important.

Suppose:

getUserAsync()

returns:

CompletableFuture<User>

and:

getAccountAsync(...)

returns:

CompletableFuture<Account>

If you use:

thenApply(...)

you may get:

CompletableFuture<
    CompletableFuture<Account>
>

That's usually not what you want.

Use:

thenCompose(...)

to flatten it into:

CompletableFuture<Account>

52. The Mental Model

A useful rule:

thenApply
    → T becomes R

thenCompose
    → T becomes CompletableFuture<R>
      and Java flattens it

Example:

future.thenApply(
        user ->
                user.name()
);

versus:

future.thenCompose(
        user ->
                getPostsAsync(
                        user.id()
                )
);

53. Full Example: Async User Dashboard

Suppose we have:

public record User(
        int id,
        String name
) {
}

public record Post(
        int id,
        int userId,
        String title
) {
}

public record Todo(
        int id,
        int userId,
        String title,
        boolean completed
) {
}

And:

public record Dashboard(
        User user,
        List<Post> posts,
        List<Todo> todos
) {
}

Then:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture =
        getUserAsync(userId);

CompletableFuture<List<Post>> postsFuture =
        getPostsAsync(userId);

CompletableFuture<List<Todo>> todosFuture =
        getTodosAsync(userId);

CompletableFuture<Dashboard> dashboardFuture =
        CompletableFuture.allOf(
                userFuture,
                postsFuture,
                todosFuture
        )
        .thenApply(
                ignored ->
                        new Dashboard(
                                userFuture.join(),
                                postsFuture.join(),
                                todosFuture.join()
                        )
        );

Now:

Dashboard dashboard =
        dashboardFuture.join();

54. The Same Idea with Virtual Threads 

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

    Future<User> userFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getUser(userId)
            );

    Future<List<Post>> postsFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getPosts(userId)
            );

    Future<List<Todo>> todosFuture =
            executor.submit(
                    () ->
                            getTodos(userId)
            );

    Dashboard dashboard =
            new Dashboard(
                    userFuture.get(),
                    postsFuture.get(),
                    todosFuture.get()
            );
}

Same concurrency.

Different programming model.

55. Which Version Would I Choose?

For this particular example, virtual threads are arguably easier to read.

The control flow is straightforward.

But if the rest of your system already uses asynchronous APIs and futures, CompletableFuture may fit better.

The important thing is not to choose the most complicated option.

Choose the model that makes the code easiest to understand and maintain.

56. Quick CompletableFuture Cheat Sheet

Start an async HTTP request 

client.sendAsync(
        request,
        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()
);

Transform result 

future.thenApply(...)

Chain another async operation 

future.thenCompose(...)

Consume result 

future.thenAccept(...)

Combine two futures 

future1.thenCombine(
        future2,
        (a, b) -> ...
);

Wait for many 

CompletableFuture.allOf(
        futures...
);

Recover from error 

future.exceptionally(...)

Handle success or failure 

future.handle(...)

Observe completion 

future.whenComplete(...)

Wait for result 

future.join()

57. Quick Virtual Thread Cheat Sheet

Create an executor:

try (var executor =
        Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {

}

Submit a blocking task:

Future<User> future =
        executor.submit(
                () ->
                        getUser()
        );

Get the result:

User user =
        future.get();

This lets you keep synchronous APIs while still achieving a high degree of concurrency.

58. Production Checklist

Before shipping concurrent HTTP code, ask:

  • Are requests independent?
  • Is concurrency bounded?
  • Are timeouts configured?
  • Are rate limits respected?
  • Are retries bounded?
  • Are errors preserved?
  • Is partial failure acceptable?
  • Are async exceptions handled?
  • Are POST retries safe?
  • Are large batches controlled?
  • Is the code still readable?
  • Would virtual threads make it simpler?

Concurrency can improve performance, but uncontrolled concurrency can create new problems.

Final Thoughts

Java now gives us several strong options for HTTP concurrency.

You can use:

HttpClient.sendAsync()
        +
CompletableFuture

for asynchronous pipelines.

Or:

virtual threads
        +
blocking HttpClient.send()

for high-concurrency code that still looks synchronous.

The key is understanding the tradeoff.

CompletableFuture is excellent when your workflow is naturally asynchronous and composed from multiple stages.

Virtual threads are excellent when you want simple blocking code but still need lots of concurrent I/O.

A useful progression is:

Simple request
    ↓
Synchronous HttpClient

Several independent requests
    ↓
CompletableFuture or virtual threads

Large-scale concurrent I/O
    ↓
Bounded concurrency + timeouts + retries + rate limits

The goal is not to make your code "more asynchronous."

The goal is to make it faster where concurrency helps, while keeping the code understandable.

title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
description:
arXiv:2611.17563v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.

title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
description:
arXiv:2611.17814v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.

title: unumsearch: a trigram index so coding agents stop re-reading 258,000 files
description:
An AI coding agent asks the same sort of question hundreds of times a day: where is this function called, which files mention that setting. A plain rg answers each one by reading every file again. That is fine on one repository. It gets slow when you run many checkouts on one machine, which is our situation.

So we built unumsearch, a search CLI for code and files that keeps an index and answers like ripgrep, usually in milliseconds. It is open source (Apache-2.0), written in Rust, and has no GPU, model or network dependency. This post is what it does, what we measured, and where it loses.

How it works

The index is a list of every three-letter piece of text and the files it appears in. A query is cut into those pieces, the index names the few files that contain all of them, and only those files are opened and checked line by line against their real contents. The index only narrows what to read; the answer always comes from the file.

Two properties matter for agents:

  • It says when it might be stale. A file watcher marks edits, changed files are searched directly until the index catches up, and every JSON answer carries fresh, backend, covered, truncated and complete fields so a client knows when to scan for itself.
  • It does not index secrets. .ssh/, .aws/, .env*, *.key, *.pem and similar are never indexed, whatever the configuration says.

What we measured

The test set is 20 regexes mined from a week of real coding-agent tool calls, on the author's machine, dated 2026-10-09.

Over the whole tree (247,535 files, warm page cache, median of three passes), ripgrep 15.1 took 347 ms per query. The unumsearch daemon took 64 ms and the one-shot CLI took 91 ms.

In a separate race of 12 patterns our agents actually issued, over about 180 worktrees (258k files), ripgrep needed 4.03 s in total and the daemon needed 217 ms, 18.6x faster, with the same files as rg on 12 of 12.

On answers: 19 of 20 queries returned exactly rg's files; the 20th differs only by .env.example files, which unumsearch never indexes on purpose. During git checkout of a branch that rewrites 44,686 Linux kernel files, the index caught up 6.4 to 7.5 s after the checkout began. Until then answers said fresh: false, and 0 of 64,454 fresh answers differed from ripgrep.

Where it loses

On a single repository of 3.7k files, ripgrep takes a median 9.8 ms. The daemon takes 2.3 ms, but the one-shot CLI, which starts a new process per query, takes 12 ms. That is slower than rg. The speed comes from a process that keeps the index open, so if you run it as a daemon, MCP server or rpc, you get the gain; if you shell out once per query on a small repo, you do not.

The benchmark file lists further weak spots, including that a busier machine made every engine about 1.7x slower in one run, so read the absolute times with that in mind.

Try it 

curl -fsSL https://github.com/corpunum/unumsearch/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
unumsearch --root ~/src/myrepo index
unumsearch search 'fn\s+main' ~/src/myrepo --text

For agents, unumsearch mcp runs it as a stdio MCP server, and the README lists setup for Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and others. The latest release at the time of writing is v0.1.12, which fixed a case where a daemon reported fresh before it had looked at its roots.

You can reproduce the race on your own code with python3 bench/race.py --root .; your numbers will differ.

Source and benchmark method: github.com/corpunum/unumsearch.

How this was written

This article was drafted by an AI model (Claude, from Anthropic) working for CorpUnum Labs, from the project's README, benchmark notes and published project facts. Its figures were checked against those files before posting. The numbers come from those files; none were measured by the model.

We are CorpUnum Labs, in Athens, building OpenUnum, a local-first runtime for user-owned agents. If you want to see what our agents do on that one mini PC, there is a playable lab here: corpunum.com/play.

title: Efficient Genotype Classification from 3D MRI in ADPKD via Density-Aware Point Sampling and E(3)-invariance
description:
arXiv:2611.17758v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Early detection of genetic kidney diseases, especially autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), is crucial because certain genotypes such as truncating PKD1 mutations cause rapid kidney growth and early progression to end-stage kidney disease. MRI-based genotype inference is a potential low-cost complement to genetic testing. However, although many deep learning methods have been developed for classifying various MR images, applying them to ADPKD remains challenging: (1) abdominal MR images are generally too large to be handled by deep learning models designed for smaller images like brain MRI, and (2) the amount of labeled data for ADPKD genetic mutations is insufficient to train deep learning models. In order to address these challenges, we propose E3PN, an efficient 3D MRI-based ADPKD genotype classification network that relies on point sampling and E(3)-invariance. We utilize a point representation of 3D MRI, which consumes less GPU memory than a voxel representation. For further memory efficiency, 3D points are sampled from a mixture distribution over the two kidneys in each image. Since E(3)-invariance has been shown to improve data efficiency, we also incorporate it into our model through coordinate canonicalization. On our ADPKD dataset, E3PN trains 163 times faster and uses 103x less GPU memory than a 3D ResNet, while also improving F1 from 0.165 to 0.226 over both baselines. These results establish a first benchmark for five-way ADPKD genotype classification from 3D MRI and show that point sampling and coordinate canonicalization yield two-orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains with a modest but consistent improvement in F1.
