A vendor-specific navigation error may be useful for maintenance engineers but insufficient for a WMS workflow. The Fleet API can expose a normalized failure category such as destination unavailable, robot unavailable, load handling failure, infrastructure failure, or mission timeout while preserving detailed vendor diagnostics for troubleshooting.

Not every failure should immediately terminate the business operation. If the assigned robot becomes unavailable before pickup, the Fleet Management Server may assign another compatible robot. If a charger, elevator, door, or traffic route is temporarily unavailable, the mission may wait or be replanned. The enterprise system should receive the operational status without having to manage low-level robot recovery logic.

Shared infrastructure must also be integrated into mission execution. Industrial robots may depend on automatic doors, elevators, conveyors, loading stations, chargers, or machine interfaces. The Fleet Management Server can represent these systems as managed resources and coordinate reservations with robot movement. WMS and ERP continue to work with business tasks rather than directly controlling each physical infrastructure component.

MES integration follows similar principles in production environments. A manufacturing operation may request raw materials, work-in-process containers, tools, or finished products to be transported between stations. The MES generates the production-related demand, while the Fleet API converts that demand into transport missions synchronized with production timing, workstation availability, and robot capacity.

Priority mapping is important because enterprise systems and robot fleets may express urgency differently. A WMS may classify an order as urgent, while the fleet scheduler uses numerical priorities or scheduling classes. The integration layer should define deterministic mapping rules so that business priorities influence mission scheduling without allowing every external application to arbitrarily override fleet-wide traffic and safety policies.

Cancellation also requires explicit semantics. An ERP or WMS may cancel a business task after the robot has already started execution. The Fleet API must determine whether the physical mission can still be cancelled safely, whether the robot should complete delivery to a safe location, or whether manual intervention is required. A cancellation request should therefore not be interpreted as proof that physical execution immediately stopped.

Inventory consistency is another critical concern. The WMS may logically reserve or transfer inventory while a robot performs the corresponding physical movement. The integration design should define when inventory states change: at mission acceptance, pickup confirmation, delivery confirmation, or another verified event. Clear transaction boundaries prevent business records from indicating that material moved when the physical transport actually failed.

A common integration pattern uses an API gateway between enterprise applications and fleet services. The gateway can provide authentication, authorization, TLS, rate limiting, request validation, routing, and audit logging. Internal Fleet APIs then handle mission orchestration, robot information, resources, events, and telemetry according to clearly defined service boundaries rather than exposing robot-specific interfaces directly to enterprise applications.

Authentication should identify the enterprise application or service submitting the request. Authorization can then restrict which facility, mission type, robot group, or API operation that application may access. A WMS responsible for one warehouse should not automatically receive control authority over robots at another site. Service identities and least-privilege policies provide controlled machine-to-machine integration.

Industrial environments often contain legacy enterprise systems that cannot directly use modern REST, gRPC, or event-streaming interfaces. Integration middleware can translate database records, file exchanges, SOAP services, message queues, or proprietary interfaces into the canonical Fleet API. This preserves a stable robot integration architecture while allowing older business systems to participate without embedding legacy behavior inside robot software.

Data mapping should be explicit and version controlled. Enterprise location identifiers may differ from robot map identifiers, and business names such as Receiving_Area_01 may need to map to a canonical fleet location or navigation target. Similar mappings may be required for material types, load carriers, priorities, mission types, facilities, and resource identifiers. Configuration should be maintained independently from application code where possible.

API versioning protects enterprise integrations as the robot platform evolves. New robot capabilities, mission parameters, or event fields should not unexpectedly break existing WMS or ERP clients. Versioned schemas, backward-compatible extensions, deprecation policies, and contract testing allow enterprise and robotics teams to upgrade their systems at different times while maintaining predictable interoperability.

Observability should span both business and physical execution layers. A transport request can be traced from an ERP order or WMS task through the API gateway, Fleet Management Server, scheduler, vendor adapter, and robot. Correlation IDs provide a common reference across these components, allowing engineers to determine whether delays originate from enterprise processing, fleet scheduling, network communication, or robot execution.

Operational metrics can combine enterprise and fleet information. Organizations can measure transport request latency, mission queue time, assignment delay, robot travel time, pickup duration, delivery duration, mission success rate, retry rate, and business-order completion time. These metrics reveal whether performance problems originate from robot capacity, warehouse workflow, scheduling rules, infrastructure constraints, or integration services.

High availability is important because enterprise logistics may depend continuously on the Fleet API. Multiple API instances, redundant databases, durable message brokers, health checks, controlled failover, and persistent mission state can prevent individual server failures from stopping warehouse operations. Recovery procedures should reconcile enterprise requests with current physical robot states before commands resume after a significant outage.

Temporary disconnection between enterprise and fleet systems should be handled deliberately. Existing robot missions may continue locally while new WMS requests are buffered, rejected, or queued according to policy. When connectivity returns, the systems should reconcile outstanding requests and completion events using stable identifiers rather than assuming that no physical work occurred during the communication interruption.

Security and safety remain separate but complementary responsibilities. Enterprise applications must be authenticated and authorized before issuing fleet commands, but successful API authorization does not replace local robot safety. Collision avoidance, emergency stopping, protective sensing, and motion limits remain enforced by robot or safety systems even when missions originate from trusted WMS, MES, or ERP applications.

A scalable industrial integration architecture therefore forms a hierarchy of responsibility. ERP and WMS express business demand, integration services convert that demand into standardized requests, the Fleet Management Server orchestrates missions and shared resources, adapters translate canonical operations into vendor protocols, and robots execute physical tasks while maintaining local control and safety.

The reverse information flow is equally important. Robots generate state and execution events, adapters normalize them, the Fleet Management Server converts them into mission-level information, and integration services deliver relevant results to WMS, MES, or ERP. This bidirectional structure creates a closed operational loop connecting digital business transactions with physical material movement.

The primary objective of industrial Fleet API integration is not simply to connect software systems through HTTP. It is to establish a stable contract between enterprise intent and physical automation. When canonical missions, identity, idempotency, asynchronous events, error normalization, resource coordination, security, observability, and recovery are designed together, WMS and ERP systems can use heterogeneous robot fleets as a dependable shared logistics capability.

Such an architecture allows robots and enterprise applications to evolve independently while preserving interoperability. New robot vendors can be introduced through adapters without redesigning WMS workflows, and enterprise systems can change without modifying every robot interface. The Fleet API becomes the controlled integration boundary that transforms individual robots into an extensible industrial fleet service supporting warehouse, manufacturing, and enterprise operations.

title: InfiHall-Bench: A Benchmark for Hallucination Evaluation in Autoregressive Text-to-Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.18053v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hallucination benchmarks for text-to-image generation are predominantly designed around diffusion models, limiting their diagnostic value for visual autoregressive (VAR) models and the development of mitigation methods. We identify two limitations in existing prompt construction paradigms: many prompts are no longer challenging for modern generators, while category-based construction relies on recurring object-attribute-relation templates and rarely tests interactions among multiple visual requirements within a single image.
  We introduce InfiHall-Bench, a controlled benchmark of 411 prompts constructed by systematically composing five foundational and visually verifiable skills: attribute binding, spatial relation, action relation, part consistency, and scene consistency. Each prompt covers 4.05 annotated skills on average, enabling the evaluation of hallucinations under diverse combinations of visual requirements. Using this benchmark, we find that hallucinations in VAR models exhibit a scale-wise persistence pattern: semantic errors can emerge at different autoregressive scales and are rarely corrected by subsequent fine-scale steps.
  Motivated by this observation, we propose Confidence-Masked Hallucination Mitigation (CMHM), which estimates the prediction confidence of target visual tokens at each autoregressive scale during teacher-forced fine-tuning. CMHM downweights reliably predicted tokens, allowing optimization to focus on uncertain predictions across scales. Experiments show that InfiHall-Bench distinguishes models that existing compositional benchmarks rate as comparable, while CMHM consistently outperforms uniform LoRA fine-tuning for VAR-based text-to-image generation.

title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.17776v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.

title: The Page Loads Fine — But Its Headers Are Telling a Different Story
description:
Last month a client's site passed every check I could think of. The pages rendered fast. The design was clean. Lighthouse gave it a green score. Then their security auditor sent back a one-page report that read like a failing grade.

Nothing on the page was broken. The problem was invisible — in the response headers. The site was missing four of the five security headers that browsers actually enforce, its pages were not being cached at all, and the server was happily announcing its exact software version to anyone who asked.

I have checked headers on dozens of sites since, and the pattern repeats. Headers are the part of a response nobody looks at until something goes wrong. Here is what they are, what they control, and the five checks I run on every site now.

What response headers actually are

Every time a browser requests a page, the server sends two things back: the HTML you see, and a set of headers you do not. Headers are short key-value instructions that travel with the response. They tell the browser how to handle the page, how long to cache it, which resources it may load, and what to do when something looks suspicious.

You can see them in any browser. Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, click a request, and look at the Response Headers section. Most developers have never opened that panel. That is the problem.

The HTML is the visible half of a response. The headers are the operating instructions. A site can look perfect and still be shipping instructions that weaken its security, waste bandwidth, or confuse search engines.

The five security headers that matter

There are dozens of response headers, but five do most of the security work. If you check nothing else, check these.

Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) tells browsers to always use HTTPS for your site, even if a link or bookmark points to the plain HTTP version. Without it, a visitor who types your domain without the scheme can be downgraded to an unencrypted connection on the first request. With it, the browser refuses to make that mistake.

Content-Security-Policy (CSP) controls which scripts, styles, and other resources a page is allowed to load, and from where. It is the strongest defence against cross-site scripting, because even if an attacker injects a script into your page, the browser will refuse to run it if the source is not on your approved list.

X-Content-Type-Options with the value nosniff stops browsers from guessing a file's type. Without it, a browser can decide that a file your server called plain text is actually executable script — and run it. This is how some old MIME-sniffing attacks worked.

X-Frame-Options (or the CSP frame-ancestors directive) stops other sites from embedding your pages in a frame. Without it, your login page can be framed inside an attacker's page in a clickjacking attack, where the visitor clicks something they cannot see.

Referrer-Policy controls how much of your URL leaks to other sites when a visitor clicks an outbound link. A strict policy keeps internal paths and query strings out of the referrer header that other sites receive.

None of these headers changes how a page looks. That is exactly why they get skipped. They are invisible work, and invisible work is the first thing cut under deadline pressure.

The missing-header trap: everything works until it doesn't

Here is the uncomfortable truth about security headers: a site missing all five will work perfectly. Pages load. Users log in. Nothing looks wrong. The protections these headers provide only matter when someone is actively attacking the site, or when an auditor checks.

That is why I now treat a header check as part of every launch checklist, next to the SSL certificate and the sitemap. A missing HSTS header is not a cosmetic issue. It is an open door that only shows itself when someone walks through it.

The same logic applies to the audit findings I see most often. The report does not say "your site is broken". It says "your site is unprotected". Those are different sentences, and the second one is the one that costs a client a contract.

Caching headers: the silent performance leak

Security is only half the story. The other half is caching, and it is where headers quietly cost real performance.

Cache-Control tells browsers and CDNs how long a response can be reused before checking back with the server. When it is missing, or set far too conservatively, every repeat visit re-downloads content that has not changed. Multiply that by every page, every asset, and every visitor, and the cost adds up.

The fix is not complicated, but it is easy to get wrong in the other direction. Versioned files such as app.3f9a.css can be cached for a year, because the filename changes when the content changes. HTML pages usually need a short lifetime, so updates reach visitors quickly.

The classic mistake is caching HTML for a year and then wondering why visitors keep seeing the old homepage. The other classic mistake is caching nothing at all, and wondering why repeat visits feel slow. Both show up in the headers, and both are visible in a single check.

The headers that give away too much

Some headers do not protect or speed anything up. They just talk too much. The Server header announces the server software and often its exact version. X-Powered-By does the same for the application framework.

Neither header breaks anything. But exact version numbers make it slightly easier for an attacker to match your stack against known vulnerabilities. Most teams strip or generalize these headers as a minor hardening step. It is not the most critical fix on the list, but it is free, and there is no reason to advertise your stack to the whole internet.

There is one more header worth watching for, and it is the one that has cost people search traffic: X-Robots-Tag. When it carries noindex, the page is hidden from search engines — even when the HTML looks completely fine. I have seen a staging configuration leak into production this way, with the header quietly deindexing pages while the team wondered why rankings were falling.

How to check headers in under a minute

You do not need a terminal or a curl command to do this, although curl works fine. The fastest way is a purpose-built tool: paste the URL, run the check, and read the findings in plain English.

When you run an http header check, you get the full response header list alongside the status code, plus a plain-English reading of what is missing. It flags the five security headers above, a missing Cache-Control, and Server or X-Powered-By values that reveal version details. It does not follow redirects, so you see the response for the exact URL you entered — which matters, because a redirect's headers are not the page's headers.

The check takes seconds. What takes longer is deciding what to do with the findings, which brings me to the part most articles skip: the order in which to fix them.

The fix order I actually use

Not every missing header is equally urgent, and fixing them in the wrong order creates new problems. This is the sequence I follow.

First, set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy. Both are safe to add everywhere. They break nothing and close real gaps. There is no reason to delay them.

Second, add X-Frame-Options or a CSP frame-ancestors directive. Unless your site is designed to be embedded in other pages, framing should be blocked. Check first that no legitimate integration depends on framing — some payment widgets do.

Third, enable HSTS — but only once HTTPS works everywhere on the site, including subdomains you plan to include. Browsers remember HSTS for the whole max-age period, and they will refuse plain HTTP for that entire time. Enabling it while some subdomain still serves HTTP will lock visitors out of that subdomain.

Fourth, roll out Content-Security-Policy gradually. Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only and watch the violation reports for a week. This shows you what the policy would block before it blocks anything. Enforcing a strict CSP on a live site without that step is how you break your own scripts in production.

Finally, fix caching. Set long lifetimes on versioned static assets and short lifetimes on HTML. Then re-check, because caching is set at several layers — the server, the CDN, the application — and one layer can override another.

The checks that catch real problems

Beyond the five security headers, there are a few header findings that have saved me real debugging time.

A missing Content-Type, or one that does not match the file, explains mysterious rendering problems. A Location header on a page that should return 200 tells you a redirect is firing that you did not expect. And a Set-Cookie header without the Secure and HttpOnly flags is a session cookie that can travel over plain HTTP or be read by JavaScript.

The pattern is always the same: the page looks fine, the headers disagree, and the headers are right. When a site misbehaves in a way the HTML cannot explain, the headers are the next place to look.

Make it a habit, not a one-off

The reason headers stay unchecked is that nobody owns them. The developer sets them, the hosting provider overrides some of them, the CDN adds its own, and the application sets a few more. Responsibility is spread across four layers, so no single person ever reads the final result.

That is why a header check belongs in the launch checklist and in the periodic audit. Run it after a server migration, after a CDN change, after a plugin update that touches security settings, and after any incident. It takes under a minute, and the findings are either reassuring or actionable. There is no third outcome.

The page your visitors see is only half the response your server sends. The other half is a set of instructions that decides how secure, how fast, and how visible that page really is. Check it before someone else does — because auditors, attackers, and search engines already are.

Further reading

  • The full list of HTTP response headers, with definitions: MDN — HTTP headers
  • The OWASP cheat sheet on security headers: OWASP — HTTP Security Response Headers Cheat Sheet
  • How caching headers work, from Google's web fundamentals: Google — HTTP Caching

If you have ever found a header problem that explained a bug nobody could reproduce, I would like to hear about it. The best checklists come from production incidents, and this one is still growing.

title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
description:
arXiv:2611.17772v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployment where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that dynamically injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. This framework offers exceptional flexibility, allowing hosts to customize target defensive styles and dynamically blend them to maximize stylistic variance. Crucially, this inference-time intervention preserves semantic utility and fluency during malicious queries, misleading adversaries into believing that they are extracting pristine teacher outputs, while standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework successfully disrupts student learning, achieving substantial anti-distillation performance while incurring negligible overhead and preserving text naturalness. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/distill-resist-38C6/.

title: Classifier-Guided Latent Diffusion for Small-Molecule Generation
description:
arXiv:2611.17650v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a promising class of generative models for molecular design because of their ability to learn complex chemical distributions and support conditional or guided generation. In this work, we investigate a latent diffusion pipeline for property-guided small-molecule generation. The proposed framework represents canonicalized SMILES strings using a frozen ChemBERTa encoder, trains a Transformer-based decoder to reconstruct SELFIES strings from molecular latent embeddings, and learns an unconditional denoising diffusion model in the ChemBERTa latent space. To enable property-directed generation, a differentiable latent property predictor is used to guide the diffusion sampling process. Generated SELFIES strings are converted to SMILES, validated using RDKit, and evaluated using molecular validity, uniqueness, novelty, and predicted property scores. We study guidance toward two drug-relevant binary endpoints: blood--brain barrier permeability and inhibition of human $\beta$-secretase 1. The results suggest that latent diffusion over pretrained molecular embeddings can generate chemically valid and novel molecules while enabling controllable steering toward desired molecular properties.

title: November 10, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Feature

TLS 1.3 for connections to backends

API Gateway is rolling out support for TLS 1.3 on connections to backend services. Once the rollout reaches a gateway, it uses TLS 1.3 with backends that support it. No configuration is required.

Agent Platform Workbench

Feature

Antigravity CLI in Agent Platform Workbench instances

Preview: The Antigravity CLI is available in Agent Platform Workbench instances that use a Debian 12 (workbench-instances-2603) or later image. The Antigravity CLI is the terminal surface of Google Antigravity, an AI agent that works in a terminal. New instances have it turned on by default. You can use the Antigravity CLI to do tasks like the following:

  • Create, explain, edit, check, and run notebooks.
  • Create a Jupyter kernel with the packages that you need.
  • Run shell commands and Google Cloud commands, such as gcloud and bq.
  • Write the code for a notebook cell from a description, with the %%agy cell magic.

The Antigravity CLI asks for your approval before it edits a file or runs a command. To turn it off for an instance, set the enable-antigravity metadata key to false. To get started, see Use the Antigravity CLI.

BigQuery

Feature

You can use graph measures to lock an aggregation to a key in order to perform complex aggregations without overcounting. Measure expressions can include the following:

  • Aggregate function calls
  • Expressions within aggregate functions
  • Conditional logic within aggregate functions
  • Conditional distinct counting
  • Scalar operations and expressions outside of aggregate functions
  • Combinations of measures wrapped in the AGG function

To query measures, you transform your graph into a flattened table by using the GRAPH_EXPAND TVF, and then query measures in that table with the AGG function. The GRAPH_EXPAND function now supports multiple fact tables. To view the output schema of the GRAPH_EXPAND function, use the BQ.SHOW_GRAPH_EXPAND_SCHEMA system procedure.

You can define extensions in the OPTIONS clause of the labels and properties in your graphs, which are string pairs that represent custom metadata for natural language querying.

Measures and graphs are supported in Data Studio through the BigQuery connector. Measures and graphs are also automatically cataloged in Knowledge Catalog, which makes them searchable by natural language or domain synonyms.

These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

BigQuery generative AI functions now support the gemini-4-carbon model. This model is generally available.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource type is publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, and Feed APIs.

  • Cloud Key Management Service
    • cloudkms.googleapis.com/KajPolicyConfig

Cloud Billing

Feature

Estimate costs for AI agents using the new cost estimator agent (Preview)

Cloud Billing is introducing cost estimation directly inside the Billing section of the Google Cloud console, starting with cost estimation for AI agents now available in Preview.

Using the new Cost estimator agent, you can generate high-level estimates based on reference architectures for agents built with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, helping you understand the potential cost of your agent before you build it.

To get cost estimates for your planned Google Cloud workloads and other cloud infrastructure, you can also use the Google Cloud pricing calculator. With the pricing calculator, you can estimate costs for a wide range of Google Cloud services and products.

Cost estimates help you set spend caps, create Cloud Billing budgets and alerts, allocate project quotas, and get financial sign-off for a launch.

For more information about the cost estimator tools, see the following:

  • Cost estimator agent
  • Pricing calculator

Cloud Logging

Feature

VM Extension Manager extension policies for the Ops Agent are now available at the folder and organization levels in Preview. Extension policies provide zonal and global Ops Agent installation, version upgrades, and configuration management. For more information, see VM Extension Manager policies for the Ops Agent.

In addition, new read-only APIs are available in Preview for querying the details and status of installed VM extensions. For more information, see View extension details and status.

Cloud Monitoring

Feature

VM Extension Manager extension policies for the Ops Agent are now available at the folder and organization levels in Preview. Extension policies provide zonal and global Ops Agent installation, version upgrades, and configuration management. For more information, see VM Extension Manager policies for the Ops Agent.

In addition, new read-only APIs are available in Preview for querying the details and status of installed VM extensions. For more information, see View extension details and status.

Compute Engine

Feature

For your regional managed instance groups (MIGs), you can view planned instance allocations across zones and machine types, check the number of instances waiting for capacity, and configure alerts based on this data. Compute Engine records these details in instance distribution logs in Cloud Logging when you create a regional MIG or increase its target size. For more information, see View instance distribution logs.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Carbon available in web app, mobile app, Workflow Builder, and AI developer tools

Gemini 4 Carbon is generally available (GA) for the Gemini Enterprise web app, mobile app, Workflow Builder, and AI developer tools.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. Gemini 4 Carbon is supported in the web app and mobile app. For more information about turning on the model, see Manage features on the web app.
  • Workflow Builder: Gemini 4 Carbon is available in Workflow Builder. For more information, see Workflow Builder.
  • AI developer tools: Enabled by default for licensed users when Antigravity authorized models uses the default selection. If your organization specifies a custom model list, an administrator must manually select Gemini 4 Carbon. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Cross-project governance for semantic governance policies

You can use semantic governance policies in a multi-project (hub-and-spoke) architecture to centrally govern agents deployed across multiple Google Cloud projects. When you configure a Resource Manager management boundary with the AGENT_MANAGEMENT capability, Agent Registry in the central management project automatically discovers agents across all member projects with their runtime identities intact. You can then provision a single Agent Gateway and semantic governance policy engine in the management project to author and enforce policies across member project agents.

For more information, see Govern agents across multiple projects and Cross-project boundaries.

Feature

Provisioned Throughput supports more detailed order statuses

Provisioned Throughput supports more granular order statuses in the Google Cloud console in General Availability (GA). You can track order lifecycle states across Declined, Cancelled, and Terminated, in addition to Pending review, Approved, Active, and Expired. For more information, see Check order status.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.20.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed patch application failures during validation on large repositories and projects with mixed LF and CRLF line endings.
    • Fixed scan error handling to properly surface permission denied errors when scanning unreadable directories instead of reporting zero findings.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber (GA)

Gemini 4 Carbon (gemini-4-carbon) and Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber (gemini-4-carbon-cyber-permissive) are generally available (GA). Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's frontier model for complex, real-world tasks across coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science, with a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit, long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens using continuation_token, configurable thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH), implicit context caching with durable caching, Microsoft Office and OpenDocument file inputs, and Provisioned Throughput support. Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber is a defensive cybersecurity variant available behind the Fairwind Program allowlist.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS prerelease notes 6.33

Here are the prerelease notes for what we expect to be the next version of Google Cloud CCaaS. When we release this version, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where numbers on the inbound blocklist weren't blocked when calling a direct line.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx calls became stuck in a queue indefinitely if a hang-up notification was lost during high-load periods.

  • Fixed an issue where callback calls that were abandoned while waiting in a queue were incorrectly recorded as system failures instead of end-user hang-ups, and didn't maintain their first-in, first-out priority order when transitioning between queue groups.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter incorrectly redialed a call immediately after hang-up, causing the participant status to fail and the mandatory disposition panel to close prematurely.

  • Fixed an issue where auto-answer calls entered an infinite re-offer loop to the same agent if a connection timeout occurred, preventing over-capacity deflection from triggering.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled callback redials were placed after their maximum deferral deadline, causing calls to reach customers later than promised.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's next status prematurely cleared and didn't appear in Agent Monitoring if a voice call's wrap-up ended while they still had active chats.

  • Fixed an issue where the logout confirmation dialog on the Agents page appeared in English when the CCaaS portal language was set to French Canadian (fr_CA).

  • Fixed an issue where virtual-agent-to-virtual-agent chat transfers failed if the transfer turn also ended the conversation.

  • Fixed an issue in the Agents view where the team filter incorrectly displayed agents from unrelated teams due to stale data records.

  • Fixed an issue where the {ACCOUNT_ID} placeholder resolved to an empty string during virtual agent chats, causing CRM API request failures.

  • Fixed an issue where large, unbounded date range queries on the Manager API calls endpoint caused request timeouts. Requests to this endpoint now require a bounded date range.

  • Fixed an issue where loading holiday settings or ending a call in the agent desktop caused significant system slowness due to inefficient database lookups.

  • Fixed an issue where retrieving agent call history caused significant performance delays and system instability.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

(2026-R47) Version updates

GKE cluster versions have been updated.

New versions available for upgrades and new clusters.

The following versions are now available for new GKE clusters, and for manual control plane upgrades and node upgrades for existing clusters. For more information about versioning and upgrades, see GKE versioning and support and About GKE cluster upgrades.

Rapid channel

Note: Your clusters might not have these versions available. Rollouts are already in progress when we publish the release notes, and can take multiple days to complete across all Google Cloud zones.
  • Version 1.37.1-gke.2097000 is now the default version for cluster creation in the Rapid channel.
  • The following versions are now available in the Rapid channel:
    • 1.34.12-gke.1698000

Feature

For more information, see Impacted resources and List impacted resources in a project.

Spanner

Feature

Spanner parameterized views are now generally available (GA). Parameterized views let you dynamically filter data based on session context parameters passed with queries, helping you isolate tenant data and restrict data access in AI agent and LLM applications.

For more information, see Create a parameterized view and Use parameterized views.

Vertex AI Search

Feature

Agent Search: Search-as-you-type for custom search apps (Preview)

You can configure schema fields to support search-as-you-type in custom search apps. Search-as-you-type returns a refreshed set of ranked documents on every keystroke before a user finishes typing a full query. Unlike autocomplete, which suggests query strings, search-as-you-type returns matching documents so that users can browse an updating result list and find the right result mid-query.

This feature is in Public Preview. For more information, see Configure field settings.

title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.17789v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.

title: Terraform plan: what to read before you press apply
description:
A plan is a preview of what will be destroyed, replaced or opened. Read the action symbols, the replacement reasons and the firewall lines before you approve.

Most of a terraform plan is routine: tags change, a size is raised, a new rule appears. A few lines are different, because applying them removes data that cannot be rebuilt or opens a service to the whole internet. This guide shows where those lines hide in the output, what each marker means, and a fixed order of reading that takes a couple of minutes. The short answer to the question in the title: read the action on every resource that holds data, read the reason behind every replacement, and read the source address of every firewall rule that was added or changed. The summary count at the bottom tells you how much to read, not whether it is safe.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/terraform-plan-read-before-apply?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: More of What You Say in Meetings Will Be Written Down by Software
description:
Join a call at many companies now and you will see a small notice that the meeting is being transcribed. When it ends, a summary appears in the chat, with a list of decisions and actions, sometimes before you have closed the window. The main video meeting tools all offer some version of this, and more organisations are switching it on by default.

That changes something quietly important about meetings. For years, a lot of what was said in them was gone the moment people left the room. Now more of it becomes searchable text that people who were not there can read, sometimes months later.

There are real benefits. People who missed the meeting can catch up. Colleagues working in their second language can check what was said. Actions are less likely to be forgotten. Used well, these tools can make meetings fairer.

But they also bring new habits worth learning early.

Read the summary, especially when you are named in it. Automated summaries can be wrong. They can attribute a point to the wrong person, turn a maybe into a decision, or miss the caveat that mattered most. If the summary says you agreed to deliver something by Friday and you did not, correct it in writing that day. Once a summary has been shared, people tend to treat it as the record.

Speak as if a stranger may read it later, because one might. That does not mean being dull or guarded. It means saying what you mean clearly, being careful with jokes about named people, and not discussing anyone's health or personal life in a meeting that is being transcribed.

Know where the off switch is, and when to ask for it. Some conversations, like personal matters, sensitive staffing discussions, or early ideas that need room to be wrong, are better held without a transcript. It is reasonable to ask at the start whether this one needs recording.

And if you chair meetings, take responsibility for the summary yourself. Check it, fix it, and send it on. The tool can write things down. Deciding what was really agreed is still a job for people.

– Asael Shinder

title: Vercel Connect adds managed Stripe API keys
description:
Vercel Connect can now create a separate restricted Stripe API key for each agent or task. When you create a Stripe connector, you can now choose Managed API Key as the connection method.

Vercel creates the key in your Stripe account, limited to the permissions you pick. The existing MCP and bring-your-own API key methods are unchanged.

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 3rOuKp0F4Nk80dMYJ5QX6U

Most apps and agents run on Stripe’s default secret key, which has full access to the account. With per-agent keys, each agent gets only the access its job needs. For example, a daily revenue report agent can be limited to read-only access to charges, and an onboarding agent can be limited to write access to customers.

Vercel creates and stores the key, so there is no secret key to paste. You can rotate it from the connector's settings without redeploying, and the old key stays valid for up to 24 hours while you switch.

Add the Stripe connector

Create a Stripe connector from the connectors directory, choose Managed API Key, pick its permissions, and attach it to your project. You can also start from the CLI, which opens the browser to finish setup:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 1I7ChkvBWny4SCOzp2xI3E

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 66OV4WkA85AVl8hbRgk4PU

To get started, add the Stripe connector or read the documentation.

title: Sample-Efficient Control of Magnetoconvective Flows via Differentiable Simulation
description:
arXiv:2611.18008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fluid flows are central to demanding engineering applications, most prominently fusion blanket cooling, where flow control is a promising tool to optimize key properties such as heat transfer. While active flow control (AFC) has recently advanced through machine learning, its application to MHD flows remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present $\phi$-PICT, a novel differentiable GPU-accelerated MHD solver targeted at AFC. We validate $\phi$-PICT against MHD benchmarks and demonstrate its high computational efficiency. Integrated into FluidGym, $\phi$-PICT enables sample-efficient gradient-based algorithms to improve heat transfer by $>25$% and allows optimizers to achieve $10^3\times$ higher accuracy in inverse design than black-box methods. $\phi$-PICT is publicly available at https://github.com/upb-sciml/phiPICT.

title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for Computational Cognitive Models: A Tutorial
description:
arXiv:2611.17608v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational cognitive modeling is an increasingly essential methodology to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human and animal cognition. By fitting models to empirical data, researchers can perform parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses to assess competing theories, quantify individual differences, and investigate neural representations. Typically, fitting these models relies on likelihood-dependent methods (e.g., Maximum likelihood estimation or hierarchical Bayesian methods). However, for many reasonable cognitive models, computing the likelihood is computationally intractable, in which case these methods become inadequate. This substantially limits the range of theories that researchers can investigate. Simulation-based inference with neural networks (neural SBI) has emerged as a powerful toolkit to overcome this hurdle. By training deep neural networks on datasets generated through model simulations, neural SBI learns the relation between observable data and cognitive models. This approach enables all the applications of standard modeling while bypassing the likelihood computation, without constraints on empirical data size. Despite its successful adoption across diverse scientific fields, neural SBI remains underutilized in cognitive modeling, partly due to a lack of accessible, domain-tailored guidance. This tutorial addresses this gap by providing a clear workflow for applying neural SBI to cognitive models. We also provide practical use cases and recommendations for reducing the computational and simulation burden, facilitating efficient implementation in real-world research settings. By lowering the technical barriers to neural SBI, this tutorial aims to empower cognitive scientists to investigate richer theory spaces and ultimately propel scientific discovery.

title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
description:
arXiv:2611.17762v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.

title: A four-eyes approval in a Uniface service - one table, two rules, and the gaps it leaves
description:
Some actions in the customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 should not be done by one person alone: writing off an open invoice, changing a price by more than a few percent, moving a customer to another account owner, paying a large supplier bill. The app got a four-eyes approval for these four cases.

It is a small service - one table, five operations - but the details decide whether it actually helps. This article walks through them, including the parts it does not cover.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition and SQLite 3.50.2, October 2026.

The table 

CREATE TABLE APPROVAL (
  APPROVAL_ID    INTEGER NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  APPROVAL_TYPE  VARCHAR(12) NOT NULL,   -- WRITEOFF, PRICE, TRANSFER, BILL
  REF_ID         INTEGER NOT NULL,       -- invoice, product, customer or bill
  AMOUNT_CENTS   INTEGER,                -- amount or new price
  NEW_VALUE      VARCHAR(100),           -- new owner for TRANSFER
  REQUEST_NOTE   VARCHAR(200),
  STATUS         VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,   -- PENDING, APPROVED, REJECTED
  REQUESTED_AT   DATETIME NOT NULL,
  REQUESTED_BY   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  DECIDED_AT     DATETIME,
  DECIDED_BY     VARCHAR(30),
  DECISION_NOTE  VARCHAR(200)
);
CREATE INDEX IX_APPROVAL_STATUS ON APPROVAL (STATUS, REQUESTED_AT);

One generic table instead of one per action type. The reference is a plain ID whose meaning depends on the type; the payload is either an amount or a short text. That is less strict than four specific tables, but the list of open requests is one query and the history of all decisions is one table.

When is an approval needed?

The thresholds are settings, so they can change without a release:

Type Needs approval when Setting (default)
WRITEOFF amount above the limit APPROVAL_WRITEOFF_CENTS (5000)
PRICE change above a percentage of the old price APPROVAL_PRICE_PCT (10)
BILL gross amount above the limit APPROVAL_BILL_CENTS (100000)
TRANSFER always -

The check is its own read-only operation, so the user interface can ask before it offers the button:

    call SETTING_NUM("APPROVAL_PRICE_PCT", "10", vLimit)
    if (vOld = 0)
        if (vAmount > 0)
            pNeeded = 1
        endif
        return 0
    endif
    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT ABS(%%(vAmount) - %%(vOld)) * 100.0 / %%(vOld) FROM (SELECT 1 AS X)", vPct)
    if (vPct > vLimit)
        pNeeded = 1
    endif

The special case vOld = 0 is not cosmetic: a product without a price would otherwise divide by zero, and any first price is a 100 % change anyway.

The request validates everything up front

REQUEST checks that the action could be executed right now: the invoice exists and is still open, the product exists, the new owner is an active user, the bill is still open. A write-off also needs a reason.

    if (vType = "WRITEOFF")
        call GET_TEXT("SELECT STATUS FROM SALES_DOC WHERE DOC_ID = %%(pRefId) AND DOC_TYPE = 'INVOICE'", vStatus)
        if (vStatus != "ISSUED" & vStatus != "PARTLY_PAID")
            pError = "The invoice %%(pRefId) does not exist or is not open."
            return -1
        endif
        ...
        if (vNote = "" | $length(vNote) > 60)
            pError = "A write-off needs a reason with at most 60 characters."
            return -1
        endif

And there can only be one open request per object and type:

    call COUNT_SQL("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM APPROVAL WHERE APPROVAL_TYPE = '%%(vType)' AND REF_ID = %%(pRefId) AND STATUS = 'PENDING'", vCount)
    if (vCount > 0)
        pError = "There is already a pending request for this object."
        return -1
    endif

Without that rule, two people can request two different write-offs for the same invoice, and the approver sees two plausible requests without knowing they compete.

Rule 1: someone else decides

Approving and rejecting require the administrator role - and the decider must not be the person who asked:

entry OTHER_ADMIN
params
    string pRequestedBy : IN
    string pUser : OUT
    string pError : OUT
endparams
variables
    string vRole
endvariables
    pError = ""
    activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(pUser, vRole)
    if (pUser = pRequestedBy)
        pError = "A request must be decided by another administrator."
        return -1
    endif
    return 0
end

This is checked on the server side, in the service, not by hiding a button. A test logs in as the requesting administrator, tries to decide the request and expects this error.

Rule 2: the approver executes

The approval is not a flag that the requester checks later. The APPROVE operation performs the action itself, by calling the same service operation that would otherwise be called directly:

    if (vType = "WRITEOFF")
        activate "SETTLE_SVC".WRITE_OFF(vRefId, vAmountText, vNote, vPaymentId, pError)
    elseif (vType = "PRICE")
        activate "PRODUCT_SVC".UPDATE_PRODUCT(vRefId, "", "", vAmountText, -1, 0, pError)
    elseif (vType = "TRANSFER")
        activate "OWNER_SVC".SET_OWNER(vRefId, vValue, pError)
    else
        activate "PAYABLE_SVC".PAY_BILL(vRefId, "", pError)
    endif
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    ...
    sql "UPDATE APPROVAL SET STATUS = 'APPROVED', DECIDED_AT = datetime('now', 'localtime'), DECIDED_BY = %%(vUserLit), DECISION_NOTE = %%(vDecisionLit) WHERE APPROVAL_ID = %%(pApprovalId)", "CUSTOMERS"

Two reasons for this order:

  • What was approved is what happens. The amount and the new price come from the request row, not from a second input. Nobody can approve 40.00 and then book 400.00.
  • The existing rules still apply. The write-off goes through the settlement service with all its checks and its own audit trail. If the invoice was paid in the meantime, the write-off fails, the operation returns the error, and the request stays PENDING for a decision.

The status is only set after the action succeeded. Action and status update run in the same transaction, so a failure in between doesn't leave an executed action with a pending request - as long as the caller rolls back on an error.

Rejecting needs a reason (1 to 200 characters) and only sets the status.

What this does not protect against

This is the part readers will ask about, so here it is up front.

The direct path still exists. SETTLE_SVC.WRITE_OFF and the other operations were there before the approval service, and they still work when called directly by a user with the right role. The four-eyes rule holds only as long as the user interface routes these actions through REQUEST. A hard guarantee would need each of the four operations to check for an approved request itself - and then the approver would need a way past that check. I chose the softer version and wrote it down.

One person with two accounts. The check compares user names. An administrator who can create users can create a second administrator account. The usual answer is organisational: user administration in different hands.

Time between request and decision. The request validates the state at request time; the approval re-validates by executing the action. A price change requested at 10 % but approved after someone else changed the price will apply the requested new price anyway. Whether that is right depends on the business; here it is accepted.

What the tests cover

  • The limits per type, including the price of 0.
  • Requests of all four types are stored as pending; a second request for the same object is refused; requests for objects that don't exist or aren't open are refused.
  • Approving executes the price change, the write-off and the customer transfer.
  • Rejecting without a reason fails and leaves the object unchanged.
  • The requester cannot decide their own request.
  • A user with only the edit role can request and list, but not decide.

One case is not automated yet: an action that fails at approval time (for example an invoice paid in the meantime) must leave the request pending. It is the next test I would add.

Takeaways

Check "who decides" in the service, not in the user interface.

Let the approval execute the action with the stored values, through the existing operations.

Validate on request and again on execution; set the status only after the action succeeded.

One pending request per object.

Write down what the design doesn't cover. Someone will ask.

title: Node.js Multipart ZIP Exports with 2-Step Retention and Signed Downloads
description:
Short answer: for a large customer-support ZIP export, have a Node.js worker use multipart object storage, explicitly complete the upload, and issue a short-lived signed download link only after completion. Keep the document's deletion deadline in durable job data. Link expiry controls access; it does not prove deletion.

For teams that value a replaceable HTTP boundary, Infrai is a reasonable adapter candidate for this job. Its public discovery endpoint exposes the request schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples without requiring a key. That makes the first integration step unusually concrete: inspect the contract, generate a thin adapter, then keep vendor details out of the export worker.

The second advantage operates at a different level. Infrai's discovery surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. A support platform that later connects its export worker to scheduling or observability can keep one credential and one bill instead of adding another set for each capability. The storage adapter still needs to remain narrow. That's what preserves the option to move.

How should a Node.js worker upload a large ZIP export and return a signed download link?

Think in two timelines. The support case might carry delete_after = 2026-09-16T12:00:00Z, while the download link should live only long enough for an authorized agent to retrieve the archive. These controls answer different questions. The deadline says when the signed documents must cease to exist. The link lifetime says how long one access grant remains usable.

Different clocks.

The worker assigns every attempt a unique key such as support-exports/case-1842/run-7f3c.zip, creates a multipart upload, and durably records its upload ID. It uploads each ZIP chunk and stores the returned part identifier. Only after every part is present does it explicitly complete the upload. If the job is cancelled, the worker explicitly aborts it. Unfinished parts don't disappear under an hourly lifecycle rule: lifecycle has a one-day minimum, and multipart fragments aren't cleaned automatically.

Keep those states boring.

The frontend never owns upload state. It receives a short-lived presigned GET URL after completion, and it must not attach the Infrai authorization header when following that URL. A separate deletion worker reads delete_after, removes the object at the deadline, and records the outcome in the application's audit trail. Use a queue or database lock around that transition because strict If-Match conditional writes aren't available. Unique object keys also stop two concurrent export jobs from overwriting the same archive.

Only then.

Here is a copyable contract check for the adapter. It calls the public discovery endpoint with a complete URL and an explicit method, verifies the exact operation the worker intends to use, and leaves request fields to the returned JSON Schema rather than freezing guessed fields into application code.

type Discovery = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: unknown;
};

async function loadMultipartCreateContract(): Promise<Discovery> {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.multipart.create",
    { method: "GET" },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery request failed with ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
  }

  const contract = (await response.json()) as Discovery;
  if (
    contract.method !== "POST" ||
    contract.path !== "/v1/storage/multipart/create/{bucket}" ||
    !contract.available
  ) {
    throw new Error("Multipart create contract did not match the required adapter boundary");
  }

  return contract;
}

loadMultipartCreateContract()
  .then((contract) => console.log(JSON.stringify(contract.params, null, 2)))
  .catch((error: unknown) => {
    console.error(error);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  });

Run that check in CI when the adapter changes, then implement the adapter from the published TypeScript example. For authenticated calls, read process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY, send Authorization: Bearer <key>, set an explicit method, and inspect every response status. On 429, honor Retry-After or use exponential backoff. Writes need a stable idempotency key so a retry can't apply the same transition twice. The returned presigned upload or download URL is a separate trust boundary and receives no Infrai bearer token.

In words, the diagram is: API creates export job -> Node.js worker streams ZIP parts -> object store assembles the object -> application marks the job ready -> frontend receives signed GET URL -> deletion worker removes the object at delete_after. The job database holds intent and progress. Storage holds bytes. The signed URL carries temporary authority.

The before-and-after migration boundary

Before the adapter, vendor assumptions tend to leak everywhere: controllers construct object keys, workers know multipart calls, and UI code treats a URL expiration as document retention. A migration then touches three layers at once.

After the adapter, the application depends on a small contract: begin an upload for a unique key, write parts, complete or abort, sign a GET, and delete at a deadline. Provider-specific request shapes live behind that contract. The distinction matters because compatibility claims are cheap; a bounded interface, a discovery assertion, and stored multipart state are concrete evidence that the application can change providers without rewriting its case workflow.

Don't hide the upload ID in process memory. A worker can be restarted between parts, and another worker should be able to continue from the durable record instead of restarting a large archive. The same record should distinguish uploading, ready, deletion_due, and deleted. If an upload never reaches ready, a cleanup job aborts it explicitly. If it does reach ready, only then may the API mint a download link.

Persist it.

This is also where observability earns its keep. Count jobs by state, alert on uploads that remain unfinished beyond the worker's expected window, and track deletion deadlines that have passed without a deleted state. I'm not sure what deletion evidence your auditor will accept; that depends on policy, and the answer should determine what the deletion worker records before production rollout. A signed URL expiring is never enough evidence by itself.

Which object storage choice keeps the export worker replaceable?

There isn't one universal winner. Amazon S3 has a mature multipart and lifecycle ecosystem. Google Cloud Storage fits teams already committed to Google IAM and regional controls. Cloudflare R2 is worth considering when an S3-compatible client boundary matches the surrounding system. Infrai fits when a self-describing REST contract and one credential across backend capabilities remove more friction than a provider-specific SDK would.

Option Fit for this support-export flow Migration and retention trade-off
Amazon S3 Multipart upload, signed access, and specialist lifecycle controls Strong choice when AWS IAM, object lock, versioning, or replication must be first-class
Google Cloud Storage Resumable transfer and signed URL patterns in the Google ecosystem Strong choice when Google IAM and regional policy already define the application boundary
Cloudflare R2 Familiar S3-compatible tooling for multipart object workflows Check required regions, governance controls, and replication before standardizing
Infrai storage Multipart completion and presigned GET behind a self-describing REST surface Thin adapter is easy to inspect; specialist immutability and cross-region controls are outside its fit

My recommendation is specific: teams building replaceable Node.js support-export workers should try Infrai for the storage adapter when public discovery and runnable TypeScript examples matter more than adopting another SDK. The supporting reason is operational: the same credential spans a broad backend surface, reducing key rotation and billing reconciliation if the workflow later adds adjacent capabilities. Neither point eliminates the need for an application-owned retention state machine.

What are the limits of signed links and lifecycle deletion?

A signed URL is temporary access, not retention enforcement. It can expire while the ZIP remains stored. Conversely, deleting the object ends future retrieval even if a previously issued URL has time remaining. Design, log, and alert on those controls separately.

The catch is that Infrai storage has no object versioning or object lock, so it isn't suitable for a financial-grade WORM archive or any workflow that must recover an overwritten object. It also lacks automatic cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration tooling. Stick with a specialist such as Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage when immutable retention, automatic geographic copies, or provider-native compliance controls are requirements.

There are narrower boundaries too. Public-read ACLs aren't supported, so this pattern isn't for permanent public links, image hosting, or static websites. Browser-direct upload is a poor fit when the team must self-configure CORS. Hour-level storage expiry doesn't fit the one-day lifecycle minimum, and server-side metadata search isn't available beyond prefix-based listing. For signed customer documents, those constraints push control back where it belongs — into the worker, queue, and job database.

The final decision rule is crisp. Choose the self-describing adapter when exports are private, the application can own deletion scheduling, and reversible integration is the priority. Choose specialist storage when the storage layer itself must enforce immutability, replication, or richer governance.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the runnable multipart guide at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/large-zip-export-multipart-upload-signed-download-link/ and keep the adapter small.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/objects/multipart-objects/

title: Vessel2Brain: Edge-Aware Multi-Scale Flow Matching for 3D Brain Image Generation from Vessel Masks
description:
arXiv:2611.17919v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating realistic 3D brain MRI volumes from sparse anatomical priors is a highly ill-posed yet clinically valuable problem, with important applications in data augmentation, simulation, and downstream neuroimaging analysis. In this work, we investigate the challenging task of synthesising full 3D brain MRI volumes conditioned solely on vascular label maps. While vascular structures provide strong anatomical and topological cues, they occupy only a small fraction of the brain volume and offer no direct information about surrounding tissue appearance. To address this challenge, we propose Vessel2Brain, an edge-aware multi-scale conditional flow matching framework that explicitly incorporates vascular structure information into the generative process. Our approach formulates vessel-guided brain image synthesis as a conditional continuous flow, enabling stable training and flexible generation while preserving structural correspondence. A multi-scale flow matching strategy is introduced to jointly model global anatomical coherence and fine-grained local details, with auxiliary velocity predictions providing additional supervision across spatial resolutions. Furthermore, we design an edge-aware objective that emphasises vascular boundaries during training, encouraging anatomically faithful tissue synthesis around vessel structures. We evaluate Vessel2Brain on two public 3D brain MRI datasets with paired vascular annotations. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative models in terms of reconstruction accuracy, structural consistency, and distributional realism.

title: Dry run first, then ask - a purge button in Uniface that shows what it will delet
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 keeps logs: imports, exports, logins, job runs, purges. A retention service deletes old rows according to rules like "import log: keep 30 days". The last stage added a form for it.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

The service

The purge operation takes a dry-run flag and returns one row per active rule (kind, days, number of rows) and the total:

public operation PURGE
params
    numeric pDryRun : IN
    string pData : OUT
    numeric pTotal : OUT
    string pError : OUT
endparams

In a dry run it only counts. Both kinds of runs are written to the purge log, with the flag.

One entry for both runs 

entry RUN_PURGE
params
    numeric pDryRun : IN
    numeric pTotal : OUT
endparams
variables
    string vData, vError
endvariables
    pTotal = 0
    activate "RETAIN2_SVC".PURGE(pDryRun, vData, pTotal, vError)
    if ($status < 0)
        rollback
        INFO.RET_DMY = vError
        return -1
    endif
    commit
    if (pDryRun = 1)
        call SHOW_PURGES(vData, "Dry run, nothing deleted:")
    else
        call SHOW_PURGES(vData, "Deleted:")
    endif
    return 0
end

After a successful call the form commits in both cases, so the purge log keeps the dry runs too. (An earlier stage of the project had a form that rolled back after a dry run and lost exactly that log row.)

The button

A separate "Purge: dry run" button exists, but "Purge now..." does not rely on the user having pressed it:

entry DO_PURGE
variables
    numeric vTotal
endvariables
    call RUN_PURGE(1, vTotal)
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    if (vTotal = 0)
        INFO.RET_DMY = "Nothing to delete."
        return 0
    endif
    askmess/question "Delete %%(vTotal) row(s) now? This cannot be undone.~Purge", "Yes,No"
    if ($status != 1)
        INFO.RET_DMY = "Purge cancelled; dry run shown."
        return 0
    endif
    call RUN_PURGE(0, vTotal)
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    INFO.RET_DMY = "%%(vTotal) row(s) deleted."
    return 0
end

The confirmation contains the number of rows that will be deleted. Without a dry run, a question like "Delete old data?" says nothing. With the number, a surprise is visible before anything happens: 2 is expected, 20000 is not.

Click test

Test data: two import log rows from early September, written into a copy of the test database before the app was started. Rule: import log, keep 30 days.

  • "Due purges": import log older than 30 days, 2 rows.
  • "Purge now...", answer No: "Purge cancelled; dry run shown." Nothing deleted.
  • "Purge now...", answer Yes: "2 row(s) deleted."
  • "Due purges" again: 0 rows.
  • The purge log had three dry runs (one from the dry-run button, two from "Purge now...") and one real run.

Notes

  • If an action deletes data, run it as a dry run first and put the result into the question.
  • If nothing is due, do not ask at all ("Nothing to delete.").
  • The dry run costs one extra pass over the data. For log tables in a desktop app that was not noticeable.
