title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.18471v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.

title: Your Integration Code Is Already a Workflow
description:
If you've worked on backend code for a while, you've probably met a function like this. It started small, it works, and nobody wants to touch it.

async function handleLabOrder(order) {
  const labRef = await labApi.submit(order);
  const results = await pollUntilReady(labRef);
  await ehr.updateRecord(order.patientId, results);

  if (results.abnormal) {
    await notifyDoctor(order.doctorId, results);
  }

  await billing.createInvoice(order);
}

This one handles a hospital lab order. It sends the test to the lab, waits for the results, saves them to the patient's record, alerts the doctor if something looks wrong, and creates the bill. That's five steps across four outside systems, written as ten lines that read neatly from top to bottom.

On a good day it does exactly what it says. The trouble is that these steps don't run in seconds. The lab might take an hour. The doctor might not look until the next morning. Any of the four systems can be down at the moment you call it. A function expects to run from start to finish in one go, and this process doesn't work that way.

So this isn't really a function. It's a long-running workflow squeezed into the shape of one, and that mismatch causes most of the trouble that comes later.

Questions this code can't answer

Ask it a few ordinary questions and the gaps show up quickly.

What happens if the process restarts while pollUntilReady is running? The lab already has the order, but your process has forgotten it. Either the order is lost, or the retry submits it a second time.

Where does the code wait while the doctor reviews abnormal results? It doesn't. notifyDoctor sends a message and moves straight on to billing. The review only exists in someone's head.

A nurse asks where order #4821 is right now. To answer, someone has to search logs across four services and hope the IDs match up.

Billing switches vendors next quarter. That means changing this function, plus every other function that copied the same invoice call.

None of these are rare edge cases. They're normal days for any process that touches several systems and involves people.

How it usually gets patched

Teams tend to fix these one incident at a time. A retry wrapper goes around the lab call. A status column appears on the orders table. A cron job checks for orders stuck longer than an hour, and a Slack alert fires when it finds one.

Each fix makes sense on its own. Add them up, though, and the real workflow ends up spread across a function, a database column, a cron job, and a chat channel. Drawing the full process on a whiteboard now means opening three repos first.

At that point it helps to call the code what it is: a sequence of steps with state, waiting, failures, and people in the middle. That kind of thing works better when it's treated as a workflow on purpose.

The same logic as a workflow

Here's the same process written as a workflow definition. It's illustrative pseudo-config, not the syntax of any particular tool.

workflow: lab_order
steps:
  - name: submit_to_lab
    call: lab.submit
    retry: { max_attempts: 5, backoff: exponential }

  - name: wait_for_results
    wait_for_event: lab.results_ready
    timeout: 24h

  - name: update_record
    call: ehr.update_record

  - name: doctor_review
    when: results.abnormal
    human_task:
      assign_to: order.doctor_id
      timeout: 8h
      on_timeout: escalate_to_on_call

  - name: create_invoice
    call: billing.create_invoice

The business logic hasn't changed. What changes is who handles everything around it.

Progress is saved after each step, outside your process. If something crashes during wait_for_results, the run picks up there instead of sending the order to the lab again.

Waiting becomes a normal step. Waiting a day for the lab or eight hours for a doctor is written into the flow, with a timeout, instead of living in a polling loop someone has to maintain.

The doctor's review gets an owner, a deadline, and an escalation path. It stops being a notification that nobody follows up on.

Finding order #4821 becomes a lookup, because the engine knows which step every run is on.

Changing billing vendors means editing one step. Adding something new, such as an AI step that summarizes abnormal results for the doctor, means adding one more step rather than rewriting the function.

When it isn't worth it

Plenty of code should stay a plain function. If the steps finish in milliseconds, the calls are safe to repeat, nobody waits on a person, and a failure can just be retried from the top, a workflow engine is extra infrastructure you don't need. A two-step script that runs once a night doesn't need a flowchart.

A rough test: if you've already added a status column, a cron job that hunts for stuck items, or an admin button that says "retry from step 3," you've built half a workflow engine by hand. The remaining question is whether you want to keep maintaining it yourself.

Code or config?

Once teams decide to treat a process as a workflow, they usually split into two camps.

One camp writes workflows as code. Steps are ordinary functions, and the engine handles saving progress and retries behind the scenes. You keep your usual language, type checking, and tests.

The other camp writes workflows as data, like the YAML above. You get a diagram that people outside engineering can read, changes that don't always need a deploy, and a clear picture of where each run stands. The risk is that a large definition can turn into a config file nobody wants to open.

Both approaches have tradeoffs, and teams land differently depending on who needs to read and change the flow.

So which one does your team use, and what pushed you that way? If you've seen a workflow-as-data setup grow into an unreadable YAML file, I'd like to hear how you got out of it.

title: Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs
description:
arXiv:2611.17469v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.

title: RecMem: Recurrent Memory Compression for Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
description:
arXiv:2611.17921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.

title: Our Node 20 image crashed on start because Docker copied the build agent's node_modules over its own
description:
Our quotes API is a Node service built by Jenkins on a pool of long lived agents. The pipeline has two stages that matter here. The test stage runs npm ci and the unit tests directly on the agent. The image stage then runs docker build with the workspace as its context, and the Dockerfile does what most Node Dockerfiles do: copy package.json and the lockfile, RUN npm ci, then COPY . . for the source.

In October we moved the image from Node 18 to Node 20. The pull request was green. The image built. In staging every pod crashed on start with an error from bcrypt: the module was compiled against a different Node.js version using NODE_MODULE_VERSION 108, and this version of Node.js requires NODE_MODULE_VERSION 115. 108 is Node 18. Nothing inside a Node 20 image should have known about it.

Our .dockerignore listed .git and the docs folder and nothing else. So the build context included the node_modules that the test stage had just installed on the agent, which still ran Node 18. Inside the image, npm ci built a correct node_modules for Node 20, and then COPY . . copied the agent's directory on top of it. COPY merges into an existing directory and replaces any file with the same name, so the native bcrypt binary from the agent overwrote the one the image had just compiled.

The uncomfortable part was not the crash. It was realising this had been happening for two years. While the agent and the image ran the same Node version, the overwrite produced identical files, and the npm ci inside the Dockerfile had been wasted work on every build. Our images contained whatever the agent had happened to install, and nobody could have told. The tests had also run only on Node 18, so the green pull request said nothing about Node 20.

node_modules is now in .dockerignore, along with coverage output and anything else a stage writes into the workspace. The test stage runs inside the same base image the Dockerfile uses, so the tests run on the Node version we ship. A check in the image stage fails the build if the context contains a node_modules directory at all.

A build context is everything in the folder, not everything in the repository, and the folder had been shaped by the stage that ran before it.

– Sergey Shinder

title: NestJS Core Architecture and How We Used It in a Real Project
description:
※ The code examples in this article are based on a real product, but project names, service names, variable names, and anything else that could identify a specific product have been changed or generalized.

(I didn't write all of this from scratch. I took AI-generated content and fixed it up, so I could use it as a kind of dictionary for the project.)

NestJS is a server-side framework built with TypeScript, known for its module-oriented architecture inspired by Angular. In this article, I'll explain the core concepts of NestJS and show how we used them in a real SaaS product (GraphQL API / multi-tenant setup).

(*Update) ↑ I made that sound impressive, but I didn't actually work on that project much, so honestly most of this article isn't in my head lol

Table of contents

  1. Module
  2. Controller / Resolver
  3. Service / UseCase
  4. DI (Dependency Injection)
  5. Guard (Authentication and Authorization)
  6. Layered Entity Definitions
  7. Prisma Integration (Repository + Mapper)
  8. How the Auth Context Flows
  9. Summary: Standard NestJS vs. a Real Project

1. Module

NestJS basics

A NestJS application is organized in units called Modules. With the @Module() decorator, you define providers (services it provides), imports (modules it depends on), and exports (services it exposes to others), which together configure the DI container.

@Module({
  providers: [CatService],
  imports: [DatabaseModule],
  exports: [CatService],
})
export class CatModule {}

In the real project

In this project, modules are split into three layers following a layered architecture.

app.module.ts
  ├─ ResolverModules (interface/di/)        ← presentation layer
  ├─ UseCaseModules (app/di/)               ← application layer
  └─ RepositoryModules (infra/prisma/di/)   ← infrastructure layer

The directory structure looks like this:

packages/api/src/
├── app/                      # Application layer
│   ├── di/                   # UseCase module definitions
│   └── useCases/             # UseCase implementations
├── domain/                   # Domain layer
│   ├── entities/             # Domain entities and type definitions
│   ├── restrictFilters/      # Permission filters
│   └── common/               # Shared types and utilities
├── interface/                # Interface layer
│   ├── di/                   # Resolver module definitions
│   ├── resolvers/            # GraphQL resolvers
│   ├── schema/               # Request/response types
│   └── auth/                 # Auth guards
├── infra/                    # Infrastructure layer
│   ├── prisma/               # Repositories and mappers
│   └── ...                   # External service integrations
└── entities/                 # GraphQL ObjectType definitions

A ResolverModule resolves its dependencies by imports-ing UseCaseModules.

@Module({
  providers: [CommentResolver],
  imports: [
    CommentUseCaseModule,
    UserUseCaseModule,
  ],
})
export class CommentResolverModule {}

A UseCaseModule imports RepositoryModules and other ServiceModules.

@Module({
  providers: [CommentUseCase],
  exports: [CommentUseCase],
  imports: [
    PrismaCommentRepositoryModule,
    PrismaRoomRepositoryModule,
    NotificationServiceModule,
  ],
})
export class CommentUseCaseModule {}

Key point: We use NestJS's module system to enforce a clean-architecture-style dependency direction (interface → app → domain ← infra).

2. Controller / Resolver

NestJS basics

For a REST API, you use decorators like @Get() / @Post() on a @Controller().

@Controller('cats')
export class CatController {
  @Get()
  findAll() { return 'All cats'; }

  @Post()
  create(@Body() dto: CreateCatDto) { ... }
}

For GraphQL, you use @Query() / @Mutation() / @ResolveField() on a @Resolver().

In the real project

This project uses GraphQL with a code-first approach, generating the schema automatically.

// app.module.ts
GraphQLModule.forRoot<ApolloDriverConfig>({
  driver: ApolloDriver,
  autoSchemaFile: join(process.cwd(), 'src/schema.gql'), // generated from TypeScript
  fieldResolverEnhancers: ['guards'],
}),

A resolver example:

@Resolver(() => GqlComment)
export class CommentResolver {
  constructor(private readonly commentUseCase: CommentUseCase) {}

  // Query: fetch data
  @UseGuards(AuthGuard)
  @Query(() => [GqlComment])
  async commentList(
    @Args('input') input: GetCommentListInput,
    @Context() context: OperationContext,
  ) {
    return this.commentUseCase.getCommentList(input, context);
  }

  // Mutation: change data
  @UseGuards(AuthGuard)
  @Mutation(() => GqlComment)
  async createComment(
    @Args('input') input: CreateCommentInput,
    @Context() context: OperationContext,
  ) {
    return this.commentUseCase.createComment(input, context);
  }

  // ResolveField: resolve a nested field
  @ResolveField('author', () => GqlUser)
  async getAuthor(@Parent() comment: Comment) {
    return this.userUseCase.findOne({ id: comment.userId });
  }
}

Main decorators

Decorator Purpose
@Resolver(() => Type) Declares the class as a resolver
@Query(() => Type) Defines a GraphQL query
@Mutation(() => Type) Defines a GraphQL mutation
@ResolveField('name', () => Type) Resolves a nested field
@Args('input') Binds input arguments
@Parent() Accesses the parent object
@Context() Gets the GraphQL context (auth info, etc.)

InputType (request type)

GraphQL input types are also defined with decorators.

@InputType()
export class CreateCommentInput {
  @Field(() => GraphQLJSON)
  content: Prisma.JsonObject;

  @Field()
  roomId: string;

  @Field(() => [Int], { nullable: true })
  imageIds?: number[];
}

This automatically generates the following GraphQL schema:

input CreateCommentInput {
  content: JSON!
  roomId: ID!
  imageIds: [Int!]
}

3. Service / UseCase

NestJS basics

You use a class with the @Injectable() decorator as a service, and gather business logic there.

@Injectable()
export class CatService {
  constructor(private readonly catRepository: CatRepository) {}

  findAll() {
    return this.catRepository.findAll();
  }
}

In the real project

In this project, we name these "UseCase" instead of "Service", and split classes by use case.

@Injectable()
export class CommentUseCase {
  constructor(
    private readonly commentRepository: PrismaCommentRepository,
    private readonly roomRepository: PrismaRoomRepository,
    private readonly notificationService: NotificationService,
  ) {}

  async createComment(input, context: OperationContext) {
    // 1. Domain validation
    const room = CoreAssert.isNotEmpty(
      await this.roomRepository.findOneById({ id: input.roomId }, context),
    );

    // 2. Create the domain entity
    const comment = createCommentSeed({
      ...input,
      userId: context.executor.userId,
    });

    // 3. Save to the DB
    const created = await this.commentRepository.create(comment);

    // 4. Notifications and external integrations
    await this.notificationService.send({ ... });

    return created;
  }
}

Key point: Inside a UseCase, the flow is domain validation → DB save → side effects (notifications, external integrations). Repositories and external services are all injected through the constructor, which makes it very testable.

4. DI (Dependency Injection)

NestJS basics

NestJS's DI automatically resolves providers from TypeScript type information. You register an @Injectable() class in a module's providers, and it's injected automatically based on the constructor's types.

In the real project

Dependencies that cross layers are controlled with imports / exports.

Resolver → constructor(useCase: CommentUseCase)     // resolved by type
UseCase  → constructor(repo: PrismaCommentRepository) // resolved by type

On the module side:

// UseCaseModule: expose CommentUseCase to the outside
@Module({
  providers: [CommentUseCase],
  exports: [CommentUseCase],          // usable from other modules
  imports: [PrismaCommentRepositoryModule],
})
export class CommentUseCaseModule {}

// ResolverModule: import the UseCaseModule to use it
@Module({
  providers: [CommentResolver],
  imports: [CommentUseCaseModule],    // CommentUseCase becomes available
})
export class CommentResolverModule {}

When you hit a circular dependency, you work around it with forwardRef().

@Module({
  imports: [forwardRef(() => RelatedModule)],
})
export class SomeModule {}

5. Guard (Authentication and Authorization)

NestJS basics

You create a guard class that implements the CanActivate interface and apply it with the @UseGuards() decorator.

@Injectable()
export class AuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const request = context.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    return validateToken(request.headers.authorization);
  }
}

In the real project

Because this project is a multi-user SaaS, we use a pattern that routes to different auth guards depending on the user type (admin / guest).

@Injectable()
export class MultiUserAuthGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(
    private readonly adminAuthGuard: AdminAuthGuard,
    private readonly guestAuthGuard: GuestAuthGuard,
  ) {}

  async canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const ctx = GqlExecutionContext.create(context);
    const request = ctx.getContext().req;
    const userType = request.headers['x-user-type'];

    if (userType === 'Admin') {
      // JWT verification (external auth service)
      return this.adminAuthGuard.canActivate(context);
    } else if (userType === 'Guest') {
      // Session token verification
      return this.guestAuthGuard.canActivate(context);
    }

    throw new UnauthorizedException();
  }
}

We also implement fine-grained permission control at the @ResolveField level.

@ResolveField('author', () => GqlUser)
@UseGuards(UserTypesGuard)
@RequiredUserTypes('ADMIN')  // metadata set via a custom decorator
async getAuthor(@Parent() comment: Comment) {
  return this.userUseCase.findOne({ id: comment.userId });
}

UserTypesGuard reads that metadata with Reflector and checks permissions.

@Injectable()
export class UserTypesGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private reflector: Reflector) {}

  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const requiredTypes = this.reflector.get<string[]>(
      'requiredUserTypes',
      context.getHandler(),
    );
    if (!requiredTypes) return true;

    const gqlContext = GqlExecutionContext.create(context);
    const user = gqlContext.getContext().req.user;
    return requiredTypes.includes(user.executor.userType);
  }
}

6. Layered Entity Definitions

NestJS basics

In a typical NestJS application, a single entity class often serves as both the DB definition and the API definition.

In the real project

This project uses three layers of entity definitions.

Layer Example file Purpose
GraphQL Entity entities/Comment.entity.ts Defines the API output type with @ObjectType()
Domain Entity domain/entities/Comment/index.ts Type-safe business model using brand types
Prisma Model prisma/schema.prisma DB schema definition

GraphQL Entity (API layer) 

@ObjectType()
export class Comment {
  @Field(() => Int)
  id: number;

  @Field(() => GraphQLJSON)
  content: Prisma.JsonObject;

  @Field()
  createdAt: Date;

  @Field(() => [CommentImage])
  commentImages: CommentImage[];  // nested field
}

Domain Entity (domain layer)

Brand types let you tell different kinds of IDs apart, even though they're all number.

// Brand type definition
type Brand<T, U> = T & { __brand: U };

// Distinguish IDs at the type level
export type CommentId = Brand<number, 'CommentId'>;
export type UserId = Brand<number, 'UserId'>;

// Type error: CommentId and UserId are not compatible
const commentId: CommentId = 1 as CommentId;
const userId: UserId = commentId; // compile error!

The domain entity definition:

export type Comment = {
  id: CommentId;
  content: Prisma.JsonObject;
  roomId: RoomId;
  userId: UserId;
  tenantId: TenantId;
  createdAt: Date;
  updatedAt: Date;
};

// Factory function
export const createCommentSeed = (payload: CommentSeed): CommentSeed => {
  return { ...payload };
};

Prisma Model (DB layer) 

model Comment {
  id        Int       @id @default(autoincrement())
  content   Json?
  roomId    String
  Room      Room      @relation(fields: [roomId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  userId    Int
  createdAt DateTime  @default(now())
  updatedAt DateTime  @default(now()) @updatedAt
}

Key point: Splitting into three layers means API spec changes don't affect domain logic, and DB schema changes don't leak into the API layer.

7. Prisma Integration (Repository + Mapper)

NestJS basics

In NestJS, it's common to use TypeORM or Prisma directly from services.

In the real project

This project uses a Repository + Mapper pattern to convert Prisma types into domain types.

Repository 

@Injectable()
export class PrismaCommentRepository {
  async create(input: CommentSeed, db = client): Promise<Comment> {
    const prismaComment = await db.comment.create({
      data: {
        contentJson: input.content,
        roomId: input.roomId,
      },
      include: { Room: true },
    });

    // Convert Prisma type → domain type
    return PrismaCommentMapper.toDomainComment(prismaComment);
  }

  async findList(input, context, db = client): Promise<Comment[]> {
    const results = await db.comment.findMany({
      where: {
        roomId: input.roomId,
        Room: { tenantId: context.tenantId }, // tenant isolation
      },
      orderBy: { createdAt: 'asc' },
    });
    return results.map(PrismaCommentMapper.toDomainComment);
  }
}

Mapper 

export class PrismaCommentMapper {
  static toDomainComment(prismaComment): Comment {
    return {
      id: prismaComment.id as CommentId,
      content: prismaComment.contentJson as Prisma.JsonObject,
      roomId: prismaComment.roomId as RoomId,
      userId: prismaComment.userId as UserId,
      tenantId: prismaComment.Room.tenantId as TenantId,
      createdAt: prismaComment.createdAt,
      updatedAt: prismaComment.updatedAt,
    };
  }
}

Transactions

Operations that span multiple tables use prisma.$transaction() to guarantee atomicity.

const result = await prisma.$transaction(async (db) => {
  const room = await this.roomRepository.create(roomData, context, db);
  await this.memberRepository.create(memberData, db);
  return room;
});

Key point: Repository methods take an optional db argument, so they're designed to work both inside a transaction and standalone.

8. How the Auth Context Flows

This is how auth information propagates in a multi-tenant SaaS.

1. GraphQL request
   ├─ Header: Authorization: "Bearer <JWT>"
   └─ Header: x-user-type: "Admin" or "Guest"

2. Guard (authentication)
   ├─ Admin → verify JWT → build OperationContext
   └─ Guest → verify session → build OperationContext
   └─ set request.user = OperationContext

3. Resolver
   └─ get it via @Context() context: OperationContext

4. UseCase / Repository
   └─ use the context for permission control and tenant isolation

OperationContext is defined type-safely with a Zod schema.

export const operationContextSchema = z.object({
  tenantId: tenantIdSchema,
  executor: z.union([
    z.object({
      userType: z.literal('ADMIN'),
      userId: userIdSchema,
      role: roleSchema,
    }),
    z.object({
      userType: z.literal('GUEST'),
      userId: userIdSchema,
    }),
  ]),
});

export type OperationContext = z.infer<typeof operationContextSchema>;

It's injected into resolvers with the custom @Context() decorator.

export const Context = createParamDecorator(
  (data: unknown, context: ExecutionContext) => {
    const ctx = GqlExecutionContext.create(context);
    return ctx.getContext().req.user as OperationContext;
  },
);

Permission filters handle tenant isolation in DB operations.

export const commentRestrictFilter = (
  context: OperationContext,
): Prisma.CommentWhereInput[] => {
  return [{ Room: { tenantId: context.tenantId } }];
};

// Usage
const comments = await prisma.comment.findMany({
  where: { AND: commentRestrictFilter(context) },
});

9. Summary: Standard NestJS vs. a Real Project

Aspect Standard NestJS Real project
API style REST (@Controller) GraphQL code-first (@Resolver)
Business logic Service UseCase (split by use case)
Data access ORM used directly Repository + Mapper pattern
Auth Single guard Guard that routes by user type
Type safety Standard TypeScript Brand types + Zod validation
Tenant isolation None OperationContext + RestrictFilter
Entity Single definition 3 layers (GraphQL / Domain / Prisma)
Module structure By feature By layer (Resolver / UseCase / Repository)

Wrapping up

NestJS is powerful enough out of the box, but it's also flexible enough to customize the architecture to fit a project's size and requirements.

In this project, we built on NestJS's DI system and added a few things:

  • Layered architecture: separate layers by module and control the dependency direction
  • Code-first GraphQL: generate the schema automatically from TypeScript decorators
  • Brand types: catch mixed-up IDs at compile time
  • RestrictFilter: turn multi-tenant data isolation into a reusable pattern

Once you understand the core NestJS concepts (Module / DI / Guard / Decorator), extending it to fit your project's needs is easy. I hope this helps.

title: Forrester analyzes the ROI of Dev Mode
description: For developers, working more efficiently isn’t just about being faster, but also reducing friction in their workflows. Forrester tells us how to save them time and headache—all in service of shipping better products.

title: When Does Oversampling Help? A Decision Framework for Imbalanced Data Streams Under Label Delay and Concept Drift
description:
arXiv:2611.17981v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For imbalanced data streams with delayed labels, is it worth adding a streaming oversampler, or does continuous re-evaluation of earlier predictions already recover the cost of the delay? We address this through an extensive experimental comparison of streaming oversampling and continuous re-evaluation under joint class imbalance, concept drift, and label delay. Streaming oversamplers are typically evaluated under the test-then-train assumption of immediate labels; their behaviour under these conditions, assessed through re-evaluation, has not been systematically studied. We close this gap with a decision framework that predicts when oversampling adds value over re-evaluation, organised around three axes: drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window, and operationalised as a competition between a recovery channel (re-evaluation) and a minority-coverage channel (oversampling). Evaluating $15$ classifiers on $6$ synthetic and $6$ real streams, we find: re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on drift-active streams but is silent on stationary ones; oversampling's marginal contribution over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration; and cost--performance Pareto recommendations from synthetic streams do not transfer to real data, where fronts partition by drift regime. Method selection should therefore be conditioned on the stream's profile and re-estimated as it evolves, not inherited from synthetic benchmarks.

title: WordPress Bozuk Veritabanı Tablolarını phpMyAdmin ile Onarma
description:
WordPress Bozuk Veritabanı Tablolarını phpMyAdmin ile Onarma konusunda kurumsal bir WordPress web sitesine sahipseniz, yaşanan teknik aksaklıklar doğrudan müşteri kaybına, Google arama sıralamalarının gerilemesine ve şirketinizin dijital prestijinin zedelenmesine yol açabilir. Bu rehberimizde hatanın kök nedenlerini, sunucu ve kod seviyesindeki kesin çözüm adımlarını detaylı olarak inceliyoruz.

** Uzman Notu:** Web sitenizde herhangi bir yapılandırma, kod veya veritabanı müdahalesi yapmadan önce mutlaka sunucunuzdan tam zaman damgalı bir veritabanı ve dosya yedeği (backup) alınız.

Sorunun Olası Kök Nedenleri

WordPress altyapısında Bozuk Veritabanı Tablolarını phpMyAdmin ile Onarma durumunun tetiklenmesine yol açan en yaygın 4 temel etken şunlardır:

  • Sunucu Kaynak ve Bellek Yetersizliği: PHP hafıza sınırının (memory_limit) veya işlem zaman aşımının (max_execution_time) aşılması.

  • Eklenti ve Tema Çakışmaları: Yeni güncellenen bir yazılımın mevcut çekirdek WordPress dosyaları veya diğer eklentilerle uyumsuzluk yaşaması.

  • Bozuk Yapılandırma Dosyaları: .htaccess, wp-config.php veya sunucu Nginx/Apache konfigürasyonundaki hatalı direktifler.

  • Veritabanı İndeks ve Bağlantı Hataları: MySQL servisinin aşırı yük altında kilitlenmesi veya tabloların çökmesi.

1. Adım: Hata Ayıklama (Debug) Modu ile Sorunun Kaynağını Belirleyin

Karanlıkta çözüm aramak yerine sorunun hangi eklentiden veya kod satırından kaynaklandığını nokta atışı tespit etmek gerekir. Bunun için web sitenizin ana dizininde yer alan wp-config.php dosyasını açarak aşağıdaki satırları ekleyin:

// Hata ayıklama modunu sessiz günlük kaydıyla açın
define( 'WP_DEBUG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_LOG', true );
define( 'WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY', false );
@ini_set( 'display_errors', 0 );

Bu ayar ziyaretçilerinize herhangi bir hata kodu göstermez; ancak sunucunuzun arka planında /wp-content/debug.log dosyasını oluşturarak çöken fonksiyonu satır numarasıyla birlikte kaydeder.

2. Adım: Sunucu ve PHP Parametrelerini Optimize Edin

Kurumsal altyapılarda modern WordPress eklentileri (WooCommerce, Elementor, WPML vb.) yüksek bellek ve yürütme süresi talep eder. Hosting kontrol panelinizden veya .user.ini dosyanızdan şu limitleri güncelleyin:

memory_limit = 256M
max_execution_time = 300
upload_max_filesize = 64M
post_max_size = 64M
max_input_vars = 3000

Eğer paylaşımlı sunucuda bu değerler güncellenemiyorsa, wp-config.php dosyasına şu satırı ekleyerek WordPress'in bellek sınırını 256MB'a yükseltebilirsiniz:

define( 'WP_MEMORY_LIMIT', '256M' );
define( 'WP_MAX_MEMORY_LIMIT', '512M' );

3. Adım: Yapılandırma Dosyalarını ve Kalıcı Bağlantıları Sıfırlayın

Bozuk yönlendirme kuralları ve güvenlik eklentilerinin bıraktığı hatalı kurallar erişimi engelleyebilir. Standart temiz .htaccess kurallarını uygulayınız:

# BEGIN WordPress
<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
RewriteEngine On
RewriteBase /
RewriteRule ^index\.php$ - [L]
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteRule . /index.php [L]
</IfModule>
# END WordPress

Ardından WordPress yönetim panelinden Ayarlar → Kalıcı Bağlantılar sekmesini ziyaret edip herhangi bir değişiklik yapmadan Değişiklikleri Kaydet butonuna basarak Apache yönlendirme önbelleğini tazeleyin.

4. Adım: Veritabanı ve Önbellek Kalıntılarını Temizleyin

Süresi dolmuş transient kalıntıları ve silinmiş eklentilerin bıraktığı sorgular veritabanını yavaşlatır. phpMyAdmin veya WP-CLI üzerinden tabloları optimize edebilirsiniz:

# WP-CLI ile önbellek ve geçici verileri temizleyin
wp cache flush
wp transient delete --expired
wp db optimize

** Kritik Güvenlik Uyarısı:** FTP veya sunucu erişim bilgilerinizi güvenli olmayan kanallardan kimseyle paylaşmayınız. WordPress Uzmanı olarak tüm şifrelerinizi AES-256-GCM ile şifrelenmiş kasamızda tutuyor, iş teslim edildiğinde otomatik olarak sistemden kalıcı olarak siliyoruz.




Ne Zaman Uzmana Başvurmalı?

Eğer yukarıdaki adımlara rağmen sitenizdeki Bozuk Veritabanı Tablolarını phpMyAdmin ile Onarma sorunu giderilemiyorsa, veritabanı tablolarında derin bozulmalar, çekirdek dosyalara bulaşmış zararlı kodlar (malware) veya sunucu seviyesinde modül çakışmaları mevcut olabilir. Bu tür kritik durumlarda deneme yanılma yapmak veri kaybına yol açabileceğinden, kurumsal sözleşmeli ve faturalı destek masamızdan Yazılı Teklif talep ederek uzman müdahalesi almanız önerilir.

Bu yazı ilk olarak wordpressuzmani.com üzerinde yayınlanmıştır.

title: One customer, many forms - passing an ID through exec in Uniface 10
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 has grown to many forms: documents, tickets, company data, channels, opportunities. Each one has its own "choose customer" button. The newest form is a customer overview that should open the others with the customer already set, so the user does not pick the same customer again.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

An optional parameter on exec

The overview itself takes the customer ID as a parameter of its exec operation. Zero means "no customer yet":

operation exec
params
    numeric pCustomerId : IN
endparams
    call SET_LABELS
    call SET_RIGHTS
    $cCust$ = 0
    if (pCustomerId > 0)
        call SET_CUST(pCustomerId)
    endif
    edit
end

The menu opens it without a customer:

entry DO_C360
    call SESSION_OK
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    activate "CRM360_FRM".exec(0)
    return 0
end

So far the overview is only opened from the menu. A call with an ID runs the same SET_CUST entry that the "Customer..." button uses after the lookup, and that path was part of the click test.

SET_CUST reads the name with a read-only query. The ID is a numeric parameter, so the value that ends up in the SQL text is a number:

entry SET_CUST
params
    numeric pId : IN
endparams
variables
    string vData, vRow, vLast, vFirst
endvariables
    sql/data "SELECT LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = %%(pId)", "CUSTOMERS"
    vData = $result
    if (vData = "")
        INFO.C360_DMY = "The customer %%(pId) does not exist."
        return -1
    endif
    getitem vRow, vData, 1
    getitem vLast, vRow, 1
    getitem vFirst, vRow, 2
    $cCust$ = pId
    CUST_NAME.C360_DMY = "%%(vLast), %%(vFirst) (#%%(pId))"
    call DO_OVERVIEW
    return 0
end

Forms that already accept the ID

The ticket form got the same kind of parameter in an earlier stage:

operation exec
params
    numeric pCustomerId : IN
endparams

The company data form follows the same pattern and loads the record right away:

operation exec
params
    numeric pCustomerId : IN
endparams
    call SET_LABELS
    call SET_RIGHTS
    $cCust$ = 0
    if (pCustomerId > 0)
        $cCust$ = pCustomerId
        CUST_NAME.PTY_DMY = "#%%(pCustomerId)"
        call LOAD
    endif
    edit
end

From the overview, opening the ticket form is one activate:

entry DO_OPEN_TICKETS
    call NEED_CUST
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    activate "TICKET_FRM".exec($cCust$)
    return 0
end

In the click test the ticket form opened with "Customer #15" filled in. A ticket created there showed up in the overview's ticket list after closing the form. The company data and channel forms opened with the same customer loaded.

Forms without a parameter

The documents form is older and has an exec without parameters. The rule for this stage was to add new forms and change only the menus, not forms from earlier stages. So the overview only opens it:

entry DO_OPEN_DOCS
    activate "DOC_FRM".exec()
    return 0
end

The user then picks the customer there. That is one extra click, and it is honest about what the form can do. Changing the documents form would have meant changing a tested component for a convenience.

Notes

  • A numeric parameter with 0 as "not set" keeps the call from a menu simple: exec(0).
  • The receiving form should load right away when it gets an ID, so the user sees data and not an empty form with a filled-in customer label.
  • When a form has no parameter yet, adding one is a change to that form's interface. In this project that waits until the form is changed anyway.

title: Color Converter: My Contrast Audit Flagged 11 Colors That Already Passed WCAG AA
description:
Color Converter: My Contrast Audit Flagged 11 Colors That Already Passed WCAG AA

Last Tuesday I ran a contrast check over our design tokens before a release. The script reported 11 failures out of 42 text/background pairs. I spent the afternoon darkening grays and pulling the brand blue down two steps, pushed it, and went home.

The next morning our designer opened the staging build and asked why the primary button looked muddy. Then axe-core in CI flagged three pairs my script had marked as clean.

Both of us were looking at the same CSS. My checker was wrong in two different directions at once, and it took me a while to see why.

The scene, with numbers

The palette was small. Body text #767676 on #FFFFFF. Brand link #5B8DEF on white. A muted placeholder #9AA4B2 on #F8FAFC. A disabled label written as eight-digit hex, #00000080.

My first script did what a lot of quick scripts do. It grabbed the three channel bytes, divided by 255, and plugged them straight into the luminance formula. No gamma step. That single omission dragged every ratio down toward 1.0, so pairs that passed looked like failures. Meanwhile the alpha bug below pushed three real failures up to a perfect score.

#767676 on white came out as 2.05:1. The real number is 4.54:1, which passes AA for body text at any size. I darkened 300-odd paragraphs for nothing.

The formula I should have used is the one in the WCAG 2.2 definition of relative luminance: linearize each channel first, then weight them 0.2126 / 0.7152 / 0.0722.

Method 1: a Python script that gets the math right

Python 3.11.1, standard library only. Save as check_contrast.py and run it.

def channel(c: int) -> float:
    c = c / 255
    return c / 12.92 if c <= 0.04045 else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4

def luminance(hex_color: str) -> float:
    h = hex_color.lstrip("#")
    r, g, b = (int(h[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (0, 2, 4))
    return 0.2126 * channel(r) + 0.7152 * channel(g) + 0.0722 * channel(b)

def ratio(fg: str, bg: str) -> float:
    a, b = luminance(fg), luminance(bg)
    hi, lo = max(a, b), min(a, b)
    return (hi + 0.05) / (lo + 0.05)

PAIRS = [
    ("#767676", "#FFFFFF", "body text on surface"),
    ("#5B8DEF", "#FFFFFF", "brand link on surface"),
    ("#9AA4B2", "#F8FAFC", "placeholder on page bg"),
]

for fg, bg, label in PAIRS:
    r = ratio(fg, bg)
    size = "AA" if r >= 4.5 else "AA-large" if r >= 3.0 else "fail"
    print(f"{label:28} {fg} on {bg}  {r:5.2f}:1  {size}")

Output on my machine:

body text on surface         #767676 on #FFFFFF   4.54:1  AA
brand link on surface        #5B8DEF on #FFFFFF   3.23:1  AA-large
placeholder on page bg       #9AA4B2 on #F8FAFC   2.41:1  fail

Read that middle line before you touch your brand color. #5B8DEF is a perfectly good link color for 24px headings and a failing one for 16px body copy. There is no single "is this color accessible" answer. Size and weight decide it, and a checker that returns one boolean will keep lying to you.

The placeholder line is the only genuine failure in that list, and it was the one pair I had not touched.

Method 2: Node, reading the tokens straight from CSS

Python is fine for a one-off list. For CI I wanted the audit to read the actual tokens.css so nobody could hand-edit a hex in the script and drift from production.

Node 22.13.1, no dependencies:

import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

const lin = (c) => (c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4);
const lum = ([r, g, b]) =>
  0.2126 * lin(r / 255) + 0.7152 * lin(g / 255) + 0.0722 * lin(b / 255);
const ratio = (fg, bg) => {
  const [a, b] = [lum(fg), lum(bg)];
  return (Math.max(a, b) + 0.05) / (Math.min(a, b) + 0.05);
};

function parse(css) {
  const hex = css.match(/^#([0-9a-f]{3,8})$/i);
  if (hex) {
    let h = hex[1];
    if (h.length === 3) h = [...h].map((c) => c + c).join("");
    const n = (i) => parseInt(h.slice(i, i + 2), 16);
    return [n(0), n(2), n(4), h.length === 8 ? n(6) / 255 : 1];
  }
  const m = css.match(/rgba?\(([^)]+)\)/i);
  if (!m) throw new Error(`unparsed color: ${css}`);
  const p = m[1].split(/[\s,\/]+/).filter(Boolean).map(Number);
  return [p[0], p[1], p[2], p.length > 3 ? p[3] : 1];
}

const over = (fg, bg) =>
  fg.slice(0, 3).map((c, i) => Math.round(c * fg[3] + bg[i] * (1 - fg[3])));

const tokens = Object.fromEntries(
  [...readFileSync("tokens.css", "utf8").matchAll(/--([\w-]+):\s*([^;]+);/g)]
    .map((m) => [m[1], m[2].trim()])
);

const bg = parse(tokens.surface ?? "#FFFFFF");
for (const [name, raw] of Object.entries(tokens)) {
  if (!name.startsWith("text-")) continue;
  const fg = over(parse(raw), bg.slice(0, 3));
  console.log(`${name.padEnd(18)} ${ratio(fg, bg.slice(0, 3)).toFixed(2)}:1`);
}

Against this tokens.css:

:root {
  --surface: #FFFFFF;
  --text-body: #767676;
  --text-muted: #8A8F98;
  --text-disabled: #00000080;
}

It prints:

text-body          4.54:1
text-muted         3.25:1
text-disabled      4.00:1

Two things to notice. text-disabled is 4.00:1, not the 21:1 my old script reported, because the alpha channel finally gets composited. And text-muted at 3.25:1 fails AA for small text, which is the kind of finding I actually wanted.

Wire this into CI with an exit code and a 4.5 threshold, and the audit stops being a thing I remember to run.

Method 3: the browser tool for the handoff

The script tells me a pair fails. It does not tell the designer what to change.

That is where a free online color converter earned a permanent tab. I paste #5B8DEF and get HEX, RGB and HSL side by side with a live swatch. The HSL row is what I forward: "same hue 220°, saturation 82%, lightness 64.7% down to 48%". She adjusts one number instead of guessing at a new hex.

The round trip matters too. When a designer sends hsl(220 82% 65%) in Slack and the codebase stores hex, this browser-based tool gives me the hex and the swatch to confirm nothing shifted. I do the ratio math in the script, not in my head. The converter handles the notation, the script handles the threshold.

One habit worth building: after you pick a shade in the color converter, check it in DevTools on the real element. Computed color can differ from the token you think you set, especially when a parent has opacity or a gradient overlay.

Three pitfalls that cost me real time

1. Missing linearization, silently. My first pass returned 2.05:1 for #767676 on white. Nothing errored. The number just looked plausible, and I acted on it. Any contrast function that does not contain a ** 2.4 or a pow(x, 2.4) is wrong. Compare against one known pair before trusting a batch of 42.

2. Eight-digit hex read as six. #00000080 sliced at h[0:2], h[2:4], h[4:6] yields black, and the 80 disappears without a warning. My audit gave text-disabled a 21.00:1 and passed it. Composited over white it is #7F7F7F, 4.00:1, below the AA floor for small text. MDN's hex color reference covers the #RRGGBBAA form; if your parser only accepts six digits, make it throw instead of truncating.

3. Interpolating hue the short way round. Building a hover ramp from a red brand color, I stepped hue from 350° to 10° in equal increments. The midpoint landed on 180°:

hue 350 -> 10, linear midpoint = #19E5E6
shortest-path midpoint         = #E61919

Cyan, in the middle of a red ramp. Hues are angles, so the shortest path crosses 0°, not the middle of the wheel. Same trap in reverse for 10° to 350°.

Also worth knowing: #767676 is HSL lightness 46.3%, not 50%. "Add 10% lightness" is not a predictable number of contrast points, so re-measure after every nudge.

Summary

Approach Good for Watch out for
Python 3.11.1 script One-off audits, exact numbers, no install Must linearize channels; no alpha support unless you add it
Node 22.13.1 + tokens.css CI gates, catching token drift Composite alpha first, then measure
Browser converter HSL handoff, notation round trips, visual check Gives you colors, not ratios

The audit did not fail because the palette was bad. It failed because my checker had no gamma correction and no alpha handling, and I trusted its output over the rendered page.

More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
description:
When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits.

Last year, we shipped just that, with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it.

More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged.

  • The first is automation: Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines.

  • The second is agents and harnesses: Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too.

As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance.

Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three.

More secure workflows

The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection.

Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end, before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools.

Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel

On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change:

Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log.

Encryption on self-hosted Worlds

Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams.

A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management. Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay:

More security work in v5

Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads.

You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0, inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability.

A redesigned trace viewer

The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development.

Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets.

Workflows in every region

In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1. Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress.

For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region. Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path.

By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration:

To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start(). That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay:

The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1.

Infrastructure reliability

Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover.

With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors.

As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug.

Agent-ready performance

In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today.

Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit.

In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes.

The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures.

Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers:

Fewer queue hops

In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout.

The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms.

Incremental replay

Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log: replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms. The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes.

WebSocket streaming

Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default. In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds.

Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression.

These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application.

Benchmark results and methodology

Measured October 8, 2026, on Vercel production in iad1, against the managed Vercel World. Each version uses a separate deployment of the same app. Steps take 1 KB of JSON in and out.

The full results, including tails, are in the performance documentation.

Worlds: the shared durability primitive

Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World: the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness, which adds durability to existing agent harnesses.

Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness.

Choose the integration around how you want to build:

  • Workflow SDK: write durable application logic with use workflow and use step.

  • WorkflowAgent: use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow.

  • fx: embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx.

  • durable-harness: keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it.

    • Supports Pi and OpenCode, with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox.

  • eve: build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds.

We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability.

Build with Workflow SDK 5

Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds:

  • In-flight cancellation with AbortController

  • Searchable run attributes

  • More framework integrations

  • And more

The v5 upgrade docs cover what changed. To start building a new workflow, install the SDK:

Workflow SDK also has a Python SDK, now in beta, with the same durable workflows, steps, sleeps, and hooks.
