title: Go Sequencing Windows — Containing Partial Batch Failures on a Delivery Tracking Map
description:
A live map has one constraint that changes the design: after a disconnect, the client must distinguish an event it never received from an event it received and then lost from memory. A faster transport cannot answer that question. Only an ordered, replayable delivery contract can.

Short answer: Assign every device-status event a stable identity and a monotonic position within its stream, acknowledge batch members individually, and reconnect from the last contiguous position rather than the largest position observed.

That choice treats a batch as a transport envelope, not a transaction. If positions 410 through 419 arrive and 414 fails validation, the dashboard may render later positions provisionally, but its durable checkpoint remains 413. The server can then backfill from 414 without guessing, while deduplication makes the repeated 415 through 419 harmless. This is the same conservative instinct used for a ledger: progress means a contiguous, auditable prefix, not a collection of optimistic successes.

How should realtime event delivery recover from batch partial failures?

Start by separating three facts that are often collapsed into one boolean: whether the producer accepted an update, whether the delivery service durably recorded it, and whether a particular dashboard applied it. An accepted: true response can establish the second fact only if the response identifies the exact member; it cannot establish the third. Likewise, a socket write completing says little about what survived a browser refresh. Don't promote transport completion into business completion.

For a medical-device delivery tracking map, a useful stream key is the tracked shipment or device journey, not the entire tenant. Each event needs an immutable event ID, a stream ID, a stream position, an occurrence time, and the status payload. The position orders changes within that one journey; it does not pretend to establish a universal order among unrelated deliveries. A correction is a new event that refers to the affected state rather than an edit that erases history. That preserves the evidence needed for reconciliation and any retention or access controls required by the applicable compliance regime. The exact retention period is a policy decision, not something the realtime protocol should invent.

The batch result must have the same granularity as the input. One response shape can classify each member as accepted, already accepted, or rejected, with a stable reason for rejection. A whole-batch success flag loses information. A whole-batch retry is acceptable only when event IDs make it idempotent; otherwise a single malformed member turns retry into duplicate state transitions.

Keep the checkpoint rule strict: advance it while next_position == checkpoint + 1, then stop at the first gap.

The batch contract is an accounting boundary

The ingest path should validate identity and sequence metadata before publishing anything downstream. It may process members independently, yet it should return one result per input event so the caller can reconcile cardinality as well as status. If the caller submits ten events and receives nine results, the response itself is incomplete and none of its apparent success should silently close the audit record.

A compact state table makes the retry rule explicit:

Member result Producer action Consumer effect
Accepted Record the event ID and position Apply once when its turn arrives
Already accepted Treat as successful retry Ignore the duplicate payload
Rejected, permanent Quarantine with the reason Do not advance across its position
Outcome unknown Retry with the same event ID Deduplicate if the first attempt committed

The permanent-rejection row deserves care. If position 414 is structurally invalid, retrying the same bytes forever cannot repair it, but silently skipping it would make the displayed route look complete when it is not. The operator needs an audited resolution: replace the invalid update with a valid, newly identified correction under a documented policy, or mark that position as deliberately resolved. Which option is lawful for device data depends on the organization's recordkeeping rules. I'm not sure a generic transport library can make that decision correctly; the evidence needed is the data classification and the approved correction policy.

Exactly-once delivery is the wrong external promise. Networks can lose acknowledgements, so a producer may have to send the same event again. The attainable contract is an idempotent write plus an exactly-once state transition at the consumer: insert the event ID under a uniqueness constraint, apply the transition in the same local transaction, and return the prior result when the ID already exists. Short version: retry facts, not guesses.

A Go consumer that refuses to checkpoint across a gap

The following state machine is deliberately smaller than a full websocket server. It shows the correctness boundary: duplicate IDs do nothing, out-of-order events wait, and the durable checkpoint moves only through a contiguous run. Persistence implementations should commit seen, pending events, derived status, and checkpoint atomically; the in-memory maps here express the contract rather than a storage recommendation.

package delivery

import (
    "errors"
    "sync"
)

type Event struct {
    ID       string
    StreamID string
    Position uint64
    Status   string
}

type Cursor struct {
    mu         sync.Mutex
    checkpoint uint64
    seen       map[string]struct{}
    pending    map[uint64]Event
    status     string
}

func NewCursor(checkpoint uint64) *Cursor {
    return &Cursor{
        checkpoint: checkpoint,
        seen:       make(map[string]struct{}),
        pending:    make(map[uint64]Event),
    }
}

func (c *Cursor) Apply(e Event) (uint64, error) {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()

    if e.ID == "" || e.StreamID == "" || e.Position == 0 {
        return c.checkpoint, errors.New("missing event identity or position")
    }
    if _, duplicate := c.seen[e.ID]; duplicate {
        return c.checkpoint, nil
    }
    if e.Position <= c.checkpoint {
        c.seen[e.ID] = struct{}{}
        return c.checkpoint, nil
    }

    c.seen[e.ID] = struct{}{}
    c.pending[e.Position] = e

    for {
        next := c.checkpoint + 1
        event, ready := c.pending[next]
        if !ready {
            break
        }
        c.status = event.Status
        delete(c.pending, next)
        c.checkpoint = next
    }
    return c.checkpoint, nil
}

There is a subtle collision the sample leaves to the persistence layer: two different event IDs must not be allowed to claim the same stream position. Enforce uniqueness on both (stream_id, position) and event_id, then retain the original payload or its integrity digest alongside the decision. Otherwise a retry with a mutated payload can masquerade as ordinary deduplication. Auditability requires being able to explain which bytes won and why.

The dashboard may still show a later location marker while a gap is open, but it should label that view as provisional and keep the durable resume token at the contiguous checkpoint. For some clinical workflows, even provisional rendering may be inappropriate; in that case hold later events in the reorder buffer and show that the feed is catching up. This is a product-policy choice with safety implications, not a transport optimization.

Reconnect is a bounded backfill protocol

On reconnect, the client presents its stream ID and last contiguous checkpoint. The server returns events after that position in ascending order, in bounded pages, before switching the connection to live delivery. The handoff needs a defined boundary so an event created during backfill is neither omitted nor applied without ordering: capture a high-water position, replay through it, and then subscribe beyond it. If live events arrive early, buffer them by position until backfill reaches the boundary.

Bound the buffer.

A device that reconnects after a long offline interval may be millions of positions behind, and letting its pending map grow without limit converts one stale tab into a memory-pressure incident. Set limits for page size, pending event count, replay duration, and maximum supported history based on load tests and retention policy. When a client exceeds a limit, stop incremental replay and fetch a versioned snapshot plus events after the snapshot position. The catch is that snapshots trade fine-grained reconstruction for bounded recovery time; they are not suitable when an auditor must reproduce every intermediate dashboard state from the client artifact alone. Stick with event replay when that reconstruction is mandatory and the retained log can meet the recovery objective.

Backpressure belongs in this protocol too. A client should advertise or imply how much work it can accept, and the server should not keep extending an unacknowledged window. Acknowledgements should report the highest contiguous applied position, not a bag of recently seen positions. That single scalar is conservative, easy to persist, and sufficient to restart replay. Selective gap information can accelerate repair, but it must not replace the contiguous cursor.

WebRTC data channels are one possible peer-to-peer transport, and the W3C recommendation defines their association and data-channel behavior. They do not remove the application-level need for event identity, durable replay, idempotent application, or an audit trail. The transport choice comes after the recovery contract.

Test the fractures, then roll out by cohort

A happy-path load test proves almost nothing here. Exercise partial acceptance at every member of a batch, a lost acknowledgement after durable acceptance, duplicate delivery with the same ID, conflicting IDs at one position, disconnects before and after checkpoint persistence, events arriving beyond a gap, snapshot handoff, and reconnect storms. Assert both the rendered device status and the audit record after every test; a green map with an unexplained cursor is still a failed test.

Operational metrics should expose gap age, pending-buffer size, duplicate rate, permanent rejection count, replay page latency, reconnect attempts, and the distance between the stream high-water position and each active client's checkpoint. Alert on sustained age and distance rather than raw reconnect count alone. Reconnects are expected. A gap that never closes is the incident.

Rollout can stay compact: first shadow-compute the new contiguous checkpoint without changing display state, then compare it with the existing resume behavior; next enable replay for an internal cohort with capped buffers; finally expand by cohort while preserving the ability to reset a client from a versioned snapshot. Record protocol version, rollout cohort, cursor transitions, and operator resolutions in the audit trail. Roll back the reader, not the event history.

The resulting design does not promise that every batch succeeds. It promises something more useful: every member has an attributable outcome, retries are idempotent, gaps remain visible, and a reconnect has one defensible place from which to resume.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: DoubleTake: Focused Verification of Visual Evidence for Long-Document Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.17853v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In long-document question answering, a vision-language model can answer incorrectly even when the retrieved pages contain sufficient evidence. Rereading those pages with the original question gives the model little guidance about which fact to check. We introduce DoubleTake, a training-free framework for focused verification of visual evidence. An initial reading produces a candidate answer and a separate evidence record that guides retrieval for a second reading. A planner compares the two candidates and their supporting evidence to formulate a factual question. A verifier answers it from the source images without seeing either candidate or evidence record, and a reasoner uses this observation to resolve the original question. With a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone, DoubleTake achieves the highest overall accuracy among the evaluated methods on each of four benchmarks. With the same pages and number of model calls, asking a focused factual question yields higher accuracy on all four benchmarks than asking the original question again. Our code is available at https://github.com/small-code-cat/double_take.

title: Ollama Tutorial: Run Your First Local LLM in Python
description:
Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/ollama-tutorial-run-local-llm.html

Quick answer

Ollama is a free program that runs open language models on your own computer, no API key or cloud account needed. You install it, download a model with one command, and talk to it from a terminal or your own code through a local HTTP API on port 11434. This post installs Ollama on Linux, pulls a small 352 MB model, and sorts four real support tickets from Python.

Picture a small software company's support inbox on a Monday morning. Four tickets waited overnight: a plan that never activated after payment, an app crashing on the settings page, a misspelled name on an invoice, and a whole team locked out since breakfast. Sorting them by hand takes a morning, and a cloud AI means uploading customer data to someone else's server and paying per message. A model on your own machine changes that trade: it sorts the tickets and sends nothing outside your computer. This post shows that setup working, with real timings.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the model fits the machine. A model file has to sit in memory with room to spare for the conversation. The model here, qwen2:0.5b, is a 352 MB download that runs on an ordinary laptop CPU. A 7B model needs around 8 GB of free RAM; a 13B model needs about 16 GB. Check free memory first, or the first run will crawl.

My second check is what the model is for. A small local model handles sorting, summarising, and drafting, but it is not as careful as the big cloud models. The demo below shows it: the 0.5B model called every ticket high urgency. For careful reasoning or long documents, a cloud model wins; local wins only when privacy matters more than polish.

My third check is whether the task repeats. Ollama earns its keep when the same job runs again and again: triage, summaries, drafted replies. One question a week does not justify an install; a repeated job makes the setup pay for itself.

My fourth check is how the model will be called. Ollama serves a local API, so a script, a service, or a tool like LangChain can call it by changing one URL. Keep the port on localhost, 127.0.0.1, so only your own machine can reach it.

My verdict, as judgement: use Ollama when the data should stay on your machine, the job repeats, and a small model fits your hardware. Start with the smallest model that works, and measure before sizing up. The recommendation flips the moment you need top-tier reasoning, long context, or a model bigger than your RAM.

Four tickets, one local model

The example sorts four support messages. Each ticket gets an urgency, a topic, and one short action, in one line. The script sends each ticket to qwen2:0.5b through the Ollama chat API, with temperature 0 and a 1024-token context. The first call deliberately asks for llama3.2, a model that was never pulled, to show the error. Here is the script, exactly as it ran:

"""Classify four support tickets with a local Ollama model.

Sends each ticket to qwen2:0.5b through the Ollama HTTP API on
http://localhost:11434 and prints the model's one-line verdict plus
timing. The first call deliberately uses a model name that has not
been pulled, to show the error Ollama returns in that case.
"""
import json
import time

import requests

API_URL = "http://localhost:11434/api/chat"

TICKETS = [
    {
        "id": "SUP-201",
        "text": "I paid for the yearly plan yesterday but my account still shows the free plan.",
    },
    {
        "id": "SUP-202",
        "text": "The app crashes every time I open the settings page on my phone.",
    },
    {
        "id": "SUP-203",
        "text": "How do I change the name on my invoice? I typed it wrong when I signed up.",
    },
    {
        "id": "SUP-204",
        "text": "Our whole team cannot log in since this morning, we keep getting a server error.",
    },
]

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You triage support tickets for a small software company. "
    "Reply in exactly one line: URGENCY: <low, medium, or high> | "
    "TOPIC: <billing, technical, or account> | "
    "ACTION: <one short action, under 10 words>."
)


def classify(model, ticket):
    """Send one ticket to the model, return the reply text and timings."""
    payload = {
        "model": model,
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Ticket: " + ticket["text"]},
        ],
        "stream": False,
        "options": {"temperature": 0, "num_ctx": 1024},
    }
    started = time.time()
    response = requests.post(API_URL, json=payload, timeout=300)
    wall = time.time() - started
    if response.status_code != 200:
        return None, response.status_code, response.text.strip(), wall
    data = response.json()
    return data["message"]["content"].strip(), response.status_code, data, wall


def main():
    print("Step 1: ask for a model that was never pulled")
    reply, status, detail, wall = classify("llama3.2", TICKETS[0])
    print(f"HTTP status: {status}")
    print(f"Response: {detail}")
    print()
    print("Step 2: same tickets, with the model that is actually on disk")
    for ticket in TICKETS:
        reply, status, data, wall = classify("qwen2:0.5b", ticket)
        tokens = data.get("eval_count", 0)
        eval_seconds = data.get("eval_duration", 0) / 1e9
        rate = tokens / eval_seconds if eval_seconds else 0
        print(f"{ticket['id']}: {reply}")
        print(
            f"    {tokens} tokens in {eval_seconds:.1f}s "
            f"({rate:.1f} tokens/sec), wall time {wall:.1f}s"
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Here is the real output from the run:

Step 1: ask for a model that was never pulled
HTTP status: 404
Response: {"error":"model 'llama3.2' not found"}

Step 2: same tickets, with the model that is actually on disk
SUP-201: URGENCY: High | TOPIC: Billing | ACTION: Contact customer support to resolve the issue.
    21 tokens in 2.0s (10.4 tokens/sec), wall time 6.0s
SUP-202: URGENCY: High | TOPIC: App crash | ACTION: Close ticket with customer support.
    20 tokens in 0.8s (25.7 tokens/sec), wall time 1.0s
SUP-203: URGENCY: High | TOPIC: Billing | ACTION: Contact customer support to resolve the issue.
    21 tokens in 0.7s (29.6 tokens/sec), wall time 0.9s
SUP-204: URGENCY: High
TOPIC: Server Error
ACTION: Contact IT Support immediately.
    19 tokens in 0.8s (24.1 tokens/sec), wall time 1.1s

The thing that went wrong is in step 1: the request asked for llama3.2, which was never downloaded, and the API answered HTTP 404 with {"error":"model 'llama3.2' not found"}. The fix is to check what is on disk first with ollama list, then pull the missing model. The first qwen2:0.5b call took 6.0 seconds of wall time against 2.0 seconds of generation, because the model was still loading; later calls took about a second each, at 24 to 30 tokens per second.

The verdicts teach a second lesson. The model called every ticket high urgency, invented a topic called "App crash" that was not in the allowed list, and split the last answer across three lines. A 0.5B model is a toy for learning the wiring, not a production classifier. Treat its output as a draft and check it with rules, the way the Pydantic post on this blog validates data first.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, asking for a model that was never pulled. The symptom is HTTP 404 with {"error":"model 'llama3.2' not found"}. The fix is to run ollama list, then ollama pull <model> before you call it, using the exact tag you pulled.

Second, calling the API before the server is running. The symptom in Python is a ConnectionError ending in [Errno 111] Connection refused. The fix is to start the server with ollama serve in a separate terminal, then check http://localhost:11434/api/tags first.

Third, trusting a tiny model's verdicts. The symptom is confident-looking output that is wrong on the details: everything high urgency, invented categories, broken formatting. The fix is to validate the reply against the allowed values in your own code, and test on ten known tickets first.

Fourth, pulling a model bigger than the machine. The symptom is a download that succeeds and a run that crawls or fails to load. The fix is to check the model size on the library page first and match it to free RAM, starting small.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a GPU to run Ollama? No. Small models run on an ordinary CPU: qwen2:0.5b generated 24 to 30 tokens per second on a 4-core machine with no GPU.

Do I need the internet after the model is downloaded? No. Once the model file is on disk, Ollama runs fully offline, and the API works with the network off.

Is my data sent anywhere when I run a model locally? No, not for local models. Ollama's FAQ says it does not see your prompts or data when you run locally. Watch out for names ending in :cloud, which run on Ollama's servers instead.

Can I use Ollama with LangChain? Yes. LangChain can point its chat model at the local Ollama API instead of a cloud provider. The LangChain tutorial on this blog shows the chain pattern; swap the model line for a local one.

What to remember

  • Ollama runs open models on your machine through a local API on port 11434, with no API key.
  • Check ollama list first, or a missing model answers with a 404.
  • The first call is slow while the model loads; later calls are much faster.
  • A tiny model proves the wiring, but validate its verdicts in your own code.

Where this leaves you

You now have a local model answering real tickets from your own code, with timings you measured yourself, and you have seen both failure modes that catch beginners: a missing model and a small model overpromising. Pick one repeated job, a daily inbox sort or a meeting summary, wire it to the local API, and run it for a week. If the small model handles it, you have a private tool that costs nothing per message. If it does not, you will know exactly what a bigger model needs to fix.

Further reading

  • Ollama, official site, https://ollama.com
  • Ollama on GitHub, https://github.com/ollama/ollama
  • Ollama model library, https://ollama.com/library

title: Representational Geometry as a Diagnostic for Adversarial Robustness
description:
arXiv:2611.17684v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adversarial training is a common technique for making neural networks more robust to small, intentionally crafted input perturbations, and robustness is commonly measured through accuracy under attack. By exploring inter-network representations across different adversarial training objectives, we can analyze whether multiple networks organize their latent representations similarly. We study Multilayer Perceptrons trained on MNIST under three adversarial training regimes and compare the resulting population training dynamics and geometry to those of a vanilla network. We use M-PHATE to embed data samples across training epochs and examine how the geometry of the data changes during training under adversarial objectives. On penultimate-layer representations we measure displacement between clean and perturbed points, distributional distance through maximum mean discrepancy, and nearest-neighbor recovery. Our visualizations and quantitative analyses show that adversarial training leads to structural changes in how networks organize internal data representations, and robust accuracy and representational stability can rank the same defenses in opposite ways. These findings support a discussion of re-evaluating how practitioners approach the auditing of model robustness by treating latent representations and their training trajectories as diagnostic artifacts across sets of networks.

title: A Multi-Layered AI Pipeline for BPMN Generation from Natural Language
description:
arXiv:2611.18157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The automated transformation of unstructured natural language process descriptions into Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams remains a challenging task, due to linguistic ambiguity and the difficulty to detect non-adjacent control-flow relationships. This paper proposes a solution for generating BPMN models from natural language descriptions through a multi-layered pipeline that integrates transformer-based architectures, Large Language Models and ontology population. The proposed method starts with natural language descriptions and separates textual processing, control-flow relation extraction, and structural validation into dedicated components. Entity extraction is performed using a fine-tuned RoBERTa-based transformer model while a control-flow engine captures non-adjacent relationships through LLM-based inference. To improve generalization under limited available data, the approach uses a dynamic few-shot strategy with con- trolled template input construction, enabling improved generalization under limited data availability. Additionally, an ontology population mechanism is introduced to represent the generated process models as semantic knowledge structures. For evaluation purposes we have used from the literature and industry reference processes. Additionally, we have validated the proposed method on a real-world heart disease patients transitional care process, capturing practical constraints and multi-actor collaboration, and serving as an expert-defined benchmark scenario. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance in the relation extraction task, achieving an accuracy of 90.7%, as well as maintaining structural alignment between the generated and reference BPMN models across multiple evaluation scenarios scenarios.

title: Agentless CSPM Explained: How It Works, What It Sees, and Where It Falls Short
description:
Few topics in cloud security generate as much debate as the question of agents. Should you install software on every workload, or collect information without touching the workload at all? Vendors have strong opinions, usually aligned with what they sell. This article offers a more neutral look at agentless CSPM: how the approach works technically, what it does well, where it has limits, and how to decide whether it fits your environment.

What "agentless" actually means

In this context, agentless means the security platform gathers data without installing its own software on your servers, containers, or virtual machines. Instead, it relies on access that the cloud provider already offers.

There are generally three data sources.

Control plane APIs. Every major cloud exposes APIs describing how resources are configured: networks, identity policies, storage settings, database options, and so on. A posture platform given read-only credentials can query these continuously and build a detailed picture of the environment.

Snapshot analysis. Some platforms go further by reading copies of disk volumes. The platform creates or accesses a snapshot of a virtual machine's storage and analyzes it outside the running system. This can reveal installed software, operating system versions, vulnerabilities, and sometimes secrets or sensitive data, without running anything on the workload.

Cloud logs and events. Audit logs, flow logs, and event streams provide information about changes and activity, which helps detect drift and unusual behavior.

Together, these sources allow broad visibility with relatively little deployment work.

Why teams like the approach

Fast time to value

Because there is nothing to install on workloads, onboarding can be quick. Connecting an account through a read-only role may take minutes, and an initial picture of risk can appear within hours. For organizations with hundreds of accounts, that speed is a major advantage.

Broad coverage by default

Agent deployments depend on every workload being enrolled. Workloads that are missed, short-lived, or managed by someone else go uncovered. API-based collection sees everything in the account automatically, including new resources as they appear.

Low operational burden

No agent means no agent updates, compatibility testing, performance tuning, or conflicts with other software. For teams that already struggle to maintain endpoint tooling, this matters.

Lower friction with engineering

Developers are often wary of additional software on production systems. Avoiding it removes a common source of resistance and reduces the risk of performance impact.

Works with services that cannot host agents

Many modern services, such as managed databases, serverless functions, and storage services, cannot run third-party agents at all. API-based assessment is the only practical way to evaluate their configuration.

What it does particularly well

  • Identifying misconfigurations across identity, networking, storage, and data services.
  • Building an accurate, near-real-time inventory.
  • Mapping relationships between resources, such as which instance can reach which database.
  • Flagging exposure, such as public endpoints and overly permissive roles.
  • Finding known vulnerabilities and installed packages through snapshot analysis.
  • Supporting compliance reporting against recognized benchmarks.
  • Highlighting attack paths, where several moderate weaknesses combine into a serious route to valuable assets. Understanding attack path analysis is increasingly central to how teams prioritize limited remediation capacity.

Where it has limits

An honest assessment should include the trade-offs.

Limited runtime visibility. Without something running on the workload, it is hard to see live behavior: which processes are executing, which network connections are active at this moment, or whether a file is being modified. Snapshots capture a point in time, not continuous activity.

Delay. Snapshot scans often run on a schedule, such as every day. A vulnerability introduced this morning may not appear until the next cycle.

Reduced ability to respond. Agents can block or kill a malicious process. A system that only observes through APIs cannot easily do that inside a workload, although it may be able to change cloud-level settings, such as isolating an instance through network controls.

Dependence on permissions. The platform can only see what its credentials allow. Overly restrictive roles produce blind spots, while overly generous ones create risk of their own.

Provider constraints. API rate limits, snapshot costs, and regional behavior can affect performance and expense, especially at large scale.

Encrypted data. Disks encrypted with customer-managed keys require additional permissions for snapshot analysis, and some organizations are uncomfortable granting them.

Agent-based approaches: when they add value

Agents are not obsolete. They shine where continuous, in-workload insight is needed.

  • Detecting active threats such as malware execution or suspicious process behavior.
  • Monitoring file integrity and runtime drift in sensitive systems.
  • Providing real-time protection for containers and hosts.
  • Supporting environments with limited cloud API visibility, such as some hybrid or on-premises estates.

Many organizations use agentless methods for broad posture coverage and add agents only to the workloads where runtime protection justifies the effort, such as internet-facing servers or systems holding regulated data.

Questions to ask when evaluating agentless platforms

  1. What permissions do you require, and can they be limited further?
  2. How often are snapshots taken, and can the frequency be adjusted?
  3. Where is snapshot analysis performed: in my account or in yours?
  4. What is stored after analysis, and for how long?
  5. How are encrypted volumes handled?
  6. What is the impact on cloud costs, such as snapshot storage and API calls?
  7. How do you handle very large environments and rate limits?
  8. Can the platform integrate with runtime tools if I need both?

Security and privacy considerations

Because agentless platforms hold powerful read access and sometimes copies of disk data, their own security matters. Check how credentials are protected, whether access is scoped to least privilege, how data is isolated between customers, and what certifications the vendor holds. Where snapshot analysis runs inside your own account rather than the vendor's, sensitive data may never leave your control, which can simplify compliance for regulated industries.

A pragmatic way to decide

Consider three questions.

Is speed of coverage your priority? If you need broad visibility quickly across many accounts, agentless is hard to beat.

Do you need runtime protection? If you are defending against active threats on workloads, plan for agents on the systems that warrant them.

What does your workload mix look like? Environments heavy on managed and serverless services lean toward agentless by necessity, while those dominated by long-lived virtual machines may benefit from a hybrid.

Closing thoughts

The agent versus agentless debate is often framed as a contest, but it is better understood as a question of fit. API and snapshot-based collection offers speed, breadth, and low overhead, making it an excellent foundation for posture work. Runtime agents add depth where active defense is required. Understanding what each can and cannot see allows you to combine them sensibly rather than overpaying for overlap or leaving blind spots you did not realize existed.

title: Cross-Linguistic Acoustic Biomarkers of Cognitive Impairment Across Interactive and Single-Speaker Speech Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.17710v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multilingual dementia detection is essential for scalable and equitable screening. In recent years, automated speech analysis has emerged as a promising approach for supporting dementia detection by enabling non-invasive and scalable assessment of cognitive function. However, existing studies that use automated speech analysis often rely on one type of task, such as picture description, and use black-box models. These studies often neglect the role of task and language. To address these gaps, we performed a cross-linguistic and cross-task acoustic analysis that integrates a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks across four languages (Spanish, Mandarin, English, Japanese). We applied statistical, linguist-/clinician-guided, and machine learning model-based feature selection to derive compact acoustic feature sets while maintaining classification performance. This enabled systematic comparison of cognitive impairment-relevant features across datasets and tasks. Our results revealed that acoustic features did not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages. Temporal features remained robust across all datasets, consistently capturing timing disruption regardless of language or task. In contrast, speech rate showed strong task dependence -- emerging as informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content and pacing, but becoming less reliable when speech content was highly individualized. Pitch-related features further exhibited language-specific patterns, favoring chroma-related features in tonal languages (e.g., Mandarin) and F0-related features in non-tonal languages. These findings caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous speech data and underscore the need for interpretable, context-aware approaches to multilingual dementia detection using automated speech analysis.

title: CharaBuddy:Running a Desktop Pet Chat on your Machine
description:
I wanted to use a desktop pet for casual roleplay without sending every message to a cloud provider. Some of the conversations I want to keep are personal, and a few notes I paste into chat would be much less comfortable uploading. CharaBuddy's Local Privacy Mode is built for that case.

Visit the CharaBuddy website

What I Expected to Happen

The setup is close to what I expected. Ollama runs on my computer, CharaBuddy connects to it, and the model replies through the desktop pet.

In local mode, prompts, conversation history, and generated results are saved locally. The model request goes to the local service instead of a third-party API.

The pet also keeps working when I disconnect the network, provided Ollama is still running. I tested this by turning off Wi-Fi during a conversation.

The Main Trade-Off Is Hardware

There is no subscription and no API credit to buy. The trade-off is that my computer does the inference, and model size matters more than it does with a hosted service.

A small model runs on my laptop, but a larger one needs a dedicated GPU and more memory. I would start with a small model and confirm the whole path before pulling a much larger one.

The setup itself is short:

  1. Install Ollama and pull a model.
  2. Choose Local model in CharaBuddy and test http://localhost:11434.
  3. Enable offline mode.

It Is Not an Automatic Privacy Win

The local model is useful, but I would not treat local mode as proof that the entire setup is private. Ollama is only one part of it. A connected MCP service may still read local files, and other software on the machine can have its own access.

What local mode does give me is control over the inference path. I know where the model request is going, and I can see that the conversation data is written locally.

Does It Work Well Enough?

For my use, yes. The responses are only as good as the local model I choose, but having the pet on the desktop and the model under my control is a better fit than a cloud chat window for casual private conversations.

CharaBuddy can also connect to local servers with an OpenAI-compatible interface, such as LM Studio, so I am not tied to one local runtime.

title: Token2Tile: Token-Wise Sparse Attention with Tile Execution through a Low-Rank Space for Video DiTs
description:
arXiv:2611.17930v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attention is essential for modeling spatio-temporal dependencies in video diffusion transformers, but its quadratic cost makes it a major inference bottleneck. Its high sparsity offers an opportunity to accelerate generation by focusing computation on important interactions. However, accuracy and execution favor different granularities: each query attends to its own key tokens, whereas GPU kernels work on tiles. We present Token2Tile, a training-free sparse attention operator that combines per-query scoring and a per-query residual with tile execution. An online low-rank space, computed directly from queries and keys to preserve attention logits, makes clustering, scoring, and residual approximation efficient. Token2Tile unites query-specific selections to allocate exact work across query clusters, then packs the selected keys into GPU tiles. On MiniMax-H3 and Wan2.1-14B, Token2Tile delivers 1.48-1.54x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3 with VBench scores within 0.5 points of dense. At comparable speeds on H3, it improves PSNR over SOL and SubBlock by 5.5-6.8 dB; on Wan, it exceeds SOL by 4.6-4.8 dB while running faster.

title: Robustness Evaluation of GPU Cloud Pricing Benchmarks under Incomplete Observations: A Controlled Missingness Study
description:
arXiv:2611.17796v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can fail when marketplace quotes are missing. This article stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four benchmark-level recovery methods. Across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations in 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days, whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 while preserving zero conditional error on published dates; composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage but produces 7.74 log points of error. A separate past-only stratum-level ablation reduces error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, using a richer information set. An observable-signal withholding rule improves the primary error-coverage criterion in 0 of 10 cases. Results concern observed asking-price measurements, not transaction prices or identified real-world missingness mechanisms.

title: Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions
description:
arXiv:2611.17603v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, $K$ state-action pairs and effective horizon $H$. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability $C\geq 4$, every estimator needs $\Omega(KCH^3/(\epsilon\max\{\epsilon,\beta\}))$ samples on some instances when $\epsilon$ is small, where $\beta$ is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when $\beta\geq 1.4H$. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as $H/\beta$; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in $1/\epsilon$, with no coverage assumption. For $\beta\geq H$ the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in $1/\epsilon$. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.

title: Contagious Fingerprints: When LLMs Inherit Another Model's Identity
description:
arXiv:2611.18104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The fingerprint by which a classifier recognizes the LLM behind a text is usually treated as a fixed property of the model. We show that it is contagious: a model that continues a conversation begun by another model inherits that model's fingerprint. This undermines audits of API relays, which can serve the first turns of a conversation with the model a customer pays for and silently hand the rest to a cheaper one. After such a handoff, detection of the substitute by a text classifier drops from 0.97 to 0.72 (DeepSeek replacing Claude Sonnet) and from 0.87 to 0.54 for a same-vendor downgrade (Haiku), and retraining on handoff data repairs only substitutes seen in training. Preregistered experiments trace the contagion to imitation of the history's style. History also moves a model away from its own fingerprint: active probes are not camouflaged, but when calibrated on fresh conversations they flag \emph{honest} models on long contexts at rates up to 1.00, and a standard MMD equality test rejects all nine models we test. Both failures come from comparing a history-dependent reply with a history-free reference. We propose \textsc{Lineup}, which samples references from the claimed model \emph{on the same history} and tests the audited reply by its rank among them. \textsc{Lineup} controls false positives by exchangeability and needs no fitted threshold or log-probabilities. With contemporaneous references on two closed models, its false-positive rate is 0.056 (preregistered bound 0.10), and it detects 0.81 of substitute sessions across six pairs after four audited turns.

title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.17780v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql

title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
description:
arXiv:2611.17899v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow

title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs
description:
arXiv:2611.17857v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.

title: From Local Prediction Error to Final Outputs: A Theory of Expert Sharing in Multi-Step Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.17879v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.

title: VACO: Vertex-Aligned Decoding for Dense Hand Contact Estimation from a Single Image
description:
arXiv:2611.17755v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dense hand contact estimation from a single RGB image is a foundational primitive for dexterous manipulation and 3D interaction analysis. Direct predictors typically decode the entire per-vertex contact map from one shared query, leaving individual vertices ungrounded in the image and smearing contact across adjacent, non-touching surfaces. We present VACO, a vertex-aligned decoder in which each MANO vertex samples local image features at its projected location. A hand-reconstruction backbone, jointly trained for reconstruction and contact, predicts these locations at inference without an auxiliary reconstructor. Training uses noise-perturbed ground-truth projections and end-to-end feature adaptation to improve robustness and contact-sensitive features. A single VACO checkpoint sets a new state of the art on five benchmarks spanning hand-object, hand-human, hand-scene, and bimanual interactions. It improves F1 by +20.7 pp over the strongest prior direct predictor on Hi4D and generalizes to the held-out HOT3D and HOCap, with gains of +5.5 and +2.7 pp. The resulting contact predictions also improve downstream HOI reconstruction.

title: Differentially Private Federated Class-Incremental Learning for EEG Mental State Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.17944v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated learning (FL) under differential privacy (DP) is typically evaluated on large client cohorts, where subsampling and cross-client averaging amplify privacy and smooth injected noise. Personal biosignal applications such as wearable EEG instead involve small federations of a handful of subjects, a regime whose interaction with formal client-level DP is largely uncharacterized. We study differentially private federated class-incremental learning in this small-cohort regime, combining a public EEG dataset with a custom four-channel MUSE 2 recording set into a K=5-client federation, and give a masked per-class training protocol that avoids degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision under class-incremental streaming. We propose FedEEG, combining Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation with a lagged adaptive FedProx term, and show it reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to FedAvg, FedProx, and a federated Learning-without-Forgetting baseline; on-device balanced-batch replay reduces mean forgetting by a further 56.7%. A class-scoping diagnosis yields $50.5\%\pm3.6\%$ accuracy with 6 seeds and 2.02 times chance. We also introduce head-scoped client-level DP, which protects the classification head and alone reduces the achievable $\varepsilon$ by 200 times at a matched round budget; combined with fewer communication rounds it reaches $\varepsilon\!\approx\!10.4$ with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.

title: When the customer changes, forget the contact - a stale id in a Uniface master-detail form
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 got a form for contact persons in stage 30. The upper part selects a customer, the lower part edits one contact person of that customer. The service behind it has simple operations: load the contacts of a customer, save one contact, delete one contact by id and version.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

The form state

The form keeps three component variables:

  • $cCust$: the customer that is shown,
  • $cContact$: the contact person that is loaded (0 = none, a new one is created on save),
  • $cVersion$: the version of that contact for the optimistic locking check.

The delete operation of the service only gets the contact id and the version:

public operation DELETE_CONTACT
params
    numeric pContactId : IN
    numeric pVersion : IN
    string pError : OUT
endparams
...

So the service cannot know which customer the form shows. Keeping the contact id in line with the customer is the job of the form.

The click test that found it

  1. Load customer 1, create the contact "Jordan Example", save. The form now has $cContact$ = 1.
  2. Load customer 2 in the same form. The list correctly says "No contact persons for this customer." The edit fields still showed Jordan's data.
  3. Type contact id 1 and press "Load contact": "Contact 1 does not belong to this customer." Correct - the load checks the list of the current customer.
  4. Press "Delete contact...". The question was: "Delete contact person 1 (Jordan Example)?" - for a contact of customer 1 while customer 2 was shown. The answer in the test was No.

The load check in step 3 was fine, but it did not touch the state. And the customer switch in step 2 did not reset it either.

Before

The tail of the entry that sets the customer:

    $cCust$ = pId
    C_ID.CT2_DMY = pId
    CUST_NAME.CT2_DMY = "%%(vLast), %%(vFirst) (#%%(pId))"
    activate "WORKSET_SVC".ADD_RECENT(pId, vError)
    if ($status < 0)
        rollback
    else
        commit
    endif
    call DO_LIST
    return 0
end

The not-found branch of the entry that loads a contact:

    if (vFound = 0)
        INFO.CT2_DMY = "Contact %%(K_ID.CT2_DMY) does not belong to this customer."
        return -1
    endif

After

The form already had an entry for the button "New contact" that resets the state and empties the fields:

entry DO_NEW
    $cContact$ = 0
    $cVersion$ = 0
    K_ID.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_NAME.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_TITLE.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_PHONE.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_EMAIL.CT2_DMY = ""
    K_MAIN.CT2_DMY = "0"
    INFO.CT2_DMY = "New contact person; Save contact creates it."
    return 0
end

It is now called when the customer changes:

    $cCust$ = pId
    C_ID.CT2_DMY = pId
    CUST_NAME.CT2_DMY = "%%(vLast), %%(vFirst) (#%%(pId))"
    activate "WORKSET_SVC".ADD_RECENT(pId, vError)
    if ($status < 0)
        rollback
    else
        commit
    endif
    call DO_NEW
    call DO_LIST
    return 0
end

DO_LIST runs afterwards and overwrites the info line, so the user sees the contact count of the new customer, not the text of DO_NEW.

A failed load resets as well and keeps only the typed id for the message:

    if (vFound = 0)
        vId = K_ID.CT2_DMY
        call DO_NEW
        K_ID.CT2_DMY = vId
        INFO.CT2_DMY = "Contact %%(vId) does not belong to this customer."
        return -1
    endif

With these two changes $cContact$ only gets a contact id in two places: after a successful load from the list of the current customer and after a save for the current customer. The delete entry itself did not need a change; it already refuses to work without a loaded contact:

entry DO_DELETE
variables
    string vError
endvariables
    if ($cContact$ <= 0)
        INFO.CT2_DMY = "Please load a contact person first."
        return -1
    endif

Retest

  • Customer 1, load contact 1, switch to customer 2: the fields are empty, "0 contact person(s)."
  • "Delete contact..." on customer 2: "Please load a contact person first." No question.
  • Contact id 1 on customer 2, "Load contact": "Contact 1 does not belong to this customer.", fields empty.
  • Back to customer 1, load contact 1, "Delete contact...", Yes: "Contact person deleted.", the list is empty.
  • The form compiled with 0 errors and the usual warning 1016 for the non-database entity.

Notes

  • A confirmation dialog that names the record helped here: the name in the question made the wrong state visible. It would not have helped a user who reads quickly.
  • The lesson for master-detail forms: every change of the master resets the detail state, and every failed detail load resets it as well.

title: Storybook for React: Build Components Without the App
description:
Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/storybook-react-component-workshop.html

Quick answer

Storybook React is a workshop that renders components on their own, outside your app, so you can see every state of a button, card, or badge without clicking through pages. You install it with npx storybook@latest init, write a story file next to each component, and open the workshop at localhost:6006. It pays off once a component has more than a couple of states, or someone else needs to see what it looks like.

You open your app to check a small change to an order badge, five clicks deep. You log in, find the order, and only then see the colour. Change one prop and you repeat the whole trip. Multiply that by five states and a ten-minute tweak turns into an afternoon of clicking. That is the problem Storybook solves. It takes the component out of the app and puts it on a bench, where you flip through its states. This post sets it up in a fresh Vite and React project, builds one real badge, and shows what breaks.

What I would check before using it

My first check is how many states the component has. A badge with five statuses earns its own workshop page, because testing each state in the full app means five different orders and five page loads. A heading with one fixed look does not, and a story for it is just overhead.

My second check is who else needs to see the component. Storybook doubles as a living catalogue, so a designer or teammate can open the badge, flip its status control, and confirm the colours without running the app. If you work alone, that audience does not exist yet, and the value drops.

My third check is the cost of keeping stories honest. A story is only useful while it matches the component, and a prop rename nobody updates in the story leaves a page that lies. I would want the type checker running over story files in CI, so a renamed prop fails the build instead of showing stale output. The demo below caught exactly that.

My fourth check is the test story. Storybook is not a replacement for unit tests. A story shows the badge; a test proves it renders the right label. The Vitest post shows how fast those tests run. Jest covers the same ground if that is what your project already uses.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt Storybook React when a component has several visual states, or when others need to review how it looks without running the app. Skip it for a one-off page or a prototype you will throw away. The recommendation flips the moment stories stop being maintained, because stale pages mislead faster than none.

One order badge, run end to end

The example is a badge from a small online shop in Karachi. An order has an id, a status, an item count, and an expected delivery date. Order PK-1042 has three items, status shipped, expected 18 Nov 2026. That is real data from the demo cart, not a textbook counter.

type OrderStatus = "placed" | "packed" | "shipped" | "delivered" | "cancelled";

const STATUS_LABELS: Record<OrderStatus, string> = {
  placed: "Order placed",
  packed: "Packed and ready",
  shipped: "On its way",
  delivered: "Delivered",
  cancelled: "Cancelled",
};

const STATUS_COLOURS: Record<OrderStatus, string> = {
  placed: "#2563eb",
  packed: "#d97706",
  shipped: "#7c3aed",
  delivered: "#15803d",
  cancelled: "#b91c1c",
};

export interface OrderStatusBadgeProps {
  orderId: string;
  status: OrderStatus;
  itemCount: number;
  expectedDate: string;
}

export function OrderStatusBadge({ orderId, status, itemCount, expectedDate }: OrderStatusBadgeProps) {
  const label = STATUS_LABELS[status];
  const colour = STATUS_COLOURS[status];
  const itemWord = itemCount === 1 ? "item" : "items";
  return (
    <div style={{ border: `2px solid ${colour}`, borderRadius: "10px", padding: "16px", maxWidth: "340px", fontFamily: "system-ui, sans-serif" }}>
      <span style={{ backgroundColor: colour, color: "#ffffff", borderRadius: "999px", padding: "4px 12px", fontSize: "14px", fontWeight: 600 }}>
        {label}
      </span>
      <p style={{ margin: "12px 0 4px", fontWeight: 700 }}>Order {orderId}</p>
      <p style={{ margin: 0, color: "#444444" }}>
        {itemCount} {itemWord} - expected {expectedDate}
      </p>
    </div>
  );
}

The story file sits next to the component and declares one story per state:

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from "@storybook/react-vite";
import { OrderStatusBadge } from "./OrderStatusBadge";

const meta = {
  title: "Shop/OrderStatusBadge",
  component: OrderStatusBadge,
  tags: ["autodocs"],
  argTypes: {
    status: {
      control: "select",
      options: ["placed", "packed", "shipped", "delivered", "cancelled"],
    },
  },
} satisfies Meta<typeof OrderStatusBadge>;

export default meta;
type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>;

export const Shipped: Story = {
  args: {
    orderId: "PK-1042",
    status: "shipped",
    itemCount: 3,
    expectedDate: "18 Nov 2026",
  },
};

export const Delivered: Story = {
  args: {
    orderId: "PK-1038",
    status: "delivered",
    itemCount: 1,
    expectedDate: "14 Nov 2026",
  },
};

export const Cancelled: Story = {
  args: {
    orderId: "PK-1045",
    status: "cancelled",
    itemCount: 2,
    expectedDate: "17 Nov 2026",
  },
};

The thing that went wrong was a small slip in the Shipped story: I typed state: "shipped" instead of status: "shipped". The type checker caught it at once:

src/components/OrderStatusBadge.stories.tsx(22,5): error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'state' does not exist in type 'Partial<{ orderId: string; status: OrderStatus; itemCount: number; expectedDate: string; }> & { orderId: string; status: OrderStatus; itemCount: number; expectedDate: string; }'.

The fix is one word: rename the arg to status. This is exactly why stories should be type-checked. Storybook's build uses esbuild and does not type-check, so without the tsc step this typo would have shipped silently and rendered with no status at all. After the fix, the type check and the Vitest render test both pass, and the build succeeds:

Rendered OrderStatusBadge for order PK-1042:
<div style="border:2px solid #7c3aed;border-radius:10px;padding:16px;max-width:340px;font-family:system-ui, sans-serif"><span style="background-color:#7c3aed;color:#ffffff;border-radius:999px;padding:4px 12px;font-size:14px;font-weight:600">On its way</span><p style="margin:12px 0 4px;font-weight:700">Order PK-1042</p><p style="margin:0;color:#444444">3 items - expected 18 Nov 2026</p></div>
---
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
--- storybook build ---
Vite built in 2.66s
Storybook build completed successfully

The built output lists four entries, the docs page plus the three stories, proving Storybook picked up the file, and the dev server answered HTTP 200 at localhost:6006. If you style the badge with utility classes, the same isolation trick works for a Tailwind CSS component, and the component's state handling follows the same rules as the React useEffect post. TypeScript is what made the typo a build error instead of a silent bug.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, naming a story arg that does not match a prop, like the state slip above. The symptom is a story rendering with a missing value, or a type error from the checker. The fix is to rename the arg to match the prop, and to run tsc over your story files, because the Storybook build alone will not catch it.

Second, putting stories in a folder Storybook does not scan. The symptom is an empty sidebar: the workshop starts fine, but your component never appears. The fix is to check the stories glob in .storybook/main.ts and confirm your file matches it.

Third, writing stories that depend on app state, like a logged-in user or a router. The symptom is a story that crashes with "useNavigate may be used only in the context of a Router" or renders a blank page. The fix is to keep components pure where you can, and wrap the story in a decorator that provides the router or context it needs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Storybook ship to production with my app? No. It is a development tool with its own build, and your app bundle never includes the stories. You can deploy the static build separately as a shared catalogue.

Do I need a separate story for every state? Not for every tiny variation, but one per state that changes how the component looks. A badge with five statuses deserves five stories, so you can see each one without staging five orders.

Can I use Storybook with plain JavaScript instead of TypeScript? Yes, the same story format works in .jsx files. You lose the type checking that caught the arg typo here, so check arg names by hand.

Does Storybook replace unit tests? No. Stories show the component; tests prove it behaves. This post does both, and the Vitest run above is the proof.

What to remember

  • One story per visual state, so every variant is one click away.
  • Run tsc over story files, because the Storybook build does not type-check.
  • Keep stories next to their components, so a prop rename is visible in the same folder.
  • Pair stories with a render test, because a story shows the component and a test proves it.
  • Share the static build as a catalogue when designers need to see components without running the app.

Where this leaves you

Storybook earns its place the moment a component has more states than you can comfortably reach inside the running app. The badge demo proved the two things that matter: the workshop builds and serves all three stories, and the type checker catches a mistyped arg before it goes silent. Seeing every state, plus a safety net for typos, is the whole point. Set it up with one command, write one story per state, and type-check in CI. If the stories stay current, the workshop saves a click-through every time a component changes. If they go stale, delete them, because a lying catalogue is worse than none.

Further reading

  • Storybook docs, getting started, https://storybook.js.org/docs/
  • Storybook docs, writing stories, https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-stories
  • Vitest Explained: Tests That Finish Before You Blink, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/vitest-explained-tests-that-finish.html
  • Jest Explained: Testing JavaScript Without the Setup Headache, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/jest-explained-testing-javascript.html
  • Tailwind CSS Explained: Styling Without Leaving Your HTML, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/tailwind-css-explained-styling-without.html
  • React useEffect Explained: When to Use It and Skip It, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/react-useeffect-explained-when-to-use.html
  • TypeScript Explained: Types That Catch Bugs Before They Run, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/typescript-explained-types-that-catch.html
  • Figma Explained: The Design Tool Developers Actually Receive, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/figma-explained-design-tool-developers.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: A Maintainer Asked Me a Design Question on My Armeria PR. Here Is How I Answered It.
description:
I recently opened a PR in Armeria, the Java microservice framework from LINE. A maintainer reviewed it and asked a design question I could not answer with a quick yes or no. This post is about how I worked through it.

The bug

Armeria has a check called validateHttp2Ciphers. HTTP/2 requires certain cipher suites, and the check makes sure your TLS configuration includes the required one.

The catch: it always asked for the TLS 1.2 cipher suite, even when the connection was configured for TLS 1.3 only. TLS 1.3 has its own, different cipher suites. So a perfectly valid TLS 1.3-only setup could be judged wrong. That is issue #7112.

My fix

The check now looks at which TLS protocols are actually enabled and picks the right required cipher suite:

  • TLS 1.3 only: require TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
  • TLS 1.2 (alone or with 1.3): behavior and error message unchanged

I read the protocols from the built SslContext, not from the TLS settings, because a customizer can change the protocols after they are set. I also added tests for TLS 1.3 only, TLS 1.2 only, both enabled, and the unsafe-cipher case. That is PR #7120.

The maintainer's question

My first version created a temporary SSLEngine just to read the enabled protocols. A maintainer asked: for connections where the TLS spec is decided dynamically, would that create an extra engine each time? He suggested wrapping the SslContext in a DelegatingSslContext and doing the check when an engine is created.

It was a fair question, and I did not want to answer from a guess. So I looked into it.

What I found

  1. How often it really runs. The validation runs once or twice per client factory or virtual host at startup. Contexts are cached, so it runs again only when a new TLS spec is created, such as certificate rotation with dynamic providers. It is per new context, not per connection.
  2. A problem with the wrapper. I checked the Netty classes with javap. DelegatingSslContext does not implement ReferenceCounted, but the code that releases contexts expects that. A wrapper would silently skip the release unless it forwarded those methods too.
  3. Failing fast still matters. Building a client factory or server is expected to fail early on a bad cipher setup, so a temporary engine would still be needed for that moment.

So instead of the wrapper, I pushed a smaller change: look up the protocols only when needed. If the cipher list already contains both required suites, no engine is created at all. Simplified, the idea is:

// If the list already has both required suites, we are done.
// No temporary SSLEngine is created on this path.
if (hasBothEssentialCiphers(ciphers)) {
    return;
}

// Only now do we look at the enabled protocols (this is where the
// temporary engine is created, and it is always released afterwards).
Set<String> protocols = enabledProtocols.get();
boolean tls13Only = protocols.contains("TLSv1.3") && !protocols.contains("TLSv1.2");

String required = tls13Only
        ? "TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256"
        : "TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256";

I explained all of this in a comment, and added that if the maintainer still prefers the wrapper, I would switch.

One more thing: scope

An automated reviewer also suggested changing how the cipher blacklist check works for TLS 1.3-only setups. The maintainer agreed it made sense but said it was optional and not part of this issue. I left it out of the PR on purpose, to keep the change focused on #7112.

What I took from it

  1. Answer design questions with evidence. Looking up how often the code really runs, and checking the class with javap, turned a debate into facts.
  2. Offer the other option. Saying "if you still prefer the wrapper, I will switch" keeps the decision with the maintainer.
  3. Keep the PR small. A good suggestion that belongs to a different issue can wait for its own PR.
  4. Explain the tradeoff, not just the result. The maintainer can now see why I chose what I chose.

As I write this, the PR is still open and under review, and I will share how it ends.

Proof of my work

Everything here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • line/armeria PR #7120 and issue #7112: the TLS 1.3 fix and the review thread
  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: extended RequireNonNullExpression rule (merged)
  • Adyen/adyen-java-api-library #1952: regex fix, shipped in SDK v42.0.0 (merged)
  • zalando/logbook #2301, #2326, #2327 and #2328: Logbook changes (merged)
  • Sionna Visualizer: my 6G + AI dashboard (live demo)
  • My GitHub

Connect with me: LinkedIn | X

If you are a maintainer, a recruiter or a team looking for someone who backs his design choices with evidence, my DMs are open. Tell me in the comments how you decide between a quick fix and a bigger refactor.

title: Designing an owner portal residents will actually use
description:
An effective HOA or condo owner portal should make common tasks easy while protecting private information. Residents need clear access to their documents, account details, request statuses, and relevant notices. Developers should prioritize role-based permissions, understandable navigation, mobile usability, accessibility, and reliable notifications before adding features that make the interface harder to use.

Model permissions before building screens

An owner portal serves several user types.

Residents may view their own records. Directors may require additional association information. Administrative users may maintain data or process requests.

These permissions should be defined on the server, not merely hidden in the interface.

A simplified model might look like this:

User {
  id
  role
  unit_ids[]
  active
}

Document {
  id
  category
  visibility
  unit_id?
}

Request {
  id
  unit_id
  category
  status
  created_at
  updated_at
}

The application must verify both the user's role and their relationship to the requested record.

A resident changing an identifier in a browser request must not gain access to another unit's private information.

Organize the document library around user needs

A large collection of files is difficult to use when everything appears in a single list.

Group documents by purpose.

Possible categories include governing documents, meeting records available to owners, community policies, insurance information approved for distribution, and forms.

Each record should have a clear title, document category, and relevant version or approval information.

Search and filtering should operate only on documents the user is authorized to access.

Make request statuses understandable

Residents should not need to interpret internal workflow codes.

Instead of displaying technical labels, show plain-language statuses such as:

  • Submitted.
  • Under review.
  • More information needed.
  • Approved or declined.
  • Completed.

These examples should be adjusted to the actual process.

A status page should distinguish the current decision from general administrative progress.

For example, a maintenance request marked completed should not imply that an unrelated architectural proposal received approval.

A useful history shows when a status changed and any information the resident is permitted to see.

Build notifications around useful events

Notifications should provide meaningful updates rather than repeat information already visible on the dashboard.

Possible triggers include a document becoming available, an authorized status change, or a scheduled community notice.

Users should be able to manage optional notification preferences where permitted.

Avoid including sensitive account information in email subjects or other channels where it could be exposed.

Notifications should guide users back into authenticated views when private details are involved.

Design for phones and accessibility

Residents may access their portal from a phone while away from home.

The interface should work with small screens, touch input, and limited typing.

Accessible design also matters.

Use readable text, descriptive labels, visible keyboard focus, appropriate contrast, and understandable error messages.

Do not rely on color alone to communicate request status.

Forms should explain what information is required and preserve entered data when validation fails.

Test tasks, not just screens

A successful test is not simply whether the dashboard loads.

Ask whether an authorized resident can locate a community rule, understand a request outcome, or recognize an important notification without assistance.

Test expired sessions, permission changes, missing documents, and incomplete forms.

The portal succeeds when residents can complete ordinary tasks confidently and the application consistently protects information they should not see.
