title: A small thing about HTML data attributes
description:
HTML data attributes are useful for passing small pieces of information to JavaScript.

For example:

<button id="save" data-enabled="false">
  Save
</button>

You can read the value using dataset:

const button = document.querySelector("#save");

console.log(button.dataset.enabled);
// "false"

The interesting part is that the value is a string, not a boolean.

So this doesn't work as you might expect:

if (button.dataset.enabled) {
  console.log("Button is enabled");
}

The message will still be logged.

That's because "false" is a non-empty string, and non-empty strings are truthy in JavaScript.

The same thing happens with numbers.

<div id="cart" data-count="0"></div>

const cart = document.querySelector("#cart");

console.log(cart.dataset.count === 0);
// false

console.log(cart.dataset.count === "0");
// true

If you need a number, convert it:

const count = Number(cart.dataset.count);

And for a boolean, you can compare the string directly:

const isEnabled = button.dataset.enabled === "true";

One other detail: even if you assign a boolean through JavaScript, it gets converted to a string.

button.dataset.enabled = false;

console.log(button.dataset.enabled);
// "false"

console.log(typeof button.dataset.enabled);
// "string"

It's not a big issue once you know about it, but it can be confusing when a condition seems to ignore a false value.

I usually just make the conversion explicit when reading from dataset.

title: Why we don't offer a free database, and what we built instead
description:
TL;DR: A free container can be free because it sleeps when nobody is looking. A database cannot sleep, so every free database you will find comes with a clock, a pause button or a shared instance. That is why there is no free database here, and why we built a $1, 12-hour trial of the real managed add-on instead. The same logic applies to Redis and RabbitMQ.

The most common question we get after "is the free tier really free?" is "why is there no free database?". Fair question.

We give away containers, and a container without a database is half an app. The answer is about what can sleep and what cannot, and it is worth explaining, because it also explains why every free database you will find comes with a clock or a pause button.

Why a container can be free

A free container on SnapDeploy sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic, and the free tier is capped at 100 container-hours a month. Most free containers are awake for a few hours a month: they serve a demo, a portfolio, a side project someone opens now and then.

The rest of the time they use nothing. Sleeping is the whole trick.

It is what lets a free tier exist without an expiry date or a card, because a container nobody is looking at is not consuming anything.

Why a database cannot

A database cannot sleep the way a web container can. If Postgres is stopped when a request arrives, the app that depends on it fails: connection refused, then a pool of dead connections, then a timeout page shown to the visitor.

So a database has to run around the clock, and it needs persistent storage that survives restarts, backups that run whether or not you visited this week, and someone to answer when the connection string stops working. None of that stops when the project is abandoned after a weekend.

A free database is a promise to keep something running forever for every account that ever clicked "create", and we would rather not make a promise we would have to quietly break later.

How the others make "free database" work

Every free database we know of solves the same problem with one of three tricks. None of them is dishonest; they are just worth knowing before you build on one.

Trick Who What it means for you
Expiry Render: free Postgres expires 30 days after creation, with a 14-day grace period Fine for a demo; a calendar reminder for anything else.
Pause when idle Supabase: projects pause after 7 days without activity; Neon: compute suspends when idle and resumes on the next query, within 100 compute-hours a month The first request after a pause is slow or fails; your app needs retry logic.
Shared, capped instance MongoDB Atlas M0: 512 MB on a shared cluster, no expiry Genuinely free for small data; throttled throughput and no dedicated resources.

Neon and Atlas are good choices for a hobby app and we say so in our own guides. Their economics work because they built engines that can pause or share at a scale we do not operate at. We are a container host; we run stock PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and MongoDB on dedicated instances next to your containers, and a dedicated instance does not pause.

What we did instead

  • A $1 trial that is the real thing. The DB Sprint Pack is 12 hours of a full Mini-tier instance (PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8, MariaDB 11, MongoDB 7, Redis 7 or RabbitMQ 3) for $1, with persistent storage, daily backups and 50 connections. Not a throttled sandbox: the same instance you would pay for monthly, for long enough to find out whether it fits. Data is kept for 24 hours after the trial ends, and converting to a monthly plan re-attaches the same volume, so nothing is migrated.
  • Plain monthly prices. Mini is $29/month for the SQL engines and MongoDB, $12 for Redis, $14 for RabbitMQ, with the admin tools (pgweb, phpMyAdmin, mongo-express) and daily backups included. The prices are on one page, they do not change with usage, and they are the same for everyone.
  • No lock-in on the free side. A free container talks to Neon, Supabase, Atlas or any other database over a normal connection string. We would rather you use a good free external database than a bad free internal one.

What the $1 trial is for, in practice

  • A demo or a hackathon. Twelve hours covers a pitch, a workshop or a weekend build day, with a real Postgres instead of a SQLite file that vanishes on the next deploy.
  • Testing a migration. Restore a dump into a Mini for a dollar, run the app against it, and know whether the schema and the connection limits fit before you commit to a month.
  • Trying an engine you have not used. The same dollar buys MongoDB, MariaDB, Redis or RabbitMQ at the same size, with the browser admin tool attached, so the comparison is between engines, not between pricing pages.

What it is not for is production. The 12 hours end, the instance stops, and after the 24-hour grace period the volume is gone unless you converted. That limit is the point: it is what lets the trial be real rather than throttled.

The same logic for Redis and RabbitMQ

People sometimes ask why the cache is not free either, since Redis is "just memory". It is a process that has to be up at 3 a.m. when your container wakes and asks for a session, and a cache that sleeps is a cache that is empty when you need it.

Redis Mini is $12/month and RabbitMQ Mini $14/month for the same reason the databases are $29: they run whether or not you do. For an app that is idle most of the time, a serverless provider such as Upstash, which charges per command and has a free plan, is the better fit, and we say so in our Redis guide.

Would we ever add one?

Maybe, in the pause-when-idle form, if we build the engine work that makes it safe: a layer that holds connections while an instance resumes, so applications see a slow query rather than an error. That is a real project, not a pricing switch. Until then, the honest answer to "why no free database" is that a database cannot sleep, and free things on this platform are free because they can.

Current prices for every add-on are on the add-on pricing page; the compute free tier (4 containers, 100 container-hours a month, no card) is on the free tier docs page. Render, Supabase, Neon and Atlas limits are as published on their pages in September 2026.

title: RecurIR: Learning When and How to Revise Restoration Policies via Recursive Self-Improvement
description:
arXiv:2611.18006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent-based image restoration has achieved promising performance by coordinating restoration tools to handle heterogeneous and coupled degradations. However, existing agents often improve their decisions through accumulated successful and failed executions, without explicitly identifying the conditions under which learned restoration strategies remain effective. Consequently, changes in degradation severity, spatial coverage, or interactions may invalidate previous decisions, while providing limited guidance on how these decisions should be revised. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RecurIR}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables restoration agents to learn when and how to revise their decision rules. Specifically, we introduce a policy-hypothesis discovery mechanism to identify testable, condition-dependent rules through matched tool executions. We then design a rule-falsification-driven task evolution mechanism to generate targeted degradation variations, examine the validity of learned rules, and identify their applicability boundaries. Based on the resulting evidence, we develop a change-conditioned policy revision mechanism that learns how variations in degradation conditions should modify tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions. We further incorporate independent verification to retain effective revisions and use the resulting feedback to guide subsequent hypothesis discovery and task evolution. Through this recursive process, RecurIR progressively refines its restoration policies as degradation conditions change. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

title: Adding a button to an existing Uniface form by XML - export, patch, import
description:
The customer app from the series Building a customer app in Uniface 10 got an administration area in its last stage. Nine new forms were generated, and one existing form needed a change: the "More functions" menu should get a button "Administration...". That button should be dimmed for users who are not administrators.

Tested with Rocket Uniface 10.4.03 Community Edition (10.4.03.021) on Windows, October 2026. The app uses SQLite through the SLE driver (SQLite 3.50.2).

New forms in this project are generated as XML and imported. For an existing form the same route works, but the starting point has to be the form as it is in the repository, not a generated copy.

Step 1: export the form

In the IDE, the main menu (≡) has an entry Export. The dialog has a field Object Name next to Component and a File Name at the bottom. With the component name and a target file, Export wrote the form with its entity and all field occurrences. The message line said: "Total number of occurrences exported: 19" - the form, its dummy entity and 17 fields.

This export is also the backup of the form before the change.

Step 2: patch the XML

Four things change in the export:

  1. the script: one label line, one check in exec, one new entry,
  2. the form picture: one more field token in the row of the last button,
  3. a new field occurrence for the button,
  4. nothing else - no other field, no entity property.

The script reads the export, applies the changes and writes the import file. Every replacement must match exactly once, otherwise the script stops:

def rep(a, b):
    global t
    assert t.count(a) == 1, a
    t = t.replace(a, b)
rep('\tBTN_DQ.MORE_DMY = "Data quality & exports..."\n', '\tBTN_DQ.MORE_DMY = "Data quality & exports..."\n\tBTN_ADMIN.MORE_DMY = "Administration..."\n')
rep(''' activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(vUser, vRole)
    INFO.MORE_DMY = "Logged in as %%(vUser) (%%(vRole))"
    edit
''', '''    activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(vUser, vRole)
    INFO.MORE_DMY = "Logged in as %%(vUser) (%%(vRole))"
    if (vRole != "ADMIN")
        $fieldsyntax(BTN_ADMIN.MORE_DMY) = "DIM"
    endif
    edit
''')
rep(''' activate "DQ_FRM".exec()
    return 0
end
''', '''    activate "DQ_FRM".exec()
    return 0
end

entry DO_ADMIN
    call SESSION_OK
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    activate "ADMIN_MNU".exec()
    return 0
end
''')
rep('        &uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_DQ&uSEP;WID=30&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;\n', '        &uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_DQ&uSEP;WID=30&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;  &uFRM;TYP=F&uSEP;NAM=BTN_ADMIN&uSEP;WID=30&uSEP;HEI=1&uFRM;\n')
occs = re.findall(r'<OCC>\n(.*?)</OCC>\n', t, re.S)
src = [o for o in occs if '<DAT name="ULABEL">BTN_DQ</DAT>' in o]
assert len(src) == 1
o = src[0]
n = o.replace('<DAT name="ULABEL">BTN_DQ</DAT>', '<DAT name="ULABEL">BTN_ADMIN</DAT>').replace('\tcall DO_DQ\n', '\tcall DO_ADMIN\n')
assert n.count('BTN_ADMIN') == 1 and 'DO_ADMIN' in n
rep('<OCC>\n' + o + '</OCC>\n', '<OCC>\n' + o + '</OCC>\n<OCC>\n' + n + '</OCC>\n')

The new field is a copy of the button next to it, with a new name and a new trigger. That keeps all widget properties (type, interface, description) the same as in the buttons that are already there. The script text in the XML is escaped, so the new entry uses < where the ProcScript has <.

Step 3: import, compile, compare

The import (≡ - Import XML...) reported "Successfully imported 20 records" - one more than the export. The form was open in an editor tab, so it had to be reloaded from the repository before compiling. The compiler reported 0 errors and the one warning that every form with a dummy entity gets (1016, entity not found in the application model).

After the import the repository was read again and compared with the intended result: the script of the form equals the script in the import file, and the form picture of the repository is contained in it unchanged. These are the two pieces of ProcScript in the repository after the import:

operation exec
variables
    string vUser, vRole
endvariables
    call SET_LABELS
    activate "USER_SVC".CURRENT_USER(vUser, vRole)
    INFO.MORE_DMY = "Logged in as %%(vUser) (%%(vRole))"
    if (vRole != "ADMIN")
        $fieldsyntax(BTN_ADMIN.MORE_DMY) = "DIM"
    endif
    edit
end

entry DO_ADMIN
    call SESSION_OK
    if ($status < 0)
        return -1
    endif
    activate "ADMIN_MNU".exec()
    return 0
end

The click test

  • As administrator, the button opened the administration menu.
  • As a user with role READ and as a user with role EDIT, the button was dimmed, and a click on it did nothing.
  • The administration menu checks the role again when it opens, so a call from somewhere else would not bypass the check.

Notes

  • Export first, patch the export, import - in that order. The export is the only reliable source for an existing form.
  • Copy an existing field occurrence instead of writing one from scratch.
  • Let the patch script fail when a search text is not found exactly once.
  • Compare the repository with the import file afterwards, not only the compiler output.

The same route added a status line to the main menu of the app; there the entity also had to grow by two rows, which is one more replacement in the form picture.

title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
description: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
description:
arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

title: Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout for Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting
description:
arXiv:2611.17752v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is prone to overfitting because only a limited number of images are available to constrain scene geometry. Dropout is one regularization strategy for alleviating this problem. We introduce the concept of a lineage family to describe a set of Gaussian primitives derived from the same founder through cloning or splitting operations. The founder Gaussians refer to all Gaussian primitives generated during initialization. Descendants within the same family often jointly contribute to the refinement of adjacent local regions. However, dropping individual Gaussians can be less effective due to the compensation effect from neighboring Gaussians for the dropped ones. To address this issue, we propose Stage-wise Lineage-aware Dropout(SLD), which applies lineage-family dropout during the structural regularization stage and switches to individual dropout during the later refinement stage. We further propose Lineage-Balanced Densification(LBD), which operates during densification by constructing an expanded candidate pool and reallocating the densification budget according to the mean gradient scores and existing descendant sizes of different families. Experiments on the LLFF, MipNeRF360, and Blender datasets show that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance in sparse-view reconstruction

title: Camera-to-Print Node.js Pipeline: How to Normalize Orientation and Validate Output
description:
The safest camera-to-print pipeline reads orientation metadata, chooses an explicit rotation that makes the pixels upright, converts the corrected image to the required print format, and validates the resulting dimensions before an order can proceed. In a Node.js application, I would put those operations behind one job boundary and persist the input checksum, chosen angle, target format, and output checksum. The decisive trade-off is quality versus bandwidth: inspect once and retain enough evidence to reverse a bad decision, but do not repeatedly move an original camera file across services just to discover that a converted asset has the wrong shape.

TL;DR: Treat metadata as an instruction, not proof that the pixels are already upright. Make the rotation explicit, validate after conversion, and make retries converge on the same output. A request that times out may still have completed, so recovery must never mean blindly applying another 90-degree rotation.

Infrai is a concrete fit at the remote inspection boundary because its one REST API and one key let an application switch providers without changing code. That contract covers 295 routes across 20 modules, requires no SDK, and has a self-describing public discovery surface; here, the useful result is less provider-specific recovery glue, not a claim that network processing is always preferable.

How should Node.js normalize camera image orientation metadata for print?

Conversion answers a format question; it does not, by itself, settle orientation or print geometry. A camera can store pixels in one direction and attach metadata describing how viewers should display them. The pipeline therefore has to read that metadata, map it to explicit degrees, rotate to upright when required, and only then convert. Reversing those stages makes diagnosis harder because the output can be a valid file and still be unsuitable for the intended print.

That distinction matters in a fintech media library that auto-tags receipt, identity-document, and dispute-evidence images for search. Search tags may be technically correct while a downstream case packet prints sideways. Worse, a retried job can rotate an already corrected derivative again if the worker uses the mutable output as its next input.

Success is not enough.

The record for each transformation should include the immutable source identifier or checksum, the orientation value observed, the explicit angle applied, the requested output format, and the final dimensions. Those fields are operational evidence: they let an operator distinguish a bad metadata interpretation from a wrong print preset and undo a rotation without guessing.

Derive the recovery contract before choosing a processor

Start with a stable job identifier derived by the application, not by the image vendor. The Node.js API can enqueue print_asset:{source_checksum}:{preset_version} and let the worker claim that identity exactly once at the storage boundary. If a response is lost, a retry looks up the same job and output rather than minting another transformation. Infrai's platform convention specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities, so the application must still retain its own durable job identity beyond that limit. Rate limiting belongs in the same state machine: HTTP 429 moves the job to delayed retry, honoring Retry-After where available, while permanent input errors stop the order.

The processing state is small: received, inspected, rotated, converted, validated, or rejected. Store the evidence at each transition. Do not infer validated from a 2xx conversion response, because the required check happens against the converted artifact, where a swapped width and height or an unexpected size can still be caught before fulfillment.

The request shape should come from discovery rather than an article that will go stale. Save a payload conforming to the current schema as metadata-request.json; this runnable client then performs the inspection call, uses Bearer authentication from the environment, honors Retry-After on 429, and surfaces the actual error body. It makes no guesses about undocumented fields.

import json
import os
import random
import sys
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request


def retry_delay(headers, attempt):
    value = headers.get("Retry-After")
    if value and value.isdigit():
        return float(value)
    return min(2 ** attempt, 30) + random.random()


def inspect_metadata(payload_path, attempts=5):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    with open(payload_path, "rb") as payload_file:
        payload = payload_file.read()
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/metadata",
        data=payload,
        method="POST",
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
    )
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=60) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai returned HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            time.sleep(retry_delay(error.headers, attempt))
    raise RuntimeError("metadata inspection exhausted its retry budget")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        raise SystemExit("usage: python inspect_metadata.py metadata-request.json")
    print(json.dumps(inspect_metadata(sys.argv[1]), indent=2))

The next runnable local reference worker uses Pillow as the concrete processor, normalizes the common EXIF orientation values into pixels, records the applied degrees, converts to a requested print format, reopens the output, and rejects dimensions that do not match the preset. The surrounding Node.js service only needs to submit and observe the stable job; keeping image mutation in one worker prevents a retry from crossing two partially completed implementations.

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image


ROTATION_BY_ORIENTATION = {1: 0, 3: 180, 6: 270, 8: 90}


def checksum(path: Path) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as stream:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: stream.read(1024 * 1024), b""):
            digest.update(chunk)
    return digest.hexdigest()


def build_print_asset(source: Path, output: Path, width: int, height: int) -> dict:
    source_hash = checksum(source)
    with Image.open(source) as image:
        orientation = int(image.getexif().get(274, 1))
        if orientation not in ROTATION_BY_ORIENTATION:
            raise ValueError(f"unsupported mirrored EXIF orientation: {orientation}")
        degrees = ROTATION_BY_ORIENTATION[orientation]
        upright = image.rotate(degrees, expand=True) if degrees else image.copy()
        if upright.mode not in ("RGB", "CMYK"):
            upright = upright.convert("RGB")
        upright.save(output, format="TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw")

    with Image.open(output) as converted:
        actual = converted.size
    if actual != (width, height):
        output.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise ValueError(f"print dimensions {actual} do not match {(width, height)}")

    return {
        "job_id": f"print_asset:{source_hash}:v1",
        "source_sha256": source_hash,
        "orientation_seen": orientation,
        "rotation_degrees": degrees,
        "output_format": "TIFF",
        "output_dimensions": [width, height],
        "output_sha256": checksum(output),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("source", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("output", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--width", type=int, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--height", type=int, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print(json.dumps(build_print_asset(args.source, args.output, args.width, args.height)))

Run it against a preset whose dimensions have already been approved for the print product:

# Execute as: python print_worker.py camera.jpg print.tiff --width 2400 --height 3000

This deliberately rejects mirrored EXIF orientations rather than pretending that rotation alone handles them. The supplied media operations take explicit rotation degrees; a mirror requires a transform that is outside this narrow contract. A production queue should classify that rejection for review, not repeatedly retry it.

Choose the boundary by failure mode, not feature count

There are at least four credible processors, and their useful differences appear at the recovery boundary rather than in a checklist of image effects.

Option Operational fit Quality/bandwidth consequence Better choice when
Sharp In-process processing close to a Node.js API Avoids an extra network transfer; the application owns native-library deployment and retry state Images can be processed near their source and the team wants direct control
ImageMagick Mature command-line or worker boundary Keeps transformation local but requires careful command construction and resource isolation The print workflow needs a broad specialist toolchain
Cloudinary Managed image transformation service Moves originals or derivatives over the network; centralizes managed transformations Delivery workflows and managed media operations matter more than a vendor-neutral contract
ImageKit Managed image optimization and delivery service Trades local processing control for a hosted media path Existing delivery and optimization requirements already align with its service
Infrai One REST boundary that can keep application code stable while the vendor behind a capability changes Reduces capability-specific integration glue, though remote processing still spends bandwidth A team values one consistent contract across media operations and wants transformation evidence at its own job boundary

Sharp and ImageMagick are not lesser fallbacks. They are often the stronger answer when originals already sit beside the worker, bandwidth is constrained, or a print specialist needs exact control over the local processing build. Cloudinary and ImageKit are reasonable managed choices when their media delivery models match the system. Infrai fits a different constraint: its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples, and its platform convention specifies idempotency for supported capabilities. The application can keep its contract while the implementation behind that capability moves.

Teams with a Node.js order service should try Infrai for the metadata/rotation/conversion boundary when they expect providers to change and want to remove per-vendor integration glue; the stable REST contract matters because retry and audit state can remain in the application. A second, concrete benefit is that one key spans a broad capability surface, so the worker does not need another vendor-specific SDK and credential lifecycle for each adjacent media operation.

There is still a limit. If the source and printer pipeline share a local network, or the print vendor mandates a tightly controlled color-management toolchain, a local Sharp or ImageMagick worker is the better design. A consistent remote API does not erase upload time, and no conversion response replaces validation against the print preset.

Make bandwidth loss visible

Quality and bandwidth should become fields in the decision, not opposing slogans. Retain the immutable original where policy permits, because reprocessing from a derivative compounds loss and makes a mistaken rotation harder to reverse. Send the original to a remote processor once per stable job identity, then retain or address the corrected result by checksum. Do not download the same result merely to learn whether the job succeeded if stored metadata can answer that question.

For auto-tagging, derive the search asset from the upright pixels. A small search derivative can reduce later transfer, while the print artifact remains tied to its validated dimensions. The tags and the print file should point back to the same source checksum and transformation record; otherwise a search result can quietly refer to a different orientation than the file included in the customer packet.

Observability needs only a few high-value facts: job identity, attempt number, processor, stage, response class, applied angle, and input/output checksums. Do not log credentials or the image itself. Alert on exhausted retries, repeated 429 responses, and validation rejection rates, but avoid interpreting one delayed attempt as a failed order.

Roll out without gambling on existing orders

Begin in shadow mode: inspect metadata and calculate the intended angle without changing the fulfillment asset. Compare the recorded decision with the current approved output, then enable mutation for one print preset. The promotion gate is mechanical: a job reaches fulfillment only after conversion and dimension validation, and a retry with the same source checksum and preset version returns the same recorded outcome.

Next, test the cases that damage recovery logic: lost responses, duplicate queue delivery, a 429 with a retry delay, orientation values for 0, 90, 180, and 270-degree outcomes, mirrored metadata, corrupt input, and a converted file with reversed dimensions. Roll back by disabling the new preset version; undo an individual bad result by replaying the immutable source with a corrected explicit angle. That is why the transformation record is part of the product, not incidental logging.

Finally, move one adjacent operation at a time. Keep the application-owned job identity and evidence schema unchanged when switching among local processing, a specialist provider, or a consistent API boundary. The processor is replaceable. The recovery contract is not.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation
  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Sharp documentation
  • ImageMagick documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • ImageKit documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current discovery schema before wiring the worker.

title: Poetry 'resurrection' from LLMs
description:
arXiv:2611.17464v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In an era where linguistic creativity is challenged by algorithmic authorship, we pose a provocative question: can artificial intelligence (AI) write an infinite poem? We set up two experiments to investigate the quantitative and qualitative output produced by AI utilizing couplets that evidence a poetic relationship between end words, the only variation in a strict anaphoric, litany structure. Our results show that while AI can generate interesting pairings, it still falls short of human-level creativity and understanding of poetic relationships. We offer commentary and a brief survey of the field of computational poetry experiments, tracing back authorial intention and distinctions of 'natural' and 'artificial' poetry, as well as justifying why couplet form is suited to testing AI's poetic output. Experiment 1 relies on manual prompting and co-creation to extend the original poem, which is developed into an animated webpage installation and interactive artwork. Experiment 2 reliably achieves automated output reaching the 1000 benchmark via an alternative method of using an LLM in combination with semantic similarity, of which Method 2 demonstrates a higher capacity for semantic and quantitative poetic output. These experiments highlight the limitations of current LLMs' generation capacity at the word level but also suggest that poetry will also respond and revive by incorporating AI workflows.

title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions
description:
arXiv:2611.17632v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.

title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
description:
arXiv:2611.17766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.

title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
description:
arXiv:2611.17616v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

title: Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding
description:
arXiv:2611.17797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.

title: Where to Predict in Retinal OCT? Anatomy-Guided Target Selection for I-JEPA
description:
arXiv:2611.17586v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised learning aims to learn meaningful representations from unlabeled data, potentially allowing models to capture subtle anatomical variations across patients and reduce the amount of labeled data needed. Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) learns by predicting target-region representations from visible context rather than reconstructing pixels. However, its uniform target placement does not account for the anatomical structure of retinal OCT, where retinal tissue occupies only part of each B-scan. We investigate anatomy-guided target selection using image intensity and predicted retinal segmentation while retaining the I-JEPA architecture and latent prediction objective. We compare anatomy-guided rectangular targets, anatomy-shaped targets and coverage-constrained placement with uniform masking, and evaluate the learned representations using linear probing for glaucoma classification on FairVision. We found that rectangular targets guided by image intensity achieved the highest linear-probe AUC in our comparisons. We show that anatomically meaningful target selection is promising for retinal OCT representation learning, while greater anatomical specificity did not consistently improve performance.

title: Java - this & final keywords
description:
this Keyword in Java

The this keyword in Java is a reference variable that refers to the current object of a class. It is commonly used to distinguish instance variables from local variables when they have the same name.

  • Refers to the current class object.
  • Used to access current class instance variables and methods.
  • Used to invoke another constructor of the same class using this().

Example

`class Student {
String name;
int age;

Student(String name, int age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
}

void display() {
    System.out.println(this.name);
    System.out.println(this.age);
}

}`

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
Student s1 = new Student("Gowtham", 20);
s1.display();
}
}

Output:

Gowtham
20

Explanation

  • this.name refers to the instance variable.
  • name refers to the constructor parameter.
  • this.age refers to the instance variable.
  • age refers to the constructor parameter.
  • The this keyword helps us avoid confusion when variable names are the same.

Common Uses of this Keyword

  1. Referring to current class instance variables.
  2. Calling another constructor using this().
  3. Calling a method of the current object.
  4. Passing the current object as an argument.

final Keyword in Java

In Java, the final keyword is used to restrict changes and make code more secure and predictable. It can be applied to variables, methods, and classes to prevent modification, overriding, or inheritance. This helps in creating constant values, stable methods, and immutable classes.

1. Final Variable

A final variable cannot be reassigned after it has been initialized.

Example:

`public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
final int age = 20;

    System.out.println(age);
}

}`

Output:

20

Here, age is a final variable, so we cannot assign another value to it.

2. Final Method

A final method cannot be overridden by a subclass.

Example:

`class Parent {
final void display() {
System.out.println("This is a final method");
}
}

class Child extends Parent {
// Cannot override display()
}`

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
Child obj = new Child();
obj.display();
}
}

Output:

This is a final method

Here, the display() method is declared as final, so the child class cannot override it.

3. Final Class

A final class cannot be extended by another class.

Example:

final class Student {
void display() {
System.out.println("Hello Java!");
}
}

public class Main {
public static void main(String[] args) {
Student s1 = new Student();
s1.display();
}
}

Output:

Hello Java!

Here, Student is a final class, so another class cannot inherit from it.

title: Window Functions vs GROUP BY, Explained the Super Simple Way
description:
What is a window function?

A window function is any function used with OVER (...).

SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY name)
  • The whole SUM(amount) OVER (...) is the window function
  • PARTITION BY goes inside it and says which groups to calculate over

PARTITION BY is optional. If you leave it out, the whole table is treated as one group.

Note: "Table partitioning" (CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION BY), which physically splits a table, uses the same keyword but is unrelated to window functions.

GROUP BY vs PARTITION BY

The short answer: this is the only difference.

  • GROUP BY: splits rows into groups and collapses each group into one row
  • PARTITION BY: splits rows into groups but keeps every row (each row gets the calculated value)

Sample table

sales table

name amount
Alice 100
Alice 200
Bob 500

With GROUP BY 

SELECT name, SUM(amount)
FROM sales
GROUP BY name;
name sum
Alice 300
Bob 500

Each name is collapsed into one row. The original "100" and "200" rows are gone.

With PARTITION BY 

SELECT name, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY name) AS total
FROM sales;
name amount total
Alice 100 300
Alice 200 300
Bob 500 500

You still have 3 rows, and each row gets the total for its name.

Why is this useful?

Because the rows are kept, you can use the original value and the total in the same row.
For example, you can get "what share of this person's sales is this one sale" in a single query.

SELECT name, amount, amount / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY name) AS ratio
FROM sales;
name amount ratio
Alice 100 0.33
Alice 200 0.67
Bob 500 1.00

ROW_NUMBER: numbering rows within each group

ROW_NUMBER() is a window function that numbers rows 1, 2, 3… within each group.
Adding ORDER BY inside OVER (...) sets the order within each group.

SELECT name, amount,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY name ORDER BY amount DESC) AS row_num
FROM sales;
name amount row_num
Alice 200 1
Alice 100 2
Bob 500 1

Each name's rows are numbered from the largest amount down.

Common pattern: get the top row of each group

Filter on row_num = 1 to get each person's highest sale.

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT name, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY name ORDER BY amount DESC) AS row_num
  FROM sales
) t
WHERE row_num = 1;
name amount row_num
Alice 200 1
Bob 500 1

row_num is created in the SELECT, so you can't use it in the WHERE of the same query. That's why it's wrapped in a subquery first.

ROW_NUMBER vs RANK

They differ in how they number ties.

amount ROW_NUMBER RANK
500 1 1
500 2 1
300 3 3
  • ROW_NUMBER: always gives a different number, even for ties (1, 2, 3)
  • RANK: gives ties the same number, then skips ahead (1, 1, 3)

title: How to Build Secure Realtime Publish Receipts for Customer Support Conversations
description:
Short answer: treat a publish acknowledgement as a signed, replay-safe receipt, and keep token authority, subscription state, and business delivery as separate records. That decision gives a support agent a useful answer to “did my message arrive?” without turning an untrusted browser acknowledgement into proof that a customer saw it.

In a customer support chat, presence accuracy is a business property, not a green dot. A browser can reconnect while an agent is away, a mobile network can duplicate a publish, and a tab can close after the server has accepted bytes but before the receipt reaches the user. The backend therefore needs a stable event identifier, an explicit acknowledgement state, and an audit trail that survives reconnects.

What should secure realtime publish acknowledgements prove?

The receipt should prove only the narrow fact the server can establish: an authenticated principal was authorized to publish event evt_8f2, and the service durably accepted that event for the conversation. It should not claim delivery to every subscriber, rendering in a browser, or human reading. Those are later observations with different evidence.

I use three monotonic states: accepted, delivered, and read. Each transition carries the event ID, actor ID, conversation ID, server time, and a hash of the canonical payload. An idempotency key binds retries to one event. If the same key arrives with a different payload hash, reject it and log the security decision; silently replacing a financial or support record is unacceptable.

The authorization check also has two dimensions. The access token must be valid and unexpired, and its scope must include the specific conversation action. Subscription membership is not authorization to publish. This distinction matters after a role change, when an agent may remain connected to a channel but lose permission to send.

How do authentication, token scope, and acknowledgements fit together?

Issue short-lived, conversation-scoped credentials from a server-side authority. The browser never receives the long-lived application secret. The generic realtime API surface exposes token issuance and revocation at /v1/realtime/token/issue and /v1/realtime/token/revoke; keep those calls behind your own authorization service so a support role, tenant, and conversation are checked before a token is minted.

Here is the critical path in Go. The transport can be WebSocket, WebRTC data channels, or another realtime protocol; the receipt contract stays the same.

package receipts

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Publish struct {
    EventID       string
    IdempotencyKey string
    Conversation  string
    Actor         string
    Payload       []byte
}

type Receipt struct {
    EventID string
    State   string
    Hash    string
    At      time.Time
}

func Accept(p Publish, authorized func(string, string) bool, seen func(string) (string, bool), store func(Publish, string) error) (Receipt, error) {
    if p.EventID == "" || p.IdempotencyKey == "" || p.Conversation == "" {
        return Receipt{}, errors.New("missing publish identity")
    }
    if !authorized(p.Actor, p.Conversation) {
        return Receipt{}, errors.New("publish scope denied")
    }
    h := sha256.Sum256(p.Payload)
    hash := hex.EncodeToString(h[:])
    if old, ok := seen(p.IdempotencyKey); ok {
        if old != hash {
            return Receipt{}, errors.New("idempotency key payload conflict")
        }
        return Receipt{EventID: p.EventID, State: "accepted", Hash: hash, At: time.Now().UTC()}, nil
    }
    if err := store(p, hash); err != nil {
        return Receipt{}, err
    }
    return Receipt{EventID: p.EventID, State: "accepted", Hash: hash, At: time.Now().UTC()}, nil
}

The durable write and the acknowledgement must have a clear boundary. Write the event and its audit record in one transaction, then emit the receipt. If the process dies before emission, the client retries with the same idempotency key and receives the original receipt. If emission happens twice, the client deduplicates by event ID. “Exactly once” is a useful storage invariant; on a network, it is a reconciliation protocol.

Short receipt. Long audit.

Which design trade-offs matter for a support chat?

Choice Strength Cost or boundary
Signed server receipt Client can verify origin and event hash Key rotation and clock handling become operational work
Plain transport acknowledgement Small implementation and low latency It cannot establish durable acceptance or caller scope
Per-conversation token Limits blast radius after disclosure More token issuance and refresh events to observe
Broad tenant token Fewer auth calls A compromised tab can probe unrelated conversations
Append-only audit log Strong reconciliation and compliance evidence Retention, erasure, and access controls need deliberate policy

The catch is that a signed receipt does not solve presence. It is unsuitable when the product promise is “the agent is watching right now”; use a separately measured presence signal with heartbeat expiry and make its uncertainty visible to operators. Stick with a plain acknowledgement when messages are disposable telemetry and no durable customer record exists. For regulated support, keep the append-only audit trail, but define a retention and deletion policy that matches the applicable privacy rules.

How should reconnect, expiry, and duplicate delivery be tested?

Build a deterministic test matrix around the event ID. Delay the receipt, drop the subscriber connection, expire the token between authorization and retry, and deliver the same event twice. The expected result is stable: one stored event, one audit identity, and a receipt that reports the same hash. A revoked token must not authorize a new publish, while a previously accepted event remains queryable for reconciliation.

I also record separate metrics for authentication failures, subscription changes, publish decisions, receipt emission, and client read markers. Combining them into one “message success” counter hides the exact failure boundary that an incident responder needs. I am not sure every team needs cryptographic signatures; the deciding evidence is your threat model, key-management maturity, and whether clients must verify receipts outside the transport session.

Presence accuracy improves when the client treats the receipt as data, not UI decoration. On reconnect, it sends the last acknowledged event ID; the server returns the missing range or a “resync required” marker, and the client reconciles by ID before showing an agent as available. In practice, that means retaining enough event metadata to answer several awkward questions at once: did authorization pass before the token expired, was the publish persisted before the socket disappeared, did a retry reuse the original idempotency key, and did the read marker arrive from the same principal that received the message? The audit record should let an operator follow those transitions without joining logs from four unrelated services, while redacting message content when retention policy requires it. This is slower than trusting a volatile browser flag, but it makes the behavior explainable during audits and customer disputes.

Don't confuse a green presence badge with evidence.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449

title: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
description:
arXiv:2611.17398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.

title: ParseBench-2: Severity-Aware Evaluation of Document Parsing
description:
arXiv:2611.17400v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Document-parsing metrics can give high scores to outputs that change important facts and penalize changes that preserve meaning. People can often judge these consequences more easily than they can design a metric to measure them. We introduce a method for developing parsing metrics from severity policies that specify how each error type should affect the score. We express these policies through test scenarios that specify how a metric should behave. We then optimize the metric implementations against these fixed expectations, using coding agents to refine comparison rules, error detectors and weights under human review. This makes stated human priorities an explicit objective of metric design. We apply this method in ParseBench-2, a comprehensive document-parsing benchmark that combines broad capability coverage with metrics calibrated to error severity. It covers 4,317 pages across six dimensions of parsing quality: text, formatting, tables, charts, visual grounding, and forms. We use detailed annotations and targeted difficult cases to check for changed facts, broken structural relationships, and missing content. We take the lower of a parsing score that measures content recovery and a severity cap that penalizes detected errors, so recovering most of a page cannot hide a serious error. Across six severity test suites, our metrics more closely match the expert judgments expressed by the scenario targets than existing metrics and penalize at most 3.4% of the tested benign variations. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation spanning frontier vision-language models, specialized document parsers and open-weight systems, comparing their overall rankings, performance across parsing capabilities and tradeoffs between accuracy and cost.

title: Building Arabic Order Forms: Labels, Phone Inputs, and Error Recovery
description:
Disclosure: This tutorial was drafted with AI assistance for the Dropsaas project. The example is a markup fragment, not a complete checkout or a claim about production conversion rates.

An Arabic order form needs more than right-aligned text. Customers may type Arabic names, Latin product codes, and phone numbers in the same flow. Make the meaning of each field explicit, then test mixed-direction content and error recovery.

Start with labels that remain visible

A placeholder disappears as soon as someone types. Keep a visible label and associate it with the input. This also gives the control an accessible name through standard HTML semantics. See the MDN label reference.

Here is a small starting fragment:

<div lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <label for="buyer-name">الاسم الكامل</label>
  <input id="buyer-name" name="buyer_name"
         autocomplete="name" dir="auto" required>

  <label for="buyer-phone">رقم الهاتف</label>
  <p id="phone-help">أدخل رقمًا يمكن التواصل معك عليه لتأكيد الطلب.</p>
  <input id="buyer-phone" name="buyer_phone"
         type="tel" autocomplete="tel" dir="ltr"
         aria-describedby="phone-help" required>
</div>

The phone field uses left-to-right direction to make its digits and international prefix easier to inspect in an otherwise right-to-left layout. That is a design choice to test with your audience, not a universal rule for every input.

The fragment deliberately has no submission endpoint or pretend validation logic. It demonstrates field semantics. A production form still needs server-side validation, error handling, transport security, authorization where relevant, and a deliberate data-retention policy.

A telephone input does not validate every country's phone numbers

Using type="tel" does not automatically prove a number is valid or reachable. Its value is still text, and telephone formats vary. Check the MDN telephone input reference.

Choose validation based on the countries you actually support. Test spaces, an international prefix, local formatting, and Arabic-Indic digits if your normalization rules support them. Do not silently change an ambiguous number into a different one. Explain what the user should enter and show the corrected representation where appropriate.

A browser-side check helps someone fix an error quickly. Your server must still validate what it receives.

Give autocomplete useful hints

The example uses autocomplete="name" and autocomplete="tel". These tokens describe the expected information to the browser; they do not guarantee every browser will autofill the field. Consult the MDN autocomplete reference when mapping address and contact fields.

Avoid requesting unnecessary details just because a template contains those fields. For a cash-on-delivery order, map every required field to a real confirmation or fulfillment task. Ask the operations team which missing details actually prevent delivery.

Design error recovery before styling the error

Write an expected result for each failure scenario. If a required address field is missing, the message should identify the missing information. Valid information in the other fields should remain available so the customer does not have to start again.

Do not rely on a red border alone. Review keyboard navigation, focus behavior after submission, and how assistive technology encounters the error. Test the rendered page with the tools and devices your customers actually use; a static code review cannot verify the full experience.

Use a small test matrix

Scenario What to inspect
Arabic name and Latin phone number Reading order, alignment, and cursor behavior
Phone pasted with spaces Normalization and understandable feedback
Missing delivery area Specific error without clearing valid fields
Longer address on a narrow screen Wrapping and horizontal overflow
Repeated submission after a network problem Clear status and investigation of duplicate orders

Record the actual result and assign one next action per failure. A screenshot of an empty form is not a substitute for these scenarios.

Keep confirmation wording accurate

If the business calls to confirm an order, the success message should say so. Do not describe a recorded request as a dispatched parcel. Match interface wording to the actual order state and the next step handled by the team.

The most useful form improvement may be a clearer label, a preserved value after an error, or an honest success message. Fix a specific failure, rerun the same scenario, and document what changed.

title: TIDE: Reclaiming Lost Performance In On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17924v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) today suffers from severe under-utilization due to long-tail rollouts. Inference engines fall idle waiting for long-tail rollouts or decode at low, inefficient batch sizes. To address this, we present TIDE, an RL training system that preserves on-policy training semantics while recovering resource utilization. TIDE does so by two complementary techniques: (1) dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training while long-tail rollouts complete and (2) dynamically migrating rollouts between inference engines to boost decoding throughput. TIDE automatically determines the right time to repurpose rollout resources through an adaptive migration policy, obtaining performance improvements that generalize across multiple applications and hardware configurations without requiring bespoke configuration. In our evaluation, TIDE provides end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-policy baselines and achieving up to 97% of optimal throughput.

title: Disentangling Forgetting from Utility: Lightweight LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Null-Space Projection
description:
arXiv:2611.17864v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) pose significant security risks by retaining private or hazardous information, creating an urgent need for unlearning techniques that excise specific knowledge without compromising general utility. However, prevailing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods struggle to achieve this balance, often suffering from computational inefficiency and unintended utility degradation due to the entangled nature of knowledge within model parameters. To disentangle forgetting from utility, we propose UUE, a theoretically grounded framework that reformulates unlearning as controllable model editing. First, UUE projects parameter updates into the orthogonal left null space of retained knowledge representations, strictly ensuring that the editing process causes minimal interference to the model's general capabilities. Second, distinct from targeted mapping, we introduce a convex untargeted objective that derives a closed-form analytical solution to effectively disrupt undesired knowledge by pushing forget-set embeddings toward their antipodal points. We implement UUE via lightweight, pluggable adapters (including a low-rank variant, UUE-L), enabling efficient deployment without modifying the frozen backbone. Extensive experiments on TOFU and WMDP benchmarks demonstrate that UUE and UUE-L achieve superior unlearning efficacy, significantly outperforming existing methods.

title: Your API URL lives in 3 dashboards. Which copy is right?
description:
Most teams do not plan to spread one app across three services. It happens a service at a time, and then the same environment variable has to be set in every place the app runs.

The Twelve-Factor App method puts config in the environment, apart from code, and asks you to keep development, staging and production as similar as possible. A database address is config too. The test it suggests is simple: your codebase should be openable to anyone without exposing a credential.
Sooner or later one copy drifts. An API URL that was updated in two dashboards but not the third. A key that was rotated in one place and left alone in two others. Nobody broke anything on purpose. The change was just made three times.

How to check it in 5 minutes:

  1. List the variables of each service in each environment.
  2. Compare them line by line.
  3. Any difference you cannot explain is drift.

How to reduce it: one source of truth for config, and rotate secrets from one place.
Source: The Twelve-Factor App, sections "Config" and "Dev/prod parity" (12factor.net).
Save this for your next deploy, and send it to the teammate who owns your environment variables.

title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
description:
arXiv:2611.17515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22.
  In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

title: AWS US-EAST-1 Outage Nov 15, 2026: Resolved, What to Do Now
description:
Updated 2026-11-15: AWS has marked the incident resolved. Its notice, "Service is operating normally: [RESOLVED] Increased Connectivity issues in US-EAST-1", was posted at 06:53 PST (20:23 IST) on the AWS Health Dashboard feed: https://status.aws.amazon.com/rss/all.rss

AWS says it experienced connectivity issues in the US-EAST-1 Region on 15 November 2026 that affected IAM Identity Center sign-in requests and AWS sign-ups, and that the issues are now resolved. AWS describes the window as between 3:05 AM and 6:10 AM PST (11:05 to 14:10 UTC, 16:35 to 19:40 IST, 06:05 to 09:10 a.m. ET). The most useful thing to do now is to retry any request that failed, as AWS recommends, and to start collecting the times and error messages you will need for any internal review or SLA claim.

Status as of 20:23 IST, 15 November 2026: AWS's latest update, posted at 06:53 PST (20:23 IST), says all services are operating normally and recommends that customers retry any failed requests. AWS has not published a post-incident summary.

What happened

All times below come from the publication times in the AWS Health Dashboard RSS feed (shown in PST by the feed). ET is Eastern Standard Time (UTC-5) on this date; IST is UTC+5:30. AWS did not publish an incident ID in the feed items. Quotes are short excerpts; the feed items are longer.

Time (PST) UTC IST ET AWS update
04:38, 15 Nov 12:38 18:08 07:38 "We are investigating reports of Connectivity issues in the US-EAST-1 Region." AWS also said IAM Identity Center sign-in requests and AWS SignUps were impacted.
05:15, 15 Nov 13:15 18:45 08:15 AWS confirmed errors when authenticating with Identity Center or services that rely on it. "For Kiro users, logins from social sign in methods are not impacted at this time." "There are no workarounds for impacted customers."
05:22, 15 Nov 13:22 18:52 08:22 "We are seeing early signs of recovery for authentication via IAM Identity Center and SignUp."
06:23, 15 Nov 14:23 19:53 09:23 AWS said most services had recovered and that the Identity Center authentication errors affecting Kiro, Connect and other services were fully mitigated. It was still investigating a Network Load Balancer (NLB) issue in a single cell in use1-az1: "we recommend creating a new NLB with targets in multiple Availability Zones." AWS said its next update would come by 7:30 AM PST.
06:32, 15 Nov 14:32 20:02 09:32 "We are seeing significant signs of recovery and are continuing to monitor for full recovery."
06:53, 15 Nov 14:53 20:23 09:53 "Service is operating normally: [RESOLVED] Increased Connectivity issues in US-EAST-1". AWS said that between 3:05 AM and 6:10 AM PST customers experienced signup errors, authentication issues and connectivity issues. It said IAM Identity Center authentication was fully mitigated at 5:20 AM, and that a subset of NLB connectivity issues in one cell in use1-az1 was fixed at 6:21 AM. It recommends customers retry any failed requests.

All items except the last carry the title "Service impact: Increased Connectivity issues in US-EAST-1". Note that AWS's own impact window starts at 3:05 AM PST, earlier than the first feed item at 04:38 PST. The interactive Health Dashboard page is dynamic and could not be loaded, so it may show details that this article does not have.

What AWS has not said, as of the latest update: the cause. This article does not guess at it.

How to check status

  • AWS Health Dashboard, Service health: open https://health.aws.amazon.com/health/status. AWS documents that you do not need to sign in or have an AWS account to view it, and that it shows only public events. Choose Open and recent issues to see the event name, the Region, severity such as Impacted or Degraded, a timeline of updates and a list of other affected services. You can show events in your local time zone or UTC.
  • Your account health: if you can sign in to an AWS account, the dashboard redirects to AWS Health Dashboard - Your account health, which shows events specific to your account.
  • Service history: choose Service history to see all service interruptions of the last 12 months, filterable by service, Region and date.
  • RSS and EventBridge: an RSS feed exists, but AWS notes the format is subject to change and recommends Amazon EventBridge for programmatic ingestion of health events.
  • Downdetector and social media: these show user reports only, not confirmed impact. Treat any user counts as claims.

What users can do now

  1. Retry any sign-in or request that failed between roughly 3:05 AM and 6:10 AM PST on 15 November 2026 (16:35 to 19:40 IST), because AWS recommends that customers retry any failed requests.
  2. If a retry still fails, check the AWS Health Dashboard for a new event before taking action; AWS's resolution notice says services are operating normally, so a continuing failure may be specific to your account.
  3. Do not reset passwords, remove MFA devices or re-create users to deal with the outage; AWS described a service-side problem, and these changes may leave you locked out later.
  4. To sign in, open your AWS access portal URL, which looks like d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start or your_subdomain.awsapps.com/start, and sign in with your company credentials (AWS documentation on signing in to the access portal).
  5. Treat it as recovered when a normal sign-in works again, in addition to AWS's resolution notice.

What admins should do

  • Communicate. Tell users that AWS has marked the US-EAST-1 incident resolved and that failed requests should be retried.
  • Check load balancers. AWS said a subset of NLB connectivity issues in one cell in use1-az1 was fixed at 6:21 AM PST. If an NLB of yours still misbehaves, AWS's 06:23 PST guidance for customers who needed immediate resolution was to create a new NLB with targets in multiple Availability Zones; confirm against your own account health first.
  • Follow your account health view and subscribe to notifications through Amazon EventBridge, as AWS recommends, so the next time you do not depend on a web page.
  • Check your own emergency access. AWS documents an emergency access configuration for the "unlikely event of an IAM Identity Center or AWS Region disruption". Per that page, it works when Identity Center is unavailable but "the IAM data plane and your external identity provider (IdP) are available". The same page warns that you should deploy it before a disruption "because you cannot create the configuration if your access to create the required IAM roles is also disrupted".
  • Review jobs that fetch credentials through Identity Center and failed during the window, and rerun them where safe.
  • Document the impact for a later review and any SLA claim: first and last failed sign-in times with time zone, the accounts and Region, error messages, affected people and business processes, and AWS case numbers.

For background on how Identity Center fits your accounts, see IAM Identity Center with Entra ID SSO and AWS IAM basics.

SLA credits

The Amazon Compute Service Level Agreement (https://aws.amazon.com/compute/sla/, last updated May 25, 2022 per the page) covers Amazon EC2 and related compute services, not IAM Identity Center, so whether this outage qualifies for any credit depends on the SLA for the specific service you use. No IAM Identity Center or Network Load Balancer SLA was opened, so this article gives no percentages or uptime figures.

What that Compute SLA says about the claim process, as a guide to how AWS handles credits:

  • "To receive a Service Credit, you must submit a claim by opening a case in the AWS Support Center."
  • The request needs the incident dates and times, the affected Region, resource IDs and supporting logs with sensitive data redacted.
  • "Your credit request must be received by us by the end of the second billing cycle after which the incident occurred."

Credits are not automatic. Start collecting evidence now, and read the SLA page for each service you depend on.

Post-incident review

As of 20:23 IST, 15 November 2026, no post-incident summary was found from AWS for this event. AWS publishes event updates on the Health Dashboard; check Service history there and AWS's own announcements for any later write-up. Any statement about the cause should come from AWS, not from forum posts.

If it happens again

Test the emergency access configuration from the AWS documentation before you need it, keep a documented break-glass procedure, and subscribe your operations team to AWS Health events through EventBridge.

What we checked

  • Read the AWS Health Dashboard RSS feed (status.aws.amazon.com/rss/all.rss) on 15 November 2026 after the resolution notice (20:23 IST). It contained six US-EAST-1 items, from 04:38 to 06:53 PST, summarized and excerpted above.
  • Confirmed the time conversions: 06:53:29 PST is 14:53:29 UTC, which is 20:23 IST and 09:53 a.m. ET; 05:22 PST is 13:22 UTC, 18:52 IST, 08:22 a.m. ET; 06:23 PST is 14:23 UTC, 19:53 IST, 09:23 a.m. ET; 3:05 AM PST is 11:05 UTC, 16:35 IST.
  • Cross-checked the resolution notice against the 06:23 PST update: both say the Identity Center authentication errors were fully mitigated and that the NLB issue was confined to one cell in use1-az1.
  • Opened status.aws.amazon.com, which redirects to health.aws.amazon.com/health/status; it is a dynamic page that could not be read, so the dashboard's affected-service list is unverified.
  • Earlier today, opened AWS documentation on the Health Dashboard, the IAM Identity Center access portal sign-in page and emergency access page, and the Amazon Compute SLA page. The sign-in URL format and the emergency access wording are quoted from those pages.
  • Claims only: any Downdetector or social media numbers; none are used here.
  • Not tested on a live AWS account; the sign-in errors could not be reproduced, and no post-incident review existed at the time.
