  • Before handing over a card, the service scrubs it and reads it back before giving it to the task.
  • After a task ends, the service reclaims the card first: reads VRAM, reads compute processes, reads the kernel log for that period. A card that threw an Xid is benched for 60 minutes, and the task is requeued onto another card.
  • A card judged faulty gets the outcome card-fault, and a human is asked on the spot to reset it. No waiting, no retrying. ### 7. Tasks that could only run on one machine

Because of resource constraints, some tasks could, believe it or not, only run on one machine. Copy the project to the second machine? Changes are far too frequent; every copy and every reconciliation makes token consumption explode.

Solution: share the codebase over NFSv4, with both machines mounting it at the same absolute path.

# This host: /etc/exports, one line per shared root
<root> <second host address>(rw,sync,no_subtree_check)

# Second host: /etc/fstab, mount at the same absolute path as this host
<this host address>:<root> <root> nfs4 rw,hard,nofail,_netdev,x-systemd.automount,x-systemd.mount-timeout=30 0 0

Three things are shared: the repository itself, the data root (working directories and shard artifacts live under it), and the session log directory. The second machine runs in the same live tree — no copying, no sending, no fetching back, not a single character of any path rewritten. What one machine writes, the other reads directly.

The only exception is the build directory: it lives on each machine's own local disk, is created fresh for every run, and is deleted afterwards. It never goes in a shared directory.

In the service this is a startup condition. On startup the service checks four things: is the configuration present, has this host exported, has the second host mounted, and can each side read a probe file written by the other in both directions. If any check fails, the service doesn't start.

The matching principle went into the project rules: no task must be bound to one machine; if one is, that's a defect. The service has no "this host only" list. If a task dispatched to the second machine goes red, let it go red and go fix the script — don't add exceptions to the service.

Well, that's more or less it. The service's own verification tasks had to queue behind those very long tasks, which made verifying and developing the service very slow. The classic awkward situation: the condition for getting in can only be met once you're in. But in the end these problems were solved.

And then, a new storm appeared.
CPU tasks were in fact solved by this point: CPU and memory form a single resource pool, and scheduling is fairly stable. But GPU tasks held their cards hostage.

8. CPU and GPU tied together

A crash-point replay task first builds and records on the CPU, and only at the very end goes onto a card to judge. Yet it holds the card from the moment it starts. Much of the time, the GPU is just waiting.

Solution: decouple. Assign no card at start; lease one only when the task reaches the step that needs it, and return it immediately after use.

The # task-server-card-lease: on-demand line in the entry file header is that declaration. For such tasks the service assigns no card and does no scrub at start, judging memory and CPU like any ordinary task. In the gate it looks like this:

# .claude/gate.d/crash-point-replay.sh (excerpt)
crash_point_replay_take_card() {
  local cards lease_exit
  [[ -z "$crash_point_replay_card_leased" ]] || return 0      # already holding one: use it
  if cards="$(crash_point_replay_card_lease take)"; then lease_exit=0; else lease_exit=$?; fi
  if (( lease_exit != 0 )) || [[ -z "$cards" ]]; then
    echo "  ✗ $1: $2 needs a card; on-demand lease refused, this run did not start"
    return 1
  fi
  crash_point_replay_card_leased="$cards"
  echo "  · $1: $2 needs a card; leased $cards on demand (returned when this run ends)"
}

Behind lease take, the service picks a free card by card priority, scrubs it, reads it back, and only then hands it over. If all cards are taken, the request waits in line, first come first served. Any card not returned when a task ends is reclaimed by the service.

The tests in the verification package were split into two stages accordingly:

  1. Record only: runs on the CPU and writes the inputs to be judged into the verdict database. Holds no card.
  2. Judge only: leases a card, reads the inputs back from the database, judges them on the card, and returns the card when done. The other half was done too: once a task has a card and enters its GPU stage, its CPU accounting switches to the number of cores actually in use during that card-holding stage. While it waits on the card's results, its CPU slots go to others.

The time a card spends in hand shrank from "the whole task" to "the part that's actually computing."

Finally, more or less there

  • Memory no longer gets eaten by several tasks starting at once. Admission is decided in exactly one place, the service, and only what qualifies gets started.
  • No task holds resources indefinitely. Stuck ones are stopped, long ones get reminders, four-hour ones are bounced.
  • Every outcome has a name, an exit code, and a next step, and it's delivered to the session that started it.

  • Verdicts from everyday runs aren't wasted; the commit-time run picks them up.
    But there are still plenty of problems:

  • Estimated runtime is historical data, not a promise. A run that reuses a lot and one that reuses little can differ enormously.

  • Starting at 4GB and bumping up by 1.5× trades reruns for convenience. A genuinely new 40GB task has to hit the cap six times before it runs stably.

  • The service is code too. Its self-tests run in a simulated world: fake memory wrappers, a fake second machine, fake cards. Running it for real is a stumbling affair.
    Fortunately, after more than 10,000 tasks, it has more or less settled down. Of course — trust me — countless bugs and optimizations are still waiting down the road.

Problems are like the tree in the yard. When the leaves fall, countless branches are laid bare...

title: Hot Switching vs Cold Switching: What Actually Kills a Coaxial RF Switch
description:
Under a cold-switching specification a coaxial switch is rated for one to five million operations. Under a hot-switching specification the same switch may be rated for fifty thousand. The hardware is identical. The difference is whether the contact opens while RF power is still flowing through it.

Almost every argument about switch life in a test rack comes down to this one clause, and it is often the least visible line on the datasheet.

What actually happens at the contact

An electromechanical coaxial switch makes contact through a spring-loaded blade pressed against a centre conductor. When the circuit is dead, the blade closes onto a clean surface and the only wear is mechanical. When the circuit is live, the blade approaches the conductor while a voltage difference still exists across the gap. Below roughly ten volts the arc does not form and the contact is effectively cold. Above that, and especially above a few tens of volts, a micro-arc erodes a small crater at the contact point on every operation.

The crater matters for two reasons. It raises contact resistance, which shows up as insertion loss creeping up over months. And it roughens the surface, which degrades the repeatability of the return loss. A switch with a million cold operations behind it can still measure like new. A switch with thirty thousand hot operations at 50 W may already be out of specification on isolation, because the eroded contact no longer seats flat.

Manufacturers know this, which is why the two ratings differ by a factor of twenty or more. What they cannot tell you is which one applies to your rack, because that depends on how the software drives the switch.

The sequence is the specification

The sequence that keeps a switch in its cold-switching rating is simple:

  1. Turn the RF source off, or set it to zero output.
  2. Wait for the source to actually settle. On many synthesizers this is longer than the command latency, and on amplifiers with a large output capacitor it can be tens of milliseconds.
  3. Switch.
  4. Wait for contact bounce to finish. A few milliseconds for a relay, microseconds for a PIN diode.
  5. Turn the source back on.

In practice most racks skip steps one and four. The switch driver fires as soon as the instrument accepts the command, and the source is still ramping down. That is a hot switch, and no amount of careful hardware selection fixes it.

The measurable symptom is a switch that meets its insertion loss specification when new and drifts by a few tenths of a dB after a year of production testing, with the drift concentrated on the channels that carry the highest power.

Where hot switching is unavoidable

Some architectures cannot avoid hot switching. A switch matrix that reconfigures while a carrier is running, a redundancy switch that has to move on failure, a calibration path that has to switch during a sweep: in these cases the specification has to be chosen for hot switching from the start, and the derating applied to power and to life.

For a switch rated 100 W cold, a hot-switching rating of 10 to 20 W at the same frequency is typical for a relay with a good contact design. For a PIN diode switch there is no arc at all, so the limit becomes the diode's power dissipation and the bias network, not contact erosion. That is one of the few real advantages of solid-state switching that survives contact with a test plan.

What to write into the test software

Three changes cover most of the exposure, and none of them costs money:

  • Put the source-off command before the switch command in the driver, not after it, and let the driver wait a fixed settling time that you have measured rather than guessed.
  • Add a per-channel operation counter to the log. A switch that is 60 percent through its hot-switching life should be scheduled for replacement, not discovered by a failed measurement.
  • Record power level with the counter. A channel that ran at 2 W for a year and then moved to 50 W has a completely different remaining life, and without the power column nobody can tell.

Choosing the part for the sequence you actually run

If a rack genuinely cold-switches, a standard electromechanical coaxial switch from SPDT to SP12T or DPDT is the right choice, and the failure mode you will meet is mechanical wear after millions of operations. If the rack hot-switches, either accept the reduced life and buy a PIN diode switch, or derate an electromechanical part and treat it as a consumable.

The same logic applies at higher frequencies where the switch is a waveguide switch: the actuator and the contact geometry change, the arc problem does not. And whatever the switch type, the unused throws still need coaxial terminations whose power rating is chosen for the same hot or cold assumption, because a termination that absorbs a live carrier during reconfiguration is doing exactly the job the switch was derated to avoid.

One last line worth writing into the RFQ: ask for the hot-switching life at the frequency and power you will actually use, not the headline cold-switching figure. The answer tells you more about the contact design than any other number on the sheet.

title: Reasoning Models Confabulate to Defend Injected Beliefs About Their Own Requests
description:
arXiv:2611.17958v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring and self-report are proposed as levers for AI oversight, on the assumption that a model's account of what it is doing is anchored to what it was asked. We show this anchor can be cut. An activation edit invisible in the prompt text, the injected forming-trace of an off-topic concept, overwrites a reasoning model's belief about its own request: across six models spanning scale, architecture, and recipe, the injected topic becomes the task it reasons about, reports back, and answers: the forced quote-back returns the injected topic in 47 of 48 model-concept cells, and on the four models with clean final haiku the injected answer follows in 99% of generations. Warnings barely move it: even one naming the true topic yields under 5% true-topic answers. Handed the truth in clean tokens, the model confabulates a story about the user ("maybe they got confused and corrected themselves") and answers with the injection anyway, its behavior and chain-of-thought corrupted together: a concrete limit on CoT monitorability. Opening the model up offers no reprieve: it attends to the true request even harder after edits, yet that attention is causally inert, and the injected content rides intact task circuits, so attention maps and circuit attributions read as on-task too; the same edit redirects the request's language and format, not only its topic. What the injection reaches is the model's reference to its own input; what it elicits is its defense of it.

title: React useState – Interview Questions & Answers
description:
Q1. What is useState in React?

  • useState is a React Hook that allows us to create and manage state (data) inside a functional component. 
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Here:
count – current state value.
setCount – function to update the state.
0 – initial value.

Q2. Why do we use useState?

  • We use useState to store and update data in a component. When the state changes, React automatically re-renders the component and updates the UI. 
import { useState } from "react";

function Counter() {

    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <>
            <h2>{count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Increase
            </button>
        </>
    );
}

export default Counter;

When we click the button, the count increases and the UI updates.

Q3. What is the difference between normal variables and useState?

  • Normal variables do not trigger a re-render when their values change, but useState updates the component UI when its state changes. Normal variable: 
function App() {

    let count = 0;

    return (
        <>
            <h2>{count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => count++}>
                Increase
            </button>
        </>
    );
}

The UI will not update when you click the button.
Using useState:

function App() {

    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

    return (
        <>
            <h2>{count}</h2>
            <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
                Increase
            </button>
        </>
    );
}

Now the UI updates automatically.

title: Réserver la place d’une image avant son chargement
description:
Sur une page d’article, un lecteur commence à lire le paragraphe qui suit la photo. La photo se charge, prend sa hauteur et repousse le texte. Le navigateur pouvait réserver cette place dès le départ si le balisage lui avait donné les proportions du fichier.

Donner les dimensions de la photo au navigateur

Supposons que escalier.jpg mesure 1 200 × 800 pixels. Renseignez ces dimensions sur l’élément img, puis laissez le CSS adapter sa largeur à celle de la colonne.

<figure class="photo-article">
  <img src="escalier.jpg"
       width="1200" height="800"
       alt="Escalier clair traversé par une ombre diagonale">
  <figcaption>La photo de l’escalier, au format 3:2.</figcaption>
</figure>

.photo-article {
  max-inline-size: 36rem;
  margin-inline: auto;
}

.photo-article img {
  display: block;
  inline-size: 100%;
  block-size: auto;
}

Dans une colonne de 360 pixels, le navigateur peut réserver 240 pixels de hauteur avant d’avoir reçu le fichier. Sur un écran large, la photo grandit avec sa colonne. Le chapitre sur les images dans le guide de web.dev détaille ce calcul et son effet sur les déplacements de mise en page.

Vérifier le résultat avec une connexion ralentie

Ouvrez les outils de développement, ralentissez le réseau et désactivez le cache le temps de l’essai. Rechargez la page en regardant le texte sous la photo. Dans l’exemple à 360 pixels de large, la hauteur réservée est restée à 240 pixels et le texte a gardé la même position. Avec les dimensions omises, la réception de la même photo a décalé le texte de 219 pixels. Pour refaire la mesure, comparez la position du texte avant et après le chargement du fichier.

Garder la même proportion entre les variantes

Si srcset propose un fichier de 600 pixels et un autre de 1 200 pixels de large, exportez-les ici en 600 × 400 et 1 200 × 800. Une image recadrée en carré pour la version mobile demande un rapport différent. Testez ce recadrage sur un écran étroit afin que l’espace réservé corresponde au fichier que le navigateur sélectionne réellement.

title: How to Deploy a Web Application to AWS Amplify Without Git: A Step-by-Step Guide Using a ZIP Folder
description:
Introduction

When developers think about deploying a frontend application to AWS Amplify, one of the first things that comes to mind is connecting a Git repository.

The typical workflow involves pushing application code to GitHub, connecting the repository to AWS Amplify, configuring the build process, and allowing Amplify to automatically deploy the application whenever changes are pushed to the selected branch.

However, connecting a Git repository is not the only way to deploy an application with AWS Amplify.

AWS Amplify also supports manual deployments, which allow developers to deploy frontend applications by uploading a ZIP archive containing their application files.

This is particularly useful when:

  • You have a static website that does not require a build process.
  • You want to deploy a frontend application without creating a Git repository.
  • You are working with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files.
  • You want to host a frontend application independently of your backend infrastructure.
  • You need a straightforward way to publish a website directly from your local machine.

In this guide, we will walk through the process of deploying a frontend application to AWS Amplify without using Git.

We will use a simple static frontend application containing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files to demonstrate the process.

By the end of this tutorial, you should have a publicly accessible website hosted on AWS Amplify.

1. Understanding AWS Amplify Hosting

Before deploying anything, it is important to understand what AWS Amplify does.

AWS Amplify Hosting is a managed hosting service designed for modern web applications and static websites.

It provides infrastructure for hosting frontend applications without requiring developers to manually configure web servers, manage operating systems, or maintain hosting infrastructure.

When you deploy an application using Amplify, AWS handles several hosting responsibilities, including:

  • Hosting and serving your frontend files.
  • Providing a publicly accessible application URL.
  • Distributing application content through its hosting infrastructure.
  • Supporting HTTPS for deployed applications.
  • Managing deployment versions.

For this tutorial, we will use Amplify's manual deployment capability.

Unlike repository-based deployments, manual deployments do not require Amplify to connect to a source code repository.

Instead, we prepare our application files locally, compress them into a ZIP archive, and upload that archive through the Amplify Console.

The deployment process looks like this:

Local application files → ZIP archive → AWS Amplify Console → Manual upload → Deployment → Live application.

2. Prerequisites

Before proceeding, make sure you have the following:

  1. An active AWS account.
  2. Access to the AWS Management Console.
  3. A frontend application you want to deploy.
  4. A ZIP utility or the ability to create ZIP archives from your operating system.
  5. A modern web browser.

You do not need:

  • A GitHub account.
  • A GitLab account.
  • A Bitbucket account.
  • A connected Git repository.
  • A configured CI/CD pipeline.
  • An EC2 instance or web server.

For this demonstration, we will use a simple frontend project with the following structure:

my-frontend-app/
│
├── index.html
├── styles.css
└── main.js

These files represent a basic static frontend application.

If your application uses React, Vue, Angular, or another frontend framework, you can also deploy it this way, provided you first generate its production build output.

For example, a React application built with Vite typically produces a dist directory. The contents of that directory, rather than the entire development project, are what you would package for deployment.

3. Prepare Your Application Files

The first step is to prepare the files that Amplify will serve.

Navigate to your frontend project directory.

Before proceeding, make sure that:

  • Your HTML file exists.
  • Your CSS and JavaScript references point to the correct paths.
  • Your application works locally.
  • All assets required by the application are included.

For applications that communicate with backend services, check that API endpoints and other environment-specific configuration values are correct for the environment you are deploying.

4. Create a ZIP Archive of Your Application

This is one of the most important steps in the entire process.

AWS Amplify expects the ZIP archive to contain the files that should be deployed.

A common mistake is compressing the entire project folder instead of compressing the contents of the folder.

For example, consider this ZIP structure:

my-frontend-app.zip
│
└── my-frontend-app/
    ├── index.html
    ├── styles.css
    └── main.js

This structure introduces an unnecessary directory level.

For a simple static application, the preferred structure is:

my-frontend-app.zip
│
├── index.html
├── styles.css
└── main.js

The index.html file should be at the root of the archive so Amplify can serve it as the website's entry point.

Creating the ZIP file using Linux or WSL

If you are using Ubuntu, Linux, or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), navigate into your frontend directory:

cd my-frontend-app

Run:

zip -r ../frontend-deploy.zip .

This creates a ZIP archive in the parent directory.

The important detail is the final dot (.).

It tells the zip command to archive the contents of the current directory rather than placing the entire directory inside the archive.

Creating the ZIP file using Windows

You can also create the archive using Windows File Explorer.

  1. Open your frontend project folder.
  2. Select the files you want to deploy.
  3. Right-click the selected files.
  4. Select Compress to ZIP file or Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder, depending on your Windows version.
  5. Give the archive a descriptive name, such as frontend-deploy.zip.

Make sure you select the application files inside the folder rather than compressing the parent folder itself.

Verify the ZIP archive

Before uploading, inspect the contents of your ZIP file.

On Linux or WSL, run:

unzip -l frontend-deploy.zip

The output should resemble:

index.html
styles.css
main.js

If you see an additional enclosing project directory, recreate the archive with the correct structure.

This small verification step can prevent unnecessary deployment problems.

5. Open the AWS Amplify Console

Now that your ZIP archive is ready, we can move to AWS.

  1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console.
  2. Search for AWS Amplify in the services search bar.
  3. Open the AWS Amplify service.
  4. Navigate to the Amplify applications dashboard.

You can also access the service directly:

https://console.aws.amazon.com/amplify/

Make sure you are working in the AWS Region where you intend to manage your application.

6. Create a New

Inside the Amplify Console:

  1. Select Create new app.

  1. Look for the option to deploy without connecting a Git provider.

  1. Select the manual deployment workflow.

Depending on the current Amplify Console interface, this option may appear as Deploy without Git provider or under a manual deployment section.

The important thing is to avoid selecting GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or another repository provider.

You are creating an application that will receive its deployment files through manual uploads.

7. Configure Your Application

The next step is to provide basic application details.

You may be asked to specify:

  • Application name.
  • Branch name.
  • Deployment method.

For example:

Setting Example value
Application name my-frontend-app
Branch name production
Deployment method Manual deployment

The application name helps identify your project in the Amplify Console.

The branch name is a deployment identifier. It does not mean you need to create or connect a Git branch.

You can use a name such as production to represent the deployment environment.

After entering the required information, proceed to the deployment configuration screen.

8. Upload Your ZIP Archive

This is where the actual deployment package is provided.

On the manual deployment screen:

  1. Locate the ZIP file upload section.
  2. Select your frontend-deploy.zip archive.
  3. If the console requests an application or branch selection, ensure you have selected the correct application and deployment branch.
  4. Review the deployment details.
  5. Start the deployment.

AWS Amplify will upload and process the archive.

Since we are deploying a static application without a build process, there is no need to configure a build specification such as amplify.yml.

Amplify can host the supplied static files directly.

Wait for the deployment to finish.

9. Verify the Deployment

Once Amplify successfully deploys your application, the deployment status should indicate that the application has been deployed.

The console will provide a default application URL.

It typically follows this format:

https://branch-name.application-id.amplifyapp.com

Open the URL in your browser.

You should see your deployed application.

If you deployed the example from this tutorial, you should see:

Welcome to My Website

This application is hosted on AWS Amplify.

Also open your browser's developer tools and inspect the Console and Network tabs.

Check for:

  • JavaScript errors.
  • Missing CSS files.
  • Missing JavaScript files.
  • Failed asset requests.
  • Incorrect API requests.

A successful deployment does not automatically mean every part of the application is functioning correctly. Always test the deployed application itself.

10. Updating Your Application Without Git

One advantage of manual deployment is that you can publish updates without pushing code to a repository.

Suppose you make changes to your frontend application.

For example, you update:

  • index.html
  • styles.css
  • main.js

The process is straightforward.

Step 1: Modify your local application files.

Step 2: Test the changes locally.

Step 3: Create a new ZIP archive containing the updated application files.

Step 4: Open the AWS Amplify Console.

Step 5: Select your existing Amplify application and deployment branch.

Step 6: Start another manual deployment using the updated ZIP archive.

Step 7: Wait for Amplify to finish deploying.

Step 8: Open your application URL and verify the changes.

You do not need to create another Amplify application every time you update your website.

You simply create a new deployment for the existing application.

11. Common Problems and How to Fix Them

Although manual deployment is relatively straightforward, a few issues can prevent an application from working correctly.

Problem 1: The deployed website displays a 404 error

One possible cause is an incorrect ZIP archive structure.

For example:

frontend-deploy.zip
└── frontend/
    └── index.html

For a simple static application, the entry point should be at the archive root:

frontend-deploy.zip
└── index.html

Solution: Recreate the ZIP archive using the contents of the frontend directory rather than the directory itself.

Problem 2: CSS files are not loading

This can happen when the paths specified in your HTML file do not match the deployed file structure.

For example:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="./styles.css">

This expects styles.css to be available relative to the HTML file.

Solution: Verify the paths and ensure all required files are included in the ZIP archive.

Problem 3: JavaScript files are not loading

Check that the JavaScript file exists and that its reference in your HTML file is correct.

For example:

<script src="./main.js"></script>

Also inspect the browser's developer console for JavaScript errors.

Problem 4: The application loads, but API requests fail

This is particularly important for applications that communicate with backend services.

Your frontend might load successfully while requests to API Gateway, Lambda-backed endpoints, or other backend services fail.

Possible causes include:

  • Incorrect API endpoint configuration.
  • CORS configuration problems.
  • Incorrect authentication tokens.
  • Invalid Cognito callback or logout URLs.
  • Backend authorization failures.

Solution: Verify the frontend configuration and inspect the browser's Network tab to identify the actual failing request.

If your application uses Amazon Cognito for authentication, make sure the deployed Amplify URL is registered as an authorized callback URL and logout URL in the Cognito app client.

Problem 5: Changes are not appearing after deployment

Sometimes your browser may continue displaying an older cached version of your application.

Solution:

  1. Confirm that the latest deployment completed successfully.
  2. Open the application in a private browsing window.
  3. Perform a hard refresh.
  4. Inspect the Network tab to verify which files are being loaded.

Also check whether your application uses a service worker or other caching mechanism.

12. Important Considerations When Using Manual Deployments

Manual ZIP deployments are convenient, but there are some limitations worth understanding.

No automatic deployment from Git

Because your application is not connected to a Git repository, Amplify will not automatically detect changes in your local project.

You must create and upload a new ZIP archive whenever you want to publish an update.

No automatic build process

A manual ZIP deployment is suitable for files that are already prepared for hosting.

For frameworks such as React, Vue, and Angular, generate the production build first and upload the resulting build output.

For example, with Vite:

npm run build

This normally generates a dist directory.

You should package the contents of that directory, ensuring that index.html is at the root of the archive.

Do not upload your entire development project with node_modules and source files when the production build output is all that is required.

Backend services are not automatically deployed

Uploading a frontend ZIP archive does not deploy your backend infrastructure.

If your application depends on services such as:

  • Amazon API Gateway
  • AWS Lambda
  • Amazon Cognito
  • Amazon DynamoDB
  • Amazon S3
  • Amazon Bedrock

Those services must already be provisioned and configured separately.

Amplify Hosting is responsible for hosting the frontend files in this deployment workflow.

Authentication and API configuration still matter

For applications that use authentication or communicate with backend services, make sure the production configuration is correct before uploading your archive.

A website can be successfully deployed while authentication or backend integration remains broken.

13. Conclusion

Deploying a frontend application to AWS Amplify does not always require a Git repository.

With manual deployments, developers can prepare their application files locally, package them into a ZIP archive, and upload the archive directly through the AWS Amplify Console.

The process is particularly useful for static websites, small frontend applications, prototypes, and projects where a repository-based deployment pipeline is unnecessary.

The overall workflow is simple:

  1. Prepare your frontend application.
  2. Ensure the required files are available.
  3. Create a ZIP archive with the correct directory structure.
  4. Open the AWS Amplify Console.
  5. Choose the manual deployment option.
  6. Upload the ZIP archive.
  7. Deploy the application.
  8. Verify the live website.
  9. Repeat the process whenever you need to publish an update.

The important lesson is that Git is not a mandatory requirement for hosting a frontend application on AWS Amplify.

If your application is already prepared for production, a ZIP archive is enough to get it deployed.

Additional Resources

  • AWS Amplify Documentation
  • AWS Amplify Hosting Documentation
  • AWS Amplify Console
  • AWS Amplify Pricing

Disclaimer: AWS Console labels and deployment screens may change over time. The exact wording of the manual deployment option may vary, but the ZIP-based deployment workflow remains the central approach described in this guide.

title: RabbitMQ Tutorial: An Order Queue That Never Loses Work
description:
Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/rabbitmq-python-order-queue.html

Quick answer

RabbitMQ is a message broker: one program puts a message into a queue, and another takes it out later, so slow work does not block the user. This post publishes three shop orders to a real queue with Python and pika, acknowledges the two good ones, and rejects the broken one into a dead-letter queue. It fits work that must survive a crash, and is overkill for a simple in-process job.

Picture a small online shop. A customer clicks buy, and the checkout code charges the card and updates stock, all inside one web request. Then the payment gateway stalls, the request times out, the customer clicks buy again, and the card is charged twice. A queue breaks the chain. The web request only has to record the order and hand it to RabbitMQ, and a separate worker takes orders one at a time and confirms each one only when the work is done. If the worker crashes halfway, the order is still in the queue, waiting for the next worker.

What I would check before using it

My first check: must the work survive a crash? If checkout dies halfway, can someone else pick up the order and finish it? When the answer is yes, a durable queue earns its place. When the answer is no, because the job can simply run again from scratch, a queue is ceremony, and a short list in Redis may do.

My second check is who runs the broker. RabbitMQ is one more service to install, watch, and back up. It needs free disk space, and stops accepting messages when the disk fills up. If nobody owns that job, a managed queue from your cloud provider is the honest alternative.

My third check is scale. RabbitMQ handles tens of thousands of messages a second on ordinary hardware, enough for most shops and internal tools. It is not the tool for replaying a year of events at massive volume. That is the job Kafka was built for.

My fourth check is how failures are handled. Every queue needs an answer for the message that can never be processed: a dead-letter queue to park it in, an alert, and a way to fix and replay it. Without that plan, bad messages vanish silently or loop forever.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt RabbitMQ when background work must not be lost, must be retried, and must be spread across workers. Skip it for a single small script or a prototype with no real users. The recommendation flips the moment nobody owns the broker, or the workload turns into an event stream that needs replay.

Three orders through a real queue

The example is a small shop selling clothes and accessories. Three orders arrive: Ayesha buys a kurta and a dupatta for Rs 12,400, Bilal buys sneakers for Rs 7,800, and Hina buys a handbag and a wallet. Hina's order has a problem: the total was never filled in. That is the kind of bad record that sails through a demo and breaks the first real order.

The script connects to a broker on localhost, declares a durable orders queue with a dead-letter exchange for rejects. Each order is published as JSON, persistent with delivery_mode set to 2. The worker takes orders one at a time and acks each one only after charging it.

"""Order queue demo for The Practical Developer (RabbitMQ, pika).

A small online shop publishes orders to a RabbitMQ queue. A worker
takes them one at a time, charges the customer, and acknowledges each
order. One order arrives without a total, so the worker rejects it and
the broker moves it to a dead-letter queue. A corrected copy of that
order is published and processed cleanly.

Run: python3 rabbitmq_demo.py (RabbitMQ must be listening on localhost:5672)
"""
import json
import pika

QUEUE = "orders"
DLX = "orders_dlx"
DLQ = "orders_dead"


def connect():
    connection = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost"))
    channel = connection.channel()
    channel.exchange_declare(exchange=DLX, exchange_type="fanout", durable=True)
    channel.queue_declare(queue=DLQ, durable=True)
    channel.queue_bind(exchange=DLX, queue=DLQ, routing_key="")
    channel.queue_declare(
        queue=QUEUE,
        durable=True,
        arguments={"x-dead-letter-exchange": DLX},
    )
    return connection, channel


def queue_depth(name):
    # A fresh connection gives the true count. Checking depth on the same
    # channel that just published returns a stale number in pika 1.4.4
    # (it lagged by one in testing: 1 after three publishes, 2 after the
    # next check), while rabbitmqctl and a new connection both said 3.
    connection = pika.BlockingConnection(pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost"))
    channel = connection.channel()
    count = channel.queue_declare(queue=name, passive=True).method.message_count
    connection.close()
    return count


def publish(channel, order):
    channel.basic_publish(
        exchange="",
        routing_key=QUEUE,
        body=json.dumps(order),
        properties=pika.BasicProperties(delivery_mode=2),
    )
    print(f"Published order {order['order_id']} for {order['customer']}")


def charge(order):
    if "total" not in order:
        raise ValueError(f"order {order['order_id']} has no total to charge")
    print(f"Charged Rs {order['total']} for order {order['order_id']}")

The second half drains the queue, acking each good order and rejecting the broken one without requeueing. Then the corrected order is published and processed.

def drain(channel):
    while True:
        method, _props, body = channel.basic_get(queue=QUEUE, auto_ack=False)
        if method is None:
            return
        order = json.loads(body)
        try:
            charge(order)
            channel.basic_ack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag)
            print(f"Acked order {order['order_id']}")
        except ValueError as exc:
            print(f"Rejected order {order['order_id']}: {exc}")
            channel.basic_nack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag, requeue=False)


def main():
    connection, channel = connect()
    print("Connected. Queue 'orders' declared (durable, dead-letter exchange set).")

    print("Phase 1: three orders published, one is broken")
    orders = [
        {"order_id": 101, "customer": "Ayesha", "items": ["kurta", "dupatta"], "total": 12400},
        {"order_id": 102, "customer": "Bilal", "items": ["sneakers"], "total": 7800},
        {"order_id": 103, "customer": "Hina", "items": ["handbag", "wallet"]},
    ]
    for order in orders:
        publish(channel, order)
    print(f"Orders waiting: {queue_depth(QUEUE)}")
    drain(channel)
    print(f"After phase 1: orders={queue_depth(QUEUE)}, "
          f"dead-lettered={queue_depth(DLQ)}")

    print("Phase 2: corrected order 103 published and processed")
    publish(channel, {"order_id": 103, "customer": "Hina",
                      "items": ["handbag", "wallet"], "total": 15300})
    drain(channel)
    print(f"After phase 2: orders={queue_depth(QUEUE)}, "
          f"dead-lettered={queue_depth(DLQ)}")
    print("Done. The broken copy of order 103 stays in the dead-letter queue.")
    connection.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Real output from the run against RabbitMQ 3.12.1:

Connected. Queue 'orders' declared (durable, dead-letter exchange set).
Phase 1: three orders published, one is broken
Published order 101 for Ayesha
Published order 102 for Bilal
Published order 103 for Hina
Orders waiting: 3
Charged Rs 12400 for order 101
Acked order 101
Charged Rs 7800 for order 102
Acked order 102
Rejected order 103: order 103 has no total to charge
After phase 1: orders=0, dead-lettered=1
Phase 2: corrected order 103 published and processed
Published order 103 for Hina
Charged Rs 15300 for order 103
Acked order 103
After phase 2: orders=0, dead-lettered=1
Done. The broken copy of order 103 stays in the dead-letter queue.

The thing that went wrong is order 103. The worker tried to charge it, found no total, and rejected it with basic_nack, requeue False, so the broker moved it to the dead-letter queue. A bad message is parked for inspection, not retried forever. The data needs its own fix: the corrected order, with the missing total of Rs 15,300 added, was published again in phase 2 and processed cleanly. The broken copy stays in the dead-letter queue for inspection. The shop API could be built with FastAPI, and the checkout endpoint follows the Node.js REST API post.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, acknowledging messages automatically. With auto_ack set to True, RabbitMQ deletes the message the moment it is delivered, so a worker crash mid-charge loses the order for good. The fix is auto_ack set to False and a manual ack only after the work succeeds.

Second, a queue that is not durable, or messages that are not persistent. The symptom is an empty queue after a broker restart, with no error anywhere. The fix is durable set to True on the queue and delivery_mode set to 2 on every publish. Both halves matter.

Third, requeueing a message that can never succeed. Calling basic_nack with requeue set to True on a poison message sends it back to the queue, so the worker fails it again and again while good orders wait behind it. The fix is requeue set to False plus a dead-letter exchange, as the demo does.

Fourth, declaring a plain queue on RabbitMQ 4. The broker closes the connection with pika.exceptions.ConnectionClosedByBroker: (541, 'INTERNAL_ERROR - Feature transient_nonexcl_queues is deprecated'). The fix is durable set to True, or exclusive set to True for a private queue.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is RabbitMQ free to use? Yes. RabbitMQ is open source under the Mozilla Public License, and running it yourself costs nothing. Only managed hosting costs money.

How is RabbitMQ different from Kafka? RabbitMQ is a queue: a message goes to one worker, then is removed. Kafka is an event log: messages stay for replay by many readers. Queues fit background jobs; Kafka fits large-scale event streaming.

Do I need Docker to run RabbitMQ? No. This demo ran on a broker installed with apt on Ubuntu, with docs for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Docker is optional, not required.

What happens to messages if the broker restarts? A durable queue with persistent messages keeps them. Anything else is lost on restart.

What to remember

  • Declare the queue durable and publish persistent messages, or a restart wipes the queue.
  • Acknowledge only after the work succeeds, never before.
  • Give every queue a dead-letter exchange, so bad messages are parked, not lost or looped.
  • Check queue depth with rabbitmqctl or a fresh connection when the numbers look wrong.
  • Own the broker: watch disk space and set an alert before it fills up.

Where this leaves you

RabbitMQ earns its place the day an order, a payment, or an email must not be lost because a process died at the wrong moment. The demo proved the three things that matter: good orders were charged and acknowledged, the broken order was rejected into a dead-letter queue instead of vanishing, and the corrected order went through cleanly. That is the whole job. Start with one durable queue, one worker, and a dead-letter queue, and watch the dead-letter queue after your first deploy. If it stays empty, your data is clean. If it fills up, you have a list of real problems, which is the better outcome.

Further reading

  • RabbitMQ tutorial, "Hello world!" with Python and pika, https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/tutorial-one-python
  • RabbitMQ docs, Dead Letter Exchanges, https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/dlx
  • pika documentation, the Python client for RabbitMQ, https://pika.readthedocs.io/
  • Kafka Explained: The Event Backbone of Big Systems, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/kafka-explained-event-backbone-of-big.html
  • Redis Explained: The In-Memory Store That Speeds Things Up, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/redis-explained-in-memory-store-that.html
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/fastapi-explained-python-apis-at-full.html
  • Build Your First REST API With Node.js and Express, https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/10/build-your-first-rest-api-with-nodejs.html

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Mockeamos la API de un proveedor para salvar el CI, y el mock nos mintió
description:
Era martes. La ejecución de GitHub Actions llevaba unos 40 minutos cuando la suite de integración murió con el mismo error por tercera vez esa mañana:

FetchError: request to https://sandbox.<proveedor>.com/v1/rates failed
  status: 429 Too Many Requests
  retry-after: 3600

Nuestro proveedor de tarifas de envío limita su sandbox a 1.000 llamadas al día por clave. Éramos cuatro desarrolladores, una clave compartida y una suite que hacía unas 180 llamadas por ejecución. Con seis pushes y un par de reintentos, la cuota se acababa antes de comer.

Esa semana perdimos casi dos días de sprint con un pipeline en rojo que nadie podía arreglar, porque en realidad no había nada roto. Al mes siguiente descubrimos que el proveedor también cobra el exceso de llamadas al sandbox. Unos 340 dólares por el privilegio de fallar nuestros propios tests.

Así que montamos un mock server. Arregló el pipeline. Y cinco semanas después dejó pasar un bug real hasta producción. Las dos mitades de la historia merecen contarse.

Lo que necesitábamos de verdad

No quería una librería de mocks repartida por los archivos de test. Ya lo habíamos hecho en un proyecto anterior con nock y cada test acabó con su propia versión, ligeramente distinta, de lo que devolvía el proveedor. Cambiar un endpoint significaba tocar 30 archivos.

Quería algo aburrido: un servidor HTTP local con las mismas rutas que el proveedor, que devuelva JSON grabado y que se active con una sola variable de entorno. El código de la aplicación no debería enterarse.

Si alguien de tu equipo no tiene claro el concepto, yo pasé por el canal interno la guía de Keploy sobre mock servers. Explica la diferencia entre hacer stubs dentro de un test y levantar un servidor aparte, que era justo la discusión que teníamos cada semana.

Son unas 30 líneas

Sin framework. El módulo http de Node es suficiente.

// mock-server.js
const http = require('node:http');
const fs = require('node:fs');
const path = require('node:path');

const fixtures = {
  'POST /v1/rates': 'rates-ok.json',
  'GET /v1/shipments/shp_123': 'shipment.json',
};

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  const url = new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost');
  const key = `${req.method} ${url.pathname}`;
  const file = fixtures[key];

  if (!file) {
    res.writeHead(404, { 'content-type': 'application/json' });
    return res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: `no fixture for ${key}` }));
  }

  const body = fs.readFileSync(path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures', file));
  res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'application/json' });
  res.end(body);
});

server.listen(process.env.MOCK_PORT || 4010, () => {
  console.log(`mock listening on ${server.address().port}`);
});

Los fixtures eran respuestas reales que capturé del sandbox con curl. En CI, el workflow arranca el mock en segundo plano y apunta la aplicación hacia él:

node mock-server.js &
VENDOR_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4010 npm test

El 404 con el nombre de la ruta resultó ser la línea más útil del archivo. Cuando alguien añade una llamada nueva y se olvida del fixture, el fallo le dice exactamente qué falta en lugar de quedarse colgado hasta el timeout.

Esa suite pasó de unos 40 minutos (casi todo reintentos y esperas) a menos de uno. Las llamadas al sandbox desde CI bajaron a cero y el cargo extra desapareció de la factura.

Durante cinco semanas pensé que habíamos terminado.

Dónde me equivoqué

El proveedor cambió su endpoint de tarifas. El campo amount, un decimal en euros, pasó a ser amount_cents, un entero. Lo anunciaron en un correo de novedades que llegó a un buzón compartido que nadie lee.

Nuestros fixtures seguían teniendo amount. Nuestros tests seguían pasando. Claro que pasaban: estaban probando contra una foto de la API de hacía mes y medio.

En producción, rate.amount llegó como undefined. El checkout mostró el envío como "NaN €" durante unas tres horas de un día laborable, hasta que nos llegó un ticket de soporte.

Eso fue culpa mía. Traté los fixtures como algo terminado cuando en realidad son una caché, y las cachés caducan. Un mock te dice que tu código maneja bien una respuesta concreta. No te dice nada sobre si esa respuesta sigue existiendo.

La comprobación nocturna

La solución no fue tirar el mock. Fue añadir un job pequeño que, una vez cada noche, compara la forma del fixture con lo que devuelve el sandbox en ese momento. Gasta un puñado de llamadas, no 180 por push.

// check-drift.js (Node 18+, usa fetch global)
const fixture = require('./fixtures/rates-ok.json');

function keys(obj, prefix = '') {
  return Object.entries(obj).flatMap(([k, v]) =>
    v && typeof v === 'object' && !Array.isArray(v)
      ? keys(v, `${prefix}${k}.`)
      : [`${prefix}${k}`]
  );
}

(async () => {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.SANDBOX_URL}/v1/rates`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANDBOX_KEY}`,
      'content-type': 'application/json',
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ from: '28001', to: '08001', weight_g: 500 }),
  });

  const liveKeys = keys(await res.json());
  const missing = keys(fixture).filter((k) => !liveKeys.includes(k));

  if (missing.length) {
    console.error('el fixture tiene campos que la API ya no devuelve:', missing);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  console.log('el fixture coincide con la API real');
})();

Es tosco. Solo mira nombres de campos, no tipos, y trata los arrays como hojas. Pero habría detectado el cambio de amount a la mañana siguiente, y ese era el listón. Corre a las 2 de la madrugada y avisa por Slack si falla.

Lo que le diría a un compañero que empieza hoy

Graba los fixtures desde respuestas reales. No los escribas a mano a partir de la documentación. La documentación miente más que los sandboxes.

Mantén el mock tonto. En cuanto empieza a tener lógica ("si el peso supera 10 kg devuelve este otro fixture") estás manteniendo una segunda versión, peor, de la API del proveedor. Si de verdad necesitas respuestas que dependan del estado o de la petición, eso ya es simulación de APIs y conviene tratarlo como un proyecto aparte, no como un if más dentro del mock.

Yo no mockearía todo. La base de datos, por ejemplo, la sigo levantando de verdad en un contenedor, porque ahí los mocks esconden justo los fallos que más duelen.

Y ponle nombre y apellido al correo de novedades del proveedor. Ese correo fue la causa real del incidente, y ninguna herramienta arregla un buzón que nadie abre.

El mock nos dio velocidad. La comprobación nocturna nos devolvió la confianza que habíamos entregado sin darnos cuenta para conseguirla.

title: Toward Universal Translatability: On the Statistical Ontology of Generative AI
description:
arXiv:2611.17963v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper argues that the problem of translation functions both as a point of origin and as a normative horizon for contemporary generative AI. In current discourse around ''world models,'' their attainment is framed as the achievement of internal consistency, cross-modal alignment, and physical grounding. Taken together, these demands converge on an ideal of the model as a universal translation machine capable of establishing lossless correspondences across linguistic, visual, and physical representation spaces. I show that this ideal presupposes a metaphysical commitment that I call a statistical ontology: the belief that reality has an underlying, computable statistical structure that can be recovered through sufficient data and modeling, rather than being shaped and accessed through situated human interpretation and labor. Tracing this commitment back to Warren Weaver's 1949 Memorandum on machine translation, I outline how translation was historically recast as code deciphering and, later, as the alignment of probability distributions across structured outputs. Finally, I contrast this paradigm with approaches in Translation Studies that foreground opacity, power asymmetries, and the translator's positionality. I argue that generative AI's statistical ontology is pre-Kantian, pre-critical and obscures the infrastructures and human labor that make machine translatability---as alignment---possible in the first place.

title: Build cache size limit on Vercel increased to 5 GB
description:
The build cache size limit on all Vercel build machines has been increased to 5 GB. This allows projects to save more installed dependencies and framework files for reuse between deployments, which can reduce install and build times.

Build machines are the compute environments that install dependencies and build your project before deployment. Previously, caches were discarded if they exceeded 1.5 GB on Basic and Standard, 3 GB on Enhanced, or 4.75 GB on Turbo, leaving the next build without a cache.

The change applies automatically across all build machine types at no additional charge, with no configuration required.

Learn more in the build cache documentation.

title: YouTube transcript APIs: existing captions or speech-to-text
description:
Choose an existing-caption API when you need the text and timestamps already published on YouTube. Choose a service with documented speech-to-text fallback when videos without captions must still yield text, and budget for minutes rather than assuming one cheap request. Official YouTube captions require video-management permission; a self-hosted library shifts operations to you. The hosted APIs below differ in both missing-track behavior and billing.

Provider Text source and timestamps Entry price and unit Free or trial When to choose it
YouTube Data API captions (official) Authorized caption-track download; the caller must be allowed to edit the video. Timed subtitle formats, not arbitrary public-video access or STT. 200 quota units per captions.download call; not a USD-per-1,000 tariff. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC Uses the project’s API quota; not a transcript trial package. Owners or authorized managers downloading their own caption tracks.
youtube-transcript-api (jdepoix) Self-hosted Python library reading existing manual or YouTube-generated tracks; timed snippets. No hosted STT fallback. Open-source software: $0 license fee; your compute and any proxy costs are separate. Not directly comparable to hosted requests. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC No SaaS trial; run it yourself. Teams comfortable operating extraction and handling blocked cloud IPs.
Supadata Existing transcripts with timestamps; AI speech recognition fallback when captions are absent. Basic: $5/month equivalent, billed $60/year, 300 credits/month. Existing transcript: 1 credit; generated: 2 credits/video minute. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC Free: 100 credits/month; generated minutes consume that budget faster than existing-track requests. Applications that need text even when no caption track exists and can budget for STT.
TranscriptAPI Transcript JSON with or without timestamps. Public pages checked do not establish whether missing captions trigger STT. Monthly: $5 for 1,000 credits; 1 transcript = 1 successful request = 1 credit. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC 100 free trial credits, no card required. A simple successful-request allowance; confirm missing-caption behavior if it is essential.
Captapi Existing captions: its FAQ says missing tracks return 404 no_captions, charged 0 credits. Transcript timestamp fields were not established by the public pages checked. Starter: $9/month for 2,000 credits. Transcript-specific credits/request not verified; do not read this as 2,000 transcripts. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC 100 lifetime credits after email verification; not a monthly refill. Teams using its wider API catalog and accepting an explicit no-captions failure.
FlashData YouTube Data Transcript defaults to YouTube automatic captions; Captions defaults to uploader tracks. Both return timed text. No generated transcription, translation or source fallback. PAYG: $0.50/1,000 standard requests; no monthly fee. Source · 2026-11-15 UTC Shared new-account trial credits; failed requests are not billed. Applications needing existing tracks with explicit source selection and timestamp segments.

FlashData’s Google Search and YouTube Download are separate products sharing the account key. Download bytes are not the billing unit for the YouTube Data row above.

An automatic YouTube caption is still an existing track

“Automatic” can describe text YouTube has already generated, or a provider generating new text from audio now. These are different operations. The jdepoix library reads available manual or generated tracks and supports YouTube-provided translations. Google’s authorized captions.download also has a translation parameter. Neither fact means FlashData translates or generates a missing track.

For FlashData, Transcript selects automatic captions by default and Captions selects uploader captions by default. The auto parameter explicitly selects the source; the API does not silently switch sources. Both return timestamp segments and full text. If the requested track or language does not exist, there is no STT fallback.

When missing captions must still produce text

Supadata explicitly documents AI speech recognition through the same endpoint when captions are absent. Its generated-transcript unit is video minutes, while existing-transcript retrieval uses credits per request. Its pricing page gives a 100-credit monthly free budget; a product-page phrase of “100 requests/month” should not be read as 100 arbitrarily long generated transcripts.

Captapi documents a no_captions error rather than an automatic transcription fallback. TranscriptAPI’s public pricing and examples establish timestamps and one-credit successful requests, but did not establish its no-caption policy in this review. If this behavior determines your choice, ask for the endpoint’s documented behavior instead of inferring it from “transcript API.”

Keep quota, request fees and usage rights separate

The official YouTube captions API requires OAuth authorization and permission to edit the video. Its 200 quota units are not a dollar rate and cannot be converted into a hosted API’s price per 1,000 requests without inventing an exchange rate. For self-hosted youtube-transcript-api, operating costs and cloud-IP blocks belong to the caller.

FlashData Extended Search has a different rate from standard YouTube Data requests and is unrelated to retrieving a transcript. A license check reports whether a video is labeled Creative Commons; it does not grant training rights. Trial credits are shared across the account. A job marked failed is not billed; a client timeout alone does not prove that the job failed.

Implementation after selection

For FlashData, read the Supadata comparison, JavaScript transcript tutorial, caption-language guide, Transcript reference and Captions reference.

Where the numbers come from

All prices are in USD. Official pages were checked on 2026-11-15 UTC. This is a vendor-document comparison published by FlashData, not an independent performance benchmark.

  • YouTube captions.download: authorization, edit permission, subtitle formats and 200 quota units.
  • youtube-transcript-api README: open-source library, existing tracks, translation and IP-blocking behavior.
  • Supadata pricing and YouTube transcript product: annual-billed Basic allowance, existing-track credits and generated minutes.
  • TranscriptAPI: monthly credits, trial and timestamp example; no verified STT price.
  • Captapi pricing and FAQ: credits, lifetime trial and no_captions behavior; transcript-specific credit cost not verified.
  • FlashData pricing, Transcript and Captions: standard data requests and existing timed tracks only.

Originally published at FlashData.

title: Microsoft 365 Is Back After a 38-Hour Global Outage — What Happened
description:
For nearly two working days, the world's most-used office suite was limping. Microsoft has confirmed Microsoft 365 is fully restored after an outage that lasted close to 38 hours and reached more than 70 countries.

The first signs appeared in Exchange Online on November 12 at about 16:17 UTC. From there, the problems spread to Outlook, Teams, Copilot and SharePoint. Full restoration landed on November 14 at 06:09 UTC, per Microsoft's confirmation, with coverage from Digital Trends, Financial Express, The Hindu and KeyXplore across November 14–15.

What caused it? According to Microsoft, an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade surfaced after a network change. The company has ruled out a cyberattack — and, notably, ruled out AI agents as the trigger. This one was an internal change that went sideways.

There's a particular sting in that cause, too. A capacity upgrade is supposed to make a network stronger. When the upgrade itself becomes the fault, it shows how fragile tightly coupled systems can be — one change, and services on every continent wobble.

Why does it matter? Thirty-eight hours is an eternity for tools that sit at the centre of the workday. Email queues stall, meetings slide, shared files stay out of reach, and staff improvise with personal accounts — a workaround with its own security headaches. Big organisations feel it; small ones, with no fallback plan, feel it more.

The uncomfortable question isn't whether Microsoft fixed it — they did. It's how many companies discovered, mid-outage, that one vendor held their mail, meetings, files and AI tools all at once. Concentration like that is convenient right up until it isn't.

A few practical moves cost little: keep a secondary channel for reaching customers, bookmark the official service health page instead of trusting rumours, and test your fallback before you need it. None of that requires leaving Microsoft 365. It just requires admitting that even the biggest cloud can have a very bad day.

My full breakdown — the timeline, Microsoft's explanation, and what businesses should change before the next outage — is on Rohan Tech Official: Microsoft 365 Fully Restored After a 38-Hour Outage Across 70 Countries

Outages this long are rare. The dependence they reveal isn't.

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

title: I replaced my budget app with a 16-page PDF
description:
Every budget app I tried wanted a subscription and a category tree before it would show me one useful number. So I built the version I actually wanted: one printable PDF, a pen, and ten minutes a week.

The Quiet Money Planner is 16 US Letter pages. It does not connect to your bank, does not ask for an email, and does not tell you what you should want. It gives you one place to write down what comes in, what goes out, and what you decide to do about the difference.

What is on the pages:

  • money in: expected and irregular income
  • fixed costs and variable costs, planned vs actual
  • the gap between in and out, with three decision prompts
  • a 31-day bill calendar
  • debt list and payoff order
  • sinking funds for known future costs
  • a weekly spending log and a no-spend week tracker
  • a subscription audit
  • a month review and a one-page year view

It is black and white with a green accent, so it photocopies cleanly. One PDF, print-ready, also readable on a tablet.

What it is not: not financial advice, not a promise that you will save a particular amount, not a bank connection, and not a course. If you have debt, tax or investment questions, talk to a qualified adviser.

I made it with reportlab, mostly because I wanted to see whether a paper tool could be simpler than the apps I kept abandoning. The numbers on the pages are yours; the workbook only asks the questions.

The Quiet Money Planner is $14: https://itfabers.lemonsqueezy.com/checkout/buy/971ae8d5-bc70-4140-9027-a66d84246380
