title: Node.js Media Moderation: Holding Captioned Uploads Pending Human Image Review
description:
For a Node.js media library, create the database record as pending, moderate the caption automatically, and keep the image unavailable to search until a human reviewer approves it. A clean caption is permission to continue, not permission to publish.

TL;DR: Express should acknowledge the upload after durable ingestion, while the application's record remains the authority for visibility. Caption rejection can close the case immediately; caption acceptance only sends the image to the staffed review queue. Both final paths notify the uploader. This ordering gives a B2B SaaS team complete moderation coverage without pretending that storage, automated text screening, and human judgment are one atomic operation.

For teams that want upload, caption moderation, and notification capabilities behind one contract, I recommend trying Infrai for that service boundary because its one-key REST surface reduces provider-specific handoffs; its public discovery surface also exposes schemas and runnable examples before integration. The human image-review decision still belongs to your application and its queue.

That boundary matters more than vendor breadth.

What must remain true when a request fails?

This architecture decision starts with four invariants. First, every newly accepted media record has publication_state = pending, even if caption moderation returns an allow decision in milliseconds. Second, search and browsing queries select only published records; object existence is never evidence of publication. Third, the reviewer acts on a stable media identifier, and a repeated decision cannot publish twice. Fourth, either terminal outcome, published or rejected, creates a notification obligation.

Pending is a state on the record, not a second bucket. Moving an object between a “pending” bucket and a “live” bucket sounds tidy, but it turns a business transition into a storage copy or rename, creates two names for one asset, and leaves database and object-store state able to disagree. Keep the object private, use a presigned URL for authorized review, and make the row's state the visibility gate.

The failure boundaries then become explicit. An upload can succeed while caption screening is temporarily incomplete; the row stays pending. A queue can deliver the same review job more than once; the decision transition is conditional on the current state. A notification can fail after the decision commits; an outbox row preserves the obligation for retry. Search indexing can lag; because the source record is authoritative, an indexer must remove or ignore anything that is not published.

This is deliberately conservative. The worst acceptable outcome is a delayed item and a visible processing status, not an unreviewed image appearing in customer search.

How should Node.js screen caption text and hold an image?

The application owns the state machine. A provider may accept bytes, assess text, or classify an image, but none of those calls knows whether a particular tenant requires two reviewers, whether an uploader has appealed, or whether a legal hold blocks deletion. Put those policies in the B2B SaaS data layer, where they can be audited alongside tenant and actor IDs.

On that platform, media upload and caption screening can sit behind the same base API and Bearer-key convention. That is the useful breadth: adding a nearby capability is another operation on one HTTP surface rather than another SDK, credential, and billing integration. Infrai exposes one REST API over plain HTTP, with no SDK to install, from any language or runtime. For an Express service, that removes a provider package and its release cycle from the upload path. The API is also genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. Discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules and provides request and response schemas plus runnable examples in 10 languages. An adapter can inspect the contract before it accepts production traffic, which removes a specific source of integration drift around field names. Those numbers describe interface coverage, not moderation accuracy, latency, or uptime.

Do not send an image to public storage while it waits. The upload must remain private or signed-only, and the reviewer should receive a short-lived presigned URL; a provider authorization header belongs on API requests, never on the returned storage URL. In Express, validate media type and size before dispatch, persist the pending row and outbox work in a transaction, then return an accepted response with the media ID and current state. The exact JSON body for a provider call should be generated from its discovery schema rather than guessed from prose.

Which moderation service fits this boundary?

The honest comparison is about ownership and coverage, not a universal winner. Automated image classifiers may help prioritize or pre-screen the human queue, but the stated policy still requires a staffed image decision.

There is no universal winner.

Option Useful boundary in this design What the application still owns Better fit when
Infrai One REST contract for upload, caption screening, and adjacent notification work Pending state, reviewer queue, image decision, search visibility, and notification outbox Integration breadth and a consistent surface matter more than a dedicated media-delivery control plane
Cloudinary Managed media upload, transformation, and delivery Caption policy, durable workflow state, reviewer UX, final publication, and notifications Existing Cloudinary asset workflows and delivery features are the larger concern
imgix Image rendering and delivery from connected sources Ingestion policy, caption screening, human review, durable state, and notifications URL-driven image processing and delivery are already the architectural center
ImageKit Media upload, optimization, transformation, and delivery Review policy, queue semantics, publication state, and uploader communication A dedicated media pipeline is preferred over a broad backend capability surface

No row in this table eliminates application orchestration. Cloudinary, imgix, and ImageKit are stronger candidates when media transformation and delivery are the center of the platform decision and adopting a specialist media integration is acceptable. The unified option is more coherent here when the desired boundary spans several backend capabilities, while human reviewers remain the authority for images.

Its limitation is equally concrete: Infrai is not a fit when the team needs a specialist media-delivery control plane or expects a provider to own the human-review operation. Choose the specialist whose documented delivery model matches that requirement, or build the review operation separately. A consistent API does not erase product boundaries.

The missing comparison metric is accuracy on your own media. Vendor category names are not a substitute for an evaluation set. Before replacing or prioritizing human review, test representative tenant uploads, document false-positive and false-negative tolerances, and decide which classes are allowed to defer, escalate, or reject. Without that evidence, any accuracy ranking would be invented.

The critical path is one conditional state transition

The following runnable Python example performs one narrow but important provider-integration step: it fetches the live schema for POST /v1/image/upload before an adapter is implemented, with an explicit method, environment-based Bearer authentication, status checks, and bounded 429 retry handling. It then models the state transition that must survive framework changes: mandatory pending status for an accepted caption, idempotent human decisions, and an outbox event for both outcomes. The same conditional update belongs inside the Node.js transaction used by an Express handler. Schema discovery is used here because the contract does not justify inventing an upload body.

import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum
from typing import Callable


class State(str, Enum):
    PENDING = "pending"
    PUBLISHED = "published"
    REJECTED = "rejected"


@dataclass
class Media:
    media_id: str
    uploader_id: str
    caption: str
    state: State = State.PENDING
    outbox: list[dict[str, str]] = field(default_factory=list)


def fetch_upload_schema() -> dict:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/image.upload"

    for attempt in range(4):
        request = urllib.request.Request(
            url,
            method="GET",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
        )
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            if error.code == 429 and attempt < 3:
                retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
                delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
                time.sleep(delay)
                continue
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            raise RuntimeError(f"Provider returned HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error

    raise RuntimeError("Schema request exhausted its retry budget")


def ingest(media: Media, caption_is_allowed: Callable[[str], bool]) -> Media:
    if not caption_is_allowed(media.caption):
        media.state = State.REJECTED
        media.outbox.append({
            "event": "media.rejected",
            "media_id": media.media_id,
            "recipient": media.uploader_id,
        })
    return media


def record_review(media: Media, approved: bool) -> Media:
    if media.state is not State.PENDING:
        return media  # Duplicate delivery cannot apply the decision twice.

    media.state = State.PUBLISHED if approved else State.REJECTED
    media.outbox.append({
        "event": "media.approved" if approved else "media.rejected",
        "media_id": media.media_id,
        "recipient": media.uploader_id,
    })
    return media


if __name__ == "__main__":
    schema = fetch_upload_schema()
    assert schema["method"] == "POST"
    assert schema["path"] == "/v1/image/upload"

    item = Media("media_1042", "user_77", "Quarterly product demo")
    ingest(item, caption_is_allowed=lambda caption: bool(caption.strip()))
    assert item.state is State.PENDING
    record_review(item, approved=True)
    record_review(item, approved=True)
    assert item.state is State.PUBLISHED
    assert len(item.outbox) == 1
    print(schema["id"], item.state.value, item.outbox[0]["event"])

Production code needs a database constraint or compare-and-set update, not merely the in-memory guard shown here. A useful SQL condition is conceptually “update this media ID only where state is pending”; zero changed rows means another worker already decided it. The decision and outbox insert must commit together. Delivery from the outbox may be at least once, so the notification consumer should deduplicate on the event ID rather than assume a queue message is unique.

Notice what is absent: the object is not copied on approval.

Publication changes one controlled state, then the search indexer reacts. That gives operators a single row to inspect when a user asks why item media_1042 is not searchable. More importantly, it prevents an awkward partial failure: if a copy completed but the row update did not, an object could occupy the “live” namespace while the application still called it pending; if the row changed first and the copy failed, search could point at bytes that were not there. One private object plus one authoritative row removes both split-brain cases from the publication transition.

Why reject publish-after-caption, and when is it valid?

The rejected design publishes as soon as automated caption moderation allows the text, then asks a person to inspect the image later. It has a shorter apparent path to search, but it fails the governing requirement: the image was never approved. A later rejection also becomes a takedown problem, with cached search results and notifications potentially advertising content that policy says should never have appeared.

There is a valid use case for that design. If a product explicitly permits post-publication sampling, accepts the exposure window, and has a documented takedown process, immediate publication can trade moderation coverage for lower latency. It is not the decision described here.

The other tempting design is to block the Express request until a reviewer responds. Reject it too. Human latency does not belong inside an HTTP request deadline, and a dropped client connection must not cancel durable review work. Return the media ID with pending, expose that state to the uploader, and send a notification after approval or rejection.

No guessing.

For this workload, the final decision rule is stable: store privately, screen the caption, hold the record, review the image, commit one terminal transition, then notify and index. If that division of responsibility fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and obtain current request schemas from discovery before implementing the provider adapter.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • Cloudinary documentation
  • imgix documentation
  • ImageKit documentation

title: HEX to Pantone is a guess: making color conversion honest in an interface
description:
Every color tool eventually ships the same sentence: closest Pantone match. It sounds authoritative, and almost every implementation behind it is an approximation. That gap between the confident label and the actual math is worth designing around, because someone will print a business card from whatever your UI claims.

Three different conversions are hiding under one button

A HEX value is an sRGB triplet with a defined transfer curve. RGB to CMYK conversion is device dependent: the real answer depends on the press, the ink set, the substrate and the ICC profile used to separate the file. Without a profile you have a formula, not a measurement. A CMYK-to-Pantone lookup is a different approximation again, because Pantone references are ink recipes and physical swatches, not RGB values.

So a converter that says "this CMYK is that Pantone" is guessing at two levels. That is fine as long as the interface says so.

Distance is the part most tools skip

If you map a color to a reference library, you have to rank candidates by something. Euclidean distance in raw RGB is convenient and visibly wrong: two colors that differ by the same RGB amount do not look equally different. Converting to CIELAB first and measuring with CIEDE2000 gets much closer to perceived difference, which matters most in the greens and blues where sRGB is coarsest.

Here is the shape of the pipeline in plain terms:

  1. Parse the input into sRGB (or take CMYK percentages as given).
  2. Convert sRGB to XYZ under a D65 white point.
  3. Convert XYZ to CIELAB.
  4. Measure CIEDE2000 against every candidate reference.
  5. Return the nearest match together with the distance, not just the name.

That last step is the honest one. A nearest neighbor with a distance of 1.2 and one with a distance of 8 are not the same answer, and the user deserves to know which they got.

Design rules that keep the UI truthful

  • Show the distance. "Nearest reference, ΔE 3.4" is information. "Exact match" is a lie unless it is one.
  • Separate coated and uncoated. They are different swatch books and they produce different nearest references. Collapsing them into one answer creates a wrong answer for half the users.
  • Keep the input reproducible. If a row in a chart shows a match, link to the converter state that produced it, so the number can be checked instead of trusted.
  • State the limits in the interface, not only in a footnote. CMYK without a profile, digital approximations of a licensed library, and the need for a physical proof all belong next to the result.

What this looks like in practice

I built HueConvert around those rules: a free converter that takes HEX, RGB, CMYK or HSL, returns the other formats, and shows the nearest Pantone coated and uncoated reference with the CIEDE2000 distance attached. The three tool pages carry printable charts of 139 references each, and every row links back to the exact input that produced it. No account, no upload, and the charts render without JavaScript.

Disclosure: I operate HueConvert. It is free, has no paid placement, and this post is a write-up of the conversion decisions, not a launch announcement.

The takeaway

Color conversion is a chain of approximations. The engineering work is not pretending otherwise; it is choosing the least misleading approximation, exposing the distance, and making the result reproducible. Users forgive an approximate answer that is labeled as approximate. They do not forgive a confident one that ruins a print run.

title: Classification with Large-Step Gradient Descent: Unifying Self-Stabilization and Convergence Rates
description:
arXiv:2611.17459v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural networks are often trained with gradient descent (GD) using step sizes that exceed classical stability thresholds, a regime where standard convergence theory no longer applies. Despite exhibiting non-monotonic loss and oscillatory dynamics, this regime frequently leads to faster convergence and better generalization. Existing theoretical perspectives offer complementary but incomplete insights: one identifies a self-stabilization mechanism that drives GD toward flat regions but does not yield convergence rates; another derives rigorous rates for specific losses but does not explain the underlying stabilization mechanism; and a third unifies these views for overparameterized least squares, but relies on the existence of a minimizer manifold, which is absent in classification settings. In this work, we extend this unified geometric perspective to exponential-tail losses, including logistic and cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, where the loss infimum is not attained at any finite parameter. We identify a curvature-defined reference subspace that replaces the role of the minimizer manifold, yielding a coupled dynamical system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by parallel progress along directions of decreasing sharpness. Under regularity conditions, which we verify for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses on symmetric data models, we derive explicit bounds for the iterates, not just the loss, covering both the unstable and stable regimes, and revealing a three-phase damping structure in the latter. Our analysis further uncovers a transient implicit bias induced by large step sizes: although GD converges asymptotically to the max-margin direction, large steps can leave persistent orthogonal residuals and, in certain geometries, amplify them, affecting finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.

title: DRA-HTR: Disentangling Representation and Adaptation for Handwritten Text Recognition
description:
arXiv:2611.18143v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Handwritten text recognition (HTR), particularly when applied to historical documents, remains challenging due to the scarcity of annotated data and the substantial domain shifts caused by variations in handwriting styles, document degradation, acquisition conditions, and linguistic characteristics. While large amounts of unlabeled target-domain data are often available, effectively exploiting them requires adaptation strategies tailored to the specific requirements of HTR. We propose DRA-HTR, an unsupervised generative domain adaptation pipeline specifically designed for HTR and built upon the DRANet framework. The proposed approach combines source-domain pretraining, unsupervised adaptation to the visual characteristics of the target domain, relying on the generation of target-style source samples for task-specific training. We further investigate the integration of post-HTR correction to complement visual adaptation with language adaptation, relying on large language models, which we introduce as DRAL-HTR. The proposed framework is evaluated across seven HTR datasets spanning four languages, using a single set of hyperparameters for all source-target combinations. The recognition model achieves state-of-the-art performance on four datasets and competitive results on the remaining three. In addition, the proposed DRA-HTR establishes a new state-of-the-art for domain adaptation across all seven datasets and substantially improves overall robustness and training stability compared to the original DRANet framework: it reduces the Character Error Rate (CER) in average by 13.52 percentage points, and the average standard deviation decreases from 7.23 to 1.11 percentage points. Finally, post-HTR correction further reduces the CER by 2.16 percentage points.

title: CamSpokenNLI: A Pilot Resource for Cross-Variety Transfer Evaluation in Cameroon Pidgin English and Camfranglais
description:
arXiv:2611.17573v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cameroon Pidgin English (a West African Pidgin English variety) and Camfranglais are widely used in Cameroon, yet to our knowledge, neither has a dedicated spoken Natural Language Inference (NLI) resource. We introduce CamSpokenNLI, a pilot dataset of 114 scenario-matched spoken NLI items in each variety (228 in total), recorded by one native speaker from Buea. Each item pairs premise audio and text with a hypothesis, an NLI label, and English glosses. The author assigned labels, so the dataset is an exploratory resource rather than a mature benchmark. The NLI experiments use the reference text; the audio is evaluated separately. XLM-RoBERTa baselines with five-fold item-level cross-validation reach 44.7% on Pidgin and 46.2% on Camfranglais (chance 33.3%). Still, neither is statistically distinguishable from hypothesis-only input, so hypothesis wording may account for much of the accuracy. Under disjoint-item cross-variety transfer, where a test item's counterpart is never seen in training, accuracy is 40.1% (Pidgin to Camfranglais) and 45.6% (Camfranglais to Pidgin). A counterpart-leak audit raises this to 60-64%, illustrating how counterpart leakage can overstate transfer. Zero-shot Whisper transcription of the recordings performs poorly: the best word error rates are 66.6% for Pidgin and 45.5% for Camfranglais, and with automatic language identification, Whisper Large-v3 labels 93 of 114 Pidgin recordings as Yoruba or Swahili. Together, the results suggest that such resources need disjoint-item evaluation and hypothesis-only controls, and that speech recognition must be adapted to these varieties before spoken NLI can be tested end to end.

title: Cracks in Embeddings: Robustness and Stability of JEPA-Based Chest X-Ray Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.17905v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models are increasingly used for medical imaging, however there is a limited understanding about robustness of these models toward real-world image changes. We test four JEPA-based chest X-ray encoders, trained on 78,468 NIH ChestX-ray14 images, under six tests: two black-box adversarial attacks (SPSA, Boundary Attack), three image corruptions (Gaussian noise, brightness shift, contrast shift), and a label-scarcity test, measuring embedding change and classification AUROC. These perturbations cause severe, model-dependent damage: encoder-level Cosine Similarity drops as low as 0.33, and AUROC falls by as much as 0.12 in the worst case (I-JEPA under the Boundary Test). We test two ways of training the small predictor on top of each frozen encoder to address this. Adversarial fine-tuning, trained on clean and perturbed images together, raises embedding consistency above 0.97 in nearly every case and improves AUROC, relative to the same perturbed baseline, for most models, with the largest gain of $+0.10$ on I-JEPA. A Vector-Quantized codebook method, trained only on clean images and evaluated on perturbed test images for the first time, instead degrades under distortion for all four models, most noticeably for I-JEPA ($-0.15$ AUROC on average), showing that its discrete bottleneck alone does not provide the robustness that comes from training on perturbed data directly.

title: Identifying Latent Neural Dynamics with Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process Dynamical Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.17487v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural circuits are densely interconnected systems, and many neural computations are thought to be mediated by the dynamical evolution of activity within these recurrent networks, a hypothesis often referred to as "computation through dynamics". Under this view, understanding computation within real neural populations depends on building models of the dynamical rules governing the temporal evolution of recorded high-dimensional neural activity. Most commonly, such models depend on explicit generative parameterisations of (i) the (nonlinear) intrinsic dynamical flow field and stochasticity, (ii) the (nonlinear) mapping from dynamical state to neuronal activity, and (iii) the variability of individual neural responses given that dynamical state. Misspecification of any of these components can bias estimates of dynamics and latent trajectories. In this paper, we circumvent generation-related issues by introducing the Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process dynamics (RP-GPdyn) model. RP-GPdyn models the dynamical flow field using a nonparametric Gaussian Process-defined transition function and models the relationship of dynamics to neural activity implicitly using the Recognition-Parametrised Model (RPM) framework. We show that this generation-free approach uncovers meaningful, behaviourally relevant latent variables and dynamics from both synthetic and experimental datasets.

title: FlexCast: Flexible Context Learning for Time Series Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2611.17862v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) based on autoregressive (AR) next-token prediction entangle two factors: variable-context conditioning and prediction-unit factorization with autoregressive rollout. Strong AR performance therefore does not reveal whether generalization stems from the flexible training distribution, the local prediction target, the left-to-right inference process, or their combination. We propose FlexCast, a flexible context-target learning framework that disentangles these factors. FlexCast reformulates forecasting as variable-length masked prediction over time series patches: during pretraining, it dynamically samples visible context and masked target patches, exposing the model to diverse context-target configurations without sequential decoding. At inference time, the same pretrained model supports one-step forecasting, confidence-based iterative refinement, and next-token-style generation through a unified mask-and-predict interface, enabling controlled comparison of inference schedules under identical architecture, data, and objective. Evaluated on BLAST and multiple zero-shot benchmarks, FlexCast achieves accuracy competitive with or better than strong TSFM baselines while substantially reducing inference latency. Ablations confirm that context diversity and contiguous target masking drive performance, while left-to-right decoding does not yield consistent gains once flexible context-target relationships have been learned, suggesting that the key benefit of AR-style TSFMs lies in flexible training rather than sequential inference. The code is available at https://github.com/BenchCouncil/FlexCast.

title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
description:
arXiv:2611.17630v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture requires resolving localized crack bands whose paths are unknown in advance and thermal boundary layers whose thickness evolves during the transient. Neural energy-based computations of thermal fracture have so far started from defects placed in advance. This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method based on multiresolution neural representations that predicts spontaneous crack nucleation, crack spacing, and selective crack propagation and arrest under transient thermal loading. Two networks, each with its own multiresolution encoding, represent the displacement and phase fields and the transient temperature, and the mechanical energy and the incremental functional of the backward Euler heat equation are estimated on integration points redrawn at every iteration. Restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying the optimizer state across load steps and decaying the learning rates within each step help prevent spurious damage accumulation. On two notched plates the initiation peak loads agree closely with an independent finite element reference. On a quenched glass strip under an analytical temperature field the crack path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched, with an oscillation threshold close to the linear stability prediction. Under a prescribed boundary temperature a quenched ceramic slab forms a crack array of the type observed in experiment, with a spacing close to that of a published benchmark. On the slab and a quenched annulus the arrays are denser than those of a finite element computation on the same material field. No crack paths, nucleation sites or crack-adapted meshes are prescribed.

title: ERGo: Energy-Efficient Hybrid Graph Neural Network Training on Processing-In-Memory Architectures
description:
arXiv:2611.17478v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Processing-in-memory (PIM) has been proposed as an alternative computing paradigm for training Deep Neural Networks, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Despite these advancements, training GNN workloads on PIM devices necessitates off-chip memory access. This off-chip access is expensive in terms of performance and energy, thereby impacting the overall energy efficiency of the training process on PIM platforms. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid training framework called ERGo that automatically switches from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase during the training process with negligible loss in predictive accuracy. The parameter-efficient phase employs low-rank representations of GNN weights, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters. This helps in reducing the off-chip access during the end-to-end training process on PIM architectures, leading to notable improvements in both performance and energy efficiency. ERGo outperforms the conventional full-parameter GNN training on a PIM-based platform by up to 3.15x in speedup and enhances energy efficiency by 10.5x. Furthermore, ERGo offers additional advantages when utilized on heterogeneous architectures incorporating non-volatile memory (NVM) and static random-access memory (SRAM). Training on the heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture typically utilizes NVM for the forward-pass and SRAM for the backward-pass. However, NVM cells suffer from low device endurance and repeated write operations due to weight updates can lead to poor lifetime. ERGo improves the lifetime of NVM devices by freezing the weights and preventing weight updates in the parameter-efficient phase. Experimental results demonstrate that ERGo improves the lifetime of heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture by up to 33x in comparison to full-parameter implementation.

title: What Do Multilingual Self-Supervised Speech Encoders Know About Sentence Meaning?
description:
arXiv:2611.17686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) have been scaled up to thousands of languages and millions of hours of audio, yet little is known about how these models structure semantic knowledge across languages. In this work, we probe sentence-level semantics in massively multilingual S3Ms across 76 languages, using linear maps from frozen speech representations into a frozen text embedding space, evaluated by cross-modal retrieval. Sentence meaning is linearly accessible but highly uneven across languages and resource tiers. Cross-lingual probes can match language-specific probes on languages never seen in probe training, but per-model monolingual decodability does not predict transfer. Within the OmniASR wav2vec family, scaling from 300M--7B disproportionately benefits high-resource languages, and ASR tuning sharply improves semantic decodability while making representations more language-specific. However, semantic content is entangled with acoustics, inflating apparent performance on single-speaker corpora.

title: Ampersand from Humans& now available on AI Gateway
description:
Ampersand from Humans& is now available on AI Gateway for free through November 13, 2026.

Ampersand is a model for group conversations. Humans& built Ampersand on Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3 and trained it with reinforcement learning in simulated group conversations that run for up to months of simulated time. Most chat models are built for one person asking a question and the model answering it. Ampersand is trained to take part in a conversation between several people. It reads every message, including the ones not addressed to it, and after each one it decides whether to reply or stay quiet.

It is designed to understand individual and shared goals, help people work through disagreements, and recognize when a contribution would be useful. That can mean asking a clarifying question, sharing relevant context, or waiting while people respond to one another.

For example:

Sam: Heads up, I'm out Friday, driving to my sister's. Alex: Have a good trip! Maya: Let's do the launch rehearsal Friday at 10 with all three of us. Ampersand: Quick flag, Maya: Sam said he's out Friday driving to his sister's, so a Friday 10am rehearsal with all three probably won't work. Might be worth picking a different time so everyone can make it.

Your application exposes these actions as caller-defined function tools. send_message delivers a contribution, while pass leaves the conversation quiet until the next human message. Your application executes both tools and records their results.

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: Photogrammetric 3D Model-Based Animal Behavior Classification
description:
arXiv:2611.17881v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Video-based behavior estimation is often implemented end-to-end from image sequences. We advocate a two-stage alternative: reconstruct 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior. This makes ambiguities of the ill-posed 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. We demonstrate the strategy with simulated interacting mice and extend it to real video.

title: SWIFT: Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning of Time-Series Foundation Models for Forecasting
description:
arXiv:2611.17915v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While current few-shot adaptation strategies for time series forecasting foundation models are predominantly dataset-centric, the necessity of obtaining an additional dataset for the finetuning process poses a significant hurdle for adoption. To address this constraint, we propose Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a novel forecasting adaptation framework that achieves fine-grained specialization by leveraging structural priors from the target instance's own history. This shift allows the fine-tuning process to be entirely transparent to the end-user, which significantly enhances the ease of adoption. To implement this framework, SWIFT synergizes Self-Retrieval for historical mining and Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, while employing Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance adaptation with general knowledge preservation. Extensive experiments across four TSFM backbones and three long-history benchmark subsets validate SWIFT, yielding average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83% across 24 combinations of four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SWIFT is the first framework to investigate sample-wise instance fine-tuning of time-series foundation models, specializing the model for an individual prediction window using only the corresponding forecasting sample's own observed history.

title: Fractional Product Designer or Full-Time Hire? How to Decide
description:
Originally published on ayurchenko.xyz.

Hire a full-time product designer when there is design work every day and someone to lead it. Bring in a fractional one when the work is real but not daily, when you need senior judgment before you can justify a senior salary, or when a first version or a relaunch needs an owner for a few months. On independent designers’ published prices, part-time senior work costs $4,000 to $8,000 a month; one designer’s comparison estimates a full-time senior product designer in the US at $14,000 to $19,000 a month, and about three months to hire. The two buy different things, so the sums alone do not decide it.

Signs you need a fractional designer

  • A first version has to be defined, and nobody on the team has done it before.
  • The product works but has become hard to use and hard to change.
  • You are about to raise or launch, and the product has to look like the company it says it is.
  • Engineers ship every week, partly with coding agents, and nobody owns how the product behaves.
  • You need a senior person now, and a senior hire would take months to find.

Signs you need a full-time designer

  • There is design work every day, across several teams or products.
  • Research, design and the design system all need an owner at once.
  • Someone on the team can lead a designer, or the hire will lead others.
  • The product will be the company’s core for years, and the knowledge has to stay inside.

What each costs, and how fast it starts

Option Cost a month Before work starts
Fractional, part-time senior $4,000 to $8,000 on published prices Days, once the scope is agreed
Full-time senior product designer, US $14,000 to $19,000, by one designer’s estimate About three months to hire, by the same estimate
Design agency $15,000 to $40,000, by the same comparison Three to six weeks

The sources and the full price table: What a freelance product designer costs.

What you give up with each

  • Fractional: fewer hours, so usually one stream of work at a time; less time in the team’s daily conversations; and what the designer learns leaves with them unless it is written down.
  • Full-time: months to hire, a salary whether or not the work fills the week, and someone to manage. In return, every day of attention, several streams at once, and knowledge that stays in the company.

What a fractional designer should own

Not tickets. The product side: what goes into the next release and what waits, how the system behaves behind the screens, and what it looks like. If the person only takes requests, you are paying senior rates for production work.

  • A seat in planning, and a say in scope.
  • Access to the repository, so they can read what ships and, if they write code, fix it.
  • One design system, kept in code, that engineers and their coding agents build from.
  • A fixed number of days a week, agreed at the start and adjusted month to month.

How to make it work

  • Start with a small, fixed piece of work, like a one-week Product Diagnosis, so both sides know what the work is before committing to months.
  • Give one founder the job of deciding with the designer, so decisions do not wait for a meeting.
  • Review what shipped every week, not what was designed.
  • Write down what the designer owns and what they do not, so nothing falls between them and the engineers.

When to switch to full-time

When the fractional days are always full and the backlog keeps growing, or when the design work splits into several streams. A good fractional designer helps you write the job description and hire for it.

Questions founders ask

Is a fractional product designer cheaper than a full-time hire?

Per month, often: $4,000 to $8,000 for part-time senior work against $14,000 to $19,000 for a full-time senior designer in the US, by one designer’s estimate. But a full-time designer is there every day and what they learn stays with you, so compare what each would own.

How many days a week does a fractional designer work?

Whatever the stage needs: agreed at the start, adjusted month to month.

Can a fractional designer lead design for the company?

Yes, for a small team: decide, design and set the system. Once there are several designers to lead, hire a full-time lead.

What does fractional product design cost with you?

From $8,000 a month. See fractional product design.

Deciding on your first designer? Send a few lines about the product and the team. I’ll tell you which one I would pick in your place. Write to me through ayurchenko.xyz.

title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors
description:
arXiv:2611.18485v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.

title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
description:
arXiv:2611.17621v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.17917v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.

title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
description:
arXiv:2611.17564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

title: Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2611.17876v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal.

title: PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers
description:
arXiv:2611.17834v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As AI conference submissions grow rapidly, AI reviewers are being considered as an alternative. However, simply imitating human reviewing is problematic because reviewing serves multiple purposes, including evaluating papers' soundness, interestingness, and clarity, the last two of which are subjective. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating soundness, the most important and objective criterion, and define the learning objective as jointly maximizing (1) precision, based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points, and (2) recall, the coverage of high-quality reference review points. Under this problem formulation, we construct a quality-labeled review point dataset, PaperSound-23K, using 1K ICLR submissions and 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. Using this dataset, we train an AI reviewer model, PaperCritic, through reinforcement learning with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. Our experiments show that PaperCritic outperforms frontier models and models trained with other AI reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set. Surprisingly, learning to review ICLR submissions also transfers to reviewing Nature-family papers and even to out-of-domain reviewing tasks (e.g., code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing).

title: Pattern-Based Matrix Analysis Under Permutations
description:
arXiv:2611.17674v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-rank approximation captures one important notion of matrix simplicity: a matrix is simple if it is well described by a low-dimensional linear model. This paper studies a complementary notion. We consider matrices that become structurally simple only after permuting rows and columns, so that their mass concentrates in a prescribed geometric pattern such as a band, block-diagonal, arrowhead, or related form. We introduce a pattern distance that measures how close a matrix is to a given pattern after optimal reordering, giving a common framework for structural problems such as latent ordering, community detection, and bandwidth minimization. The problem is NP-hard in general; we derive an alternating algorithm based on Linear Assignment subproblems. We further introduce a pattern-plus-low-rank decomposition that combines permutation-structured fitting with a low-rank residual, whose permutation step is pattern fitting on the residual; its gains across pattern families persist at a matched parameter budget and are substantially reduced under a density-matched random-mask control. We evaluate the framework on synthetic recovery tasks, real correlation and graph adjacency matrices, and transformer attention heads, showing that a single universal algorithm recovers qualitatively different forms of matrix structure.

title: gspread APIError 429: Quota exceeded for 'Write requests per minute per user' (and the 3-layer fix)
description:
You loop over your data and write it to a Google Sheet, and after a few dozen calls:

gspread.exceptions.APIError: APIError: [429]: Quota exceeded for quota metric
'Write requests' and limit 'Write requests per minute per user' of service 'sheets.googleapis.com'

A time.sleep(1) did not fix it, or it fixed it and now the job takes hours. This is what is going on.

What Google counts

Google's Sheets API usage limits page lists, for both reads and writes: 300 requests per minute per project and 60 requests per minute per user per project. Read and write each have their own bucket. A batchUpdate request counts as one request, however many operations it contains. Google's advice for a 429 is exponential backoff. (Limits change, so check the page.)

Three consequences:

  • The unit is the request, not the cell. One cell and one 60,000-cell block both cost one request.
  • The binding limit for a script is usually the per-user one: 60 per minute. A service account counts as one user.
  • It is a speed limit per minute, not a ban. Without retry code a throttled job simply crashes.

The arithmetic

Writing a 5,000-row, 12-column table:

How you write it Requests Minimum time at 60/min
update_cell in a double loop 60,000 about 1,000 minutes
append_row in a loop 5,000 about 84 minutes
one block with ws.update 1 under a minute

Layer 1: make fewer requests (this fixes most 429s) 

import gspread

gc = gspread.service_account(filename="service_account.json")
ws = gc.open_by_key("YOUR_SHEET_ID").worksheet("Data")

rows = [["date", "usd"], ["2026-10-27", 1.115]]   # your whole table as a list of lists
ws.update(values=rows, range_name="A1", value_input_option="USER_ENTERED")   # one request

Note the argument order of gspread 6: values first, then the range. Also read once (ws.get_all_values()) and work in memory: every ws.cell() and ws.col_values() call is a request. To add rows below existing data in one request use ws.append_rows(rows, value_input_option="USER_ENTERED").

Layer 2: slow down on purpose

A well-batched job can still exceed 60 a minute when it touches many tabs. Keep a small sliding window and sleep when you are about to go over (55 calls per 60 seconds leaves headroom under the documented 60).

import time
from collections import deque

class PerMinuteLimiter:
    def __init__(self, max_calls=55, window=60):
        self.max_calls = max_calls
        self.window = window
        self.times = deque()

    def wait(self):
        now = time.monotonic()
        while self.times and now - self.times[0] >= self.window:
            self.times.popleft()
        if len(self.times) >= self.max_calls:
            time.sleep(self.window - (now - self.times[0]))
            return self.wait()
        self.times.append(time.monotonic())

limiter = PerMinuteLimiter()  # 55 calls per 60 seconds
# before every Sheets call: limiter.wait()

Layer 3: retry politely, with backoff and jitter 

import random, time, gspread

def call_with_backoff(fn, *args, tries=8, **kwargs):
    for n in range(tries):
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except gspread.exceptions.APIError as e:
            if e.code not in (429, 500, 502, 503, 504) or n == tries - 1:
                raise                                   # not retryable, or out of attempts
            time.sleep(min(2 ** n + random.random(), 64))

limiter.wait()
call_with_backoff(ws.update, values=rows, range_name="A1", value_input_option="USER_ENTERED")

Two details that matter:

  • Retry only what is worth retrying. A 403 "permission denied" or a 404 will never fix itself; retrying hides the real problem. e.code comes from the JSON error body; for a normal Sheets 429 it is the integer 429.
  • Wait longer than one quota window. A per-minute quota needs about a minute to recover. In my own test with one Cloud project, writes became possible again between under 10 and about 130 seconds after a burst (usually 40 to 60; about eight trials). A version that gave up after six retries (about 66 seconds in total) failed in three of those trials. Your numbers will differ, but eight retries with a 64-second cap is a safer default than three.

The jitter (the random.random()) stops many jobs from retrying at the same instant.

Estimate before you run

A job with more than about 50 requests per run needs a redesign, not more retries. Open the spreadsheet by ID (1 request), read each tab once, write each output block once, and put all formatting changes in one batchUpdate.
