title: Deploying a Containerized Web Application on AWS ECS Fargate using Terraform and AWS CodeBuild
description:
Table of Contents

Introduction
Business Requirements
Architecture
Pre-requisites
Implementation Steps in Words
Technical Implementation Steps
Pipeline Configuration
Key Benefits
Conclusion

1. Introduction

Modern application delivery demands speed, scalability, and reliability. Running workloads on traditional servers often introduces overhead — managing OS patches, scaling infrastructure manually, and dealing with environment inconsistencies between development and production.
This blog walks you through a fully automated, Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) driven deployment of a containerized web application on AWS ECS Fargate using Terraform and AWS CodeBuild. The entire infrastructure — from container registry to load balancer — is provisioned and torn down through automated pipelines, eliminating manual intervention and enabling repeatable deployments.
By the end of this guide, you will understand:

How to containerize a simple Apache web server using Docker
How to provision AWS ECS Fargate infrastructure using Terraform
How to automate the full deploy and destroy lifecycle using AWS CodeBuild buildspec files.

2. Business Requirements

Organizations moving to the cloud typically have the following non-negotiable requirements:

Requirement How This Project Addresses It
Zero server management AWS Fargate removes the need to provision or manage EC2 instances
Automated deployments AWS CodeBuild pipelines handle build, push, and deploy automatically
Cost control Infrastructure can be destroyed on demand using the destroy pipeline
High availability ECS service runs 2 task replicas across multiple private subnets
Security Containers run in private subnets; only the ALB is internet-facing
Centralized logging All container logs are shipped to AWS CloudWatch with KMS encryption
State management Terraform remote state is stored in S3 for team collaboration

3. Architecture

                        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │                        AWS Cloud (us-east-1)                 │
                        │                                                               │
   User Request         │   ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────┐  │
 ──────────────────────►│   │  Application  │        │        VPC (custom-vpc)       │  │
        Port 80         │   │ Load Balancer │        │                               │  │
                        │   │  (internet-  │        │  Public Subnets               │  │
                        │   │   facing)    │        │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │  │
                        │   │              │◄───────┤  │ public-1 │ │ public-2 │   │  │
                        │   │  SG: SG_LB   │        │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘   │  │
                        │   └──────┬───────┘        │                               │  │
                        │          │ Port 8080       │  Private Subnets              │  │
                        │          ▼                 │  ┌──────────────────────┐    │  │
                        │   ┌──────────────┐        │  │  ECS Fargate Service │    │  │
                        │   │  Target Group │        │  │  (desired count: 2)  │    │  │
                        │   │  (Ubuntu-tg)  │───────►│  │                      │    │  │
                        │   │  Health: /    │        │  │ ┌────────┐ ┌───────┐ │    │  │
                        │   └──────────────┘        │  │ │Task 1  │ │Task 2 │ │    │  │
                        │                            │  │ │Ubuntu  │ │Ubuntu │ │    │  │
                        │   ┌──────────────┐        │  │ │:8080   │ │:8080  │ │    │  │
                        │   │  Amazon ECR  │        │  │ └────────┘ └───────┘ │    │  │
                        │   │ (ubuntu-repo)│        │  │  SG: sg_ecs          │    │  │
                        │   └──────────────┘        │  └──────────────────────┘    │  │
                        │                            └──────────────────────────────┘  │
                        │   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐  │
                        │   │  CloudWatch  │   │   KMS Key    │   │   S3 (State)  │  │
                        │   │  Log Group   │   │ (Encryption) │   │  terraform-   │  │
                        │   └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘   │  state-files  │  │
                        │                                           └───────────────┘  │
                        └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Traffic Flow:

  • User sends an HTTP request to the ALB on port 80.

  • ALB listener forwards the request to the Target Group on port 8080.

  • Target Group routes traffic to one of the two ECS Fargate tasks running in private subnets.

  • The Ubuntu container responds with a dynamic hostname-based message
    Container logs are streamed to CloudWatch Logs, encrypted with KMS.

4. Pre-requisites

Before you can run this project, ensure the following AWS resources are already created in your account:

  • VPC named custom-vpc with public and private subnets tagged public-* and private-*.

  • Security Groups: SG_LB (for the load balancer) and sg_ecs (for ECS tasks).

  • IAM Roles: ecsTaskExecutionRole and ecsTaskRole with appropriate ECS permissions.

  • S3 Bucket: terraform-state-files-8759855 for Terraform remote state storage.

  • AWS CodeBuild Projects: One for deploy (deploybuildspec.yaml) and one for destroy (destroybuildspec.yaml)
    Docker must be enabled in the CodeBuild environment (use a build image that supports Docker)

5. Implementation Steps in Words

Here is the high-level journey from code commit to a live application:

Step 1 — Dockerize the Application
A simple Ubuntu-based Apache web server is containerized. The Dockerfile installs Apache, reconfigures it to listen on port 8080 (instead of the default 80), and serves a dynamic HTML page showing the container's hostname.

Step 2 — Define Infrastructure as Code
All AWS infrastructure is defined using Terraform across modular .tf files. Variables are cleanly separated from resource definitions, and all sensitive configuration lives in terraform.tfvars.

Step 3 — Provision ECR and Push Docker Image
The deploy pipeline first creates the ECR repository using a targeted Terraform apply, then builds the Docker image locally, authenticates to ECR, and pushes the image with the latest tag.

Step 4 — Provision Full AWS Infrastructure
With the image available in ECR, Terraform provisions the full stack: CloudWatch log group, KMS key, ECS cluster, task definition referencing the pushed image, ECS Fargate service, ALB, target group, and listener.

Step 5 — Application Goes Live
ECS pulls the container image from ECR and starts 2 task replicas in private subnets. The ALB distributes traffic across them. The application is accessible via the ALB DNS name.

Step 6 — Teardown on Demand
The destroy pipeline runs terraform destroy to cleanly remove all provisioned resources, ensuring no lingering costs.

6. Technical Implementation Steps

6.1 Dockerfile

FROM public.ecr.aws/docker/library/ubuntu:24.04

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y apache2 && apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN sed -i 's/80/8080/g' /etc/apache2/ports.conf

RUN sed -i 's/<VirtualHost \*:80>/<VirtualHost *:8080>/' /etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf

RUN echo "ServerName localhost" >> /etc/apache2/apache2.conf

CMD ["/bin/bash","-c","echo \"This is web server $(hostname)\" > /var/www/html/index.html && exec apache2ctl -D FOREGROUND"]

EXPOSE 8080

The Dockerfile starts from the official Ubuntu 24.04 image pulled from the public ECR gallery. It installs Apache2, then uses sed to reconfigure Apache's listening port from the default 80 to 8080 — both in ports.conf and the default virtual host config. At container startup, it dynamically writes the container's hostname into index.html, making it easy to verify load balancing by seeing different hostnames on page refresh. Apache runs in the foreground as the main container process.

6.2 Terraform/provider.tf — Backend & Provider Configuration

terraform {
    backend "s3" {
        bucket = "terraform-state-files-8759855"
        key    = "ecs.tfstate"
        region = "us-east-1"
    }
    required_providers {
        aws = {
            source  = "hashicorp/aws"
            version = "6.51.0"
        }
    }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}

This file does two critical things. First, it configures an S3 remote backend to store the Terraform state file (ecs.tfstate), which is essential for team collaboration and pipeline-based deployments — the state is never stored locally. Second, it pins the AWS provider to version 6.51.0, preventing unexpected breaking changes from provider upgrades. The region is kept dynamic via a variable.

6.3 Terraform/data.tf — Reading Existing AWS Resources

data "aws_vpc" "custom-vpc" {
  filter { name = "tag:Name"  values = ["custom-vpc"] }
}

data "aws_subnets" "public" {
  filter { name = "tag:Name"  values = ["public-*"] }
}

data "aws_subnets" "private" {
  filter { name = "tag:Name"  values = ["private-*"] }
}

data "aws_security_group" "sg_lb"  { name = "SG_LB" }
data "aws_security_group" "sg_ecs" { name = "sg_ecs" }

data "aws_iam_role" "task_exec" { name = "ecsTaskExecutionRole" }
data "aws_iam_role" "task_role" { name = "ecsTaskRole" }

Rather than recreating foundational resources like VPC, subnets, security groups, and IAM roles, this file uses Terraform data sources to reference resources that already exist in the AWS account. This follows the principle of separation of concerns — the networking layer is managed independently, and this project simply reads its outputs. Subnets are looked up by tag name pattern (public-, private-), making the code flexible across multi-AZ setups.

6.4 Terraform/ecr.tf — Amazon ECR Repository

resource "aws_ecr_repository" "ecr" {
  name                 = var.ecr_repo_name
  image_tag_mutability = "MUTABLE"

  image_scanning_configuration {
    scan_on_push = true
  }
}

This creates the Amazon Elastic Container Registry repository where the Docker image is stored. image_tag_mutability = "MUTABLE" allows the latest tag to be overwritten on each pipeline run, enabling a simple continuous deployment pattern. scan_on_push = true enables automatic vulnerability scanning every time an image is pushed, providing a built-in security gate without any additional tooling.

6.5 Terraform/ecs.tf — ECS Cluster, Task Definition & Service

# CloudWatch Log Group
resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "cw_log" {
  name = var.cloudwatch_log_group
}

# KMS Key for encryption
resource "aws_kms_key" "kms" {
  description             = "kms key required for encryption"
  deletion_window_in_days = 7
}

# ECS Cluster with encrypted exec logging
resource "aws_ecs_cluster" "ecs" {
  name = var.ecs_name
  configuration {
    execute_command_configuration {
      kms_key_id = aws_kms_key.kms.arn
      logging    = "OVERRIDE"
      log_configuration {
        cloud_watch_encryption_enabled = true
        cloud_watch_log_group_name     = aws_cloudwatch_log_group.cw_log.name
      }
    }
  }
}

# Task Definition
resource "aws_ecs_task_definition" "task_def" {
  family                   = var.ecs_task_definition.family
  requires_compatibilities = var.ecs_task_definition.requires_compatibilities
  network_mode             = var.ecs_task_definition.network_mode
  cpu                      = var.ecs_task_definition.cpu
  memory                   = var.ecs_task_definition.memory
  task_role_arn            = data.aws_iam_role.task_role.arn
  execution_role_arn       = data.aws_iam_role.task_exec.arn
  container_definitions    = jsonencode([...])
}

# ECS Fargate Service
resource "aws_ecs_service" "ecs_service" {
  name            = "susseta"
  cluster         = aws_ecs_cluster.ecs.id
  task_definition = aws_ecs_task_definition.task_def.arn
  desired_count   = 2
  launch_type     = "FARGATE"
  load_balancer { ... }
  network_configuration {
    assign_public_ip = false
    security_groups  = [data.aws_security_group.sg_ecs.id]
    subnets          = data.aws_subnets.private.ids
  }
}

This is the core of the infrastructure. It creates four interconnected resources:

CloudWatch Log Group — captures all stdout/stderr from running containers
KMS Key — encrypts ECS Exec session logs and CloudWatch logs for security compliance
ECS Cluster — the logical boundary for your containerized workloads, configured with encrypted exec command logging
Task Definition — the blueprint for the container: 1 vCPU, 2 GB RAM at the task level (800 CPU units and 1500 MB reserved for the container), pointing to the ECR image URL, with awslogs log driver configured
ECS Service — maintains 2 running replicas of the task using the Fargate launch type, placed in private subnets with no public IP, wired to the ALB target group.

6.6 Terraform/alb.tf — Application Load Balancer

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "tg" {
  name        = var.target_group.name
  port        = var.target_group.port
  protocol    = var.target_group.protocol
  target_type = var.target_group.target_type
  vpc_id      = data.aws_vpc.custom-vpc.id
  health_check {
    enabled           = var.target_group.health_check_enable
    healthy_threshold = var.target_group.healthy_threshold
    interval          = var.target_group.interval
    path              = var.target_group.path
  }
}

resource "aws_lb" "alb" {
  name               = var.lb.name
  load_balancer_type = var.lb.load_balancer_type
  internal           = var.lb.internal
  ip_address_type    = var.lb.ip_address_type
  security_groups    = [data.aws_security_group.sg_lb.id]
  subnets            = data.aws_subnets.public.ids
}

resource "aws_lb_listener" "listener" {
  count             = length(data.aws_subnets.public.ids)
  load_balancer_arn = aws_lb.alb.arn
  port              = var.lb_listener.port
  protocol          = var.lb_listener.protocol
  default_action {
    type             = var.lb_listener.type
    target_group_arn = aws_lb_target_group.tg.arn
  }
}

Three resources work together to expose the application to the internet. The Target Group (Ubuntu-tg) uses ip as the target type — required for Fargate — and performs health checks against the root path / every 30 seconds, requiring 5 consecutive successes to mark a target healthy. The ALB (frontend-lb) is internet-facing, deployed across public subnets, and protected by the SG_LB security group. The Listener watches on port 80 and forwards all HTTP traffic to the target group, with one listener created per public subnet.

6.7 Terraform/var.tf & terraform.tfvars — Variables

# var.tf — type definitions and descriptions
variable "ecs_task_definition" {
  type = object({
    family                   = string
    network_mode             = string
    requires_compatibilities = list(string)
    cpu                      = number
    memory                   = number
    cpu_allocations          = number
    memory_allocations       = number
    container_name           = string
    container_port           = number
    log_driver               = string
  })
}

# terraform.tfvars — actual values
ecr_repo_name        = "ubuntu-repo"
cloudwatch_log_group = "aws-cloudwatch-group-ubuntu"
ecs_name             = "Ubuntu-cluster"
ecs_task_definition = {
  family                   = "Ubuntu-td"
  network_mode             = "awsvpc"
  log_driver               = "awslogs"
  requires_compatibilities = ["FARGATE"]
  cpu                      = 1024
  memory                   = 2048
  cpu_allocations          = 800
  memory_allocations       = 1500
  container_name           = "Ubuntu"
  container_port           = 8080
}
aws_region = "us-east-1"

The variable strategy cleanly separates type safety (var.tf) from runtime values (terraform.tfvars). Using object() types for complex variables like ecs_task_definition, target_group, lb, and lb_listener groups related settings together, avoids variable sprawl, and lets Terraform validate the entire object shape at plan time. To deploy to a different environment, only the .tfvars file needs to change — the resource definitions remain untouched.

6.8 Terraform/output.tf — Outputs

output "public_subnet_ids" {
  value = data.aws_subnets.public.ids
}

output "private_subnet_ids" {
  value = data.aws_subnets.private.ids
}

Outputs make key infrastructure values accessible after terraform apply, useful for debugging, downstream automation, or cross-stack references. Here, the resolved public and private subnet IDs are exported — helpful for verifying that the correct subnets were selected by the tag-based data source filters.

7. Pipeline Configuration

The CI/CD automation is powered by two AWS CodeBuild buildspec files that handle the complete infrastructure lifecycle.

7.1 Deploy Pipeline — deploybuildspec.yaml

version: 0.2

env:
  variables:
    TF_VERSION: "1.8.5"
    TERRAFORM_DIR: "Terraform"
    URL: "009846316881.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/"
    REPO: "ubuntu-repo"
    TAG: "latest"

phases:
  install:
    commands:
      - curl -fsSLo terraform.zip "https://releases.hashicorp.com/terraform/${TF_VERSION}/..."
      - unzip -q terraform.zip -d /usr/local/bin/

  pre_build:
    commands:
      - terraform init && terraform validate
      - terraform plan -target=aws_ecr_repository.ecr -out=tfplanecr
      - terraform apply -target=aws_ecr_repository.ecr tfplanecr
      - docker buildx build -t $URL$REPO:$TAG .
      - aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $URL
      - docker push $URL$REPO:$TAG

  build:
    commands:
      - terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
      - terraform apply -input=false tfplan

The deploy pipeline is split into three phases:

Install Phase: Downloads and installs the pinned Terraform version (1.8.5) directly from HashiCorp releases into /usr/local/bin, ensuring a consistent toolchain regardless of the CodeBuild base image.

Pre-Build Phase: This is the most critical phase. It first creates only the ECR repository using a targeted apply (-target=aws_ecr_repository.ecr). This is necessary because the ECS task definition references the ECR image URL — the repository must exist before the full plan can succeed. Then it builds the Docker image using buildx, authenticates to ECR using the AWS CLI's temporary credential mechanism (get-login-password), and pushes the image. A 60-second sleep is included to allow ECR to fully register the pushed image.

Build Phase: With the image safely in ECR, a full Terraform plan and apply provisions the remaining infrastructure — ECS cluster, task definition, service, ALB, target group, and listener.

7.2 Destroy Pipeline — destroybuildspec.yaml

version: 0.2

env:
  variables:
    TF_VERSION: "1.8.5"
    TERRAFORM_DIR: "Terraform"

phases:
  install:
    commands:
      - curl -fsSLo terraform.zip "https://releases.hashicorp.com/terraform/${TF_VERSION}/..."
      - unzip -q terraform.zip -d /usr/local/bin/

  pre_build:
    commands:
      - terraform init -input=false

  build:
    commands:
      - terraform plan -destroy -input=false -out=destroy.tfplan
      - terraform apply -input=false destroy.tfplan

The destroy pipeline is intentionally lean. It installs the same Terraform version, initializes the backend to load the existing state, generates a destroy plan (-destroy flag), and applies it. Using a plan file (destroy.tfplan) before the apply adds an extra layer of safety — you can inspect what will be destroyed before it happens. This pipeline is typically triggered manually to tear down the environment and stop incurring costs.

7.3 Pipeline Flow Diagram

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    DEPLOY PIPELINE                               │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌───────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ INSTALL  │──►│    PRE_BUILD      │──►│       BUILD        │ │
  │  │          │   │                   │   │                    │ │
  │  │ Download │   │ terraform init    │   │ terraform plan     │ │
  │  │ Terraform│   │ terraform validate│   │ terraform apply    │ │
  │  │ v1.8.5   │   │ Apply ECR only    │   │ (full infra)       │ │
  │  └──────────┘   │ docker build      │   └────────────────────┘ │
  │                  │ docker push       │                           │
  │                  └───────────────────┘                           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    DESTROY PIPELINE                              │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌───────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ INSTALL  │──►│    PRE_BUILD      │──►│       BUILD        │ │
  │  │          │   │                   │   │                    │ │
  │  │ Download │   │ terraform init    │   │ terraform plan     │ │
  │  │ Terraform│   │ (loads S3 state)  │   │ -destroy           │ │
  │  │ v1.8.5   │   └───────────────────┘   │ terraform apply    │ │
  │  └──────────┘                            │ (destroys all)     │ │
  │                                          └────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

8. Key Benefits

No Server Management ECS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers. There are no EC2 instances to patch, resize, or monitor. AWS manages the underlying infrastructure entirely.

Immutable Infrastructure Every deployment produces a fresh infrastructure state from code. There is no configuration drift because resources are never modified in place — they are planned, applied, and optionally destroyed.

Security by Default

  • Containers run in private subnets with no public IPs.

  • Only the ALB is exposed to the internet.

  • Container logs are encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key.

  • ECR scans every pushed image for vulnerabilities automatically.

  • IAM roles follow least privilege — the task execution role and task role are separate.

Cost Efficiency Fargate charges only for the vCPU and memory reserved per running task. The destroy pipeline ensures you can completely eliminate costs when the environment is not needed, such as in a dev or demo setup.

Repeatable and Portable The entire stack is defined in code. Deploying to a new AWS region or account requires changing a handful of values in terraform.tfvars and re-running the pipeline

Observability Built In Every container's stdout and stderr are automatically captured by CloudWatch Logs under the aws-cloudwatch-group-ubuntu log group, with stream prefix app. No additional logging agents are needed inside the container.

9. Conclusion

This project demonstrates a production-aligned pattern for containerized application deployment on AWS. By combining Docker for application packaging, Terraform for infrastructure provisioning, and AWS CodeBuild for CI/CD automation, the entire lifecycle — from code to running container to teardown — is managed as code with no manual steps.
The architecture enforces security best practices by keeping workloads in private subnets, using encrypted logging, and leveraging IAM roles for all AWS API access. The modular Terraform structure makes it straightforward to extend — adding auto-scaling policies, HTTPS listeners, or additional services requires minimal changes to the existing files.
Whether you are building a proof of concept or a foundation for a production microservice, this approach gives you a reliable, auditable, and cost-controlled deployment platform on AWS.

Repository Structure

aws-app-deployment-ecs/
├── Dockerfile                  # Container image definition
├── deploybuildspec.yaml        # CodeBuild spec for deploy pipeline
├── destroybuildspec.yaml       # CodeBuild spec for destroy pipeline
└── Terraform/
    ├── provider.tf             # AWS provider & S3 backend config
    ├── data.tf                 # Data sources for existing AWS resources
    ├── ecr.tf                  # ECR repository resource
    ├── ecs.tf                  # ECS cluster, task definition & service
    ├── alb.tf                  # ALB, target group & listener
    ├── var.tf                  # Variable type definitions
    ├── terraform.tfvars        # Variable values
    └── output.tf               # Stack outputs

Built with ❤️ using AWS ECS Fargate, Terraform, and AWS CodeBuild

title: Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions
description:
A few years ago a client's support team got a call from a customer whose payout bank account had been changed overnight. The login itself looked normal: correct password, a known browser, a session that had been open for eleven days on a shared office machine. Someone had simply walked up to an unlocked laptop, opened the billing page and swapped the IBAN. Nothing in our stack asked "are you still you?" before a change that moved real money. The fix was not a stronger password policy. It was step-up authentication on the handful of actions that actually matter.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every snippet against current OWASP Authentication and Session Management cheat sheets, NIST SP 800-63B, the WebAuthn Level 3 spec, Laravel 11 and Node 22. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi with 9+ years across PHP/Laravel, Vue, Node and .NET microservices, and I build the free developer tools at PixelValut. This is the final part of the series, and everything here is about hardening an app you own.

📚 Series Navigation — Passkeys & Session Hardening for Web Apps

  • Part 1: Rolling Out Passkeys Without Locking Users Out
  • Part 2: Session Lifecycle Hardening: Rotation, Timeouts & Server-Side Revocation
  • Part 3: CSRF in 2026: SameSite, Fetch Metadata & Origin Checks
  • Part 4: Account Recovery Hardening: The Side Door Next to Your Passkey
  • Part 5: Protecting Login Endpoints: Credential-Stuffing Signals & Adaptive Rate Limits
  • Part 6 (This Post): Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions

Related earlier posts: Browser Secrets That Leak: Token Storage, Quotas & Outbound Controls · OAuth 2.1, OIDC ID Tokens & PKCE Forensics

What is step-up authentication and when should you use it?

Direct answer: Step-up authentication asks an already signed-in user to prove their identity again, freshly and often more strongly, before a sensitive action. Use it for money movement, credential and MFA changes, data exports, role changes and destructive deletes. Record when and how the user re-authenticated, allow the action only within a short window, and log every elevated action.

Classify actions before writing code

The mistake I see most is protecting everything or nothing. If every settings page asks for a passkey, users learn to click through prompts and complain until you remove them. Start by putting actions into tiers:

Tier Example actions Required proof Freshness window Notify user?
0 – Normal Read dashboards, edit profile name Valid session Session lifetime No
1 – Sensitive View API keys, export personal data, invite users Re-auth with any enrolled factor 15 minutes Optional
2 – Critical Change email, password, MFA, payout account; create API keys Phishing-resistant factor (passkey) preferred, else TOTP 5 minutes Yes, to old and new contact
3 – Destructive Delete organisation, transfer ownership, disable audit log Passkey + typed confirmation; optional second approver Single use Yes, to all admins

Keep this table in your repository. When someone adds a new endpoint, the review question becomes "which tier is this?" instead of a debate.

Record how and when the user authenticated

Step-up only works if the server knows how fresh and how strong the current authentication is. OpenID Connect already has the vocabulary: auth_time for when the user last actively authenticated, amr for the methods used and acr for the assurance level. Even if you do not use OIDC, store the same facts in your session.

In Laravel, I set them on every successful login or re-auth:

// app/Support/AuthContext.php
final class AuthContext
{
    public static function record(Request $request, string $method, int $level): void
    {
        $request->session()->put('auth.time', now()->timestamp);
        $request->session()->put('auth.amr', $method);   // 'pwd', 'otp', 'hwk'
        $request->session()->put('auth.level', $level);  // 1 = password, 2 = passkey/otp
        $request->session()->regenerate();               // new ID on privilege change
    }

    public static function satisfies(Request $request, int $level, int $maxAgeSeconds): bool
    {
        $time = (int) $request->session()->get('auth.time', 0);
        $have = (int) $request->session()->get('auth.level', 0);

        return $have >= $level && (now()->timestamp - $time) <= $maxAgeSeconds;
    }
}

Regenerating the session ID on elevation matters for the same reason as on login: privilege changed, so the identifier should too (Part 2 covers rotation in detail).

Enforce it with middleware, not page logic

Put the check in one middleware so no controller forgets it. When the check fails, return a clear machine-readable error that tells the frontend what to ask for:

// app/Http/Middleware/RequireStepUp.php
public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next, int $level = 2, int $maxAge = 300)
{
    if (AuthContext::satisfies($request, $level, $maxAge)) {
        return $next($request);
    }

    $request->session()->put('stepup.intended', $request->fullUrl());

    return response()->json([
        'error'      => 'step_up_required',
        'acr_values' => $level >= 2 ? 'passkey otp' : 'any',
        'max_age'    => $maxAge,
    ], 401)->header('WWW-Authenticate', 'Bearer error="insufficient_user_authentication"');
}

// routes/web.php
Route::put('/billing/payout-account', UpdatePayoutAccount::class)
    ->middleware(['auth', 'stepup:2,300']);
Route::delete('/org', DeleteOrganisation::class)
    ->middleware(['auth', 'stepup:2,60', 'confirm.typed']);

The insufficient_user_authentication error code comes from RFC 9470 (OAuth 2.0 Step-Up Authentication Challenge). If you run an API with access tokens, follow that RFC and let the client request a new token with acr_values and max_age.

Node/Express version with short-lived elevated tokens

For APIs and SPAs, I avoid making the whole session elevated. Instead, the re-auth endpoint issues a separate, short-lived token scoped to the action:

// stepup.js
import { SignJWT, jwtVerify } from 'jose';
const key = new TextEncoder().encode(process.env.STEPUP_SECRET);

export async function issueElevation(userId, action, amr) {
  return new SignJWT({ act: action, amr: [amr] })
    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: 'HS256' })
    .setSubject(String(userId))
    .setIssuedAt()
    .setExpirationTime('5m')
    .setJti(crypto.randomUUID())
    .sign(key);
}

export function requireElevation(action) {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    try {
      const token = req.get('X-Step-Up-Token');
      const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, key, { algorithms: ['HS256'] });
      if (payload.sub !== String(req.user.id) || payload.act !== action) throw new Error('scope');
      if (await usedJti(payload.jti)) throw new Error('replay');   // single use
      await markJtiUsed(payload.jti, payload.exp);
      return next();
    } catch {
      return res.status(401).json({ error: 'step_up_required', action });
    }
  };
}

app.put('/billing/payout-account', requireElevation('payout.update'), updatePayout);

Binding the token to one user, one action and one use stops an elevated token from being reused for something else. When I debug these, I paste the token into the JWT decoder to check sub, act and exp, and use the JWT signature verifier with a test key to confirm the signing setup. Never paste production secrets into any web tool.

Use passkeys for the re-auth itself

Passkeys from Part 1 make step-up fast: one fingerprint or face check. The important detail is to require user verification, not just presence, so the authenticator actually confirms the person:

// Browser: request a fresh assertion for step-up
const options = await fetch('/webauthn/stepup/options', { method: 'POST' }).then(r => r.json());
const assertion = await navigator.credentials.get({
  publicKey: {
    ...decodeOptions(options),
    userVerification: 'required',          // biometric or PIN, not just a tap
    allowCredentials: options.allowCredentials, // only this user's credentials
  },
});
await fetch('/webauthn/stepup/verify', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(encode(assertion)) });

On the server, verify that the UV flag is set, the challenge is fresh and single-use, and the credential belongs to the signed-in user. Only then record auth.level = 2 and the new auth.time. If the user has no passkey, fall back to TOTP; avoid SMS for critical tiers where you can.

UX rules that keep step-up from becoming nagware

  • Ask at the moment of action, not on page load. Show what is about to happen: "Confirm to change payout account ending 4421."
  • Reuse a fresh elevation within its window, so three related edits do not trigger three prompts.
  • Keep the user's input. After re-auth, replay the pending request instead of making them fill the form again.
  • Show a clear cancel path that leaves nothing half-changed.
  • For destructive actions, add a typed confirmation (the organisation name) on top of re-auth.

Log, notify and allow undo

Every tier 2+ action should produce an audit entry and a notification:

{
  "event": "payout_account.updated",
  "user_id": 4821,
  "auth_time": 1763271840,
  "amr": "hwk",
  "ip": "203.0.113.24",
  "user_agent_hash": "9f2c…",
  "old_value_suffix": "1180",
  "new_value_suffix": "4421",
  "request_id": "a1b2c3"
}

Send the notification to the old contact details as well as the new ones, include a "this wasn't me" link that freezes the change and revokes sessions, and for payout changes consider a short hold before the first transfer. This is the same side-door thinking from Part 4: assume one control will eventually fail and make the damage reversible.

Diagnostic checklist

  • [ ] Every sensitive endpoint is assigned a tier in a version-controlled table
  • [ ] Sessions record auth_time, method (amr) and level after login and re-auth
  • [ ] Session ID rotates on every elevation
  • [ ] Step-up enforced in middleware, not in individual controllers or the UI
  • [ ] API responses use a clear step_up_required / insufficient_user_authentication error
  • [ ] Elevated tokens are bound to user, action and single use, with ≤5 minute expiry
  • [ ] Passkey step-up requires user verification and a fresh challenge
  • [ ] SMS not accepted for critical or destructive tiers where alternatives exist
  • [ ] Pending request is replayed after re-auth; elevation reused within its window
  • [ ] Tier 2+ actions audited and notified to old and new contacts with a freeze link
  • [ ] Payout and ownership changes have a short delay or second approver

FAQs

Isn't a short session timeout enough?

No. Short timeouts annoy everyone and still leave the riskiest minutes unprotected. Step-up lets normal sessions stay comfortable while the few critical actions get fresh proof.

What if the user has no second factor enrolled?

Ask for the password again at minimum, and use the moment to prompt passkey enrolment. For tier 3 actions, consider requiring enrolment before allowing the action at all.

How does this work with SSO users?

Send the user back to the identity provider with prompt=login or max_age=0 and the desired acr_values, then check auth_time and acr in the returned ID token before allowing the action.

Should admins be exempt?

The opposite. Admin and support accounts can do the most damage, so they should face step-up on impersonation, role changes and data exports, with every use logged.

Can I store the elevated state in localStorage?

Avoid it. Keep elevation server-side in the session, or in a short-lived token held in memory and sent per request. My earlier token-storage post explains why long-lived secrets in browser storage are risky.

How do I test step-up flows?

Write feature tests that call each protected endpoint with a stale auth_time, a low level and a replayed token, and assert a 401 step_up_required. Then test the happy path within the window.

That wraps up Passkeys & Session Hardening for Web Apps. The thread across all six parts: authentication is not a single gate at login. It is a lifecycle — enrolment, sessions, CSRF, recovery, login defences and step-up — and each stage needs its own control.

title: Conflict, Feasibility, Faithfulness, Displacement: Four Quantities That Come Apart in Federated Dual-Cone Aggregation
description:
arXiv:2611.18014v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: FedFV, FedGH and FedMGDA+ aggregate client updates with multi-objective gradient aggregators to remove conflict between them. We examine this rationale with UPGrad, which increases no client's loss to first order, in a comparison that changes only the direction of FedAvg's update. Four quantities the rationale treats as one -- conflict between client updates, feasibility of their weighted mean, faithfulness of the transmitted updates to the clients' gradients, and displacement of the update -- come apart. Under Dirichlet partitioning UPGrad improves CIFAR-10 accuracy by +0.78 pp (14/15 seeds, p < 0.001), only with full participation; on Oxford-IIIT Pet its +0.52 pp gain vanishes (+0.07 pp) once the data our protocol left unused are kept. Varying only the Dirichlet concentration, the gain grows with heterogeneity, yet the split with the most conflict shows none. Uniform client weights, blind to conflict, match the CIFAR-10 gain and exceed the Pets gain; a matched random rotation does neither. No fairness effect survives multiplicity correction, and on CIFAR-10 the guarantee does not reach the clients' gradients. We state what evaluations should report.

title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
description:
arXiv:2611.17501v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture.
  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

title: Deployments now show build cache size
description:
Deployment summaries now show the size of the build cache each deployment saved and how close it is to the limit for its build machine. The same information is in the CLI with vercel inspect on version 65.1.0 or newer, and in the get-deployment REST API endpoint.

Uploading the build cache is billable build time, and a cache that goes over the limit is discarded, so the next build starts without one.

This is on by default on all plans for deployments built on or after October 21. See the maximum build cache size for each build machine in the docs.

title: How Much Does a Freelance Product Designer Cost in 2026?
description:
Originally published on ayurchenko.xyz.

Six independent product designers who publish their prices, read on 7 November 2026, give these ranges: $50 to $180 an hour, $900 to €1,500 for an audit of about a week, $15,000 for a three-week UX audit, and €2,500 to $8,000 a month for part-time work. Six sellers are a sample, not the market. One designer’s comparison estimates a full-time senior product designer in the US at $14,000 to $19,000 a month and a design agency at $15,000 to $40,000. Every outside figure below is linked to the page it came from.

Prices by type of work

Type of work Price in this sample Who states it, and how
By the hour $50 to $180 Utkarsh Panwar publishes $50; Batzorig prices by the engagement and states an implied $120 to $180; Dejan Veljanoski’s comparison estimates $80 to $150 for freelancers
UX or product audit, about a week $900 to €1,500 Bear Liu, an audit of one product problem, US$900; Utkarsh Panwar, a UX audit, from $900; Julia Slipenchuk, a product and UX audit for when users leave, €1,500; my Product Diagnosis, of the product and the decisions behind it, from $900
UX audit, three weeks $15,000 Alora Tishok, $15,000
Design system audit $700 to $12,000 My Consistency Review, an inventory of what ships, from $700; Batzorig, a design system audit, from $12,000
One flow or a sprint Sprints from $2,500 Bear Liu, a sprint from US$2,500; Julia Slipenchuk, from €3,000
Part-time, monthly €2,500 to $8,000 Julia Slipenchuk, €2,500; Bear Liu, from US$4,000; Utkarsh Panwar, from $4,500; Batzorig, from $6,000 for one day a week; my fractional product design, from $8,000
Building a design system $8,000 to $40,000 My design system work, from $8,000, about a month; Batzorig, from $40,000

Against an agency and a full-time hire

Dejan Veljanoski publishes a comparison on his hiring page. These are one designer’s estimates, not survey data, but they are the clearest public numbers I found:

Option Cost a month Time to first screens
Full-time senior product designer, US $14,000 to $19,000 About three months to hire, then two weeks
Design agency $15,000 to $40,000 Three to six weeks
Freelancer by the hour, at $80 to $150 $10,000 to $20,000 Days, once matched

These are not like for like. Part-time work buys an agreed number of days; a salary buys every day, and what the hire learns stays in the company; an agency brings several people. Compare what each would own, not only the monthly sum. More: Fractional or full-time product designer.

Why one audit costs $900 and another $15,000

  • Scope. The number of flows, user types and platforms in it. Utkarsh Panwar quotes his audit on exactly those.
  • Depth. A pass over the screens is quick. Interviews, analytics and a look at the decisions behind the screens take weeks.
  • Output. A list of issues, a plan of what to keep, cut and change, or redesigned flows.
  • Who does it. Years of experience, and whether they have worked in your kind of product before.

How to compare two quotes

  • Check that both describe the same scope: the same flows, the same platforms.
  • Ask what you hold at the end: a report, Figma, or working code.
  • Ask who does the work: the person you spoke to, or someone they hand it to.
  • Ask what the fee becomes if you continue. Some designers, Bear Liu and me among them, credit an audit toward the next piece of work.
  • Prefer a fixed price when the scope can be written down, and hourly only for open-ended work.

What I charge

Service Price What it is
Product Diagnosis From $900 One week, a written plan: what to keep, cut, change and do next
Consistency Review From $700 An inventory of what the product actually ships, in 3-5 working days
UX redesign Quoted per flow Flow by flow, each priced after an audit
Design system work From $8,000 Usually about a month
Fractional product design From $8,000 a month Part-time, an agreed number of days a week

Questions founders ask

How much does a freelance product designer charge per hour?

In this sample, Utkarsh Panwar publishes $50 an hour, Batzorig states an implied $120 to $180, and one designer’s comparison estimates $80 to $150 for freelancers. Many, me included, do not sell by the hour: audits have a fixed price, redesigns are quoted per flow, longer work is monthly.

How much does a UX audit cost?

On the pages above, a UX or product audit of about a week costs $900 to €1,500, a three-week UX audit $15,000, and a design system audit from $12,000. They check different things, so compare what each one covers.

Is a fractional designer cheaper than a full-time hire?

Per month, often: €2,500 to $8,000 for part-time work on the pages above, against $14,000 to $19,000 for a full-time senior designer in the US by one designer’s estimate. They buy different things: part-time days, or every day and knowledge that stays in the company.

Should I pay by the hour or a fixed price?

A fixed price when the scope can be written down, so you know the total before work starts. By the hour for open-ended work, like support or small fixes.

What does a product designer cost for an MVP?

Design alone is usually monthly work, €2,500 to $8,000 a month on the pages above, or a fixed project. Designing and building a first version with me starts at $8,000, with the scoping week counted in.

title: SQL Challenge : ROW_NUMBER() vs RANK() vs DENSE_RANK() – What's the Difference?
description:
SQL window functions are useful when working with employee rankings, sales reports and business data.


Three commonly used ranking functions are "ROW_NUMBER()", "RANK()" and "DENSE_RANK()". Although they look similar, they produce different results when multiple records have the same value.

If you want to understand SQL window functions in more detail, including "PARTITION BY", "LAG()", "LEAD()", running totals and interview questions, you can also explore this "SQL Window Functions and Analytic Functions Guide" (https://www.sankalandtech.com/Tutorials/sql-plsql-faq-interview/window-functions-analytic-functions-sql-faq.html).

The Problem

Suppose you have an employees table containing employee IDs, employee names, departments and salaries.

emp_id| emp_name| department| salary
101| Amit| IT| 90000
102| Rahul| IT| 80000
103| Priya| HR| 80000
104| Neha| HR| 70000
105| Karan| IT| 80000
106| Sneha| HR| 65000

You need to compare the results of three SQL ranking functions when employees have equal salaries.

SQL Solution (Oracle)

SELECT
emp_id,
emp_name,
department,
salary,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id
) AS row_num,
RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY salary DESC
) AS salary_rank,
DENSE_RANK() OVER (
ORDER BY salary DESC
) AS dense_rank
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id;

Expected Output

emp_id| emp_name| salary| row_num| salary_rank| dense_rank
101| Amit| 90000| 1| 1| 1
102| Rahul| 80000| 2| 2| 2
103| Priya| 80000| 3| 2| 2
105| Karan| 80000| 4| 2| 2
104| Neha| 70000| 5| 5| 3
106| Sneha| 65000| 6| 6| 4

Understanding the Difference

  • "ROW_NUMBER()" assigns a unique sequential number to every row.
  • "RANK()" assigns the same rank to equal salaries and skips subsequent rank numbers.
  • "DENSE_RANK()" assigns the same rank to equal salaries without skipping rank numbers.

Your Turn

Suppose you want to find the top three distinct salary levels in each department, including all employees who share the same salary.

Which SQL ranking function would you use?

Share your answer in the comments!

For more practical SQL examples and interview preparation, explore the SQL window functions guide linked above.

title: ECS 建站上线前，把“能打开”变成可交接的验收记录
description:
作者说明：本文由 YunECS Pro 所属团队整理，文末链接指向我们维护的独立技术指南，与阿里云官方没有隶属关系。

网站在自己的电脑上打开一次，只能说明一条访问路径在那个时间点成功。正式上线还需要回答：值班人员能否接管，数据能否恢复，用户失败时有没有告警，以及发布出现问题后能否回退。下面给出一套适用于小型 ECS 网站的验收方法。文中的例子是操作设计示例，不是已经完成的客户实测。

先写通过条件，再改配置

建立一张资源台账，至少记录账号主体、地域、可用区、实例标识、系统版本、应用版本、磁盘、域名与负责人。随后写清本次发布窗口、检查项目、通过条件和回退触发条件。例如，一个带询价表单的网站，需要验证的不只是首页状态码，还包括表单是否真正被后端接收、失败是否有日志、负责人是否收到通知。每条记录留下测试时间与证据，避免交接时只能依赖口头描述。

维护人员使用符合职责的 RAM 身份，提前验证常用管理通道和应急通道。应用访问云 API 时，评估实例角色与临时凭据，不要为了部署方便把长期高权限密钥写进代码库。台账可以保存身份用途和密钥保管负责人，不应保存密钥本身。

沿着真实请求路径验收网络

从应用本身开始检查：进程是否存活，监听地址与端口是否正确，本机请求是否成功。随后检查系统防火墙，再检查 ECS 实际关联的安全组。测试来源、协议、端口和方向必须对应同一次请求。管理端口只向必要维护来源开放；数据库和缓存按实际应用路径授权。

如果网站经过 CDN 或负载均衡，把用户到入口、入口到源站分开记录。浏览器访问成功可能是命中了缓存，不能直接证明源站健康。健康检查的来源与业务回源来源也可能不同，应按所用产品说明核对。每次仅修改已定位的问题，先保留原配置和维护连接，修改后使用新连接复测，排障结束处理临时规则。

域名与 HTTPS 要覆盖所有计划入口

核对 DNS 托管方、A 与 AAAA 记录、实际公网入口，以及根域名和使用中的子域名。对使用 IPv6 的访问者，只验证 IPv4 不够。证书检查覆盖域名、有效期和链，使用代理时还要分别检查对外 TLS 与回源连接。若部署 Nginx，可先做配置语法检查，再按维护流程重载，最后验证跳转、静态资源和接口。

测试表中应包含正常页面、缺失页面、HTTP 到 HTTPS 的跳转和主域名规范化。证书自动续期也需要负责人和失败告警。中国大陆地域承载网站时，应提前核实适用的备案要求，不能把服务器已经创建视为网站可以直接公开上线。

备份完成之后，还要证明能恢复

将代码、配置、数据库和上传文件分别列入保护范围，并为每一类数据确定恢复目标。磁盘快照与数据库一致性备份解决的问题不同：有快照不代表应用事务已经处于可恢复状态。发布前应保存备份标识、完成时间和一致性条件。

优先在隔离副本中演练恢复，检查应用版本、数据、挂载点、文件权限与外部依赖是否一起恢复。记录实际恢复时间，再判断是否满足业务要求。回滚原盘会覆盖快照之后的变更，因此需要事先约定新订单、新文件或数据库写入如何处理。只写“失败就回滚”无法指导值班人员处理数据。

让告警真的抵达一个人

确认 CPU、磁盘、网络和应用错误有持续数据，所需操作系统指标具备相应采集条件。除了实例指标，再从外部检查关键 URL。安排一次受控告警测试，验证通知到达、负责人响应、故障恢复后可以复核。阈值应结合业务基线，避免把演示阈值直接复制到生产。

最终上线记录应能回答：谁在什么时间，以哪个版本，通过了哪些功能测试；哪些问题尚未通过，由谁处理；何时需要回退，回退后怎样验收。需要逐项填写时，可使用我们整理的 ECS 上线检查清单。它适合作为验收起点，具体限制和操作前置条件仍需对照当前官方文档与自己的部署环境。

title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
description:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above.

title: How I Built a Fast Book Search & Cataloging System in React 19 Using Redux Toolkit
description:
The Problem: Managing Complex Book Data Without Prop Drilling

When I started building AYUBOOKS, a digital cataloging and reading platform inspired by Letterboxd, the initial prototype relied heavily on local component state (useState). Everything worked smoothly with just a handful of books.

However, as the catalog grew and I introduced real-world features—such as instant search filtering, category tagging, tracking reading statuses, and user reviews—three major bottlenecks quickly emerged:

  1. Severe Prop Drilling: Passing book lists, search queries, and state-updating functions down through multiple layers of nested components (from the main layout to search bars, filter sidebars, and individual book cards) made the codebase rigid and hard to refactor.
  2. State Synchronization Bugs: Updating a book's status in one view (like marking it as "Read" inside a modal) didn't always reflect immediately in the main catalog grid or user statistics without messy workarounds.
  3. Unnecessary Re-renders: Every keystroke in the search bar triggered state updates at the top level, causing large portions of the UI tree to re-render and making the filtering experience feel sluggish.

To keep AYUBOOKS fast, scalable, and maintainable, I needed a centralized, predictable state management solution—which led me to refactor the core architecture using Redux Toolkit.

The Architecture: Centralizing State with Redux Toolkit

Instead of reaching for boilerplate-heavy classic Redux, I integrated Redux Toolkit (RTK) alongside React 19 and Vite. RTK gave me a single source of truth for the entire book catalog while keeping the logic modular and easy to debug.

Here is how I structured the Redux store folder inside the project:


text
src/
├── app/
│   └── store.js          # Configures the central Redux store
└── features/
    └── books/
        ├── booksSlice.js # Manages catalog data, search query, and status updates
        └── BookList.jsx  # Renders the filtered book grid cleanly`// src/features/books/booksSlice.js
import { createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';

const initialState = {
  items: [], // Populated with book objects { id, title, author, category, status }
  searchQuery: '',
  selectedCategory: 'All',
};

const booksSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'books',
  initialState,
  reducers: {
    setBooks: (state, action) => {
      state.items = action.payload;
    },
    setSearchQuery: (state, action) => {
      state.searchQuery = action.payload;
    },
    setCategoryFilter: (state, action) => {
      state.selectedCategory = action.payload;
    },
    toggleReadStatus: (state, action) => {
      const book = state.items.find((b) => b.id === action.payload);
      if (book) {
        book.status = book.status === 'Read' ? 'Want to Read' : 'Read';
      }
    },
  },
});

export const { 
  setBooks, 
  setSearchQuery, 
  setCategoryFilter, 
  toggleReadStatus 
} = booksSlice.actions;

export default booksSlice.reducer;`
// src/features/books/booksSlice.js

const initialState = {
  items: [], // Populated with book objects { id, title, author, category, status }
  searchQuery: '',
  selectedCategory: 'All',
};

const booksSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'books',
  initialState,
  reducers: {
    setBooks: (state, action) => {
      state.items = action.payload;
    },
    setSearchQuery: (state, action) => {
      state.searchQuery = action.payload;
    },
    setCategoryFilter: (state, action) => {
      state.selectedCategory = action.payload;
    },
    toggleReadStatus: (state, action) => {
      const book = state.items.find((b) => b.id === action.payload);
      if (book) {
        book.status = book.status === 'Read' ? 'Want to Read' : 'Read';
      }
    },
  },
});

export const { 
  setBooks, 
  setSearchQuery, 
  setCategoryFilter, 
  toggleReadStatus 
} = booksSlice.actions;
